passages.text: The Sultanate of Aïr, centred on Agadez in present-day Niger, connected Saharan caravan routes with a distinctive urban society. Its history survives in earthen houses, mosques, craft traditions and continuing local institutions.

passages.title: Building a city from earth
passages.text: Agadez’s irregular neighbourhoods preserve the outlines of earlier Tuareg encampments. Streets, houses and shared spaces therefore record how settlement grew through existing social groupings. The surviving plan is evidence of an urban history shaped by communities as well as by rulers.

passages.title: Building a city from earth
passages.text: Traditional houses are built around courtyards that admit light and air. The entrance vestibule can receive visitors, accommodate grain pounding, or support craft production and sales. Earthen benches beside doorways provide seating and help protect wall bases. Domestic architecture joined household work, sociability and maintenance.

passages.title: Building a city from earth
passages.text: Measured study of the Great Mosque identified successive building campaigns rather than a single original design. Cressier proposed an early prayer hall before 1449 and an eastern enlargement before 1515. His reconstruction combines dimensions, surviving fabric, written references and oral tradition; the dates remain approximate.

passages.title: Building a city from earth
passages.text: The mosque’s later minaret should not be presented as untouched medieval fabric. Cressier proposed a major nineteenth-century campaign around 1844 or 1847. Rebuilding and continued use are part of the monument’s history, and explain why the visible structure contains evidence from different periods.

passages.title: Building a city from earth
passages.text: The historic centre’s importance extends beyond the palace and mosque to its many earthen dwellings. UNESCO’s assessment identifies neighbourhood chiefs and committees as part of local protection. Keeping a living city usable involves residents and everyday repairs alongside the conservation of celebrated monuments.

passages.title: Provisioning, exchange and adornment
passages.text: Agadez depended on exchange with farming regions as well as on long-distance caravans. Baier’s study of neighbouring Damergu describes villagers taking millet to Agadez, then increasingly sending it south toward Nigeria after 1900. The change connects the desert city’s fortunes to cultivators and the movement of staple food.

passages.title: Provisioning, exchange and adornment
passages.text: The same study describes villagers exchanging tanned goat skins and ostrich feathers for imported cloth and other goods. When trans-Saharan commerce declined, grain and livestock became more important. These are documented regional responses to changing demand, not evidence that every household in the sultanate followed one occupation.

passages.title: Provisioning, exchange and adornment
passages.text: An Agadez-cross ornament at the Musée des Confluences, inventory 2015.32.3, is catalogued as a twentieth-century silver-alloy piece from Azawagh, associated with Iwellemmeden Kel-Denneg Tuareg. Its name connects it with a recognizable regional jewellery form, but does not prove manufacture in Agadez or under its medieval sultans.

passages.title: Provisioning, exchange and adornment
passages.text: The museum records the ornament’s collection between 1990 and 2011 and its later donation. It describes the form as worn mainly by women in necklaces and ear ornaments. These details document use and collecting history while leaving this particular object’s maker and exact manufacture date unidentified.

passages.title: Recording and renewing practical knowledge
passages.text: A recent conservation project used photographs to build three-dimensional records of the Great Mosque and historic homes, including the Baker’s House. Local representatives learned documentation techniques. The resulting records help plan repairs and preserve measurable evidence of buildings whose earthen surfaces change through weathering and maintenance.

passages.title: Recording and renewing practical knowledge
passages.text: Local craftspeople made fitted leather bags for manuscripts kept at the Abawagé mosque, replacing damaged protective coverings. This project links leatherworking with the care of written knowledge. The conservation account documents the intervention, but does not provide dates or contents for every manuscript.

passages.title: Recording and renewing practical knowledge
passages.text: House rehabilitation included crack repair, wall-base reinforcement, replastering, roof work and improved drainage. Young residents learned from masons while occupied homes were repaired. The project’s 2021 campaign shows the continuation of building knowledge through paid work and training, as well as through the monuments themselves.

French occupation changed the sultanate’s political position. The revolt of 1916 to 1917 challenged colonial control, but the institution continued afterward and within independent Niger. Loss of sovereignty was not the disappearance of Agadez’s communities or the abolition of every local office.

passages.text: The Ais lived along Florida’s central Atlantic coast south of Cape Canaveral. Fishing and water travel supported their communities, while encounters with shipwrecks and foreign vessels helped their leaders build influence during the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries.

passages.title: Homes, food and excavated traces
passages.text: At Herman’s Bay on Hutchinson Island, site 8SL1146, excavators found evidence of a house, a cooking hearth and discarded animal remains. The project places these traces in the Okeechobee period, about 1000 to 1513 CE. They illuminate the region’s earlier coastal life, but the report does not identify the occupants specifically as Ais.

passages.title: Homes, food and excavated traces
passages.text: Herman’s Bay animal bones point to fishing and turtle consumption, with resources drawn especially from the Indian River estuary and Atlantic shore. Very small schooling fish led researchers to infer fine-mesh nets or similar gear. The bones are observed evidence; the proposed equipment is an interpretation, not a surviving net.

passages.title: Homes, food and excavated traces
passages.text: A community excavation led by Alan Brech at Cape Canaveral’s site 8BR1936 recovered pottery, bone and shell beads, shell tools and food remains. Field Manor reports work from 2015 to 2019 and a proposed identification with Savochequeya, a village on Mexía’s 1605 map. That town identification remains a proposal.

passages.title: Homes, food and excavated traces
passages.text: At the same site, dark post molds marked the positions of decayed wooden supports; pits and hearths also survived. These soil traces help reconstruct buildings and household activity even where the wood has disappeared. They offer a different kind of evidence from the names and routes recorded by European visitors.

passages.title: Homes, food and excavated traces
passages.text: Three early glass beads and European metal were reported alongside local pottery and shell objects at 8BR1936. A possible copper-alloy button was also identified. The finds show access to imported materials, but the button’s identification is tentative and individual objects cannot establish the route by which every item reached the settlement.

passages.title: Homes, food and excavated traces
passages.text: At Jece in 1696, Dickinson recorded baskets of dried berries arriving from other towns and being delivered to a chief. He thought these deliveries were tribute. His observation documents stored food and movement between settlements; the explanation as tribute is his interpretation, not an independently recorded rule for every Ais community.

passages.title: Salvage, exchange and maritime knowledge
passages.text: Ferdinando argues that the Ais used existing aquatic skills to recover goods and castaways from wrecked Spanish, French, English and Dutch ships. Redistributing these resources to other Native communities, St. Augustine and passing Europeans increased their influence. Salvage was part of an active political economy, rather than simply the collection of accidental treasure.

passages.title: Salvage, exchange and maritime knowledge
passages.text: Dickinson saw tools, knives, wooden ship fittings and a razor bearing the name Thomas Foster at Jece. These objects give his account a concrete material dimension. He did not learn the full history of their arrival, so the record cannot show whether each item came through wreck salvage, exchange or another encounter.

passages.title: Salvage, exchange and maritime knowledge
passages.text: A resident of Jece told Dickinson that ambergris could buy a mirror, an axe, knives and tobacco at St. Augustine. The passage links a coastal resource with desired tools and consumer goods. It records one person’s expected exchange, not a fixed price list or proof that all residents traded on identical terms.

passages.title: Salvage, exchange and maritime knowledge
passages.text: Maritime expertise also exposed Native people to enslavement. Ferdinando describes late-seventeenth-century English buccaneers capturing coastal divers for work on a wreck in the Bahamas and subsequently selling survivors in Caribbean markets. Skill could support local autonomy while also attracting coercive exploitation.

passages.title: Survivors in the colonial record
passages.text: Worth identifies a 1711 town near St. Augustine containing more than a hundred Ais and other coastal refugees. The number describes a mixed community, not a census of all Ais people. Subsequent mission lists still named Ais, showing why a story of abrupt disappearance would conceal a documented history of survival and displacement.

Raiding and displacement undermined the Ais coastal political order in the early eighteenth century. Ais survivors are documented near St. Augustine, but the evidence cited here does not establish one final dissolution year or trace every later family. Wider migrations to Cuba should not be converted into an unsupported claim that all Ais died or left together.

sectionTitles: Community decisions and caring for the land

passages.text: Akaitcho Dene refers here to communities associated with Dettah, Ndilǫ, Łutsël K’é and Fort Resolution in Canada’s Northwest Territories. The Yellowknives Dene, Łutsël K’é Dene and Deninu K’ue First Nations retain distinct community histories within their shared regional political relationship.

passages.title: Objects, materials and household work
passages.text: The Yellowknives Dene exhibition at the Prince of Wales Northern Heritage Centre includes a copper bar made by hammering smaller pieces together and an unfinished knife blade, both labelled early nineteenth century. They preserve intermediate stages of manufacture. The labels do not identify a named maker or excavation context.

passages.title: Objects, materials and household work
passages.text: A displayed fish net uses the inner bark of willow. Twisted lengths are intertwined and knotted into mesh. In accompanying testimony, Fred Sangris describes women making such nets to span rivers. Material preparation, knotting and knowledge of fishing places together supported this work; the display supplies no manufacture date for the net.

passages.title: Objects, materials and household work
passages.text: Sophie Potfighter made a caribou-skin coat at Dettah in the 1970s. Its front could accommodate an added panel during pregnancy and hold a baby inside. Her daughter Alizette Lockhart remembered its use in the bush and its inheritance within the family, connecting skilled sewing with warmth, childcare and practical household needs.

passages.title: Travel, provisioning and practical knowledge
passages.text: Akaitcho’s people supplied meat to Fort Providence and negotiated the terms of work with Franklin. In 1820 the chief challenged the expedition’s slow travel and its hope of reaching the coast in one season. Establishing winter quarters acknowledged a practical limit identified by people who knew the country.

passages.title: Travel, provisioning and practical knowledge
passages.text: Yellowknives rescuers brought assistance to the starving expedition in November 1821. Akaitcho subsequently received the survivors and personally helped care for them. The episode shows how European exploration depended on Indigenous food, travel knowledge and decisions to provide support, not merely on the explorers’ equipment and plans.

passages.title: Travel, provisioning and practical knowledge
passages.text: A study coauthored by Fred Sangris describes his use of successive low stars to maintain a travelling direction across open country. As each star moved, he selected another near the original bearing. Once he reached a familiar lake or trail, he returned to navigation by landmarks. The account documents his learned practice, not a universal Dene method.

passages.title: Travel, provisioning and practical knowledge
passages.text: Sangris also described stone cairns marking routes and the importance of remembering landforms when cloud hid the stars. Knowledge passed through his father and grandfather and developed through travel. The study connects sky observation, constructed markers, memory and experience; it does not treat navigation as a single instrument or an unchanging inherited formula.

passages.title: Community decisions and caring for the land
passages.text: In their 2004 parliamentary submission, Akaitcho representatives explained how negotiations with Tłı̨chǫ leaders turned a territorial dispute into a Shared Use Area. They described agreed boundaries alongside an area of mutual interest. This is a documented example of diplomacy between neighboring Dene peoples, whose institutions and territories should not be collapsed into one.

passages.title: Community decisions and caring for the land
passages.text: The same submission recalls people travelling by canoe to the 1900 gathering at Deninu K’ue and its centennial reenactment in 2000. The account links political memory with routes across Great Slave Lake. It is also the First Nations’ own explanation of why continuing treaty negotiations concern living communities and inherited responsibilities.

passages.title: Community decisions and caring for the land
passages.text: At Thaidene Nëné, Łutsël K’é Dene guardians and research partners installed cameras and sound recorders in 2021 to establish a wildlife baseline. When the management board noticed a gap near an important caribou area northeast of Artillery Lake, it added sites. Community knowledge directly shaped where the research looked.

passages.title: Community decisions and caring for the land
passages.text: The monitoring project combines recordings with Dene knowledge to study animal distribution and environmental change. Its account also records limitations: snow blocked some cameras and equipment sometimes failed, including a camera damaged by a bear. Recognizing such gaps is necessary before interpreting missing photographs as missing animals.

Akaitcho Dene communities and their institutions continue. Land, resources and self-government are subjects of negotiation with Canada and the territorial government. Neither the imported map interval nor Chief Akaitcho’s death represents the end of these peoples.

sectionTitles: Household tools, food and living heritage

passages.text: Akan describes several related peoples, including the Asante and Fante, rather than one kingdom. Their histories include distinctive local institutions and connections with neighbors. Weaving shows how shared skills and changing fashions can cross political and linguistic boundaries without making every community identical.

passages.title: Excavated craft and trading communities
passages.text: Begho included quarters associated with local Brong communities and others occupied by Mande-speaking Muslims. Posnansky’s account of the 1970s excavations reports spindle whorls and dye pits, concrete evidence for textile work. The town’s mixed population cautions against assigning every recovered technology to one ethnic group.

passages.title: Excavated craft and trading communities
passages.text: Brassworking took place in Begho’s Dwinfuor artisans’ quarter, while iron was smelted outside the town at Dapaa. Weights made from stone and terracotta also survived. These different materials connect specialist production with measurement and exchange; they do not mean every household performed the same work or possessed equal wealth.

passages.title: Excavated craft and trading communities
passages.text: The excavations also uncovered decorated ivory trumpets and a shrine room containing inverted offering cups. Posnansky interpreted these as evidence for the ritual character of Brong chieftaincy. The objects and their arrangement are observations; the explanation of their political and religious role is an interpretation informed by local historical research.

passages.title: Metal, cloth and skilled production
passages.text: The Met’s brass shell-form object, catalogue 1978.412.450, is dated broadly from the nineteenth to mid-twentieth century. The catalogue explains lost-wax casting: a model is enclosed in clay, removed by heating, and replaced by molten metal. This is a museum object with a broad regional attribution, not a find from Begho.

passages.title: Metal, cloth and skilled production
passages.text: Gold-dust exchange required scales, containers, spoons and carefully adjusted weights. The Met’s recent discussion distinguishes geometric weights from figurines often grouped under the same name. Some figurines may instead have circulated as embodiments of proverbs or moral ideas. A familiar museum label therefore does not establish every object’s original function.

passages.title: Metal, cloth and skilled production
passages.text: Kente cloth is assembled by sewing narrow woven strips edge to edge. Asante and Ewe centres developed related but distinguishable repertoires, and later exchanged styles and materials. Kraamer’s research traces these interactions and competing origin stories; it does not support reducing the whole tradition to one securely dated invention by a single people.

passages.title: Household tools, food and living heritage
passages.text: In Mpraeso, Kwahu women potters shape clay into coils and build vessels on a raised working surface. A study published in 2020 records a wooden paddle, sabroba, used to flatten bases and a metal scraper, ponoye, used inside pots. The named tools show how control of shape and surface depends on practiced handwork.

passages.title: Household tools, food and living heritage
passages.text: The potters pack vessels on firewood for open firing in their backyards. Some fired pots are placed in sawdust to blacken them. The study follows production through sale, connecting material preparation and firing with a working household economy. These observations concern the surveyed Mpraeso potters, not an unchanged practice everywhere in Akan history.

passages.title: Household tools, food and living heritage
passages.text: Mpraeso grinding bowls, apotoyowa, have ridged interiors for preparing vegetables with wooden pestles. Other vessels store drinking water, cook food or serve meals. Their shapes meet different household tasks, so pottery history includes ordinary food preparation and water storage as well as objects used in ceremonies.

passages.title: Household tools, food and living heritage
passages.text: Asante shrine compounds near Kumasi use timber and bamboo frames with mud plaster, organized around courtyards. Reliefs on the walls carry animal, plant and geometric forms associated with meanings and beliefs. These surviving buildings document one Akan architectural tradition; they should not be treated as a standard house type for every Akan community.

passages.title: Household tools, food and living heritage
passages.text: Many of the protected shrine buildings have been reconstructed or modified, including replacements of thatched roofs and earthen floors. Conservation involves chiefs, Elders, residents and museum staff. Their survival reflects continued decisions about use and repair, rather than the preservation of buildings entirely untouched since the Asante kingdom’s height.

Akan peoples do not share a single fall date: individual kingdoms and political institutions have separate histories. Living shrine traditions and community participation in their preservation demonstrate continuity. The end of the map’s Akan interval in 1715 must not be read as the disappearance of these communities.

passages.text: Akawaio, also spelled Akawayo, identifies Indigenous Cariban-speaking communities of the Guiana Highlands. Their histories overlap with neighboring peoples without making those peoples interchangeable. Historical collectors used names inconsistently, so objects labeled Akawaio, Patamona or Kapon require attention to their particular collection records.

passages.title: Food, tools and household skill
passages.text: A basket sieve called tonga, NMAI_61541, combines twill-plaited plant fibers with wood and cordage. The museum records it from the Lower Essequibo and says Verrill collected it in 1916. Its classification connects basketry to food preparation. That collection date does not establish when the object was made or when the technique began.

passages.title: Food, tools and household skill
passages.text: A food grater from the Upper Cuyuni, NMAI_214381, brings together carved wood, stone and tree pitch or gum. The record tentatively associates its collection with a 1937 or 1938 expedition and records its donation in 1939. These materials document a composite household tool; the uncertain collecting history should not become a precise manufacture date.

passages.title: Food, tools and household skill
passages.text: Bulkan’s 2019 comparison emphasizes women’s knowledge and work in transforming bitter cassava into food and drink. The study distinguishes the Makushi and Akawaio cases. Its detailed discussion of Makushi plant varieties cannot simply be transferred to all Akawaio gardens, but the comparison shows why food history includes skills and social responsibilities.

passages.title: Food, tools and household skill
passages.text: The same study describes eki siku, an Akawaio young-cassava festival within the areruya religious tradition. Cassava and women’s roles are affirmed through sacred texts and prophetic visions. The account treats cultivation, belief and social relationships together, rather than reducing a staple crop to its nutritional value.

passages.title: Language, materials and geographic knowledge
passages.text: The 2014 dictionary was developed with Akawaio speakers from the Upper Mazaruni and linguists Ray and Dee Stegeman. Its introduction describes work on an alphabet, reading books and a lexical database. Recording pronunciations, meanings and alternative forms makes a practical resource for speakers and learners while preserving variation within the language.

passages.title: Language, materials and geographic knowledge
passages.text: The dictionary records simari, with the variant sumari, for a cassava grater. Its si’na’ entry describes both a tree whose inner bark supplies carrying straps and the straps themselves. These entries connect vocabulary with material knowledge and transport. They do not identify a botanical species or date the origin of either tool.

passages.title: Language, materials and geographic knowledge
passages.text: Clarke’s botanical expedition report credits Akawaio Isaac Jerry and Adrian Thompson with establishing a western route up Mount Ayanganna from Chinowieng. Earlier scientific parties used that route. Naming the guide makes visible the local geographic expertise on which collecting expeditions depended, rather than treating a scientific visit as the first human knowledge of a landscape.

passages.title: Land, evidence and continuing institutions
passages.text: For the mapping project begun in 1995, Indigenous team members learned surveying and GPS methods. Communities supplied names and categories for settlements, resource areas, burial grounds and other significant places. Griffiths’s account explains how younger people worked with Elders, turning knowledge normally transmitted locally into a map that outsiders could examine.

passages.title: Land, evidence and continuing institutions
passages.text: The published map made land uses visible that official maps could overlook, including hunting and fishing reserves. Griffiths reported that the government had not accepted it as a legitimate ownership claim when he wrote in 2002. Producing evidence and winning legal recognition were different steps; the map alone did not settle the dispute.

passages.title: Land, evidence and continuing institutions
passages.text: At the 2025 Waramadong meeting, village representatives discussed social, environmental and economic concerns with public agencies. Leaders also renewed a request for formal recognition of their District Council. This is evidence of active collective decision-making, not a claim that official recognition had already been granted.

passages.title: Land, evidence and continuing institutions
passages.text: In 2026, the Upper Mazaruni council joined other Indigenous councils in training on digital mapping and data management. Participants practiced collecting, organizing and interpreting information and preparing reports. These methods support community monitoring and advocacy, showing the continued adoption of new tools alongside local knowledge.

Akawaio communities continue to organize, maintain knowledge and pursue recognition of their institutions and land rights. The 2025 council meeting documents ongoing work, not a completed settlement of every claim. The map’s 1500 endpoint is a coverage limit and does not mark a conquest or the disappearance of the people.

passages.text: Akimel O’odham means River People. Gila River and Salt River communities belong to a wider O’odham world while retaining local identities. Pima is a name applied by outsiders. Their history connects farming and environmental knowledge with continuing efforts to sustain himdag, their way of life.

passages.title: Farming and the changing rivers
passages.text: The Salt River Community’s history describes ancestral canals dug by hand to carry water to villages beyond the riverbanks. Some old canal courses remain in use. The achievement was a coordinated irrigation landscape, requiring both construction and water distribution; a surviving route does not mean every canal has operated continuously without rebuilding.

passages.title: Farming and the changing rivers
passages.text: Early historic Gila villages grew corn, beans, squash and cotton, supplemented by gathered and traded foods. The irrigation project’s account distinguishes floodwater farming from later distribution canals and notes the introduction of wheat and fruit crops. Agricultural practices changed with new crops and contacts rather than remaining one fixed system.

passages.title: Farming and the changing rivers
passages.text: When newcomers diverted the rivers, fields lost water and the riparian environment changed. The community history describes the loss of cottonwood and willow stands as well as farmland. This affected food production and access to materials for everyday objects; water loss reached beyond the boundaries of individual cultivated plots.

passages.title: Shelter, shade and everyday work
passages.text: The Huhugam Ki: Museum explains a partly sunken house built with mesquite posts, bent willow branches and arrow-weed thatch. Earth over the roof helped exclude rain. These structures provided sheltered space and storage. The museum’s example teaches a building method; it is not presented here as an excavated house dated to 1492.

passages.title: Shelter, shade and everyday work
passages.text: A brush-covered ramada provided an open, shaded place for cooking, preparing materials and sleeping. The museum describes a water vessel wrapped in a wet cloth for evaporative cooling. Managing shade and moving air was part of household technology, alongside the more visible engineering of irrigation canals.

passages.title: Shelter, shade and everyday work
passages.text: For outdoor cooking, a circular arrangement of poles and brush formed a windbreak around a central fire. The materials could include willow, mesquite, arrow weed, cattail or cornstalks. The museum presents this practical structure alongside the house and ramada, showing a household spread across several purpose-built spaces.

passages.title: Makers, exchange and public culture
passages.text: Mary Sampson’s 1964 basket, NMAI_248732, combines cattail, willow, devil’s claw and mountain-mahogany bark using coiling. Its maker and materials are recorded, and collector Byron Harvey bought it from Sampson herself. This object preserves an individual artist’s work and a documented transaction, not an anonymous survival from an undated ancient tradition.

passages.title: Makers, exchange and public culture
passages.text: The Blackwater Trading Post supplied groceries and accepted basketry, pottery and other goods in exchange when customers lacked cash. In 2010 the Gila River Community bought the property and its collection. An inventory and oral history helped document the objects, which entered the Community’s heritage holdings.

passages.title: Makers, exchange and public culture
passages.text: The Huhugam Heritage Center cares for archaeological holdings and O’odham baskets alongside the trombone and memorabilia of Akimel O’otham jazz musician Russell Moore. Placing these collections together makes cultural history broader than a display of ancient objects: it includes named artists and participation in changing musical worlds.

passages.title: Makers, exchange and public culture
passages.text: Built in 2003, the center adapts ancestral architectural forms for present use. Its ball-court-shaped community space hosts celebrations and performances, while metal shade arbors recall structures still used locally. These features are deliberate contemporary designs, not ancient remains uncovered beneath the museum.

passages.title: Ancestors, sovereignty and continuity
passages.text: The Salt River Community distinguishes huhugam, its word for departed ancestors, from Hohokam, the narrower archaeological label derived from that word. Huhugam is not confined to one excavated period. This distinction matters when large settlements change: an archaeological phase can end while descendants, language and relationships to place continue.

passages.title: Ancestors, sovereignty and continuity
passages.text: The community-curated exhibition Rekindling Our Connections links water loss with wider changes in cultural life. Curators Jacob E. Butler Sr. and Aaron Sabori present traditional knowledge as a resource for young people’s future. Their work places communities themselves at the center of interpreting environmental history and sovereignty.

Akimel O’odham communities continue. The loss of river water transformed farming and daily life, while communities continued to assert their rights. Gila River and Salt River cultural institutions document ongoing work, knowledge and self-representation. The map’s endpoint in 1500 is therefore a coverage limit, not a fall date.

sectionTitles: Later records and living community memory

passages.text: Akokisa, also recorded as Orcoquiza and Arkokisa, refers to Indigenous communities of the upper Texas coast around Galveston Bay and the lower river valleys. Historical scholarship places their language within the Atakapan grouping. Mission documents provide only a partial view of their communities and choices.

passages.title: What archaeology can show
passages.text: At Lake Miller, shell-midden site 41CH22 contained Rangia clam shells and fish remains, including gar, catfish and striped mullet, alongside deer and turtle. These traces document the use of aquatic and terrestrial foods. The investigators proposed an Akokisa camp here, but explicitly said the recovered objects did not establish that identification.

passages.title: What archaeology can show
passages.text: At 41CH22, sandy-paste and grog-tempered pottery suggested occupation from perhaps around 1000 CE into the contact period. A blue glass bead came from the surface near a pipeline corridor. This broad ceramic range and imported object cannot securely date every deposit or identify its occupants.

passages.title: What archaeology can show
passages.text: At 41CH57, investigators recovered blue-on-white majolica, green bottle fragments and part of a metal buckle over an older shell midden. The site is associated with the trading post and first presidio location. These mixed materials show why objects from a colonial installation should not automatically be assigned to an Akokisa household.

passages.title: Exchange, missions and daily choices
passages.text: French traders exchanged European goods for furs, skins and bear grease, traveling by water and overland. These networks gave local resources value beyond their place of production and shaped colonial competition around the lower Trinity.

passages.title: Exchange, missions and daily choices
passages.text: Spanish authorities removed French traders without replacing their supply network. The mission and presidio lacked basic provisions and sufficient trading stock. A military establishment offered different economic possibilities from a trading post, despite occupying the same area.

passages.title: Exchange, missions and daily choices
passages.text: Some Akokisa entered San Ildefonso Mission near present-day Rockdale in 1748 to 1749, then left when it closed in 1755. Campbell’s account describes participation by part of the population. It does not establish that every Akokisa household moved there or accepted mission authority.

passages.title: Exchange, missions and daily choices
passages.text: After the Spanish departure, Akokisa people used El Orcoquisac’s buildings for meetings and trade with Atakapa and Karankawa people. Reuse gave the place another role: a garrison’s abandonment was not immediate abandonment by everyone.

passages.title: Later records and living community memory
passages.text: Campbell identifies reports of two Akokisa settlements in 1805, one near the lower Colorado and another near the coast between the Neches and Sabine. He treats later movement into Atakapa communities in Louisiana as probable. Sparse outside records support caution, not a precise date when a whole people supposedly disappeared.

passages.title: Later records and living community memory
passages.text: In a 2021 interview, Mary Leblanc identified herself as Akokisa within the Atakapa Ishak community and connected the name with the San Jacinto River. Her account describes family ties to the Big Thicket. This is living testimony about identity and homeland, alongside the much narrower perspective preserved in colonial records.

passages.title: Later records and living community memory
passages.text: Leblanc describes families seeking safety in less accessible wetlands and recalls discrimination and attacks during her own youth. She also describes an active community gathering for ceremonies. Her account shows why limited visibility to outsiders cannot be treated as proof that cultural and social life had ended.

The Spanish mission’s closure was not an Akokisa fall date. Mary Leblanc’s 2021 account describes continuing Akokisa identity and Atakapa Ishak community life despite displacement and violence. The map’s interval ending in 1500 cannot establish extinction, and the sources reviewed do not support assigning one conqueror or a single final year.

passages.text: Aksum linked the northern Ethiopian highlands to the Red Sea through Adulis. Its monuments and inscriptions reveal a kingdom connected to African and Mediterranean exchange networks. The city also retained religious and ceremonial importance after its political power diminished.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Stoneworkers carved enormous stelae from single blocks. Some imitate multi-storey buildings, preserving an architectural vocabulary in stone.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: The carved stelae belong especially to the third and fourth centuries CE. Royal tombs and later palace ruins reveal several phases of monumental construction.

passages.title: Writing and ideas
passages.text: King Ezana's fourth-century inscriptions used Greek, Sabaean and Ge'ez. Their multiple languages make connections across the region visible.

passages.title: Writing and ideas
passages.text: Christianity was introduced during the fourth century. Church building subsequently became part of the city's sacred landscape.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Adulis connected maritime commerce with inland routes, while ivory trade linked Aksum with Sudan.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Later Ethiopian emperors continued to be crowned at Aksum. Political decline did not erase its ceremonial role.

sectionTitles: A basket, its materials and its geometry
Social knowledge and caring for land

passages.text: Akwẽ is a self-name of the Xerente, a Jê-speaking Indigenous people of the Tocantins region of Brazil. This entry concerns Xerente communities near Tocantínia, between the Tocantins and Sono rivers. Their relationships with the Xavante and Xakriabá do not make these distinct peoples interchangeable.

passages.title: A basket, its materials and its geometry
passages.text: A golden-grass basket given to researcher Elisângela Melo during fieldwork in 2006 later became the subject of Wesley Coelho de Sousa’s mathematics study. Its known history is a gift and a research collection, not an archaeological excavation. The basket’s maker is not named in the account.

passages.title: A basket, its materials and its geometry
passages.text: The studied basket has bundled golden-grass fibers joined with fine buriti-palm fiber. Its tightly coiled base supports open sides with repeated triangular forms and a firm rim. The different arrangements of the same materials produce both a containing surface and a visible decorative structure.

passages.title: A basket, its materials and its geometry
passages.text: Sousa used the basket to explore geometric forms and possibilities for mathematics teaching. Pandemic restrictions prevented interviews with its makers. His analysis of shapes therefore cannot establish the maker’s own terminology, intentions or mathematical explanations. It remains an interpretation of a particular object.

passages.title: Homes, meals and shared work
passages.text: Fieldwork in Porteira and Funil in 2013 to 2014 recorded adobe houses with palm roofing. Sleeping and living rooms occupied one small building, while cooking occupied another; washing facilities stood outside. This household arrangement connected shelter, food preparation and surrounding yards.

passages.title: Homes, meals and shared work
passages.text: The same study observed refrigerators, stoves and other electrical appliances, alongside some continued wood-fire cooking. Instant noodles, powdered drinks and packaged biscuits appeared among purchased foods. These observations describe changing household practices in the two studied villages, rather than a timeless menu for all Xerente people.

passages.title: Homes, meals and shared work
passages.text: Some households continued growing cassava, yams and pigeon peas. Residents described hunting peccaries, deer and armadillos; researchers also recorded craft production as a source of income. Cultivation, hunting, making goods and buying food formed overlapping livelihoods.

passages.title: Homes, meals and shared work
passages.text: In interviews during 2019 to 2020, people described sharing large hunted animals among hunters and then their relatives. The researchers observed particular care to include elders. Food distribution expressed social obligations as well as meeting household needs.

passages.title: Homes, meals and shared work
passages.text: Dona Pizadi of Salto recalled communal planting and harvest gatherings with shared food and singing. Other participants described more recent family plots and home gardens. Valcir Sinã connected difficulties with riverbank cultivation to changed water levels below the hydroelectric dam. These attributed accounts record change without declaring farming extinct.

passages.title: Social knowledge and caring for land
passages.text: Ethnographic accounts describe the Doí and Wahirê social divisions, connected by reciprocal duties and clan relationships. Circular and linear body-painting motifs identify affiliations. Designs applied with carved buriti-pith stamps show how knowledge of materials and visual forms can communicate a person’s place in social life.

passages.title: Social knowledge and caring for land
passages.text: The GATI report describes ABIX working with Ibama’s Prevfogo program to combine Xerente fire knowledge with environmental management. Participants mapped vulnerable areas, forests, wildlife refuges and wetlands containing golden grass. This was a specific collaborative project, not evidence that every fire or ecological problem had been controlled.

passages.title: Social knowledge and caring for land
passages.text: ABIX also established a plant nursery at Funai’s Tocantínia site. Seedlings were intended for restoring cleared areas and for household fruit gardens. The report connects nursery work with exchanges and training, including agricultural projects in 2015 to 2016, showing land care as organized community work.

Xerente communities continue to transmit knowledge and adapt their livelihoods. The 2019 to 2020 fieldwork records living participants debating changes in hunting, farming and food sharing. Territorial losses and environmental pressures are real, but the map’s endpoint in 1500 is not a supported extinction date or the fall of a Xerente state.

passages.text: The Alabama people belong to the Indigenous history of the southeastern woodlands, including towns around the Alabama River. Alabama is a Muskogean language, closely related to but distinct from Koasati. Long associations with Coushatta communities produced shared institutions without making the two names or languages identical.

passages.title: Town life, food and diplomacy
passages.text: Eighteenth-century towns governed their affairs through a headman, elders and a war chief. Kinship connected neighboring settlements, while leaders negotiated alliances with other Indigenous towns and European powers. Political coordination grew from local institutions rather than requiring every town to surrender its autonomy.

passages.title: Town life, food and diplomacy
passages.text: Families linked Alabama and Coushatta towns with the French garrison through intermarriage. Shuck-Hall describes children of Indigenous women and French men receiving their mothers’ clan membership. This continuity in kinship organization complicates any simple equation between imported trade goods and the loss of community identity.

passages.title: Town life, food and diplomacy
passages.text: Drawing on an April 1831 census, historian Harriet Smither places Alabama households in villages on the Neches, including Peach Tree Village. Her account describes corn, beans, sweet potatoes and peas, with surplus produce sold or shared with visitors. Farming supplied households and supported exchange and hospitality.

passages.title: Town life, food and diplomacy
passages.text: Smither also describes seasonal hunting journeys with family members, bedding, tents and cooking equipment. Dressed skins and bear oil reached the Nacogdoches market. This account connects settled villages with mobile work and trade; it does not imply that agriculture and hunting belonged to separate kinds of people.

passages.title: Town life, food and diplomacy
passages.text: The tribe’s history credits Colabe, second chief during Antone’s leadership, with speaking Alabama, English, French and the Mobilian trade language. He interpreted and attended conferences. His work illustrates how multilingual knowledge supported representation and negotiation across the changing political world of nineteenth-century Texas.

passages.title: Making baskets and sustaining materials
passages.text: The Gorman Museum catalogs a basket made by Florena Robinson in 1973 under the Alabama Coushatta affiliation. It entered the collection as a gift from Carol and Don Tallman. A named maker and dated object preserve an individual contribution to basketry; the catalog provides no archaeological findspot or manufacturing account.

passages.title: Making baskets and sustaining materials
passages.text: In a 2021 interview, Elliot Abbey described learning around his basket-making aunts, then using single stitches and a newer wheat-stitch pattern in his own work. Abbey is Coushatta from Louisiana; his wife and children are Alabama-Coushatta. Their life in Texas shows how artistic knowledge crosses closely related communities through families.

passages.title: Making baskets and sustaining materials
passages.text: Abbey recalled harvesting pine needles near home with his family in 2019 after new plantings made them accessible. The same report describes Gesse Bullock’s work managing prescribed burns for the tribe. Forest management helped sustain material needed by basket makers, linking a household craft with community stewardship.

passages.title: Language, records and continuing institutions
passages.text: Cora Sylestine, Heather K. Hardy and Timothy Montler produced the Dictionary of the Alabama Language, published in 1993. Its online form followed in 1999. Their introduction treats Alabama and Koasati as separate languages, cautioning that close relationship does not guarantee mutual understanding.

passages.title: Language, records and continuing institutions
passages.text: The dictionary’s pronunciation guide distinguishes short and long vowels, tone and consonant length. It gives kolbi for basket and oki for water. Its spelling guidance records differences that ordinary English spelling could obscure, making written documentation more useful to readers learning how words are pronounced.

passages.title: Language, records and continuing institutions
passages.text: The Briscoe Center preserves copies of three deeds concerning transfers through Texas to the Alabama Indians in 1854 to 1855, plus a record concerning one seller’s purchase. Its finding aid says the community holds the originals. These are specific documentary traces of the reservation’s creation, not evidence of an unrestricted historical homeland.

passages.title: Language, records and continuing institutions
passages.text: A separate history continued in Oklahoma. Alabama-Quassarte Tribal Town traces its community through removal from the Southeast and continued ceremonial government near Wetumka. Its account identifies April 1939 as approval of its constitution. This institution should not be confused with the later federal restoration of the Texas tribe.

The Alabama did not disappear when this map interval ends in 1783. Displacement led to different community histories, including Alabama-Coushatta government in Texas and Alabama-Quassarte Tribal Town in Oklahoma. Their continuing institutions make an extinction date inappropriate. Federal termination and restoration in Texas concern political recognition, not the beginning or end of a people.

sectionTitles: Settlements, households and the evidence of graves

passages.text: Alemanni, also written Alamanni or Alamans, names groups associated with the Upper Rhine and southwestern Germany in late antiquity. Early descriptions come from Roman outsiders. Historians do not treat them as one unchanged migrating people or assume that a single king governed every community.

passages.title: Houses, water and metalworking
passages.text: At Vörstetten’s Grub site, excavated building traces informed the museum’s reconstruction of a house combining living and livestock areas. Its timber posts and clay-coated wattle walls make the work of construction understandable. The standing museum building is a modern interpretation of archaeological evidence, not a surviving ancient house.

passages.title: Houses, water and metalworking
passages.text: Circular marks in the settlement soil suggested a round well shaft. They did not establish whether its lining used boards or woven willow. The museum therefore distinguishes the excavated indication of water supply from choices made in rebuilding the well. Preserved traces do not always determine every construction detail.

passages.title: Houses, water and metalworking
passages.text: Iron-ore fragments and smelting slag found at Vörstetten document local iron production. The museum interprets one building plan as a possible smithy, but keeps that attribution tentative. Slag is evidence of a manufacturing process; assigning that process to a particular building requires an additional argument.

passages.title: Furniture, drink and music
passages.text: A beechwood bed from grave 27 at Lauchheim-Mittelhofen is dated to 703 to 704. Pegged joints, a stabilizing wedge and traces of leather and plant-fiber padding suggest use for sleeping. Added end boards converted it for burial. The object connects skilled joinery, household comfort and funerary reuse.

passages.title: Furniture, drink and music
passages.text: A maple flask from Trossingen grave 58, dated around 580, was hollowed on a lathe and closed with a separate plate sealed with resin. Its suspension loops and standing base allowed different uses. Beer remains survived inside, linking woodworking techniques with the handling of drink.

passages.title: Furniture, drink and music
passages.text: The lyre from the same grave is cataloged around 560. Its pegs indicate six strings; the strings themselves are missing. Playing wear, replaced pegs and small repair nails show continued use and maintenance. Charcoal emphasized engraved decoration, joining musical function with visual craftsmanship. Its maker and repertoire remain unidentified.

passages.title: Settlements, households and the evidence of graves
passages.text: At Lauchheim-Mittelhofen, archaeologists investigated settlement remains dating from the sixth through eleventh centuries, close to the Wasserfurche cemetery. Ground-level building plans and sunken structures provide evidence beyond grave gifts. They reveal where people built and worked, helping balance the prominence of elite objects in museum collections.

passages.title: Settlements, households and the evidence of graves
passages.text: The Mittelhofen project compares settlement plans with cemetery records to investigate social and economic organization. Such comparison matters because a lavish burial describes a particular treatment of the dead, while houses record another part of community life. Neither evidence alone supplies a complete picture of every household.

passages.title: Settlements, households and the evidence of graves
passages.text: Niederstotzingen’s burial ground, used roughly from 580 to 630, contained weapons, armor and horse equipment associated with several distant regions. A 2018 genetic study identified close relatives among people buried with differently associated goods. Object style therefore cannot simply be read as the wearer’s ancestry or place of birth.

passages.title: Settlements, households and the evidence of graves
passages.text: The same study found people without detectable close kinship buried alongside relatives. Its authors interpreted the group through both family relationships and fellowship. They also cautioned that this richly furnished, predominantly male burial group was not representative of the wider population. A small cemetery cannot stand for all Alemannic society.

passages.title: Institutions and historical interpretation
passages.text: Geuenich emphasizes that the early name is preserved in outsiders’ accounts. Similar pottery and other objects can demonstrate connections between regions without proving that all their users shared one identity. The formation of Alemannic communities was a process, not a securely documented founding ceremony or a single migration.

passages.title: Institutions and historical interpretation
passages.text: Alemannic legal texts distinguish free, dependent and unfree people and describe courts and offices. Their categories do not map automatically onto richly or poorly furnished graves. Written rules and burial evidence answer different questions about rank, rights and power.

Frankish control developed through victories around 500, acquisition of Ostrogothic territories in 536 to 537, and the suppression of resistance at Cannstatt in 746. The last event strengthened Carolingian control within the Frankish realm. It ended a phase of political autonomy, not the lives or identity of the region’s communities.

sectionTitles: Fields and the traces of ordinary work

passages.text: The Alans were Iranian-speaking communities known around the Black Sea, Caspian and North Caucasus. Their history includes mobile pastoral groups, westward migrations and the medieval kingdom of Alania. These were changing communities and political arrangements across many centuries.

passages.title: Herding, households and ancient descriptions
passages.text: Ammianus describes families moving with covered wagons, tending herds and choosing fresh pasture. Milk and meat feature in his account, and he stresses the care given to horses. This connects movement with household subsistence, although the account belongs to a Roman author describing outsiders in the fourth century.

passages.title: Herding, households and ancient descriptions
passages.text: The same passage surrounds practical details with claims about savagery and warfare. Its hostile comparisons warn against treating it as a neutral survey. In particular, its assertion that Alans did not plow cannot describe the farming settlements documented centuries later in the North Caucasus.

passages.title: Fields and the traces of ordinary work
passages.text: Researchers in the Kislovodsk basin identified terraces associated with Alan communities in the first millennium CE. These differ in form and date from much older Koban agricultural terraces. Aerial photographs, geographic mapping and field investigation allow cultivated landscapes to be studied alongside settlements, rather than reducing life to graves and weapons.

passages.title: Fields and the traces of ordinary work
passages.text: The later fields largely avoided ground made infertile during earlier Koban land use. This finding shows that cultivation was shaped by the inherited condition of the landscape. It does not identify an individual inventor of terracing or establish that every Alan settlement organized farming in the same way.

passages.title: Fields and the traces of ordinary work
passages.text: Around Podkumskoe-3, a settlement associated with Alan culture in the fifth to eighth centuries, investigators found pottery, charred cereal grains and straw in soils. Together with chemical and biological soil changes, these traces identify agricultural activity beyond the settlement itself. Food production can leave evidence even where buildings do not survive.

passages.title: Fields and the traces of ordinary work
passages.text: The study identifies early medieval plowing and fertilization within roughly 500 to 600 meters of Podkumskoe-3. Farther away, the researchers instead found evidence of older Bronze Age cultivation. Distinguishing these layers prevents all nearby farmland from being assigned to one period or population.

passages.title: Clothing, craftsmanship and uncertain provenance
passages.text: The Met’s Alanic kaftan, cataloged around the seventh to ninth centuries, preserves fine linen, patterned silk edging and traces of fur. These materials combined a practical garment with costly decoration. The museum’s complete-looking coat includes reconstruction; the surviving original front fragment runs from neck to hem.

passages.title: Clothing, craftsmanship and uncertain provenance
passages.text: The coat’s silk includes animal and rosette designs within beaded roundels. The catalog relates such patterns to Iran and Central Asia without identifying a single workshop. Its back slits accommodated riding. Textile structure and garment shape reveal different aspects of making and wearing the clothing.

passages.title: Clothing, craftsmanship and uncertain provenance
passages.text: Harper identified Moshchevaja Balka as the coat’s probable origin by comparison with excavated textiles and correspondence with the site’s researcher. The coat entered the art market, however, and lacks a securely documented grave context. Similarity to excavated material supports an attribution, not a claim that its burial was recorded.

passages.title: Clothing, craftsmanship and uncertain provenance
passages.text: A renewed conservation study compared the coat with other textiles and used specialized imaging and chemical dye analysis. Digital drawings and photomicrographs helped document its construction. These methods show how fragile fragments can answer technical questions while leaving the original owner and exact burial context unresolved.

passages.title: Writing and political identity
passages.text: A Greek inscription at Senty Church dated 965 names the rulers David and Maria and the metropolitan Theodore. Its Byzantine architectural setting shows how Christian institutions and political authority were expressed together. Latham-Sprinkle cautions that adopting these forms does not prove replacement of the local population by Byzantine settlers.

passages.title: Writing and political identity
passages.text: Linguistic evidence connects Alanic with modern Ossetic. Surviving traces include an inscription in Greek letters, phrases recorded by the Byzantine writer Tzetzes, and a Jász-Latin vocabulary. These records preserve language across different settings; they do not imply that every community retained an identical identity.

Alania fragmented into competing principalities before the Mongol invasions of 1238 to 1240. Latham-Sprinkle therefore separates the collapse of royal unity from later conquest. Communities and language outlasted the kingdom, with Alanic an ancestor of modern Ossetic. No single fall year describes the full history of the Alans.

Aerial photographs, geographic mapping and field investigation allow cultivated landscapes to be studied alongside settlements, rather than reducing life to graves and weapons.

passages.title: Fields and the traces of ordinary work
passages.text: The later fields largely avoided ground made infertile during earlier Koban land use. This finding shows that cultivation was shaped by the inherited condition of the landscape. It does not identify an individual inventor of terracing or establish that every Alan settlement organized farming in the same way.

passages.title: Fields and the traces of ordinary work
passages.text: Around Podkumskoe-3, a settlement associated with Alan culture in the fifth to eighth centuries, investigators found pottery, charred cereal grains and straw in soils. Together with chemical and biological soil changes, these traces identify agricultural activity beyond the settlement itself. Food production can leave evidence even where buildings do not survive.

passages.title: Fields and the traces of ordinary work
passages.text: The study identifies early medieval plowing and fertilization within roughly 500 to 600 meters of Podkumskoe-3. Farther away, the researchers instead found evidence of older Bronze Age cultivation. Distinguishing these layers prevents all nearby farmland from being assigned to one period or population.

passages.title: Clothing, craftsmanship and uncertain provenance
passages.text: The Met’s Alanic kaftan, cataloged around the seventh to ninth centuries, preserves fine linen, patterned silk edging and traces of fur. These materials combined a practical garment with costly decoration. The museum’s complete-looking coat includes reconstruction; the surviving original front fragment runs from neck to hem.

passages.title: Clothing, craftsmanship and uncertain provenance
passages.text: The coat’s silk includes animal and rosette designs within beaded roundels. The catalog relates such patterns to Iran and Central Asia without identifying a single workshop. Its back slits accommodated riding. Textile structure and garment shape reveal different aspects of making and wearing the clothing.

passages.title: Clothing, craftsmanship and uncertain provenance
passages.text: Harper identified Moshchevaja Balka as the coat’s probable origin by comparison with excavated textiles and correspondence with the site’s researcher. The coat entered the art market, however, and lacks a securely documented grave context. Similarity to excavated material supports an attribution, not a claim that its burial was recorded.

passages.title: Clothing, craftsmanship and uncertain provenance
passages.text: A renewed conservation study compared the coat with other textiles and used specialized imaging and chemical dye analysis. Digital drawings and photomicrographs helped document its construction. These methods show how fragile fragments can answer technical questions while leaving the original owner and exact burial context unresolved.

passages.title: Writing and political identity
passages.text: A Greek inscription at Senty Church dated 965 names the rulers David and Maria and the metropolitan Theodore. Its Byzantine architectural setting shows how Christian institutions and political authority were expressed together. Latham-Sprinkle cautions that adopting these forms does not prove replacement of the local population by Byzantine settlers.

passages.title: Writing and political identity
passages.text: Linguistic evidence connects Alanic with modern Ossetic. Surviving traces include an inscription in Greek letters, phrases recorded by the Byzantine writer Tzetzes, and a Jász-Latin vocabulary. These records preserve language across different settings; they do not imply that every community retained an identical identity.

Alania fragmented into competing principalities before the Mongol invasions of 1238 to 1240. Latham-Sprinkle therefore separates the collapse of royal unity from later conquest. Communities and language outlasted the kingdom, with Alanic an ancestor of modern Ossetic. No single fall year describes the full history of the Alans.

sectionTitles: Language books shaped by their readers
Caring for land and sustaining institutions

passages.text: Alawa people are Traditional Owners in the Northern Territory of Australia. Many live at Minyerri, near the Hodgson River on the Alawa 1 Aboriginal Land Trust. Their history connects country, kinship, language and artistic expression with the struggle to regain control over land and community life.

passages.title: Country, houses and family life
passages.text: Edmonds’s account of Minyerri in 2003 describes people adapting houses, yards and temporary shelters to relationships with kin and country. A settlement’s street grid did not determine every use of space. Residents continued moving between households and communities for family obligations and other changing circumstances.

passages.title: Country, houses and family life
passages.text: At Roper Mission, families had been separated by boundaries between staff buildings, dormitories and outside camps. Edmonds contrasts these imposed divisions with residents’ own arrangements reflecting language and country affiliations. Architecture was part of colonial control, but it never fully determined how people understood their relationships.

passages.title: Language books shaped by their readers
passages.text: Alawa-Kriol-English dictionaries launched in Katherine on 31 October 2001 grew from Margaret Sharpe’s fieldwork and later collaboration with Alawa speakers. Community workshops in 1999 found the large draft difficult for some readers to use. The response was to prepare shorter and longer versions with different levels of detail.

passages.title: Language books shaped by their readers
passages.text: The shorter dictionary and the plant book Ruwu Alawirryunu used larger print, more space and illustrations. The plant book connected vocabulary with uses of plants for food, tools and other purposes. Design choices made documented knowledge more approachable for readers with different literacy experience.

passages.title: Language books shaped by their readers
passages.text: The books could be searched through Alawa, Kriol and English lists. The longer dictionary also included examples showing words in use. These parallel routes connected the heritage language with languages people used in daily life, rather than assuming every reader would start from English.

passages.title: Paintings and public expression
passages.text: Barney Ellaga’s Dum-nyun-ngadanyana, Big Lagoon in Alawa, painted in 2004, contrasts bright, stippled stripes with a blue central form. In her exhibition review, Cath Bowdler relates the surrounding marks to native bees traveling across country toward a waterhole. The work makes landscape and movement legible through abstraction.

passages.title: Paintings and public expression
passages.text: Bowdler describes Tibby Ellaga’s Deelinginji, painted in 2005, as using a strong vertical form across colored stripes. Although Tibby had worked with Barney, her paintings expressed her own relationships and stories. The reviewer distinguishes their individual work instead of presenting one uniform Alawa painting style.

passages.title: Paintings and public expression
passages.text: Willie Gudupi’s Alawa story is held in the Araluen Art Collection. It jointly won the 1993 Alice Prize and entered the collection through the Alice Springs Art Foundation. This documented work shows Alawa cultural expression circulating in contemporary exhibitions and public collections, beyond archaeological or ethnographic displays.

passages.title: Paintings and public expression
passages.text: The 2019 Indigenous Languages commemorative coin includes the Alawa word gudaru. The Mint lists meanings including rock, hill and coins, showing how vocabulary can encompass both landscape and introduced objects. Its multilingual design places Alawa alongside other distinct Australian languages in an everyday public medium.

passages.title: Caring for land and sustaining institutions
passages.text: A 2009 Indigenous Land Corporation report describes Minyerri residents working on fencing, water points, sheds and other station infrastructure. Senior Traditional Owners helped assess works with a sacred-site specialist. This connected employment and practical construction with protection of culturally significant places and teaching younger custodians.

passages.title: Caring for land and sustaining institutions
passages.text: The same account records Traditional Owners and Minyerri Rangers preparing a land-management plan covering weeds, feral animals and fire. Pastoral workers and rangers could coordinate their tasks. The report describes an approach to managing a particular property, not proof that all environmental problems had been solved.

passages.title: Caring for land and sustaining institutions
passages.text: The Ngukurr Language Centre works with Alawa alongside Marra, Ngandi, Ngalakgan and other heritage languages. It also works with Kriol. An Indigenous board drawn from local speakers, educators and language workers oversees the organization, keeping documentation and teaching connected to community participation.

Alawa people continue to maintain community institutions and relationships with country. Return to Minyerri and community enterprise show ongoing efforts to direct their own lives. The map’s endpoint in 1878 is a coverage limit, not an extinction date or the fall of an Alawa kingdom.

sectionTitles: Discoveries in parish and historical records
Irrigation, local government and collective action

passages.text: Alazapa communities lived in what became the Nuevo Reino de León in northeastern Mexico. Spanish colonization brought raids, captivity and demands for labor, alongside continued resistance. The name identifies particular people in colonial records; it should not be treated as a synonym for every Indigenous community in the region.

passages.title: Colonial pressure and everyday survival
passages.text: Von Mentz’s study places Alazapas among the peoples targeted by expeditions associated with Luis de Carvajal’s colonization. Captives were drawn into a market for Indigenous labor. These campaigns help explain why movement in later records cannot automatically be interpreted as voluntary migration.

passages.title: Colonial pressure and everyday survival
passages.text: The term Chichimeca often grouped together peoples with different languages and histories. Von Mentz examines how such classifications supported conquest and servitude. A colonial label alone cannot establish a common language, a single political organization or an identical way of life for Alazapas and their neighbors.

passages.title: Colonial pressure and everyday survival
passages.text: Garza Martínez’s introduction describes seasonal movement between Indigenous country and colonial estates for gathering, harvests and work. Alazapa rancherías from the north seldom appear at southern estates. These patterns suggest regional ties and changing labor arrangements, rather than one permanently wandering population.

passages.title: Colonial pressure and everyday survival
passages.text: At Santo Domingo in February 1685, an inspection recorded the Alazapa captain Christóval with Diego, Joseph and Lorenzo. Their account included shortages of food and clothing. The document makes ordinary material needs visible within a labor regime described by officials and estate owners.

passages.title: Colonial pressure and everyday survival
passages.text: Christóval also complained that his wife was being kept in the estate kitchen against his wishes. The governor ordered that she be released from that obligation. Her own words were not recorded, and the order alone does not establish whether the owners complied.

passages.title: Discoveries in parish and historical records
passages.text: A Charcas parish entry from 1653 names an adult Francisco as Alazapa and describes his parents as non-Christian. This is evidence of a particular person beyond the later Bustamante settlement. It gives no explanation for his journey and cannot establish that an entire community moved with him.

passages.title: Discoveries in parish and historical records
passages.text: In a note accompanying that entry, Martínez Sánchez points to Alazapas at Bustamante in the nineteenth century. He records Governor Santiago Vidaurri’s acknowledgment of their support during the Reform War of 1858 to 1860. Recognition under the Alazapa name therefore continued long after Spanish conquest.

passages.title: Irrigation, local government and collective action
passages.text: The 1711 division placed Alazapas north of a separating street and Tlaxcaltecas south. Each community had local officers. They shared an irrigation channel, church and mill, linking distinct communities through agricultural infrastructure.

passages.title: Irrigation, local government and collective action
passages.text: In November 1823, Alazapas authorized José Antonio Pérez to challenge dispossession and loss of control over communal resources. A 1826 ruling recognized their right to one-third of the shared irrigation water.

passages.title: Irrigation, local government and collective action
passages.text: Enforcing water rights required more than a judgment. Pérez complained that the community’s allotted turn was being denied. Later disputes involved a channel and aqueduct, with competing claims about effects on crops and mills. Marrufo traces continuing litigation through 1846.

Municipal incorporation did not erase Alazapa identity: Martínez Sánchez documents its persistence at Bustamante into the mid-nineteenth century. These sources do not establish a final disappearance date for all Alazapa communities. The map’s endpoint in 1500 marks its coverage, not the end of the people.

sectionTitles: Photography as craft and a record of life

passages.text: Albania declared independence in 1912 and developed national institutions amid international pressure and war. Occupation, communist rule and the transition of the early 1990s repeatedly changed the relationship between citizens and the state. Its cultural history also includes skilled photography, textile making and communal music that crossed these political divides.

passages.title: Photography as craft and a record of life
passages.text: The Marubi studio in Shkodër grew from Pietro Marubbi’s nineteenth-century work into a family tradition continued by Kel and Gegë. Early wet-collodion images gave way to dry gelatin on glass. This was a local mastery of changing photographic methods, not an Albanian invention of photography.

passages.title: Photography as craft and a record of life
passages.text: The archive records births, weddings and funerals alongside political figures. Studio compositions were deliberately staged. Photographs reveal clothing, gestures and social relationships, while reflecting choices made by photographers and their subjects. They do not transparently represent an entire society.

passages.title: Photography as craft and a record of life
passages.text: The private Marubi studio closed in 1952, and Gegë worked with other photographers in a state cooperative. His family archive entered state custody in 1970, and he continued organizing it. The collection therefore preserves both a photographic tradition and evidence of how socialist policies transformed private creative work.

passages.title: Currency and political authority
passages.text: The Bank of Albania’s catalog identifies a 1926 note bearing both 5 lek and 1 frank ari as the first national banknote. Printed by Richter in Naples, it circulated only briefly. The object ties Albania’s new monetary institution to overseas printing skills and a currency expressed in related units.

passages.title: Currency and political authority
passages.text: A 1939 issue reused a 1926 banknote with an eagle stamped over Ahmet Zogu’s portrait. A 100-franga note issued in May 1940 carried Victor Emanuel III’s portrait in its watermark. These alterations show political authority changing on an everyday object.

passages.title: Clothing, work and collective music
passages.text: The xhubleta worn by women and girls in northern highland communities has an undulating bell shape. Makers prepare shajak, cut and sew it, then add embroidered motifs. Its form and decoration once communicated social and economic standing as well as requiring knowledge passed between skilled makers.

passages.title: Clothing, work and collective music
passages.text: UNESCO’s account links declining xhubleta use to changes under socialism in the 1960s. The garment was impractical for work in agricultural cooperatives, while collectivization reduced access to materials. Its inclusion on the urgent safeguarding list in 2022 recognized a living skill whose transmission had become vulnerable.

passages.title: Clothing, work and collective music
passages.text: Iso-polyphonic singing combines a melody, countermelody and a supporting vocal drone. Tosk singers sustain the drone through staggered breathing; Lab performances can make it rhythmic and attach words to it. Songs accompany weddings, funerals and harvest celebrations. The coordination of voices is part of social participation as well as musical accomplishment.

passages.title: Survival, surveillance and civic rights
passages.text: A 1943 photograph preserved by the U.S. Holocaust Memorial Museum connects Gavra Mandil with Refik Veseli. The Mandils were Jewish refugees from Yugoslavia; photographic work in Tirana brought the families together. When danger increased under German occupation, Veseli arranged refuge at his family’s home in Krujë, where the Mandils survived.

passages.title: Survival, surveillance and civic rights
passages.text: The House of Leaves museum preserves miniature cameras, recorders, microphone transmitters and official instructions for surveillance. Such equipment required purchasing, maintenance and trained operators. The collection shows technical expertise serving political repression under communism, rather than treating every technological development as a social benefit.

passages.title: Survival, surveillance and civic rights
passages.text: Another exhibit displays a telephone interception list from the Ministry of Internal Affairs archive. The museum explains that household telephone access in 1970s Tirana required special authorization and favored officials, their connections and certain essential services. A phone could offer practical advantages while also enabling the state to monitor private conversations.

passages.title: Survival, surveillance and civic rights
passages.text: The 1998 constitution provides for freely formed political parties and separates state powers. It also protects expression, religious choice and the cultural and language rights of minorities. These provisions record the republic’s declared civic framework; the text itself cannot demonstrate how completely those guarantees were realized in daily life.

Albania continues as a state. Italian occupation interrupted its independence in 1939, and the communist system later gave way to political change in the early 1990s. These were transformations of rule, not the disappearance of Albanian society. The 1998 constitution established the framework of a parliamentary republic.
