sectionTitles: Settlements and the work of sharing water
Food, dress and knowledge passed between generations

passages.text: Algeria’s modern history includes French colonial rule, independence in 1962 and continuing national life. Its communities brought distinct regional practices into that history, from the oasis settlements of the M’Zab to households linked by migration. Colonial and independent Algeria are different political settings, not two unrelated peoples.

passages.title: Households, schools and migration
passages.text: Colonial institutions did not provide equal citizenship or education. The Crémieux decree of 1870 granted French citizenship collectively to many Algerian Jews while leaving Muslim Algerians under a restricted status. The immigration museum’s exhibition also documents separate schooling arrangements and the particular exclusion experienced by Muslim girls.

passages.title: Households, schools and migration
passages.text: From the late nineteenth century, some Kabyle families and village assemblies organized men’s labor journeys to France. Workers saved for relatives at home, and networks helped newcomers find jobs and lodging. Land dispossession and rural poverty shaped these movements; they were not simply an expression of individual wanderlust.

passages.title: Households, schools and migration
passages.text: A photograph used by the immigration museum shows Mr. and Mrs. Messaoudi in their grocery shop in Levallois-Perret during the 1950s. This named household makes family enterprise visible alongside histories of industrial labor. It is one documented example, not a census of how Algerian migrants earned their living.

passages.title: Settlements and the work of sharing water
passages.text: In the M’Zab Valley, the fortified settlements of El-Atteuf, Bounoura, Melika, Ghardaïa and Beni-Isguen form an ensemble with cemeteries and palm groves. Water capture and distribution supported cultivation in a dry environment. The layout embodies the practices of particular Ibadi communities, rather than a model for every Algerian settlement.

passages.title: Settlements and the work of sharing water
passages.text: The water measurers of Touat and Tidikelt calculate shares, repair distribution combs and guide water through foggara channels. Their work combines calculation with practical maintenance. Owners, laborers and accountants also participate, showing that the operation of irrigation depends on social agreements as well as physical structures.

passages.title: Settlements and the work of sharing water
passages.text: The 2018 UNESCO inscription identified threatened transmission of these water-management skills. Urbanization, changed ownership relations and weakened communication between elders and younger people were among the pressures. Recognizing the technology does not mean it maintains itself: practical teaching and experienced workers are essential to its continued use.

passages.title: Painting, cinema and women’s voices
passages.text: Baya’s first major Paris exhibition in 1947 presented an artist developing her own language of forms and colors. She also worked in ceramics at Vallauris in 1948. The later Institut du monde arabe exhibition examined both her work and correspondence, challenging descriptions that reduced her achievement to an unexplained miracle or merely naive art.

passages.title: Painting, cinema and women’s voices
passages.text: After a period devoted to family life, Baya resumed painting around independence. The national fine arts museum in Algiers exhibited and acquired her work in 1963. Musical subjects became part of her painting during the 1960s, alongside the vividly colored women, plants and creatures explored in the retrospective.

passages.title: Painting, cinema and women’s voices
passages.text: Assia Djebar prepared La Nouba des Femmes du Mont Chenoua by listening to rural women’s memories of the war. Produced for Algerian television in Arabic and French, the film combined documentary material with fiction. It was shown at Carthage in 1978 and received an international critics’ prize at Venice in 1979.

passages.title: Food, dress and knowledge passed between generations
passages.text: Preparing couscous connects cereal cultivation, milling, hand-rolling semolina and steaming with the making of clay and wooden utensils. Recipes vary with place, season and occasion. Algeria’s joint UNESCO nomination with Mauritania, Morocco and Tunisia recognizes a shared tradition; it does not assign exclusive national ownership or identify a single inventor.

passages.title: Food, dress and knowledge passed between generations
passages.text: Tlemcen’s wedding costume brings together woven golden silk, embroidered velvet, jewelry and a conical hat. Experienced women help dress the bride, while girls learn the practices from an early age. Making and wearing the costume join skilled work to relationships between families and generations in this particular community.

passages.title: Changing sovereignty and preserving evidence
passages.text: The Évian settlement followed eighteen months of discussions rather than a single meeting. The French Diplomatic Archives edition brings together records of negotiations with the National Liberation Front. Agreements were signed on 18 March 1962; the independence referendum and recognition followed in July. A negotiated settlement did not make the peace immediately secure.

passages.title: Changing sovereignty and preserving evidence
passages.text: In testimony published by Human Rights Watch in 2003, Zakia Belkhaznadji described keeping prison-visit permits while searching for her son Fouad Lakel. The paperwork conflicted with accounts officials gave her about his whereabouts. Her effort shows how families preserved documents and pressed institutions for answers after the violence of the 1990s.

Colonial rule ended in 1962. July’s referendum, French recognition on 3 July and UN admission on 8 October were distinct steps. Algeria remains independent. The map’s 1938 and 1960 boundaries describe coverage, not independence or disappearance.

Agreements were signed on 18 March 1962; the independence referendum and recognition followed in July. A negotiated settlement did not make the peace immediately secure.

passages.title: Changing sovereignty and preserving evidence
passages.text: In testimony published by Human Rights Watch in 2003, Zakia Belkhaznadji described keeping prison-visit permits while searching for her son Fouad Lakel. The paperwork conflicted with accounts officials gave her about his whereabouts. Her effort shows how families preserved documents and pressed institutions for answers after the violence of the 1990s.

Colonial rule ended in 1962. July’s referendum, French recognition on 3 July and UN admission on 8 October were distinct steps. Algeria remains independent. The map’s 1938 and 1960 boundaries describe coverage, not independence or disappearance.

sectionTitles: Embroidery and the evidence of objects

passages.text: The Regency of Algiers developed within the Ottoman world around a Mediterranean port. Its history includes maritime diplomacy, artisans’ work and the everyday institutions of a densely built city. Surviving houses, fountains, textiles and agreements reveal different aspects of that society.

passages.title: Water, streets and waterfront homes
passages.text: The Kasbah brought houses, markets, bathhouses, mosques and palaces together on a steep site. Builders worked with earthen bricks, lime and earth renders, stone and wood. This urban fabric connected worship, trade and household life; the architecture was an accumulation of building traditions rather than the work of one ruler.

passages.title: Water, streets and waterfront homes
passages.text: Public fountains depended on both benefactors and administration. Donations of property, known as habus, supported their operation, while an official called the khudjat al-uyun oversaw the associated funds. Water supply therefore involved maintaining an institution as well as constructing a basin and channel.

passages.title: Water, streets and waterfront homes
passages.text: An inscription dates a fountain commissioned by Husayn to 1820 near Bab al-Djazira. Its praise of the patron preserves his public message, not proof that everyone received enough water. Later records trace the fountain’s relocation, including a move in 1867, showing why a monument’s present setting may differ from its original one.

passages.title: Water, streets and waterfront homes
passages.text: The Palais des Raïs preserves part of the waterfront neighborhood of Qaâ Es-Sour: palaces, sailors’ homes, a mosque, covered passages and a defensive battery. The site’s history dates Palace 18 to 1750 and records its purchase by Dey Mustapha Pacha in 1798. Elite residences belonged to a larger working urban district.

passages.title: Embroidery and the evidence of objects
passages.text: An eighteenth-century turban cover in the Walters collection is embroidered in silk on linen. The museum explains that such cloths protected turbans when they were removed and stored without being unwound. An ornate textile could therefore serve a practical household purpose as well as expressing care for an item of dress.

passages.title: Embroidery and the evidence of objects
passages.text: The Walters record identifies an Algerian origin but gives no named maker or original wearer. Henry Walters’s acquisition date and method are unknown; the museum received the piece through his 1931 bequest. These gaps matter: a surviving object can document skilled work without revealing exactly who commissioned, used or transported it.

passages.title: Embroidery and the evidence of objects
passages.text: A separate eighteenth-century panel at the Metropolitan Museum combines linen, silk and metal-wrapped thread. Its catalog describes Algerian embroidery as receptive to designs from Istanbul while retaining distinctive colors and stitches. Exchange within the Ottoman world supported adaptation, rather than making every region’s textile work identical.

passages.title: Merchants, captives and translated agreements
passages.text: The 1795 treaty set a five-percent duty on American goods sold in the regency’s ports and permitted unsold goods to leave without that charge. This specific arrangement placed American merchants alongside several European trading partners. It describes negotiated rules, not unrestricted commerce for every visitor.

passages.title: Merchants, captives and translated agreements
passages.text: The same agreement protected some Americans against enslavement while still recognizing owners’ claims over captives. Article 11 required the return of fugitives reaching American warships; article 12 addressed negotiated redemption. These provisions show the limits of bilateral protection within an economy that continued to exploit enslaved people.

passages.title: Merchants, captives and translated agreements
passages.text: The edition warns that the original English version differed substantially from the Turkish text. J. H. Kramers therefore prepared a new translation in 1930. Comparing versions is part of historical research: apparent agreement between governments does not guarantee that surviving translations express identical obligations.

passages.title: Merchants, captives and translated agreements
passages.text: The 1815 treaty changed those terms. It rejected American tribute, required the release and exchange of captives, and allowed Christian captives reaching American warships to remain there. It also prohibited enslaving future prisoners captured between the two parties. These were defined protections, not a declaration abolishing slavery everywhere in the regency.

passages.title: Conquest, reuse and preservation
passages.text: The dey signed a surrender agreement on 5 July 1830 after French forces landed in June. Resistance elsewhere continued, including under Ahmed Bey in the east and Abd el-Kader in central and western Algeria. The capture of the capital did not mean that the whole country immediately accepted French control.

passages.title: Conquest, reuse and preservation
passages.text: Palais des Raïs later housed families before its evacuation for restoration. Work involved Algerian specialists and an Italian firm under UNESCO supervision, with work on site beginning in 1988. Its preserved appearance reflects conservation decisions as well as historical construction; the buildings also have a history of residential reuse.

The regency ended with the French capture of Algiers in 1830. Its inhabitants and urban traditions continued. The imported map extends this record to 1878, which should not be read as the duration of the dey’s government.

sectionTitles: Evidence of exchange and knowledge of rivers
Leaders, livelihoods and protecting community life
Language and art in community education

passages.text: The Algonquin are an Indigenous people with longstanding ties to the Ottawa River watershed and neighboring lands in present-day Quebec and Ontario. Their communities have distinct local histories. Algonquin names a people; Algonquian names a much larger language family and should not be used as though it described one nation.

passages.title: Seasonal movement and household skills
passages.text: Seasonal activities connected fishing, hunting, trapping and gathering. Summer brought larger gatherings and marriages; families then returned to hunting grounds for the winter. These movements joined social relationships to the availability of food and materials. They did not mean people lacked a homeland or moved without knowledge of particular places.

passages.title: Seasonal movement and household skills
passages.text: Morrison’s material-culture notes describe lodges with pole frames and portable birchbark coverings sewn with spruce roots. Families could roll the coverings for transport while leaving a frame for reuse. Bedding was spread at night and moved aside during the day, making the same interior serve several household purposes.

passages.title: Seasonal movement and household skills
passages.text: Snowshoe makers selected materials for different jobs: ash for frames, cedar or red pine for crosspieces, and hide strips for webbing. Shapes also varied with conditions. Long, narrow designs suited travel along rivers, while shorter, rounder ones served in deep snow. Both men and women made snowshoes.

passages.title: Seasonal movement and household skills
passages.text: Birchbark containers held foods such as maple sugar and berries. Split spruce roots joined bark panels, and scraping the darker inner surface could reveal a lighter design. Morrison also records woven basswood containers in southern areas where the material was available. Craft practices reflected local resources as well as shared knowledge.

passages.title: Evidence of exchange and knowledge of rivers
passages.text: Excavations on Allumette and Morrison islands recovered stone and bone tools and native copper implements. Morrison’s historical synthesis places this evidence within occupation beginning about six thousand years ago and traces materials to distant regions. The finds support long-distance exchange; assigning every ancient object directly to a later named nation remains an interpretation.

passages.title: Evidence of exchange and knowledge of rivers
passages.text: Place names recorded different parts of the river system rather than applying one name to the entire watershed. Morrison discusses Mattawa as a meeting or dividing of waters and Temiskaming as deep water. Such naming preserved detailed geographical relationships useful for travel, memory and communication.

passages.title: Canoe making as shared work
passages.text: The Canadian Canoe Museum’s 2019 field notes identify boats by William and Mary Commanda, Peter Carle, Jocko Carle and Basil Smith among its Algonquin holdings. Naming the makers preserves individual and family contributions. The collection also documents Kitigan Zibi’s role in a revival of birchbark canoe building around the 1970s.

passages.title: Canoe making as shared work
passages.text: During the same visit, Pinock Smith described learning through observation and participation from childhood. His workshop held canoe models, toboggans, drum frames and cradleboards. He emphasized the community needed to build a canoe, showing how teaching depends on relationships and repeated practice as well as an individual craftsperson’s skill.

passages.title: Leaders, livelihoods and protecting community life
passages.text: Kitigan Zibi’s account credits Chief Antoine Pakinawatik with three canoe journeys to Toronto to seek protection for community land. It also records opposition to placing the reserve in missionaries’ trust. This history presents community members as negotiators defending their own priorities, rather than passive recipients of a reserve arranged entirely by outsiders.

passages.title: Leaders, livelihoods and protecting community life
passages.text: Chief John Cayer’s ability to speak three languages helped him interpret for people who did not speak French or English. The community history also describes hunting and trapping, with summer work guiding visitors for fish and game clubs. Families combined knowledge of the land with changing opportunities for paid work.

passages.title: Leaders, livelihoods and protecting community life
passages.text: Pikwàkanagàn’s account explains the Seven Grandfather Teachings through honesty, humility, respect, courage, wisdom, love and truth. It connects these principles with responsibilities to other people, future generations and the land. This is a community’s description of its values, not a claim that all individuals hold identical beliefs or practices.

passages.title: Language and art in community education
passages.text: The school’s 1980 to 2010 anniversary brochure describes Mokasige partial immersion, with pupils learning Algonquin through activities including games, cooking, songs and storytelling. Joan Tenasco’s account distinguishes this language-learning class from teaching every school subject in Algonquin. The detail shows how educators adapted methods to support oral language use.

passages.title: Language and art in community education
passages.text: The same brochure records John Tenasco’s art teaching with collage, three-dimensional work and charcoal. Students’ work was exhibited at the Cultural Centre on 22 May 2009. This named event documents a setting where young people could develop and publicly share their ideas, alongside the school’s other academic and cultural activities.

Algonquin communities continue in Quebec and Ontario. Colonial settlement and resource extraction restricted land use and changed livelihoods, while communities maintained institutions and developed their own services and education. The map’s endpoint of 1530 marks an imported coverage boundary, not conquest, extinction or the end of Algonquin history.

passages.text: The Almohads made Marrakesh a center of government and learning while maintaining a major Iberian center at Seville. Monumental mosques, gates and city walls gave their rule an enduring architectural presence.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: The Kutubiyya mosque and minaret formed a major landmark in Marrakesh. Walls and monumental gateways also shaped the imperial capital.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Almohad decoration emphasized organized geometric patterns and increasingly schematic ornament.

passages.title: Ideas and learning
passages.text: The courts at Marrakesh and Seville supported Islamic learning within a program of religious reform.

passages.title: Urban life
passages.text: Fez expanded under the Almohads, with the old city reaching the extent described by UNESCO as its present-day size.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Almohad Marrakesh remained a capital into the thirteenth century. Later dynasties inherited a city whose monuments continued to structure urban life.

passages.text: The Almoravids governed from Marrakesh and connected Saharan routes with North African and Iberian towns. Their rule supported major religious buildings and crafts, while their capital helped shape the urban geography of the western Islamic world.

passages.title: Technology and towns
passages.text: Marrakesh was an Almoravid foundation. Its palm grove is traditionally attributed to their period, linking the capital with a managed cultivated landscape.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Ali ibn Yusuf commissioned a richly worked mosque minbar in 1137. It later became associated with the Kutubiyya Mosque.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Textile manufacture in Almeria shows that Almoravid cultural production included luxurious fabrics as well as mosque building.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Almoravid power connected important ports with trans-Saharan commerce. The state's economy crossed both sea and desert.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The Almohads replaced Almoravid rule in Marrakesh in the mid-twelfth century and retained the city as a capital.

passages.text: Alsea communities lived along the central Oregon coast, with villages around the Alsea River and Cape Perpetua. Their history survives through community knowledge, language records, ethnographic testimony and the continuing Siletz confederation.

passages.title: Food and winter households
passages.text: The Cape Perpetua area offered several kinds of food. Families hunted and fished, while the intertidal zone supplied clams and mussels. Villages near the cape, Seal Rock and the Alsea estuary connected people to these resources. Coastal life depended on knowing different environments, not on a single food source.

passages.title: Food and winter households
passages.text: In accounts recorded by Drucker, women prepared salmon with shell knives and preserved it through drying and smoke. Stored fish hung in baskets or bundles inside winter houses, where warmth helped protect it from damp. Harvesting a seasonal run required skilled processing and storage to feed households later.

passages.title: Food and winter households
passages.text: Winter houses were described as rectangular excavated spaces lined with cedar planks, with posts supporting overlapping roof boards. Larger houses accommodated several families, each with its own space and hearth. These are remembered construction practices recorded from speakers, not a newly excavated building assigned to a precise ancient year.

passages.title: People who preserved knowledge
passages.text: Leona Ludson of Siletz supplied much of Drucker’s account, supplemented by John Albert of Oakville. Their conversations took place in 1933 and appeared in print in 1939. Identifying these contributors makes clear that the publication depended on Indigenous expertise, even though the anthropologist organized and interpreted the resulting text.

passages.title: People who preserved knowledge
passages.text: The introduction to Alsea Texts and Myths names Alsea George and U. S. Grant as contributors to Livingston Farrand’s 1900 collection. William Smith and Thomas Jackson later worked with Frachtenberg, mainly in 1910 and again in 1913. The 1920 book therefore brings together several people’s contributions made at different times.

passages.title: People who preserved knowledge
passages.text: Frachtenberg also explained that he revised Farrand’s notes with help from his own contributors because their sound-writing systems differed. He reworked translations and paragraphing. The printed stories are valuable language records, but their presentation reflects choices by speakers, translators and editors rather than an untouched transcript of one conversation.

passages.title: People who preserved knowledge
passages.text: A Smithsonian finding aid describes an aluminum disc recorded by John Paul Marr with John Albert in May 1941 at Oakville. Cataloged as NAA INV.00000550, it includes Albert’s Bear and Wren story in English and vocabulary in Alsea and English. This preserves a different documentary medium from the earlier printed collection.

passages.title: Place names and interpreting evidence
passages.text: Patricia Whereat Phillips traced different forms of Cape Perpetua’s name in Alsea, Hanis and Lower Umpqua. She consulted linguist Eugene Buckley about a possible meaning related to an open or exposed place. Her discussion keeps the proposal tentative: John Albert preserved the Alsea name without giving its meaning.

passages.title: Dispossession, resistance and continuing institutions
passages.text: The Siletz tribal history challenges descriptions of land around Yaquina Bay as empty when it was opened to settlers in 1865. It identifies Alsea and other Indigenous families living and farming there, then being displaced from homes and fields. The account links the change in reservation boundaries to losses in daily subsistence.

passages.title: Dispossession, resistance and continuing institutions
passages.text: An 1875 council transcript reproduced by historian David G. Lewis records Coos leader Jack Rogers resisting another removal from the Alsea area. Rogers stressed homes people had built and nearby food supplies. He was a Coos representative living in the subagency, not an Alsea chief; the distinction reveals the different peoples forced together there.

passages.title: Dispossession, resistance and continuing institutions
passages.text: Lewis compares removal orders with agents’ letters about unavailable funds, competing plans and negotiations. His study places the move from the former Alsea Reservation toward Salmon River at least as late as 1878. An order issued in 1875 cannot therefore be treated as proof that every family moved that year.

passages.title: Dispossession, resistance and continuing institutions
passages.text: The 1977 Siletz Restoration Act restored recognition and access to federal services, including eligibility without requiring residence on a reservation. Restoration concerned an existing community that had organized to regain its legal standing. It was neither the creation of a new people nor the automatic return of every lost homeland.

Alsea history continues within the Siletz confederation. Dispossession and forced relocation transformed community life, and federal termination later removed recognition before restoration in 1977. These changes did not make the people extinct. The map’s 1500 cutoff describes coverage rather than a historical ending.

passages.text: Alutiiq/Sugpiaq homelands extend across coastal south-central Alaska, including Prince William Sound, the outer Kenai Peninsula, Kodiak and the Alaska Peninsula. Archaeology, community knowledge, language records and living artists reveal a continuing maritime culture. The examples here chiefly concern Kodiak, rather than every community across this broad region.

passages.title: What excavations reveal
passages.text: At Nikllirtuusqaq on Karluk Lake, excavators found a deeply dug house with a stone-lined entrance and central hearth. Notched pebble net weights and fish-cleaning knives were common finds. The museum presents the site with camps of roughly 1,300 years ago, interpreting the houses and work areas as places repeatedly used for autumn fishing.

passages.title: What excavations reveal
passages.text: Seven small blue-schist adzes from Nikllirtuusqaq have differently shaped cutting edges. Researchers suggest they could have belonged to a carver’s tool set. The tools establish woodworking at the camp; their ownership as one set remains an interpretation. An engraved pebble also bears a design resembling parka decoration.

passages.title: What excavations reveal
passages.text: A different Karluk Lake house, dated to about 3,000 years ago, contained fishing equipment and traces of household life. Its destruction by fire preserved fragments of woven matting. The charred material adds evidence of furnishings that usually decay; the report does not identify an attacker or establish why the fire began.

passages.title: Homes, containers and skilled making
passages.text: A ciqlluaq combined an excavated floor, timber framework, split driftwood boards and insulating sod. Related women and their families shared a central room for cooking, sewing, repairing tools and receiving visitors, with side rooms for sleeping and storage. As frame houses spread, older sod buildings could remain places for bathing, food preparation and gatherings.

passages.title: Homes, containers and skilled making
passages.text: Bentwood boxes required carefully prepared planks bent into sides, joined with lashings or fasteners and fitted to a separate base. Small containers carried food and supplies in kayaks. The museum distinguishes this known construction from the exact Alutiiq steaming method, which was not recorded; a documented Tlingit technique cannot simply be assigned to Alutiiq makers.

passages.title: Homes, containers and skilled making
passages.text: A painted wooden box panel from Karluk One, dated around 1550, depicts an erupting volcano. Other pieces include a miniature skin-working board showing an otter. Artists prepared colors from plants and crushed minerals mixed with binders. These surviving surfaces show that everyday wooden objects could also carry carefully composed images.

passages.title: Homes, containers and skilled making
passages.text: Catalog UAM:EH:0568-5577 describes an adze from Karluk whose maker fastened a metal rasp blade to a wooden handle with cotton cord. The object shows a familiar tool form made with introduced materials. Charles Lucier collected it around 1952; that collection date does not establish when it was manufactured.

passages.title: Colonization, displacement and rebuilding
passages.text: At Awa’uq, a refuge off Sitkalidak Island, families sought protection in a naturally defensible place. Russian traders attacked with cannon in 1784, killed many people and took hostages. The museum identifies this massacre as the loss of Kodiak Alutiiq political autonomy, not the disappearance of Alutiiq society throughout its wider homeland.

passages.title: Colonization, displacement and rebuilding
passages.text: The Russian settlement at Three Saints Bay relied on Alutiiq hostages forced to hunt and prepare food. When traders moved their settlement to Kodiak in 1793, the Native community remained. Its subsequent movements form part of Old Harbor’s history, which also includes families arriving from other villages after epidemics and later disruptions.

passages.title: Colonization, displacement and rebuilding
passages.text: The 1964 earthquake and tsunamis destroyed much of Afognak village. Residents evacuated and established Port Lions in nearby Settler Cove; families entered new houses that December. The move involved creating homes and community infrastructure after a disaster, while carrying relationships and village history into a new location.

passages.title: Language, memory and living art
passages.text: Mission and secular schools under American rule punished children for using Alutiiq, sometimes physically. The museum explains how this pressure affected parents’ decisions about teaching the language at home. Reduced transmission was shaped by coercive institutions, while later community teaching projects sought to make public speaking and learning possible again.

passages.title: Language, memory and living art
passages.text: The museum’s language archive describes Joe Kelly’s interviews with Larry Matfay about sod-house construction, Deborah Robinson’s interviews with speakers from several villages, and recordings from the 2003 to 2007 master-apprentice project. These collections connect language with biographies and practical knowledge. Their catalog descriptions identify the contributors; they are not substitutes for listening to the recordings.

passages.title: Language, memory and living art
passages.text: In 2024 the museum selected oil lamps by Rolf Lee Christiansen made from cobbles gathered below Refuge Rock. One has a carved face designed to emerge as its oil burns. It also selected Cheryl Lacy’s beaded mask How Big Was Your Fish?, which reworks older mask forms through beadwork rather than wood carving.

Alutiiq/Sugpiaq communities continue across their homeland. Russian violence brought colonial domination on Kodiak, and later schools and displacement caused further losses. Community institutions, language projects and living artists carry knowledge forward. The map’s 1500 cutoff is a coverage boundary, not the end of these people.

sectionTitles: Food, families and the work behind a meal
Building, making and connecting a city
The past in homes and classrooms

passages.text: Alwa’s capital, Soba, lay on the Blue Nile in what is now Sudan. Kings and church leaders shared this city with people who built, traded and prepared food. Its buried buildings and everyday objects let us look beyond royal history.

passages.title: Food, families and the work behind a meal
passages.text: At Soba, Deposit 7 in trench 1/GN contained six lower grinding stones and fourteen handheld grinders. Large basin-shaped stones paired with disc-shaped grinders probably supported processing such as turning grain into flour. The investigators also suggest smaller tools served smaller tasks. Making a meal could start with an arm workout: no button marked “blend”. The exact foods processed on each stone remain uncertain.

passages.title: Food, families and the work behind a meal
passages.text: Researchers examining Soba samples reported charred broomcorn millet and grape seeds. The samples came from contexts including vessel fills and ash-bearing deposits. These tiny remains add plants to the story told by pots and grinding stones. Grapes do not automatically mean wine, and the preliminary report does not reconstruct a complete family menu. Many uncharred remains were considered modern contamination.

passages.title: Food, families and the work behind a meal
passages.text: A 2024 study examined tooth enamel from fourteen people buried at Soba’s Cemetery OS. Chemical traces formed during childhood point to heavy reliance on foods from a plant group that includes millet and sorghum, and possibly products from animals eating similar plants. Teeth can preserve clues to childhood meals, but they cannot hand us a recipe or identify every ingredient.

passages.title: Food, families and the work behind a meal
passages.text: Comparisons between people, animals and regional water chemistry led the same researchers to suggest seasonal movement between the Nile valley and nearby grasslands. In their interpretation, some herders may have travelled with family members, including children. This is a possible explanation of the chemical evidence, not a recovered travel diary or proof that every Soba household lived the same way.

passages.title: Building, making and connecting a city
passages.text: In trench 1/OS, excavators found mud-brick walls and evidence that an open area later became a roofed room. An impression left by a palm log helped identify its roof supports. These remains show a space changing over time; they do not identify the household, room occupants or purpose of every activity inside.

passages.title: Building, making and connecting a city
passages.text: Another excavation on Mound OS found lime deposits and kiln remains. Radiocarbon samples place the production deposit around the early eleventh century. Making building materials left traces as well as constructing the finished buildings: the city required skilled work behind the scenes.

passages.title: Building, making and connecting a city
passages.text: A 2023 study tested twenty-three glass beads from Soba. Their chemistry linked most samples to glass made in northern India, with others connected to Egypt and the Middle East. Small ornaments could therefore participate in enormous exchange networks. A bead’s ingredients can suggest its origin, but cannot tell us every stop on its journey or the identity of its wearer.

passages.title: Building, making and connecting a city
passages.text: Excavations in 2019 to 2022 recovered glass fragments and an object identified as a cosmetic bottle. Analysis of thirty fragments linked their glass to production in Egypt, the Levant and the Middle East. Glass served purposes beyond jewellery, including vessels and windows. The bottle’s label is not a chemical identification of its original contents, and these finds do not prove every home had glass windows.

passages.title: Building, making and connecting a city
passages.text: The project begun in 2019 used magnetic surveys to detect buried structures, then tested interpretations by excavating selected places. In Area F, the survey suggested closely packed mud-brick houses and irregular streets. This reveals a neighbourhood’s layout without digging up every square metre, although a magnetic pattern still needs interpretation and cannot name the family living behind a wall.

passages.title: The past in homes and classrooms
passages.text: Interviews reported in 2021 found that some modern Soba households kept old grinding stones and displayed pottery fragments. Women connected such objects with memories of family homes. An archaeological object can become part of somebody’s living room, not only a museum collection. Modern reuse does not prove an unbroken custom stretching back to Alwa.

passages.title: The past in homes and classrooms
passages.text: In December 2022, workshops in Soba schools asked children to discuss archaeology and draw their ideas about the past. Pictures included brick houses, water containers and objects used at home. Researchers noted that classroom discussion and textbooks influenced the drawings. Children were contributing their own ideas, while the pictures remained modern interpretations rather than illustrations made by medieval residents.

passages.title: The past in homes and classrooms
passages.text: During research in early 2023, women in Soba and the Mahas region discussed clothing, food and homes in interviews and meetings, including conversations over coffee and sweets. Researchers compared local traditions instead of assuming one uniform Sudanese way of life. Their work records modern women’s knowledge; it does not make every present-day resident a direct descendant of medieval Soba’s population.

Later accounts link Soba’s conquest by Sennar’s first ruler to 1504. Excavation reveals districts abandoned at different times, with some buildings still used in the thirteenth century. Alwa’s final political transition remains uncertain. The map’s 1530 endpoint is not a verified fall year, and collapse did not mean everyone disappeared.

sectionTitles: Clothing and evidence of household life

passages.text: Amahuaca are an Indigenous Amazonian people with communities in Peru’s Ucayali and Madre de Dios regions. Their history includes horticulture, skilled manufacture, displacement and continuing community life.

passages.title: Growing, storing and preparing food
passages.text: Dole’s ethnographic account describes hilltop gardens combining maize, sweet manioc and bananas. Planting followed a sequence: maize first, manioc cuttings among the young plants, then banana shoots before the rains. Cultivation depended on knowledge of crop growth and seasonal timing, alongside hunting and gathering rather than replacing them.

passages.title: Growing, storing and preparing food
passages.text: Maize was stored on the cob in granaries with raised floors of split palm. Toasted kernels were ground in a trough made from a palm log, using a rocking pestle carved from a tree’s buttress root. These implements connected forest materials with the work of keeping harvests and preparing meals.

passages.title: Growing, storing and preparing food
passages.text: The same account describes palm-wood bows and cane arrows with specialized points, along with smoking racks used for meat and fish. People selected different materials for shafts, cutting edges and other tools. This combination of gardening, hunting and processing required several kinds of expertise within everyday household work.

passages.title: Clothing and evidence of household life
passages.text: The Ministry of Culture’s account describes women’s woven cotton skirts and dyes made with annatto, bark preparations and clay. It also records red and black body designs using plant pigments. Spinning, weaving and coloring were distinct stages of skilled work; these historical descriptions do not imply that every family dresses identically today.

passages.title: Clothing and evidence of household life
passages.text: A Smithsonian catalog describes C. L. Chester’s July 1910 photograph, NAA INV.04325900, showing a plank-and-bamboo house with a thatched roof, a metal pot at the hearth and bundles hanging above. Its recorded setting is the Perene coffee colony. This is evidence of one photographed household setting, not an untouched precolonial village.

passages.title: Language as living knowledge
passages.text: Amahuaca grammar can mark whether connected actions involve the same people or different people, and whether events overlap or follow one another. Clem’s study illustrates the distinction with singing and dancing, and with eating and washing dishes. Speakers’ explanations of ordinary sentences help linguists understand a system that differs from English.

passages.title: Language as living knowledge
passages.text: In a 2025 study, three Amahuaca speakers translated sentences from Spanish and reviewed them with researchers. The team then annotated a subset to show grammatical relationships, including small markers that attach to other forms. This creates a resource for language research while making the speakers’ role in producing and checking the evidence explicit.

passages.title: Learning, making and returning records
passages.text: Amahuaca teacher Carlos Melendez Piño proposed a cultural center at Nuevo San Martin on the Inuya River. Community members built it and prepared pottery, headdresses, necklaces and armbands for the opening. Hewlett’s account describes young people making their own adornments, so the project transmitted practical skills as well as displaying finished objects.

passages.title: Learning, making and returning records
passages.text: The center brought photographs and film from earlier research back into community discussions. Melendez explained images taken by Carneiro and Dole in 1960 and 1961, and people watched footage showing themselves or relatives. The center’s inclusive name made room for Yaminahua and Ashaninka neighbors, alongside the formation of a local Indigenous federation.

passages.title: Learning, making and returning records
passages.text: In a 2024 interview at Boca Pariamanu, Alberto Inuma described learning plant knowledge from his grandfather and uncle, then training as a nurse. The report follows him gathering materials with Walter Pacaya and visiting the community’s planted medicinal garden. This documents learning across generations and institutions, without establishing the clinical effectiveness of particular remedies.

passages.title: Displacement, rights and continuity
passages.text: The rubber economy exposed Amahuaca families to capture and exploitation. The Ministry of Culture also records epidemics and raids by other groups seeking captives. Movement into less accessible areas could be a response to these threats. Describing dispersion only as a preference for wandering would miss the violence shaping where people could live.

passages.title: Displacement, rights and continuity
passages.text: A decree published in July 2016 assigned Murunahua the category of Indigenous reserve and explicitly included Amahuaca people in initial contact among its beneficiaries. The document’s stated purpose concerned protection of people and habitat. It recognizes a particular legal situation; it does not classify every Amahuaca community as isolated or newly contacted.

Amahuaca communities continue through local institutions, cultural projects and the transmission of knowledge. The map’s 1500 cutoff is not an extinction date. Initial-contact protections apply to particular groups and must not erase the different experiences of other Amahuaca communities.

sectionTitles: Cave finds and what they can tell us
Food, water and connections between places
Painting, performance and passing on knowledge

passages.text: Amangu are among the Aboriginal peoples of Western Australia’s Mid West, including the Geraldton region. Amangu identity continues within wider Southern Yamatji and Yamatji relationships. Archaeology, place-based knowledge and living artists illuminate this history without reducing its communities to the boundaries of an imported map.

passages.title: Cave finds and what they can tell us
passages.text: At Yellabidde Cave, researchers recovered stone artifacts and charcoal from deposits extending back about 25,500 calibrated years before present. A younger charcoal fragment in a deep layer was judged intrusive. The sequence records intermittent occupation, not uninterrupted residence or proof that today’s named identities had identical boundaries throughout that span.

passages.title: Cave finds and what they can tell us
passages.text: Quartz and limestone fragments at Yellabidde were interpreted as debris from making or modifying tools. Later layers also contained ochre and plant remains near hearths. Animal bones require another distinction: people, owls and mammalian predators all contributed to the deposit, so the whole bone collection cannot be read as a human menu.

passages.title: Cave finds and what they can tell us
passages.text: Amangu Traditional Owners helped name the site Yellabidde after the emu eggshell found there. The cave had long been known locally before the 2014 archaeological excavation. Scientific investigation added dated evidence to a place already present in community knowledge; it did not discover an unknown landscape for its custodians.

passages.title: Food, water and connections between places
passages.text: The city’s Yamaji heritage trail describes Champion Bay as a sheltered fishing ground used by people from across the Mid West. Nearby Chapman River offered camping places, while Greenough’s permanent waterholes supported wildlife and edible plants. These are connected regional examples, not evidence that only Amangu people used each location.

passages.title: Food, water and connections between places
passages.text: The Old North Road Stock Route followed a landscape already structured by Aboriginal pathways and water sources. Its heritage assessment records how colonial droving and settlement changed access to these places. Wells and road infrastructure therefore preserve a history of pastoral transport alongside the disruption of much older relationships with water and Country.

passages.title: Painting, performance and passing on knowledge
passages.text: Nicole Dickerson’s Connection of Our People is an acrylic painting that links ancestors, stars, rivers and the ocean. The artist’s statement accompanies it in the Mid West Development Commission’s 2024 to 2025 report. Dickerson has Amangu, Naaguja, Wilunyu and Ngarluma connections; her individual work should not be treated as a generic design shared identically by all groups.

passages.title: Painting, performance and passing on knowledge
passages.text: For Winthu Wangga in July 2024, Dickerson collaborated with poet Charmaine Papertalk Green on a drone-light and sound performance at Geraldton. Images and narration followed wind across inland and coastal Country. The production combined artistic knowledge with animation and sound design, creating a new medium for public storytelling.

passages.title: Painting, performance and passing on knowledge
passages.text: Amangu performer Lucia Richardson appears in Star Dreaming, a 2021 film connecting a journey through radio astronomy with encounters with Yamaji artists. Its study guide records her explanation that painting, dancing and conversation pass knowledge between people. Her participation offers an example of young people contributing to cultural storytelling, rather than appearing only as its audience.

passages.title: Identity, institutions and continuity
passages.text: YMAC’s 2017 report traces changes from the Amangu claim to Wilunyu and then Southern Yamatji. It also states that earlier project agreements remained in force and that an elected Amangu working group continued making decisions about their implementation. Changes in a legal claim’s name therefore did not mean that Amangu identity had ceased.

passages.title: Identity, institutions and continuity
passages.text: The Yamatji Nation agreement names Amangu alongside other identities and explicitly recognizes continuing relationships with land and waters. It describes responsibilities guided by traditional laws and customs. This regional arrangement preserves distinctions among its constituent identities, rather than declaring that every group has one language or a single interchangeable history.

passages.title: Identity, institutions and continuity
passages.text: The Department of Justice dates the consent determination to 7 February 2020 and formal execution of the agreement to 24 February. It distinguishes recognized native title over particular parcels from the wider agreement and its benefits. A broad settlement area is not proof of exclusive title over every place inside it.

Amangu people continue as part of the region’s living communities. Colonial land use disrupted access to Country, while later agreements and institutions address aspects of those losses. Amangu identity remains explicitly recognized within Yamatji Nation. The map’s 1878 cutoff marks the end of this imported coverage, not the people’s history.

sectionTitles: Journeys and images of a changing world

passages.text: Amurdak people are connected with Country around Awunbarna, also called Mount Borradaile, in northwestern Arnhem Land. The map’s older label, Amarak, also appears in language catalogues. Rock paintings, oral histories and language records reveal artistic experimentation and relationships with neighbouring peoples and overseas visitors.

passages.title: Objects in lived places
passages.text: Awunbarna shelters contain grindstones, grinding hollows, shell middens, spears and wooden artifacts alongside introduced glass, metal and steel bed frames. The blue-painting study recorded these materials without excavating them. They bring food processing, equipment and changing household possessions into view, but do not supply a securely dated sequence for every object.

passages.title: Objects in lived places
passages.text: Amurdak oral and written histories describe trade, marriage and ceremonial relationships with neighbouring peoples. Encounters with British settlements, buffalo shooters and missionaries later altered those networks. This was a connected social landscape: neither imported goods nor contact-themed paintings demonstrate that earlier relationships simply vanished.

passages.title: Inventive materials and decorated hands
passages.text: At the Major Art Site, AW22, artists used laundry blue in decorated hand paintings, including a hand placed over an earlier fish image. A material sold for whitening fabric became a strong ultramarine pigment. The sequence shows deliberate reuse of both a new material and an already painted surface.

passages.title: Inventive materials and decorated hands
passages.text: Painted Hands combine a recognizable hand or hand-and-arm outline with added internal designs and sometimes a surrounding line. At Awunbarna they go beyond leaving a simple stencil. The 2020 study interprets their elaboration as a way of communicating identity and sustaining relationships during colonial upheaval, rather than proving one meaning for every hand.

passages.title: Inventive materials and decorated hands
passages.text: A small horse painted across the border around an Awunbarna hand image provides a relative sequence: that horse was added after the border. Overlapping images, comparisons with documented works and recollections help researchers place paintings in time. Such evidence should not be turned into an exact calendar date for each image.

passages.title: Journeys and images of a changing world
passages.text: Two paintings at inland Awunbarna depict boats that researchers identify as Moluccan fighting vessels. Their forms connect this rock-art landscape with seafaring worlds beyond Australia. The 2026 paper compares the images with historical evidence of Aboriginal voyages and longstanding Amurdak relationships with Iwaidja neighbours to the north.

passages.title: Journeys and images of a changing world
passages.text: Alamurdie, also known as Jack White, visited Tanimbar, Aru and Kei aboard a ship in 1839. Researchers propose that his experience could explain who made the boat paintings. This is an argued possibility, not a signed attribution or proof that every Amurdak person undertook such voyages.

passages.title: Journeys and images of a changing world
passages.text: Awunbarna’s large Rainbow Serpent paintings combine snake bodies with features of other creatures. Researchers distinguish recent examples through their upper positions in overlapping sequences, style and use of white clay pigment. White clay weathers differently from red ochre, so surviving colour and condition matter when interpreting the sequence.

passages.title: Journeys and images of a changing world
passages.text: The 2026 study proposes that making especially large ancestral figures helped reassert cultural authority amid the changes brought by European settlement. Size is directly observable; this explanation of its social purpose is the authors’ interpretation. A recent painting can therefore be innovative while remaining part of a much longer tradition.

passages.title: Language, memory and authorship
passages.text: AIATSIS lists a 1977 Amurdak wordlist with Lucy Wirlmaga as its knowledge holder and a comparison involving Amurdak, Garig and Iwaidja with Lily Marriyulgij. The catalogue restores named contributors to the history of language documentation. It describes records that can be located, rather than certifying that every word was independently checked for this card.

passages.title: Language, memory and authorship
passages.text: The educational guide for Language Matters identifies Charlie Mungulda’s Amurdak narration of the Warramurrungunji creation story. The recording preserves language used in an extended account, beyond a list of isolated words. The guide’s speaker information belongs to the documentary’s context and is not a present-day population census.

passages.title: Language, memory and authorship
passages.text: Mungulda appears as a coauthor of research on Amurdak encounters, bringing a songman’s knowledge into historical interpretation. The conference abstract describes a history built through oral accounts, rock paintings and documentary records. Community knowledge here participates in explaining the evidence, rather than serving only as an anonymous subject of study.

There is no supported fall of an Amurdak kingdom to attach to this people’s history. Colonial encounters transformed life, and language transmission has faced severe loss. Amurdak knowledge nevertheless continues through custodianship, recordings and collaborative research. The map’s 1878 endpoint is a coverage limit, not evidence of disappearance.

passages.text: This map category spans many Amazonian societies, not a single civilization. Evidence from particular places shows hunting, fishing, gathering, cultivation and settlement in different combinations. The examples below describe those places; none defines everyone within the map’s broad outline.

passages.title: Early food and tools
passages.text: At Caverna da Pedra Pintada near Monte Alegre, excavators found triangular stone spear points, other tools and paintings in a stratified cave site. Radiocarbon dates on charred plant remains and luminescence measurements support a late Pleistocene occupation. The evidence documents people living in a tropical environment long before the map’s first appearance of this category.

passages.title: Early food and tools
passages.text: Charred tree fruits, wood and animal remains at Pedra Pintada indicate a varied forest-and-river economy. The inhabitants cannot be described only as big-game hunters. Their food debris gives evidence of gathering and using local environments, although surviving remains are not a complete menu of everything eaten.

passages.title: Early food and tools
passages.text: At Isla del Tesoro in Bolivia’s Llanos de Moxos, layers of burnt and unburnt apple-snail shells occur with other animal remains. Broken deer bone, localized burning, sediment chemistry and stratigraphy together support human food preparation. A shell accumulation by itself would not establish that people, rather than animals or natural processes, made the mound.

passages.title: Early food and tools
passages.text: The Isla del Tesoro study interprets repeated burnt lenses as intermittent, possibly seasonal use. Snails may have supplemented other foods despite dominating the preserved deposit. As refuse accumulated, the mound became a raised place within wetland surroundings. This is evidence of changing a landscape through repeated activity, without requiring a planned monumental construction.

passages.title: Cultivation and useful soils
passages.text: At Llanos de Moxos forest islands, microscopic silica traces left by plants identify manioc, squash and maize. The 2020 study reports manioc at about 10,350 calibrated years before present and maize later, around 6,850. These are dated local attestations, not proof that one crop appeared everywhere at once or that gathering immediately ended.

passages.title: Cultivation and useful soils
passages.text: At Hatahara in central Amazonia, dark soil contains fragmented charcoal, bone and pottery. At nearby Caldeirão, excavations reveal mounds and pits, including a pit with well-preserved vessels. These archaeological contexts support a strong human role in forming fertile soils, rather than treating every dark patch as a natural river deposit.

passages.title: Cultivation and useful soils
passages.text: The 2023 dark-earth study compared modern Indigenous settlements with archaeological sites in the Upper Xingu. Similarities in soil composition and distribution, together with documented soil-enriching practices, support deliberate management as one explanation for ancient fertile patches. The comparison is a model grounded in evidence, not direct access to every ancient household’s intentions.

passages.title: Cultivation and useful soils
passages.text: Researchers at Kuikuro II observed people spreading hearth ash, charcoal and manioc-processing waste, and planting crops in enriched ground near houses. Farmers explained the intended improvement of the soil in interviews. These observations connect everyday cooking, cleaning and food preparation with cultivation, while leaving room for variation between households and statements.

passages.title: Villages, pottery and regional differences
passages.text: Excavation at the Upper Tapajós site Mt-04 found pottery and charcoal within dark earth inside a ditched enclosure. Charcoal associated with pottery near the deposit’s base dated to 1410 to 1460 CE. The dense domestic remains support settlement use; the ditch alone would not establish how the place functioned.

passages.title: Villages, pottery and regional differences
passages.text: Mt-04 pottery differs in decoration from ceramics reported in Acre, Bolivia and the Upper Xingu. Communities could share the practice of constructing earthworks while retaining different craft traditions. That variation matters when interpreting a map that gives large areas a single label.

passages.title: Villages, pottery and regional differences
passages.text: Dark-earth chemistry does not translate directly into a population count. The 2022 assessment explains that people concentrated food residues and other materials from a wider catchment into settlement areas. Understanding ordinary refuse disposal is therefore essential before using enriched soil to infer farming intensity or the size of a community.

passages.title: Continuing histories
passages.text: Kuikuro oral history recounts slave-raiding encounters before peaceful exchanges with Karl von den Steinen in the nineteenth century. Later influenza and measles caused severe losses and movements closer to medical posts. This documented community history shows why village abandonment and population decline must be distinguished from the disappearance of Indigenous peoples.

This regional category has no single founding, conqueror or fall. Individual societies followed different paths through colonial violence, disease, migration and continuing community life. Kuikuro history provides one example of that continuity. The map’s 1800 cutoff does not mark the extinction of Amazonian peoples or the end of foraging.

passages.text: The Ambaló, also called Ampiule, are an Indigenous people of the Central Cordillera around Silvia in Cauca, Colombia. Farming, collective organization and the Ampiu Wam language connect community life with this mountainous territory. Their history includes dispossession and renewed self-government, as well as continuing work to pass knowledge between generations.

passages.title: Clothing, language and belonging
passages.text: CRIC’s Ambaló profile describes sheep-wool ruanas and woven bags among men’s clothing, and dark wool anacos and rebozos among women’s garments. The materials connect dress with pastoral work and the cold highland environment. This contemporary account does not establish when each garment first came into use.

passages.title: Clothing, language and belonging
passages.text: Ampiu Wam is described as a variety of Namtrik, a language also associated with neighboring peoples. A shared linguistic relationship does not erase Ambaló identity. The community’s own organization, history and territory matter alongside language, especially where recovery movements brought people of different backgrounds together.

passages.title: Plants, water and everyday learning
passages.text: In 2009, Nancy Bravo Chantre reported that students from two Ambaló educational centers were characterizing local plant species with CRIC’s education program. They considered plants still conserved and others needing recovery. The work brought observation and comparison into the care of the resguardo’s cold-climate environment.

passages.title: Plants, water and everyday learning
passages.text: The same account links this plant research with organic production and learning through schools. It presents food autonomy as the ability to choose and maintain local production. Its wider lists of foods and regional exchanges should not be read as an inventory of crops grown by every Ambaló household.

passages.title: Plants, water and everyday learning
passages.text: The UAIIN-CRIC catalog describes Corredor biológico, a film about a teaching project in Ambaló. Students, teachers and community members identified waterfalls, streams and rivers, gathered native seeds and plants, and undertook reforestation. The catalog documents the project’s subject, but supplies no filming date or measured ecological outcome.

passages.title: Plants, water and everyday learning
passages.text: Miraflores teachers’ 2014 garden project proposed visits to family gardens and illustrated writing about their practices. José Luis Chávez was assigned garden visits and knowledge-sharing activities, while Patricia Pechene’s tasks linked collected information with short texts and graphics. Literacy could grow from observing familiar work and discussing it.

passages.title: Plants, water and everyday learning
passages.text: Another part of the Miraflores plan assigned Robinson Rivera Otero land preparation and seed planting. Measuring distances and counting or selecting seeds joined mathematics to agricultural tools and work. The schedule records an educational design; it does not by itself demonstrate improved harvests or prove that every planned activity occurred.

passages.title: Rebuilding institutions and sharing skills
passages.text: Ambaló’s 2016 anniversary statement describes government as a collective responsibility involving the traditional authority, work committees, program teams, the Indigenous Guard and different generations. Family, school and community spaces all matter in transmitting knowledge. This account presents an ongoing practice of organization, rather than a single leader’s achievement.

passages.title: Rebuilding institutions and sharing skills
passages.text: Sources date the rebuilding of authority in different ways. The September 2016 statement celebrates its thirty-third anniversary, while CRIC’s people profile records an assembly choosing a state-recognized cabildo in 1984. Both place renewed organization in the early 1980s; this card does not force them into one exact reconstitution date.

passages.title: Rebuilding institutions and sharing skills
passages.text: At the April 2021 communication workshop in Popayán, Ambaló communicator Miguel Ulchur helped moderate discussion alongside Nasa communicator Erika Hilamo. Participants from several peoples connected radio and video with their own histories, assemblies, gardens and other community activities. The event shows collaboration without making those peoples culturally interchangeable.

passages.title: Rebuilding institutions and sharing skills
passages.text: The workshop also focused on how to ask useful research questions and learn from elders and people living through events. Media-making involved gathering and interpreting testimony, as well as operating equipment. This is documented work in producing knowledge, not a claim that the community invented radio or video.

passages.title: Rebuilding institutions and sharing skills
passages.text: José Miguel Niquinás, an Ampiulle man from Ambaló, recalled leaving in 1986 to join land recovery at Caloto. CRIC’s 2025 account connects his experience with the later community economy of López Adentro. Its Kwe’sx rice project belongs to that setting, illustrating a person’s contribution beyond his home territory.

Ambaló communities continue. Their own history distinguishes the mid-twentieth-century loss of collective land and the cabildo from renewed organization in the 1980s. Recovery has involved land, institutions and cultural knowledge, amid continuing pressures. The map’s 1500 cutoff is a limit of its imported coverage, not an extinction date.

sectionTitles: What petitions reveal about daily life
Reading changes in population and identity

passages.text: Ambocas names an Indigenous population and a colonial province in Ecuador’s Loja region. Colonial writers connected the population with Cañari ancestry, but this name does not identify a precisely bounded kingdom with a known founding and fall.

passages.title: Land, work and making things
passages.text: Loja’s municipal account of Santiago de Ambocas describes fields, grazing land, woodland and accessible water in a cool environment. Its language about supposedly unused land reflects a colonial assessment of usefulness. Such a description helps reconstruct a farming landscape, but is not a neutral survey of Indigenous land rights.

passages.title: Land, work and making things
passages.text: A colonial observer distinguished Ambocas builders who laid adobe from other workers who made the blocks. Brito Román cites this account in discussing Cañari connections. It provides evidence for skilled building labor, while the observer’s ethnic ranking should not become a judgment of people’s abilities or worth.

passages.title: Land, work and making things
passages.text: The municipal history of El Cisne says difficult, steep terrain led colonial authorities to allow community land beyond the usual surrounding allocation. The account links settlement with the practical need for usable ground. It does not provide enough surveyed evidence to reconstruct every boundary on this map.

passages.title: Land, work and making things
passages.text: El Cisne’s account describes Indigenous residents commissioning a Virgin Mary image from Diego de Robles in 1595. The carved cedar sculpture connects local patrons with a wider colonial artistic world. Accounts of an apparition belong to devotional tradition; they are not archaeological proof of when Ambocas people first occupied the region.

passages.title: What petitions reveal about daily life
passages.text: The February 1639 letter from leaders of Ambocas, Calbas, Paltas, Chuquiribamba and Malacatos challenged excessive tribute. The catalog describes their complaint that rolls had not been corrected for people who were absent or dead. Household obligations depended on records, so outdated lists could impose burdens on those who remained.

passages.title: What petitions reveal about daily life
passages.text: Those petitioners asked for an Audiencia official to examine the accounts and presented their request as beneficial to the royal treasury. The document’s description shows coordinated advocacy across communities and an understanding of colonial procedures. It does not tell us whether the requested investigation occurred or whether payments were reduced.

passages.title: What petitions reveal about daily life
passages.text: Antonio Montoya’s 1787 petition concerns concrete work: caring for horses, domestic service and baking for the local priest. Identified as a cacique, he appealed to the dignity of his position. The catalog preserves his allegation of compelled service, not a court finding that independently verifies every detail.

passages.title: What petitions reveal about daily life
passages.text: The rejected 1732 appointment of a lieutenant in Ambocas illustrates conflict within colonial administration. The corregidor’s nomination faced a legal objection before the Audiencia. Formal restrictions on officials could create grounds for resistance, although this one case cannot establish that communities were consistently protected from interference.

passages.title: Reading changes in population and identity
passages.text: El Cisne’s municipal history attributes severe population losses to smallpox and measles. It also distinguishes surrounding communities such as Ari, Ganajapa and Nona. A count of tribute-paying people at a settlement would exclude others, so it should not be turned into a complete census or a claim that all Ambocas vanished.

passages.title: Reading changes in population and identity
passages.text: Brito Román discusses a Cañari connection and possible Inca-era resettlement, while comparing different proposed locations for Ambocas. Resettlement is an interpretation of historical testimony, not a directly dated migration recovered by excavation. The surviving name does not establish that provincial and ethnic boundaries were identical.

passages.title: Reading changes in population and identity
passages.text: Santiago’s municipal history cites a 1778 census organized by Pedro Xavier de Valdivieso y Torres. It is evidence for a particular settlement under colonial rule. A town census should not be used as the population of every community associated with the larger Ambocas province.

Colonial government reorganized Ambocas communities through tribute, labor and church institutions. This research has not established a single ending year for their collective identity. Brito Román records Ambocas heritage among the traditions claimed by Loja’s modern communal federation. The map’s 1500 cutoff is not evidence of extinction.

passages.text: American Samoa is a United States territory in the eastern Samoan archipelago, with a cultural history much older than that political relationship. Basalt quarries, siapo barkcloth, schools and government records illuminate skilled work, community life and changing authority. Its history is connected with, but politically distinct from, the independent state of Samoa.

passages.title: Stoneworking and archaeological discovery
passages.text: Tutuila's Tataga-matau quarry above Leone formed part of a wider landscape of basalt extraction and tool making. Te Rangi Hiroa investigated it in 1927 with information from village elders. Quarry research combines physical remains with knowledge retained by local communities.

passages.title: Stoneworking and archaeological discovery
passages.text: A 2007 study analyzed geological samples from four Tutuila quarries and distinguished their chemical signatures. This supplies a way to test where a stone tool originated. It does not, by itself, date a tool or identify the person who carried it between islands.

passages.title: Siapo, makers and technical knowledge
passages.text: Hamilton Library in Hawaii holds a siapo mamanu made by Mary Pritchard around 1965, using mulberry bark and organic dyes. A named artist and a dated work make it possible to follow a particular contribution to Samoan art instead of treating every cloth as anonymous tradition.

passages.title: Siapo, makers and technical knowledge
passages.text: Siapo makers soften bark, scrape it with shells and beat it on a wooden anvil. Joining sheets creates larger surfaces for decoration. Pattern-board printing and freehand mamanu painting offer different ways to arrange designs, with hand finishing allowing variation between repeated forms.

passages.title: Siapo, makers and technical knowledge
passages.text: Pritchard recalled learning in Leone from Kolone Fai'ivae Leoso and other women while helping cultivate and harvest paper mulberry. Her account links artistic training to gardening, preparation, conversation and shared work, rather than only the final painted surface.

passages.title: Siapo, makers and technical knowledge
passages.text: Pritchard also described exporting siapo and adapting designs to shirts, dresses and household cloth. Those recollections show artists responding to markets while teaching and sustaining their practice. Innovation and cultural continuity could be parts of the same working life.

passages.title: Food, education and daily institutions
passages.text: An umu uses heated stones and layers of leaves to cook food for family gatherings. Taro, breadfruit, fish and other ingredients can share the cooking space. Preparing such a meal joins knowledge of heat, plant materials and timing with cooperative work.

passages.title: Food, education and daily institutions
passages.text: Palusami combines taro leaves with coconut cream, wrapped and cooked until tender. The dish makes two cultivated plants central to a shared meal, alongside other foods that vary with the household and occasion.

passages.title: Food, education and daily institutions
passages.text: Atauloma Girls School on Tutuila opened in 1900 through the London Missionary Society, with funds raised by Samoan residents. Classrooms and dormitories made formal schooling possible away from home, while its preparation of future pastors' wives reflected a particular religious and gendered purpose.

passages.title: Food, education and daily institutions
passages.text: The National Park Service's 1993 lease included village-owned land managed through the matai system. A later Traditional Use Study documented knowledge of plants, marine resources and culturally important places. Continuing local access is part of maintaining that knowledge.

passages.title: Reading political change through records
passages.text: The 1900 Tutuila and Aunu'u deed transferred sovereignty while promising protection of land and property and qualified retention of chiefly control of towns. Its clauses reveal which powers and protections were being negotiated; the document alone cannot represent every resident's view.

passages.title: Reading political change through records
passages.text: The Manu'a deed of 1904 was signed by Tuimanu'a and island chiefs. American Samoa's archives emphasize his annotation concerning equality and tradition. The territorial commission later stressed that US authority had already been proclaimed before the cessions, complicating a simple story of voluntary transfer.

passages.title: Reading political change through records
passages.text: President Truman's executive order transferred administration from the Navy to the Interior Department effective 1 July 1951. Voters first elected a governor in 1977. These changes concerned how the territory was governed, while Samoan family and village institutions continued.

American Samoa continues as a US territory. Naval government ended in 1951, and later constitutional and electoral changes expanded local political institutions. Those transitions did not end Samoan communities, language, chiefly relationships or artistic practice, nor did they unite the territory politically with independent Samoa.
