passages.text: The Amorúa are an Indigenous people of the Orinoco region, with communities in Vichada and Casanare and histories of movement across the Colombia-Venezuela border. Their own research emphasizes remembered routes, relationships among communities, food knowledge and self-government. Rural settlements, resguardos and urban neighborhoods are all part of their recent history.

passages.title: Food, equipment and seasonal knowledge
passages.text: The La Esmeralda study documents a sebucán, called woboto, used to squeeze bitter manioc. It connects the implement with plants gathered for household production. This is evidence of working material knowledge in a living community, not an archaeological object or proof that the Amorúa invented manioc processing.

passages.title: Food, equipment and seasonal knowledge
passages.text: At La Esmeralda, fishing depended on access to rivers, channels and a lagoon. Residents described lower river levels during the dry season and changes in available catches. Knowledge of water and season helped households obtain food; the account does not establish an unchanging calendar for all Amorúa communities.

passages.title: Food, equipment and seasonal knowledge
passages.text: Families sold manioc products such as mañoco and casabe in Agua Verde and bought soap, salt and other supplies. To reduce transport costs, one person could carry goods for several households. The documented arrangement shows practical cooperation connecting local food production with river travel and market exchange.

passages.title: Weaving and innovation at Guáripa
passages.text: Guáripa artisans describe extracting fibers individually from young moriche leaves, cooking them in water and drying them in shade. They also explain harvesting leaves without felling the palm and allowing plants to recover. Preparing material and sustaining its supply are part of the same craft knowledge.

passages.title: Weaving and innovation at Guáripa
passages.text: The Guáripa booklet shows hand-twisted fiber and coiled basketry. Its dye chart associates orange with onoto and brown with algarrobo. The artisans describe using inherited knowledge and experimenting with plants. Their work therefore includes investigation and refinement, rather than simply copying a permanently fixed set of designs.

passages.title: Weaving and innovation at Guáripa
passages.text: The group’s account credits Rosa Juana with encouraging women to renew weaving. Organization brought coordination of materials, better-quality work and opportunities to sell beyond nearby towns. The narrative records a particular community’s achievement; it does not suggest that weaving had disappeared among all Amorúa people.

passages.title: Homes and community decisions
passages.text: Gobierno Mayor describes homes using palm roofs, timber supports, board walls and earth floors, alongside brick buildings. Hammocks form part of this domestic setting. The account shows several building materials in use; it should not be turned into a rule that every family lives in the same kind of house.

passages.title: Homes and community decisions
passages.text: The same Indigenous organization describes a captain who represents the community administratively and politically while consulting traditional authorities. Elders and knowledgeable people remain part of decision-making. This account distinguishes a community leadership role from kingship and does not imply a single centralized government over all Amorúa settlements.

passages.title: Homes and community decisions
passages.text: In the study based on 2013 fieldwork, Amorúa speakers recalled making temporary shelters with platanillo leaves during journeys. The authors relate movement to remembered territory and criticize stereotypes that treated mobility as inferiority. Temporary residence was a way of using and knowing a landscape, not evidence of having no homeland.

passages.title: Research, learning and exchange
passages.text: Community researchers in 2013 drew routes of arrival and discussed their maps with younger and older residents. They also recorded food varieties, fishing and craft practices. Their books and drawings are concrete research products that preserve knowledge while allowing communities to question present problems of territory, education and autonomy.

passages.title: Research, learning and exchange
passages.text: Casanare’s rural education plan records work with Amorúa and other peoples to develop community educational projects. Elders, authorities and teachers contributed knowledge for study plans addressing territory, history, language and identity. The document reports a shared program; its combined student total cannot be assigned to the Amorúa alone.

passages.title: Research, learning and exchange
passages.text: A 2012 SENA report records Amorúa and Sikuani participants presenting fiber and natural-dye work at an exchange in Mitú. Demonstrations introduced visitors to moriche bags and baskets, while a forum addressed organization and fair commerce. Craftsmanship also provided a means of exchanging knowledge with other Indigenous makers.

passages.title: Displacement and collective repair
passages.text: Kanalitojo’s secretary described families fleeing armed groups, some crossing into Venezuela, and losses of territory. The community’s reparation process began in 2015. By July 2024, the responsible agency reported completion of twelve measures, including a cultural hall, agricultural initiatives and recovery of knowledge. This is a specific program’s reported outcome.

Amorúa communities continue despite displacement, land pressures and discrimination. Kanalitojo’s 2024 reparation milestone illustrates ongoing collective organization alongside other Indigenous peoples. Completion of that plan does not establish that every harm has been resolved. The map’s 1500 endpoint is not an extinction date or the end of Amorúa history.

sectionTitles: Food and exchange in the archaeological record

passages.text: ’Amuwu is associated with the Chumash community at Mission La Purísima Concepción near present-day Lompoc, California. The detailed evidence here concerns the nineteenth-century mission settlement, rebuilt in 1813 after an earthquake. Its residents maintained relationships, skills and exchange networks while living under coercive colonial institutions.

passages.title: Homes, work and water
passages.text: Excavators found an earthen floor beneath collapsed roof tiles in an adobe building occupied by a Chumash family. A dense deposit behind the building contained discarded material and traces of activity. Studying the room together with its backyard reveals how domestic space was used and maintained.

passages.title: Homes, work and water
passages.text: A larger refuse deposit farther north may mark an area of tule-thatched houses, according to the investigators. Differences in food remains, beads and displayed wealth suggest social distinctions within the community. The house identification and status explanation are interpretations, not a complete reconstruction of every household.

passages.title: Homes, work and water
passages.text: The district’s waterworks connected reservoirs, tile channels, distribution boxes and filtering structures with fields and shared facilities. Supplying water required coordinated construction and maintenance. The historic nomination credits Native craftsmanship; today’s park also includes restored or reconstructed structures that should not be confused with untouched mission-era fabric.

passages.title: Homes, work and water
passages.text: Chumash laborers made bricks, worked wood and built the relocated mission. These were skilled contributions to substantial buildings and working infrastructure. Describing that expertise does not turn the mission labor system into a voluntary building project or attribute the achievement solely to its Franciscan overseers.

passages.title: Food and exchange in the archaeological record
passages.text: The 2019 excavations recovered cattle and sheep bones together with remains of local animals and marine fish. California mussels dominated the identified shellfish assemblage. These finds show a diet combining introduced livestock with continuing use of coastal resources, rather than a complete replacement of older foodways.

passages.title: Food and exchange in the archaeological record
passages.text: One floor tile in the Chumash residential building preserved a hoofprint. The study identifies it as an ungulate print, probably from a calf or sheep. It records an animal encountering the tile while the material was impressionable; it does not establish that livestock normally lived inside the room.

passages.title: Food and exchange in the archaeological record
passages.text: Shell beads occurred with Olivella manufacturing debris, evidence that residents made beads locally. Many recovered beads had been drilled with introduced steel needles. The authors connect production with continuing exchange networks. The debris supports manufacture more directly than finished beads alone, which could also have arrived through trade.

passages.title: Reconsidering a household collection
passages.text: A concentration of glass and ceramic vessels was found under a floor in the adobe barracks. Earlier researchers associated the objects with a European resident. Brown and Liguori reexamined the collection and argued that an Indigenous family had occupied the room, challenging identification based simply on imported possessions.

passages.title: Reconsidering a household collection
passages.text: The same study proposes that the household belonged to a Native official or another influential couple known through mission roles such as interpreter, nurse, witness or godparent. It interprets the vessels as a Mexican-period cache. These are argued possibilities, not a securely identified owner’s personal inventory.

passages.title: Knowledge, resistance and living connections
passages.text: Brown’s public archaeology account describes continued manufacture of water-bottle baskets lined with asphaltum, a natural bitumen. It also records ceramic and glass fragments shaped into projectile points. Residents combined established technical knowledge with newly available materials; adoption of imported goods did not require abandoning all older practices.

passages.title: Knowledge, resistance and living connections
passages.text: Chumash collaborators used the Samala-English Dictionary to identify Amuwu as a place name connected with La Purísima. Tribal Historic Preservation Officer Nakia Zavalla emphasized calling archaeological objects belongings. These contributions link language and material evidence with present community relationships, rather than treating the site as an exclusively vanished world.

passages.title: Knowledge, resistance and living connections
passages.text: The 1824 occupation and its military suppression were followed by further institutional change under secularization. The later land grant to Elceario and Pastor Choyama documents Native people acting within the transformed landscape. Neither the end of Franciscan management nor the deterioration of mission buildings meant the disappearance of Chumash people.

Mission authority and residence patterns changed through revolt, secularization and movement to ranchos. Chumash descendants continue to interpret this history through language, family accounts and participation in archaeology. The map’s 1500 endpoint does not describe the end of this community, and its early polygon is not established by the later mission evidence.

passages.text: The Anambé are an Indigenous people of Pará in northern Brazil, with a community on the Cairari River in the Moju basin. Their language belongs to the Tupi-Guarani family. Histories of movement and severe disruption coexist with continuing family life, farming, craft knowledge and cultural renewal.

passages.title: Food and household work
passages.text: ISA’s account describes gardens producing maize, rice and manioc flour, with surplus sold locally or to river traders. Hunting, fishing and gathering also supported households. These descriptions concern a changing twentieth-century economy, not a fixed diet shared by every family throughout Anambé history.

passages.title: Food and household work
passages.text: The same account records locally made carrying baskets, fans, sieves, spindles, mortars, boats and bows alongside purchased equipment. Useful skills persisted while materials and tools changed. Buying manufactured goods did not erase community identity or make the locally produced objects merely decorative.

passages.title: Baskets as evidence and memory
passages.text: The 1969 Cairari collection includes objects gathered from daily use and others made when researchers asked about less-used forms. Lisboa’s study distinguishes these circumstances. A museum collection can reveal skilled techniques without being a statistical sample of everything households used equally often.

passages.title: Baskets as evidence and memory
passages.text: Anambé baskets served different tasks: containers stored belongings, carrying baskets moved manioc, the jamaxim helped transport game, and a patrona held shotgun cartridges. Makers used fibers including timboí and arumã. Form and material therefore connect weaving knowledge with food production, transport and changing hunting equipment.

passages.title: Baskets as evidence and memory
passages.text: Lisboa brought photographs of collection objects to the village. Dona Tapira recalled gathering vines with her parents and recognized equipment associated with relatives. These conversations connected material descriptions with named people and lived experience. The encounter used photographs; it was not a physical return of the collection.

passages.title: Children making and learning
passages.text: In the study published in 2022, elders remembered dolls made from parts of palm fruit clusters, miriti toy cars and small clay dishes. These were recalled childhood objects, not excavated artifacts. Turning familiar plants and earth into toys required knowledge of materials as well as imagination.

passages.title: Children making and learning
passages.text: The researchers also observed children using handmade miniature bows, softwood or miriti boats, and clay dishes alongside shop-bought toys. They interpreted making models as practice in skills relevant to later work. The observations do not prove that every child followed the same learning path.

passages.title: Children making and learning
passages.text: Children explained pisei, a game played on a ground drawing divided into squares. Players moved with closed eyes while asking a companion whether they had crossed a line. The account records rules, cooperation and attention to space, showing learning occurring through play outside a formal lesson.

passages.title: Contemporary making and cultural renewal
passages.text: Luakam Anambé’s 2021 interview describes the largely handmade Anaty dolls. She and her daughter made the clothing, while other workers helped with filling, hair and coloring. Her account makes visible the division of labor behind a finished object and connects craft income with family collaboration.

passages.title: Contemporary making and cultural renewal
passages.text: Luakam also spoke about an Indigenous language teacher in the community and her own plans to take lessons. She described receiving words from the teacher while living away from Pará. The testimony shows language renewal as deliberate learning and sustained relationships, rather than assuming that every Anambé person is already fluent.

passages.title: Contemporary making and cultural renewal
passages.text: Funai’s profile follows Luakam from sewing clothes by hand to factory work, buying a sewing machine and building a doll business. It also describes her Mãos de fadas project to help women acquire a trade. This is one maker’s documented achievement, not a timeless craft attributed to every Anambé household.

passages.title: Contemporary making and cultural renewal
passages.text: The 1991 decree identifies the Anambé area as traditionally and permanently occupied Indigenous land. Its boundary description uses rivers, streams and survey markers. This legal document is evidence for recognition of a specific territory; it does not verify this map’s much broader historical polygon or represent an ethnic founding date.

Anambé people continue in the Cairari community and elsewhere. Migration, family ties, craft work and language learning are parts of that living history. Luakam’s account shows continuing relationships across distance. The imported map’s 1500 endpoint must not be read as the disappearance of the people.

passages.text: Ancestral Pueblo communities farmed, built villages and made distinctive pottery and textiles across the Four Corners region of the American Southwest. Mesa Verde and Chaco Canyon represent different parts of this history. Present Pueblo and Hopi communities maintain ancestral relationships with these places; they are not the remains of a vanished people.

passages.title: Making homes
passages.text: The Mesa Verde pithouse reconstruction shows a living space sunk into the ground, roof-support posts, a hearth with an air deflector and an adjoining space for storage. These features connect architecture with heat, air movement and stored food. They describe an early house form, not every dwelling used across the Southwest.

passages.title: Making homes
passages.text: Pueblo Bonito at Chaco Canyon grew through repeated building campaigns between about 850 and 1150 CE. Its long construction history matters: the surviving complex combines work by multiple generations. It should not be imagined as one building erected in a single event or as the home of all Ancestral Pueblo people.

passages.title: Making homes
passages.text: Mesa Verde cliff dwellings used shaped sandstone blocks and mud mortar fitted to alcoves. Smaller rooms behind and above living spaces are interpreted as storage areas. The architecture therefore records a practical problem of arranging households and supplies within irregular rock shelters, alongside communal spaces whose purposes require additional interpretation.

passages.title: Making homes
passages.text: At Square Tower House, original timber ceilings and floors survive with painted walls. Thelma Jean Atsye’s tour also describes a reed mat, feathered cloth and a human figurine found inside. These traces give a fuller picture of furnished homes and artistic work than bare masonry alone.

passages.title: Growing food and carrying water
passages.text: Mesa Verde’s museum gallery pairs a mano, the handheld stone, with a metate, the grinding surface, to explain preparing corn before cooking. Food production did not end with harvest: repeated household labor transformed kernels into usable food. The gallery does not identify a precise excavated room or manufacture date for the displayed pair.

passages.title: Growing food and carrying water
passages.text: The same farming account describes check dams and other devices for conserving rainfall and soil. Growing crops in a short season required choosing suitable plants and managing runoff. These practices show adaptation to local conditions; irrigation methods and water availability varied across Ancestral Pueblo regions.

passages.title: Growing food and carrying water
passages.text: Ollas were ceramic jars for carrying and storing water. At Mesa Verde, seep springs emerge through sandstone cliffs; some households had to walk to reach them. A water jar links pottery-making with the recurring work of fetching a heavy, necessary household supply, rather than serving only as a decorated museum object.

passages.title: Fiber, pottery and exchange
passages.text: Bandelier’s plant-use account describes stripping yucca leaves for fibers and making rope, baskets and sandals. Wrapping turkey feathers or rabbit fur around fiber cord produced warm blankets. A single plant could therefore support carrying, clothing and household work through different manufacturing techniques.

passages.title: Fiber, pottery and exchange
passages.text: Yucca also supplied painting tools: softening the end of a leaf exposed fibers that could function as a brush. Bandelier’s account connects such brushes with decorating pottery. Craft production joined knowledge of plants to the preparation and application of designs, rather than separating useful objects from art.

passages.title: Fiber, pottery and exchange
passages.text: Black-on-white vessels at Mesa Verde combined containers for cooking, eating and storage with carefully transmitted geometric designs. Painted domestic objects and murals show artistic work integrated into everyday surroundings. Patterns can help investigate community relationships, but a decorative resemblance alone cannot identify an individual potter or a fixed political border.

passages.title: Fiber, pottery and exchange
passages.text: At Pueblo Bonito, Room 28 yielded a remarkable concentration of cylinder jars. Later residue analysis of sherds dated by decoration to about 1000 to 1125 CE found theobromine in pieces thought to belong to cylinder jars. Researchers interpreted this as evidence for a cacao drink, linking pottery with long-distance exchange.

passages.title: Fiber, pottery and exchange
passages.text: Cacao grows in tropical environments far from Chaco. Its identification therefore indicates that a valued substance moved through exchange networks. Suggestions that these drinks had ceremonial or elite uses remain interpretations of vessel form and restricted distribution; the residue does not reveal a complete recipe or show that every household drank it.

passages.title: Names and living relationships
passages.text: Laguna Pueblo ranger Thelma Jean Atsye asks visitors to use Ancestral Pueblo instead of the older archaeological label Anasazi. Her account places innovation, migration and survival within an ongoing Pueblo history. The older name remains searchable here so that an inherited map label does not prevent visitors from finding that history.

Mesa Verde’s large-scale residential occupation ended through migration in the late thirteenth century. Drought, pressures on resources and social change contributed, with choices differing between communities. People joined or founded other settlements, and Pueblo and Hopi histories continue. Neither the departure from Mesa Verde nor this map’s 1000 CE cutoff represents extinction.

sectionTitles: Country and the limits of the map

passages.text: Antekerrepenh, also recorded as Andegerebenha, names an Aboriginal people and an Arandic language associated with country around the Tarlton and Toko ranges and the Field and Hay rivers. Historical descriptions qualify the southern limits of this country. Language names and broad mapping should not be mistaken for the boundaries of a centralized state.

passages.title: Material skills and exchange
passages.text: Roth describes people he called Undekerebina traveling from the Toko Ranges to meet Yaroinga traders at Gordon’s Creek or by the Georgina River. They brought pituri, possum-fibre twine and blankets, returning with ochre, boomerangs, stone knives and hair belts. Trade connected different resources and skills.

passages.title: Material skills and exchange
passages.text: The same account describes sandstone grinding slabs and handstones made around Walaya and the Toko ranges. Makers cut and shaped stone for movement through regional markets. These tools linked food preparation with skilled manufacture and transport; the regional description does not identify the maker of every surviving specimen.

passages.title: Material skills and exchange
passages.text: Roth’s description of an Undekerebina sign for making a net imitates rolling fibre along the thigh while the other hand twists. A sign for wild orange imitates plucking and biting. These recorded gestures connect communication with embodied knowledge of working materials and gathering food.

passages.title: Food, shelter and environmental knowledge
passages.text: AIATSIS identifies a July 31, 1970 Boulia recording with Tiger George that covers food plants, tools, fire, clothing and shelter. Its catalogue makes ordinary work visible within the language record. It does not supply a house plan or prove that every listed tool remained in everyday use.

passages.title: Food, shelter and environmental knowledge
passages.text: A neighboring recording catalogs Tiger George’s words concerning water, direction and time. The same tape later changes to Pitta Pitta speech by Nora Jacks. Keeping those sections separate prevents knowledge from one language from being assigned to another simply because they share an archival reel.

passages.title: Food, shelter and environmental knowledge
passages.text: Bill Jenkin and Jack Marshall contributed plant names and conversation in Antekerrepenh at Dajarra on August 12, 1970. The archive distinguishes their exchange from subsequent Warluwarra recordings on the same reel. Spoken conversation provides a different kind of language record from isolated vocabulary prompted by a researcher.

passages.title: Relationships, performance and intellectual work
passages.text: In 1976, Jack Marshall gave Breen a sentence about addressing two brothers-in-law, then corrected the form the researcher proposed. That correction exposed a grammatical distinction tied to relationships. The example records Marshall’s active role in explaining his language and changing an outside scholar’s analysis.

passages.title: Relationships, performance and intellectual work
passages.text: Breen later found related forms on a recording he had made in 1967 without recognizing their significance. His survey also records variation in how speakers accepted these forms. The resulting analysis is a history of learning and revision, rather than proof that one grammatical rule applied identically everywhere.

passages.title: Relationships, performance and intellectual work
passages.text: AIATSIS catalogs performances and explanations by Didgeroo Jack and Noble Burke that include choruses from marambala, identified as an Antekerrepenh corroboree, alongside Wangkangurru songs. The record shows a multilingual performance setting. The catalogue establishes attribution and context; it does not authorize invented lyrics, meanings or ceremonial details.

passages.title: Relationships, performance and intellectual work
passages.text: Jack Marshall’s Dajarra sessions continued in August 1976, including work on possessive expressions. AIATSIS preserves a sequence of associated recordings, making it possible to trace sustained work with a named contributor. Its finding aid distinguishes permission to listen from conditions governing publication of the audio.

passages.title: Country and the limits of the map
passages.text: The AUSTLANG-derived profile links the language to the Field and Hay river region, but explicitly qualifies its southwestern extent and the role of changing flood conditions. This is a reminder that a broad language-area map summarizes relationships with country; it cannot by itself certify a fixed territorial boundary.

Andegerebenha remains named among the First Nations whose country is acknowledged by James Cook University’s regional health centre. Language loss and archival preservation are separate from the existence of a people and their connections to country. The imported map ending in 1815 records neither a verified conquest nor extinction.

sectionTitles: Finding and teaching an ancestral language

passages.text: Andwa, also written Andoa, communities live in the Amazonian borderlands of Ecuador and Peru. Many speak Kichwa while maintaining a distinct Andwa identity. Their history includes mission pressures, rubber exploitation, divided families and collective efforts to recover Katsakati, their ancestral language.

passages.title: Food, work and community decisions
passages.text: NAPE’s life plan describes household livelihoods that combine cultivated gardens, fishing, hunting, gathered fruit and small livestock. Gardens include cassava, plantains, maize, peanuts and peppers. These activities connect family provisioning to different parts of the forest and river landscape.

passages.title: Food, work and community decisions
passages.text: The plan records pottery-making alongside the weaving of bags, baskets, hammocks and fishing nets. Such objects served practical domestic and river tasks as well as exchange. Its account also recognizes migration for wage work, rather than portraying community life as isolated from wider economies.

passages.title: Food, work and community decisions
passages.text: Community authorities described in the plan organize collective work, maintain shared property and address internal disputes. They coordinate with NAPE’s governing council. This arrangement brings local responsibilities together with representation to provincial and national institutions; the plan distinguishes these connected levels of government.

passages.title: Finding and teaching an ancestral language
passages.text: During 2009 fieldwork, María Santi, Dionisia Arahuanaza and Lidia Arahuanaza helped researchers check remembered vocabulary. In Kapawari, Hipólito Arahuanaza contributed recorded narratives in 2010, with Kichwa mediation. Documentation depended on Indigenous memories and multilingual collaboration, not simply on an outsider locating an unknown language.

passages.title: Finding and teaching an ancestral language
passages.text: Funding difficulties interrupted further recording, and researchers learned of Arahuanaza’s death in 2012. The surviving material included narratives with sometimes incomplete Kichwa translations. These limitations matter: a recording collection preserves valuable speech without providing a complete account of every word, grammatical pattern or social use.

passages.title: Finding and teaching an ancestral language
passages.text: In the December 2013 Quito workshop, participants wrote stories and dramatized selected examples for video recording. Teaching resources included vocabulary cards, dice, interactive posters and a teacher’s guide. The activities connected language learning with meaningful situations and creative work.

passages.title: Clay, storytelling and public exchange
passages.text: The Dagua family women who hosted a 2016 university project identified as Andwa and spoke Kichwa. They made mukawas, tinajas, callanas and human-shaped ceramic figures. Calling themselves weavers, they shaped vessels with lengths of clay, demonstrating a skilled process that students learned through participation.

passages.title: Clay, storytelling and public exchange
passages.text: The collaboration linked pottery with spoken stories, music, bodily expression and visual design. At Interactos in Guayaquil in November 2016, students presented a short documentary, information booklets and edited oral texts. Five women from Canelos and a Kichwa translator participated in a workshop and conversation.

passages.title: Achievements and continuing identity
passages.text: Kupukwano, the Andwa language dictionary, was publicly introduced on February 16, 2023 by Daniel Dagua, then president of the nationality. The project partner describes a gathering of leaders, representatives and young people at Amazon State University. The publication is a concrete resource for language work, not evidence that everyone has regained fluency.

passages.title: Achievements and continuing identity
passages.text: Erika Rosado’s 2022 to 2023 interviews examine how leaders use Katsakati in public life, including greetings before continuing in Kichwa or Spanish. The research links these practices with claims to recognition and territory. It treats language recovery as political and cultural work, not a simple test of authentic identity.

Andwa communities continue through political organization, skilled work and language recovery. The loss of an elder speaker did not mean the disappearance of the people. The imported map’s endpoint in 1500 is a coverage limit, not an extinction date or an end to this history.

passages.text: Andorra is a Pyrenean principality whose institutions developed between powerful neighbors and within communities of mountain valleys. Agreements between the bishop of Urgell and the count of Foix established shared lordship in 1278 and 1288. Farming, herding, ironworking and cross-border exchange supported livelihoods long before the growth of tourism and finance.

passages.title: Working a mountain landscape
passages.text: The Madriu-Perafita-Claror Valley preserves shepherds’ stone huts, stables, cheese-making facilities, terraced fields and barns for hay and grain. These structures connect seasonal movement of livestock with food production and storage. Together they show how mountain households coordinated work across different elevations and times of year.

passages.title: Working a mountain landscape
passages.text: Partly paved tracks and low stone walls link the valley’s agricultural and pastoral places. UNESCO also identifies a communal land-management system with medieval roots and four communities owning land within the property. Maintaining this landscape involves collective decisions as well as individual work; declining agriculture is a stated conservation concern.

passages.title: Working a mountain landscape
passages.text: Casa Rull in Sispony interprets a prosperous rural household whose family, property and working life formed a social unit. Rooms contain furnishings and tools associated with farming and livestock. Several generations could live together, and better-resourced households also employed servants or day laborers, making the house a workplace as well as a home.

passages.title: Working a mountain landscape
passages.text: Casa Cristo in Encamp presents a more modest household from the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. Its tools, stone slab sink and christening robe passed through a family make ordinary work and inherited possessions visible. Preserved domestic objects help explain lives that appear less prominently in political chronicles.

passages.title: Craft, trade and religious art
passages.text: Farga Rossell operated during the mid-nineteenth century, closing in 1876. Its reconstructed interpretation centre explains the conversion of ore into iron ingots and their sale in Catalan markets, including demonstrations of the forge hammer. The surviving industrial site connects local skilled work with a wider trading economy.

passages.title: Craft, trade and religious art
passages.text: The twelfth-century murals of Santa Coloma include religious imagery that once formed part of a church interior. Most were removed in the twentieth century and later recovered for Andorra; originals are displayed at Espai Columba. Digital projections inside the church help show their former setting, but are modern reconstructions.

passages.title: Craft, trade and religious art
passages.text: The government’s historical account connects twentieth-century commercial growth with Andorra’s border position, the Spanish Civil War and the Second World War. Trade in goods and currency preceded expansion of tourism and financial services. This economic transformation changed the setting of older farming and industrial livelihoods.

passages.title: Buildings and objects of government
passages.text: Casa de la Vall’s entrance bears a shield dated 1580, linking the building with its origins as a Busquets family house. Its reuse as a public meeting place in 1702 illustrates institutional adaptation of an existing building. Later alterations, notably in 1962, also form part of the house visible today.

passages.title: Buildings and objects of government
passages.text: Inside Casa de la Vall, the former entrance became a criminal courtroom, while a kitchen and later dormitory accommodated practical needs of council members. These spaces show the material work behind public administration: representatives needed places to gather, eat, stay and conduct proceedings. The rooms changed function over time.

passages.title: Buildings and objects of government
passages.text: The assembly room retains a bell associated with opening parliamentary sessions and the Seven Keys cabinet associated with its archival role. Such objects helped organize meetings and preserve records. The present chamber also incorporates a seating arrangement created during the 1962 renovation, so its appearance combines different periods.

passages.title: Representation and constitutional change
passages.text: The council’s history explains that the 1419 privilege provided for two or three representatives from each parish, elected annually. It also strengthened the position of leading households. The development of representative institutions therefore needs to be read alongside the exclusion of less wealthy household heads from office.

passages.title: Representation and constitutional change
passages.text: The 1866 reform widened the electorate among household heads, but retained limitations, including the absence of a secret vote. The council’s account connects demands for reform with economic hardship and concerns over public money. Broader representation emerged through conflict and negotiation rather than a single uninterrupted expansion.

passages.title: Representation and constitutional change
passages.text: The Constitution states that sovereignty belongs to the people and identifies Catalan as the official language. It preserves two co-princes, the bishop of Urgell and the French president, within a parliamentary system. The document is evidence of a negotiated redistribution and definition of public authority, not the disappearance of Andorra’s institutions.

Andorra continues as a sovereign parliamentary co-principality. Its 1993 Constitution transformed the basis and allocation of political authority while retaining the co-princes within a constitutional framework. The imported map’s 1938 to 2020 coverage neither dates the principality’s creation nor indicates that it ended in 2020.

sectionTitles: Everyday work, food and learning on country
Carving and the lives of objects

passages.text: Adnyamathanha people are the people of the rocks of South Australia’s Flinders Ranges. Their communities maintain connections to country through family knowledge, skilled work and cultural teaching. Pastoral settlement restricted movement and access to land, but community histories describe adaptation and continuing identity, not disappearance.

passages.title: What archaeology reveals at Warratyi
passages.text: At Warratyi rock shelter, dating of sediments, hearth charcoal and eggshells supported occupation around 49,000 years ago. Worked red ochre was identified on a silcrete tool in the oldest excavated unit. This is evidence of pigment handling in a specific archaeological context, without identifying a surviving painted design.

passages.title: What archaeology reveals at Warratyi
passages.text: A sharpened bone point from Warratyi’s SU3 layer was dated by its context to about 40,000 to 38,000 years ago. Its shape resembles tools interpreted elsewhere as awls or needles for working skins. Manufacture is evident, while its precise task remains an interpretation from comparison.

passages.title: What archaeology reveals at Warratyi
passages.text: Resin residues and associated polish on stone artefacts support attaching flakes to handles or shafts. At Warratyi, these traces reveal composite tools whose wooden components need not survive. Microscopic analysis adds evidence of manufacture that a stone’s shape alone may not provide.

passages.title: Everyday work, food and learning on country
passages.text: Nepabunna’s community history recalls fathers and uncles working skillfully on pastoral stations. It also describes how leases forced people to camp together and curtailed travel. Paid station work and continued family life developed under those constraints, rather than replacing all earlier relationships with country.

passages.title: Everyday work, food and learning on country
passages.text: Iga Warta’s food programme credits cooking knowledge passed down by the family’s mother. Its meals combine bush foods with adaptations such as kangaroo lasagne or meatloaf. Campfire offerings include damper and quandong jam. These examples show inherited knowledge being used creatively in a community-run enterprise.

passages.title: Everyday work, food and learning on country
passages.text: The same programme teaches seasonal plant foods, ochre and local social history. Its explanation of Yura Muda connects land, ancestral journeys, behavior and belonging. Teaching takes place through Elders’ knowledge and encounters with country, bringing environmental understanding together with social responsibilities.

passages.title: Carving and the lives of objects
passages.text: Museums Victoria’s Wapma figure, X 94829, is catalogued as made around 1930 in the Copley area. The wooden snake has an upturned body, cut surface patterns and a darkened head. Its maker is unrecorded, and its later collection date must not be mistaken for its production date.

passages.title: Carving and the lives of objects
passages.text: The South Australian Museum describes Ted Coulthard trading carefully made walking sticks, snakes, lizards, boomerangs and shields while working with pastoralists. Its 2024 exhibition places that work within a continuing family tradition, including Kristian Coulthard’s carving near Blinman. Selling objects and transmitting cultural knowledge formed connected parts of this practice.

passages.title: Language as shared intellectual work
passages.text: The Adnyamathanha Culture Guide and Language Book is jointly credited to Terrence and Josephine Coulthard. The Mobile Language Team describes a two-way dictionary alongside grammar, kinship, music and social history. The volume draws on many speakers and Elders, making their contributions part of a substantial resource for future learners.

passages.title: Language as shared intellectual work
passages.text: Museums Victoria also identifies Aunty Lily Neville’s contribution through Adnyamathanha translations and publications. Her work includes songs, wordlists, family stories, observations of bush life and annotated drawings. Such records preserve forms of knowledge that a vocabulary list alone could not fully convey.

passages.title: Land management and public institutions
passages.text: The Nantawarrina case study describes community planning for a property managed by Nepabunna people with traditional ties to it. Training covered environmental management, fencing, tourism, feral-animal control and identifying threatened species. These are practical skills used to care for country and sustain organized work.

passages.title: Land management and public institutions
passages.text: Recorded management activities included revegetation, weed and feral-animal control, interpretation of sites and tracks, and maintaining visitor facilities. Work also provided water supplies for camps and huts. The programme combined cultural responsibilities with the routine infrastructure required for people to use and care for a place.

passages.title: Land management and public institutions
passages.text: The 2009 park determination recognizes specified rights to access, camp, gather resources, conduct ceremonies and teach the significance of places, subject to its terms. These non-exclusive rights coexist with other interests. A native-title determination is legal recognition of defined rights, rather than a declaration that colonial dispossession never occurred.

passages.title: Land management and public institutions
passages.text: ATLA’s 2013 report records the purchase of Wilpena Pound Resort and sets out objectives for Adnyamathanha employment and cultural tours. Its mission emphasizes cultural information shared by Adnyamathanha people. The purchase is a documented institutional achievement; the report’s employment targets are plans, not proof that every target was fulfilled.

Adnyamathanha people continue to live on and care for their country through community life, cultural work and public institutions. Pastoral dispossession changed access and mobility, but did not end the people. The map’s 1815 endpoint is a coverage limit, not a verified conquest or extinction date.

sectionTitles: Work and the transformation of territory
A new generation records its own history
Institutions, land and the right to decide

passages.text: Angaité names an Indigenous people of Paraguay’s Chaco whose histories include the Ko’ahlvok, Koieteves and Konjanava groups. Their language belongs to the Enlhet-Enenlhet family. Industrial expansion, ranching and loss of access to land transformed community life, while families continued to build institutions and maintain their own accounts of the past.

passages.title: Work and the transformation of territory
passages.text: Puerto Pinasco’s tannin industry depended on quebracho timber brought from inland cutting camps. Villagra’s historical study describes railways, fenced pastures and ranches extending across Indigenous country. These installations reorganized both labor and movement, while cattle occupied water sources around which Indigenous settlements had already developed.

passages.title: Work and the transformation of territory
passages.text: Falling tannin prices and the company’s later break-up disrupted employment and settlement. The study follows families dispersing among ranches and moving into communities with land of their own. An industrial company’s decline therefore did not mark the disappearance of Angaité people; it changed the conditions under which families lived.

passages.title: Food, materials and everyday work
passages.text: For La Patria, the 2002 census atlas lists squash, sweet potatoes, cassava, watermelon and beans among household crops. It also records fishing, hunting and gathering palm shoots and algarrobo. The combination shows cultivated food and knowledge of uncultivated environments contributing to livelihoods in this particular community.

passages.title: Food, materials and everyday work
passages.text: The same record lists wool, cotton, karaguatá, palm leaves and takuara among materials used in craft production. Agriculture, beekeeping, forestry and craft work appear among occupations. These entries document several kinds of practical expertise; they do not establish that every household practiced every activity or that techniques never changed.

passages.title: Language research with community participation
passages.text: The Koahlvo consultation publication brought together Angaité leaders’ and community representatives’ assessments of language use. In her 2023 conference account, Ladislaa Alcaraz identifies three areas of their proposals: writing the language, recording it, and encouraging its use and wider recognition. The publication itself was written in Spanish.

passages.title: Language research with community participation
passages.text: At 6 de Marzo / La Patria, Félix Navarro and Herminia Rivero contributed names and traditional uses of plants to a language-recording project reported in July 2024. Their knowledge was recorded audiovisually in kovahlok. The report documents a language and cultural resource, not clinical testing of the plants.

passages.title: A new generation records its own history
passages.text: In the 2024 workshops, young Angaité participants recorded mothers and grandmothers and learned to select cuts and combine images with sound. The project report notes that some no longer understood many words used by their Elders. Editing therefore involved careful listening as well as learning how to make a film.

passages.title: A new generation records its own history
passages.text: The report distinguishes the Angaité work on medicinal-plant names from a parallel Qom group’s recording of fiber weaving. Both groups made their own material, but their projects had different subjects. This distinction preserves who contributed each form of knowledge instead of treating neighboring peoples as interchangeable.

passages.title: A new generation records its own history
passages.text: Memorias Angaité brings together sound recordings, photographs, audiovisual material and written works about the people in Presidente Hayes. These different media can preserve voices, images and narratives alongside published history. The archive’s existence is a documented achievement in making community memory accessible; individual recordings require their own context and attribution.

passages.title: Institutions, land and the right to decide
passages.text: The La Patria account describes villages with their own social and political autonomy. Its history of a territorial dispute emphasizes community assemblies as well as engagement with state courts. This is evidence of organized decision-making, rather than a story in which outside institutions were the only actors.

passages.title: Institutions, land and the right to decide
passages.text: The project’s account includes Jacinta Barreto’s intervention at the assembly, linking respect for community decisions to earlier restrictions on hunting and gathering. Her testimony connects territorial rights with feeding families and living on the land. It is an attributed participant’s account, rather than a substitute for the complete court record.

Angaité communities continue despite dispossession, industrial upheaval and serious pressures on language transmission. Their history includes community institutions, recording projects and efforts to regain control over territory. The map’s 1500 endpoint is a coverage boundary, not a documented date when the people ended.

sectionTitles: Discovering village work at Wharram Percy
Castles as architecture and statements of power
Craft, devotion and connections across the Channel
Records, legal practice and ordinary obligations

passages.text: The Angevin Empire was the collection of lands brought together under Henry II and his family, including England, Normandy, Anjou and Aquitaine. Inheritance, marriage and political expansion joined these territories under related rulers. Family rivalries and conflict with the French monarchy eventually broke apart much of this cross-Channel dominion.

passages.title: Discovering village work at Wharram Percy
passages.text: At Wharram Percy in Yorkshire, excavators found postholes and beam slots beneath later houses. These traces indicate timber-built dwellings before the thirteenth century. They preserve evidence of ordinary construction even where the wood has disappeared, and help distinguish earlier households from the stone buildings visible in later phases.

passages.title: Discovering village work at Wharram Percy
passages.text: Excavation beside the village stream revealed successive low clay dams and a millpond for a horizontal water mill. This system began before Angevin rule and remained in use into the thirteenth century. Its successive alterations show a community maintaining water-powered grain processing over generations.

passages.title: Castles as architecture and statements of power
passages.text: Dover’s great tower had a long approach through a forebuilding, with stairs reaching the second floor before descending into a hall. Its paired hall-and-chamber arrangement and conspicuous exterior suited grand receptions. Historians interpret these features as evidence for ceremony and hospitality as well as defense.

passages.title: Castles as architecture and statements of power
passages.text: The tower was built without fireplaces and used hearths and braziers for heat. English Heritage links its elaborate rebuilding to high-ranking visitors traveling to Becket’s shrine. That connection is a historical interpretation from architecture and events; the modern furnished rooms are reconstructions of a possible royal interior.

passages.title: Castles as architecture and statements of power
passages.text: Richard’s Château-Gaillard was constructed above the Seine between 1196 and 1198 to help protect the river route and Rouen. Its position and defensive design show the importance of controlling approaches through Normandy. The stronghold’s capture in 1204 also demonstrates that an imposing fortress could be overcome.

passages.title: Craft, devotion and connections across the Channel
passages.text: A Limoges reliquary now in the British Museum is made of gilded copper alloy with champlevé enamel and is dated to about 1210 in the exhibition catalogue. It depicts Becket’s murder near an altar and his ascent to heaven. Its materials and imagery connect specialized metalwork with the expanding cult of an English saint.

passages.title: Craft, devotion and connections across the Channel
passages.text: The catalogue compares the reliquary with a similar example in the Louvre. Differences in Becket’s posture show makers adapting a shared religious subject. These are devotional images made after the killing, not eyewitness pictures. The British Museum object’s known collecting history does not establish its original medieval owner.

passages.title: Records, legal practice and ordinary obligations
passages.text: The surviving English pipe rolls become a nearly continuous series from 1155, although an earlier roll covers 1129 to 1130. Their survival gives historians an unusually long sequence of royal financial records. The start of the continuous series under Henry II should not be mistaken for the invention of royal accounting.

passages.title: Records, legal practice and ordinary obligations
passages.text: The 1166 Assize of Clarendon required sworn reports from twelve men of a hundred and four from each village about suspected serious offenders. Accusation could lead to the ordeal of water. This was a procedure for presenting suspects, with forms of proof very different from a modern criminal jury trial.

passages.title: Records, legal practice and ordinary obligations
passages.text: The same text required sheriffs to coordinate with justices, instructed counties without jails to build them, and ordered written lists of fugitives. These provisions show government depending on messengers, buildings, timber and clerical work. They describe official requirements, not proof that enforcement was identical in every county.

passages.title: Power, conflict and lasting institutions
passages.text: Eleanor of Aquitaine’s inheritance was central to the dynasty’s continental position, and she continued to exercise political authority. Her long captivity after the revolt and her renewed activity under Richard reveal both the reach of a queen’s power and its vulnerability within the royal family.

passages.title: Power, conflict and lasting institutions
passages.text: Magna Carta addressed baronial rights, property and practical grievances against the king. Its provisions concerning lawful judgment and access to justice later acquired broader meanings. The 1215 settlement did not establish equal rights for everyone, and its immediate failure to end conflict belongs alongside its enduring reputation.

passages.title: Power, conflict and lasting institutions
passages.text: Later rulers reissued the charter after John’s death. The U.S. National Archives displays a 1297 version that was entered into England’s statute rolls. Distinguishing that surviving document from the 1215 agreement shows how an institutional legacy could be reshaped long after the Angevin territorial union weakened.

The Angevin dominions broke apart through warfare and dynastic conflict. John lost Normandy and Anjou to the French monarchy, while the Plantagenet dynasty continued to rule England. This was a loss of territorial power, not the disappearance of the populations and institutions of those lands. The map’s 1279 endpoint does not date a single imperial fall.

sectionTitles: Art as skilled work and historical expression
Community research and care for Country

passages.text: Anggamudi is a map spelling associated with Angkamuthi people of northern Cape York. Community histories connect waterways, movement and family knowledge with continuing cultural life. Their history includes displacement and settlement at Injinoo, as well as contemporary art, language work and care for Country.

passages.title: Waterways, movement and everyday work
passages.text: Seven Rivers Aboriginal Corporation describes fishing in estuaries, gathering bush foods and learning seasonal changes as connected responsibilities. Its account links the Jardine, Skardon and other rivers with family knowledge and cultural practice. These activities belong to a living relationship with Country, not a fixed picture of life in one historical year.

passages.title: Waterways, movement and everyday work
passages.text: The corporation records that colonial intrusion pushed Angkamuthi families north toward Cowal Creek, later called Injinoo. Movement did not erase their identity or connections to earlier places. The account describes both displacement and the continuing work of Elders and families to pass knowledge forward.

passages.title: Waterways, movement and everyday work
passages.text: By 1918, government reports described Cowal Creek residents managing a council and supporting themselves through gardens and maritime trade. Oysters, bananas and pumpkins were taken to Thursday Island for sale. This was a settlement shared by several peoples; its activities should not be assigned exclusively to Angkamuthi residents.

passages.title: Waterways, movement and everyday work
passages.text: In April 2025, Community Enterprise Queensland reported expanding groceries at the council-owned Injinoo service station. Staff redesigned shelving and stocked a broader range to reduce journeys for supplies. This specific project illustrates a practical concern of everyday life in a remote community, without proving that all food-access problems were resolved.

passages.title: Language evidence and teaching
passages.text: The Crowley finding aid lists Angkamuthi narratives about visiting friends, cooking for soldiers and a canteen. Their presence records speakers discussing social life and work in their language. The catalog identifies the materials; reconstructing the events, words or individual experiences requires the underlying recordings and transcripts.

passages.title: Language evidence and teaching
passages.text: Northern Peninsula Area State College records that Sandra Sebasio joined Atambaya and Yadhaykenu Elders in language renewal with Pama Language Centre from 2015. The school also describes a multilingual region. Cooperation in an Injinoo program does not make Angkamuthi, neighboring languages and Torres Strait Creoles interchangeable.

passages.title: Art as skilled work and historical expression
passages.text: Teho Ropeyarn combines carving with printmaking in large vinyl-cut works. The Art Gallery of South Australia describes a work carved across six panels over two months, with colored sections prepared before the overall printing. This process turns careful cutting, inking and alignment into a contemporary means of conveying inherited knowledge.

passages.title: Art as skilled work and historical expression
passages.text: In his published gallery transcript, Ropeyarn describes growing up at Injinoo and learning while camping and traveling with family and Elders. His Angkamuthi and Yadhaykana connections inform his art. The account gives the artist’s own explanation of that learning rather than treating the work as anonymous traditional decoration.

passages.title: Art as skilled work and historical expression
passages.text: QAGOMA’s account of Athumu Paypa Adthinhuunamu, made in 2022, identifies a freshwater turtle associated with Angkamuthi among figures representing four Injinoo clans. Water and ancestral beings connect the panels. These meanings are attributed to the artwork and its explanation, not presented as a universal symbol system for all Aboriginal peoples.

passages.title: Community research and care for Country
passages.text: Angkamuthi and other Traditional Owner representatives help guide the Apudthama ranger program. Angelina Williams’s July 2024 report lists clearing access tracks, maintaining campsites and graves, removing marine debris and working with schools. These tasks connect cultural responsibility with ordinary maintenance, education and environmental observation.

passages.title: Community research and care for Country
passages.text: The same report describes turtle monitoring through beach sectors, daily track records and observations of nest predation. Rangers use these repeated observations to document nesting activity. Counting tracks is a particular field method, not a direct census of every turtle living offshore or a guarantee that all nests survive.

passages.title: Community research and care for Country
passages.text: A December 2024 survey with Angkamuthi partners sampled seabed habitats and used baited underwater cameras. TropWATER reported 80 fish species, including diverse sharks and rays, alongside low seagrass cover in the surveyed area. These are findings from a defined survey, not totals for all of Angkamuthi Sea Country.

passages.title: Community research and care for Country
passages.text: The project also includes training in survey methods and fish-video analysis, with bilingual maps planned to reflect community values. Its August 2026 update records further intertidal work. Such research builds information for future monitoring while recognizing that management decisions involve Traditional Owners as well as scientists and government agencies.

passages.title: Continuity and decisions about rights
passages.text: A Cape York Land Council notice called Ankamuthi members to an Injinoo meeting in March 2025 to consider a claim over an undetermined part of Endeavour Strait. The notice documents community decision-making and a proposed legal step. It does not establish that the meeting approved the application or that a court granted it.

Angkamuthi people continue to maintain identity, cultural work and responsibilities to Country. Colonial displacement and changes in language use are not an ending of the people. The map’s 1815 cutoff describes available coverage, not extinction or a verified loss of all territorial rights.

sectionTitles: What survives of houses and working spaces
Food and textiles in daily life
Migration revealed without reducing identity to ancestry
Sutton Hoo and the reach of elite exchange
Books as works of art and instruments of learning

passages.text: Anglo-Saxon is a collective label for several peoples and societies that developed in early medieval England. Migration across the North Sea, interaction with Britain’s existing population, competing kingdoms and Christian institutions shaped this history. A single name should not imply one unchanging people, kingdom or way of life across the entire period.

passages.title: What survives of houses and working spaces
passages.text: At West Stow, rows of postholes outline timber halls, while smaller structures left rectangular hollows with posts at their ends. The remains reveal different building forms within an early medieval settlement. Reconstructed houses help test explanations, but they are modern experiments rather than surviving Anglo-Saxon buildings.

passages.title: What survives of houses and working spaces
passages.text: Burnt remains in West Stow’s building SFB 15 included loom weights lying on planks. Preserved timber helped support an interpretation of a suspended floor above the hollow. The combination of structural traces and working equipment challenges the older assumption that people simply lived and worked on the bottom of a pit.

passages.title: What survives of houses and working spaces
passages.text: West Stow also produced a clay heap and pottery-decorating stamps, alongside finished pots, worked bone and antler combs. These finds reveal production skills as well as objects brought into homes. Timber buildings themselves required repeated carpentry, repair and replacement, making woodworking another substantial part of village labor.

passages.title: Food and textiles in daily life
passages.text: Animal bones from West Stow document sheep, cattle and pigs, along with fishing, wildfowling and deer hunting. Plant remains indicate cereals supplemented by gathered foods. Loom weights and other textile tools, considered together with sheep husbandry, support weaving as an important skill; surplus cloth exchange remains an interpretation.

passages.title: Food and textiles in daily life
passages.text: A laboratory study identified impressions of hulled barley in West Stow’s Anglo-Saxon pottery, with less certain traces of other cereals. The marks formed when plant material entered soft clay before firing. They are small physical traces of contact between pottery manufacture and the plant materials handled in the settlement.

passages.title: Food and textiles in daily life
passages.text: The study cautions that grain impressions cannot be converted directly into crop-production totals. Whole grains and flour leave different traces, and fruit, leaves or roots are less likely to appear in clay. The apparent dominance of barley in this evidence therefore does not establish an exclusively barley-based diet.

passages.title: Migration revealed without reducing identity to ancestry
passages.text: A 2022 ancient-DNA study found substantial continental northern European ancestry among its early medieval English samples, alongside people with more local ancestry. Hatherdene Close in Cambridgeshire showed variation within one cemetery. The results support large-scale migration and interaction, while ancestry alone cannot identify a person’s language or political allegiance.

passages.title: Migration revealed without reducing identity to ancestry
passages.text: The researchers compared ancestry with burial furnishings. Women with continental ancestry were more often buried with goods in the sample, but weapon graves among men did not follow a simple immigrant-versus-local division. A sword or brooch therefore cannot by itself reveal a buried person’s birthplace or ethnic identity.

passages.title: Sutton Hoo and the reach of elite exchange
passages.text: At Sutton Hoo, a purse contained 37 Frankish gold coins, three blanks and two small ingots. The coins’ composition and minting dates help place the burial in the early seventh century. This is a closely studied elite assemblage, not a measure of how much money ordinary households possessed.

passages.title: Sutton Hoo and the reach of elite exchange
passages.text: The burial also held a nested group of ten silver bowls identified as sixth-century Byzantine work. Their presence in an English grave shows objects traveling across great distances and remaining valuable over time. It does not establish a direct voyage by their final owner or identify every intermediary in their journey.

passages.title: Books as works of art and instruments of learning
passages.text: The Lindisfarne Gospels, Cotton MS Nero D IV, combines Latin Gospel texts with decorated initials, Evangelist portraits, carpet pages and tables linking passages. The book required skilled work on parchment and careful organization. Its attribution to Eadfrith comes from a later note, so it is an attribution rather than a contemporary signed statement.

passages.title: Books as works of art and instruments of learning
passages.text: Aldred’s tenth-century additions placed Old English between the Latin lines and recorded information about the book’s makers. They show later readers using and interpreting an older object. Separating these additions from the original text reveals several generations of linguistic and religious work within one surviving manuscript.

passages.title: Conquest and continuing lives
passages.text: Norman victory changed royal and ecclesiastical leadership and brought extensive castle and church building. It did not empty the country of its inhabitants. English and Norman communities interacted over subsequent centuries, while English continued to develop and eventually displaced French as the dominant language.

The Norman conquest of 1066 ended the pre-Conquest English ruling order, with William of Normandy defeating Harold at Hastings. Communities and language continued under new rulers and changing institutions. Anglo-Saxon society was transformed rather than physically extinguished; the map’s 600 endpoint is only the end of this particular imported coverage interval.

sectionTitles: Archives that preserve people and decisions
Independence, war and the work of peace

passages.text: Angola’s history connects African polities, Portuguese colonial expansion, independence in 1975 and civil war. Archives, objects and living practices reveal distinct regional experiences within this changing political setting.

passages.title: Archives that preserve people and decisions
passages.text: The Ndembu archives were created and kept by African authorities in northern Angola. Their documents include letters, wills, product lists, receipts and legal cases. Portuguese writing incorporated Kimbundu vocabulary, allowing rulers and their scribes to conduct diplomacy and record disputes in an adapted written language alongside oral traditions.

passages.title: Archives that preserve people and decisions
passages.text: The Angolan National Archive’s codex 240 contains outgoing colonial correspondence from 1798 to 1854, addressed to African authorities. Its survival alongside Ndembu collections lets researchers compare different sides of political relationships. Conservation work on the wider collections has included repairing tears and treating damage associated with iron gall ink.

passages.title: Archives that preserve people and decisions
passages.text: Books compiled mainly between 1856 and 1875 recorded enslaved and freed people by name, birthplace, age and occupation, as well as identifying owners. Angola, Cabo Verde and Mozambique jointly nominated the surviving collection. These records can restore individual details, but their categories reflect a system that treated people as property.

passages.title: Trade, labor and material evidence
passages.text: Ovimbundu traders connected the Bié Plateau with Benguela in the nineteenth century. Later colonial infrastructure included the Benguela Railway linking Lobito with the mining region of Katanga. These changing routes connected inland work and coastal commerce, while Portuguese conquest constrained African political independence.

passages.title: Trade, labor and material evidence
passages.text: The Met’s Pwo mask, attributed to a Chokwe artist in Angola’s Xassenge region, dates to the first quarter of the twentieth century. Wood, plant fiber, pigment, fur and metal combine in the object. Its 2003 museum acquisition date is separate from when the artist made it.

passages.title: Trade, labor and material evidence
passages.text: Pwo honors founding female ancestors in a society that traces descent through mothers’ lines. The Met explains the cheek motifs in relation to the pride and sorrow surrounding sons’ initiation. Such interpretations connect carving with performance and family relationships; they describe Chokwe practices, not a single culture shared by every Angolan.

passages.title: Cities, stories and mathematical skill
passages.text: Mbanza Kongo preserves the royal, religious and civic spaces of the former Kingdom of Kongo. Its customary court, sacred tree and royal burial places sit within a history that also includes Portuguese-style churches. This older kingdom was a distinct polity, not simply an earlier name for the modern Angolan state.

passages.title: Cities, stories and mathematical skill
passages.text: The Jesuit College at Mbanza Kongo is associated with a Kikongo catechism written in 1624. The city’s religious buildings and educational history reveal exchanges involving African languages and Christianity. UNESCO’s 2017 recognition also acknowledges living customary institutions, rather than treating the place solely as an abandoned ruin.

passages.title: Cities, stories and mathematical skill
passages.text: Sona practitioners mark points with their fingers in a damp surface covered with sand, then draw lines around them. Among Lunda Cokwe and neighboring peoples in eastern Angola, the resulting figures carry stories and collective knowledge. The process joins spatial reasoning to narration, teaching and decorative art.

passages.title: Cities, stories and mathematical skill
passages.text: Sona knowledge is transmitted through initiation and practical teaching. Educational institutions have also used its patterns to explore mathematics and anthropology. UNESCO’s 2023 inscription recognizes an existing, changing practice; it does not date its invention or imply that classroom use replaces the authority of experienced community practitioners.

passages.title: Independence, war and the work of peace
passages.text: The Alvor Agreement recognized the MPLA, FNLA and UNITA as negotiating representatives and set 11 November 1975 for independence. It also provided for a transitional government before that date. The document records an intended transfer of power; renewed fighting meant that its planned arrangements did not become a stable shared government.

passages.title: Independence, war and the work of peace
passages.text: RTP’s archive identifies separate independence speeches by Agostinho Neto and Jonas Savimbi. The accompanying account places the MPLA declaration in Luanda and the FNLA-UNITA declaration in Huambo. These competing proclamations show why the end of Portuguese sovereignty did not immediately settle who would govern the country.

passages.title: Independence, war and the work of peace
passages.text: The April 2002 Luena Memorandum required a ceasefire and addressed the demobilization of UNITA forces. It also called for shelter, food and preparation for civilian employment. Those provisions show that ending armed organization required practical support for people as well as agreement between military leaders.

passages.title: Independence, war and the work of peace
passages.text: In November 2002, UN monitors reported no ceasefire violations since the agreement. They also described continuing searches for weapons. This dated observation supports the importance of the settlement while leaving room to examine its implementation; it is not evidence that every local conflict or hardship had disappeared.

passages.title: Farming and negotiating shared resources
passages.text: An FAO project in southwestern Angola combined seasonal grazing knowledge with discussion through Jango Pastoril forums. Moving herds toward uplands in the rainy season and back toward river plains in the dry season helped coordinate access to land. The approach depended on agreements among people as well as the movement of animals.

passages.title: Farming and negotiating shared resources
passages.text: Agro-pastoral field schools brought farmers and herders together to test land-management practices and exchange experience. FAO’s 2022 account describes rehabilitation planting and work around water points. These are examples of practical collaboration in particular project areas, not proof that drought, land degradation or competition for resources have ended nationwide.

Portuguese colonial rule ended with independence on 11 November 1975. Angola continued as a state through civil war; the 2002 government-UNITA settlement marked a different transition. The map’s separate Angola records and gaps represent coverage, not repeated national disappearances.

passages.text: The Alvor Agreement recognized the MPLA, FNLA and UNITA as negotiating representatives and set 11 November 1975 for independence. It also provided for a transitional government before that date. The document records an intended transfer of power; renewed fighting meant that its planned arrangements did not become a stable shared government.

passages.title: Independence, war and the work of peace
passages.text: RTP’s archive identifies separate independence speeches by Agostinho Neto and Jonas Savimbi. The accompanying account places the MPLA declaration in Luanda and the FNLA-UNITA declaration in Huambo. These competing proclamations show why the end of Portuguese sovereignty did not immediately settle who would govern the country.

passages.title: Independence, war and the work of peace
passages.text: The April 2002 Luena Memorandum required a ceasefire and addressed the demobilization of UNITA forces. It also called for shelter, food and preparation for civilian employment. Those provisions show that ending armed organization required practical support for people as well as agreement between military leaders.

passages.title: Independence, war and the work of peace
passages.text: In November 2002, UN monitors reported no ceasefire violations since the agreement. They also described continuing searches for weapons. This dated observation supports the importance of the settlement while leaving room to examine its implementation; it is not evidence that every local conflict or hardship had disappeared.

passages.title: Farming and negotiating shared resources
passages.text: An FAO project in southwestern Angola combined seasonal grazing knowledge with discussion through Jango Pastoril forums. Moving herds toward uplands in the rainy season and back toward river plains in the dry season helped coordinate access to land. The approach depended on agreements among people as well as the movement of animals.

passages.text: Agro-pastoral field schools brought farmers and herders together to test land-management practices and exchange experience. FAO’s 2022 account describes rehabilitation planting and work around water points. These are examples of practical collaboration in particular project areas, not proof that drought, land degradation or competition for resources have ended nationwide.
