sectionTitles: Building and caring for village life

passages.text: The Aparai are a Cariban-speaking Indigenous people associated with the Paru de Leste region of northern Brazil. Long relationships with Wayana neighbors include shared villages, marriages and artistic work, while distinct languages and identities remain important. Their history connects forest and river livelihoods with exchange, changing government policies and community-led cultural work.

passages.title: Clay, tools and household knowledge
passages.text: O Livro da Argila documents women building vessels from coils of clay and smoothing them with pieces of gourd. Corncobs help shape surfaces, while wet pieces of bracket fungus smooth rims. These tools show how ceramic skill depends on selecting familiar materials and controlling texture by hand.

passages.title: Clay, tools and household knowledge
passages.text: A bird-shaped ceramic roof ornament described in the book carries a vessel on its back. It belongs to the ceremonial house and is connected with a creation narrative. The associated roof vessels also help exclude rain, bringing narrative meaning and a practical architectural function into the same object.

passages.title: Art, teaching and exchange
passages.text: The pottery book grew from women’s efforts to record their expertise. Contributors shaped its contents and revised the texts, making the publication a collective expression of knowledge that remained in use.

passages.title: Art, teaching and exchange
passages.text: The graphic-art book presents designs as knowledge passed on and recreated between generations. Its museum description connects stories about the origins of art with marks applied to bodies and objects. This relationship matters when interpreting a design: its significance cannot be reduced to a detached decorative pattern.

passages.title: Art, teaching and exchange
passages.text: Barbosa’s ethnographic account follows basket production between trips to gardens and fishing. Collecting and preparing arumã stems, weaving and finishing required intermittent work over months. Finished baskets and seed necklaces could enter trade for household goods. The account links artistic skill to schedules of subsistence and exchange.

passages.title: Art, teaching and exchange
passages.text: The same study describes collective work on roofs and gardens, organized by households that provided fermented drinks. Barbosa distinguishes this hospitality from simply paying wages. Cooperation rested on relationships among residents, even while village trading outlets also used debts, prices and manufactured goods.

passages.title: Art, teaching and exchange
passages.text: Craft markets did not begin with a single recent project. The Instituto Socioambiental account traces missionary-supported trading outlets, later Funai involvement and Indigenous association initiatives. Selling work could alter its forms and intended uses, while providing access to goods that households wanted. This was a changing relationship, not the end of Aparai making.

passages.title: Building and caring for village life
passages.text: At Kurupohpano, Aparai and Wayana residents opened a new Tukusipan in November 2024. Palm thatch and forest timber required coordinated gathering and construction, supported by food prepared for work parties. The house replaced an older structure whose materials had deteriorated, showing that maintaining architecture involves repeated skilled renewal.

passages.title: Building and caring for village life
passages.text: The Tukusipan accommodates meetings, visitors, craft work and celebrations. Community members use it to discuss collective concerns as well as to make objects and share knowledge. Forest management matters to its future because useful construction materials have become harder to obtain close to the village.

passages.title: Building and caring for village life
passages.text: Manioc supplies flour, flatbread and fermented drinks. In 2026, a crop-disease education project worked with Indigenous associations on Aparai and Tiriyó translations and narration. The resulting animation joins garden observation with communication in local languages. It records an organized response to a contemporary threat, without establishing that the disease has been eliminated.

passages.title: Territory, political change and continuity
passages.text: A 2024 expedition revisited the lower Paru after decades of concentration farther upriver. Its aims included territorial monitoring and testing a river connection toward Laranjal do Jari, where residents could reach services and trade. Funai’s account links the earlier concentration to outside settlement and state installations, rather than to a voluntary abandonment of ancestral connections.

passages.title: Territory, political change and continuity
passages.text: The Pakará Fund grew from a territorial plan and consultation process shared by several peoples. Its public account describes Indigenous assemblies setting priorities and choosing a management committee, with Iepé initially supplying technical and financial support. This is a contemporary institution for collective decisions, not evidence that the peoples it serves have merged into one identity.

Aparai communities continue to shape village life, teach knowledge and organize through Indigenous associations. Outside settlement and state policies changed residence and access to territory, but no single conquest date describes their history. The map entry’s endpoint in 1500 is a limit of its imported snapshot, not the disappearance of the people.

sectionTitles: Food, trade and organizing a community

passages.text: The Apiaká are an Indigenous people of the upper Tapajós river system, with histories tied to the Arinos, Juruena and Teles Pires. Their Tupi-Guarani language, river knowledge, skilled making and community institutions distinguish them from neighboring peoples, despite long relationships and intermarriage. Apiaká communities survived severe violence and continue cultural and political work.

passages.title: Objects, buildings and historical evidence
passages.text: Florence’s April 1828 image of an Apiaká dwelling shows a thatched structure, a visible timber framework and a hammock beneath the roof. People wear different body designs and ornaments. The image provides concrete evidence of how an observer represented residence and appearance, while its composition cannot establish a complete household census or a universal building plan.

passages.title: Objects, buildings and historical evidence
passages.text: A 2009 Apiaká schoolbook reproduced in the exhibition places copies of Florence’s scenes beside later drawings of people, vessels and a village. Historical images thus became material for community memory and education. Their reuse is a new act of interpretation, not proof that every depicted practice remained unchanged.

passages.title: Objects, buildings and historical evidence
passages.text: An ethnographic survey describes residents making baskets, sieves, paddles, canoes and ornaments from seeds and beads. Forest materials also supply house frames and thatch. These linked skills turn knowledge of plants, rivers and construction into objects for transport, food preparation and daily shelter.

passages.title: Food, trade and organizing a community
passages.text: Manioc flour, flatbread and tapioca sit alongside fish, game, cultivated tubers and gathered fruits in the documented food repertoire. Different foods require gardens, fishing grounds and forest access. A description of that repertoire does not mean that every household ate the same foods or could obtain them in every season.

passages.title: Food, trade and organizing a community
passages.text: A community history recalls journeys from Anipiri carrying salted fish and meat, Brazil nuts, honey, oils and cotton hammocks for exchange. Desired goods included salt, metal graters, hooks, beads and cooking pots. This testimony shows people evaluating useful new materials while maintaining skills and products of their own.

passages.title: Food, trade and organizing a community
passages.text: Mayrob residents describe forming ACAIM, a community association, to coordinate trade and collective activities, including schooling. Their account connects products such as Brazil nuts, açaí, manioc flour and handmade sieves with the need to manage negotiations. Economic organization was therefore also a matter of community authority and education.

passages.title: Food, trade and organizing a community
passages.text: The same community account remembers escape from coercive rubber work, a difficult journey and losses through disease before families reached the Rio dos Peixes. It is a history of survivors rebuilding relationships and residence, rather than a claim that the Apiaká ceased to exist when outside observers lost track of them.

passages.title: Language knowledge and cultural achievement
passages.text: In their published language account, Apiaká contributors explain that rubber and timber employers imposed Portuguese under threat of punishment. Language shift was connected to unequal labor relations and attempts to navigate an unfamiliar economy. Their later commitment to teaching Apiaká responds to that history, rather than indicating that community identity depends on perfect fluency.

passages.title: Language knowledge and cultural achievement
passages.text: The museum documentation project brought Indigenous researchers Angelo Krixi and Evanilson Crixi Morimã into work with linguists. Its archive included photographs, video and recorded speech. The project distinguished preserving evidence from developing effective school lessons: possessing recordings alone was not treated as sufficient to restore everyday conversation.

passages.title: Language knowledge and cultural achievement
passages.text: The project’s activity record identifies a 2009 workshop with community women concerned with Apiaká body designs, alongside training for Indigenous language researchers. It makes women’s knowledge and community participation visible within cultural documentation. A workshop record establishes that work took place, without measuring how widely each practice subsequently spread.

passages.title: Language knowledge and cultural achievement
passages.text: During 2014 fieldwork, Sousa worked with Luzia Kamassuri and Fernando Paleci and taught lessons requested by residents. In Mayrowi, learners wanted to progress beyond an existing primer. This example shows research responding to a locally expressed educational need, with elders contributing knowledge to younger people’s learning.

passages.title: Language knowledge and cultural achievement
passages.text: Sousa later recorded vocabulary for parts of the body with Kamassuri and Paleci, comparing their contributions toward an illustrated teaching resource. Her 2017 thesis describes this as work in progress. The account documents careful listening and comparison, not a claim that the proposed glossary was already completed or that all learners became fluent.

passages.title: Land and continuity
passages.text: The September 2024 declaration concerned a territory used by Apiaká, Munduruku and peoples in voluntary isolation. Funai described physical demarcation and presidential approval as later stages. This particular administrative milestone should not be confused with a new ethnic founding, a state conquest or proof that every territorial concern had been resolved.

Apiaká communities continue through collective institutions, language work and territorial claims. Severe exploitation and displacement transformed their circumstances without ending the people’s history. The imported map interval ends in 1500, centuries before the documented experiences described here; it supplies no valid date for cultural disappearance or the fall of a unified kingdom.

sectionTitles: Objects and the skills behind them

passages.text: The Apinayé, also written Apinajé, are a Jê-speaking Indigenous people of northern Tocantins, in the region between the Araguaia and Tocantins rivers. Their history includes village autonomy, ceremonial associations, mixed gardens, music and skilled work with forest materials. Communities continue to defend their territory and teach knowledge across generations.

passages.title: Objects and the skills behind them
passages.text: A bag from São José, catalogued as 70.03.012 at the UFG museum, uses woven palm leaflets and a carrying handle. Its function was to store and transport personal belongings. The museum purchased it in 1970 but did not record its maker. It preserves evidence of practical weaving, while leaving an individual craftsperson’s story unknown.

passages.title: Objects and the skills behind them
passages.text: Necklace 91.06.133 combines buriti fiber with differently colored seeds, bamboo sections, quills and green feathers. Its pendant repeats several of those materials. Making such an ornament involved selecting and assembling contrasting textures and colors, not simply finding a single decorative substance. The collection records its entry in 1991, without establishing when it was made or who made it.

passages.title: Objects and the skills behind them
passages.text: A gourd flute, object 79.01.0881, hangs from a cord of plant fibers. The museum acquired it by purchase in 1979. Its dossier mentions a seed pendant that is now missing, a reminder that surviving objects can change after collection. The instrument documents material choices for making sound; its catalogue alone cannot recover the music once played on it.

passages.title: Gardens, food and village life
passages.text: The ethnographic account describes gardens associated with women’s households, with men clearing vegetation and women participating in planting corn, manioc and other crops. Rice, corn and manioc grow together; later beans can climb the standing corn stalks. This arrangement combines crops with different growth habits and makes a field a sequence of linked tasks.

passages.title: Gardens, food and village life
passages.text: Villages act as local political communities, with household relationships, leaders and ceremonial groups organizing collective life. Families may establish a new settlement rather than remain permanently within one village. This helps explain why a single outline on a map does not represent a centralized Apinayé kingdom with one ruler over every community.

passages.title: Gardens, food and village life
passages.text: In a January 2015 statement, the PEMPXÀ association described gardens begun in 2013 and supported again in 2014. Families planted manioc, beans, bananas, corn and rice. Seeds came through exchanges with farmers in the Bico do Papagaio region and fairs held by Kayapó and Krahô peoples, linking household food security with wider relationships.

passages.title: Gardens, food and village life
passages.text: The association emphasized that children and grandchildren learned planting, seed conservation and care for land and water while joining family garden work. It also reported concern about drought and limited support. Its account presents food production as both skilled labor and education, with future harvests depending on environmental conditions as well as knowledge.

passages.title: Music and environmental knowledge
passages.text: Singer Cleonice Apinagé told researcher Célio Ribeiro Dias Apinajé that she learned by attending celebrations with her mother and listening to singers. She also described women completing parts of a song in collective performance. The account connects musical knowledge with participation and repeated listening, rather than treating a written score as the only route to learning.

passages.title: Music and environmental knowledge
passages.text: Other interviewees described recordings as useful for learning and wanted stronger support for music in schools. At Boi Morto’s 2018 gathering, the researcher observed people singing together indoors by day and in the plaza at night. These discussions show singers actively considering how teaching can adapt while preserving relationships between music, memory and community.

passages.title: Music and environmental knowledge
passages.text: A project led by the Pyka Mex association at Prata reported establishing a nursery and collectively producing about 5,000 seedlings. Women, young people and elders joined seed-collecting expeditions; plants and seeds went to neighboring communities and partners. Territorial visits and conversations with elders connected plant work to knowledge of local history, boundaries and threats.

passages.title: Land, historical records and continuity
passages.text: Fagundes and Barbosa’s archival study identifies nineteenth-century records of Apinayé gardens supplying both local residents and boats on the Tocantins. Those records connect agricultural work with regional exchange. They also explain why excluded fertile lands mattered materially, alongside their significance in community history and relationships with particular places.

passages.title: Land, historical records and continuity
passages.text: The 1985 demarcation followed Indigenous mobilization, but its boundary excluded land west of the Transamazonian highway. A later presidential decree, dated 3 November 1997, formally approved the administrative demarcation. Recognizing this sequence avoids confusing one legal act with the beginning of Apinayé ownership or the resolution of every land claim.

Apinayé communities continue through gardens, teaching, associations and territorial action despite restrictions on their land. The map’s interval of 1492 to 1500 is imported coverage; 1500 is not a cultural ending, conquest date or the dissolution of an Apinayé state.

passages.text: The Appamattuck, also called Appomattoc, lived along the lower Appomattox River in Virginia. They belonged to the core of Powhatan’s paramount chiefdom while maintaining local leaders and communities. River foods, cultivated land, skilled travel and diplomacy shaped their history, which continued through repeated colonial attacks and restrictions.

passages.title: Water, food and ordinary work
passages.text: The Appomattox delta supplied fish such as shad and sturgeon, waterfowl and edible wetland plants. Upland ground provided garden soils, deer and other game. Moving among river, marsh and woodland gave households access to different resources across the seasons; fishing was one part of a broader food system.

passages.title: Water, food and ordinary work
passages.text: Timber from the river’s uplands could become dugout canoes and house frames, while ravines connected freshwater springs with landing places. These details explain how settlement depended on more than fertile fields. Woodworking, water access and routes between houses and river landings were connected parts of everyday life.

passages.title: Water, food and ordinary work
passages.text: A Charles City County payment recorded in 1658 compensated Appomattuck people for killing wolves. This small administrative trace shows hunting skills entering a colonial economy that valued protection of livestock. It documents particular paid work, not the disappearance of Indigenous hunting for food or the wholesale adoption of a new livelihood.

passages.title: Authority, ornaments and historical evidence
passages.text: Opossunoquonuske ruled one Appamattuck town and was the sister of the chief Coquonasum. English visitors called her a queen, but her local title was weroansqua. At her reception of Newport’s party in May 1607, attendants and rules about approaching her made authority visible in the arrangement of people and space.

passages.title: Authority, ornaments and historical evidence
passages.text: The same account describes copper ornaments at her head, ears and neck. These were observed objects of status, rather than treasures recovered from her burial. The description preserves evidence of adornment and political display, filtered through English observers’ unfamiliarity with the community.

passages.title: Authority, ornaments and historical evidence
passages.text: A copper badge inscribed for the King of Appomattock was reported found in Dinwiddie County in the early twentieth century. The NPS study suggests that it may be a colonial identification insignia. Its inscription is evidence of an official designation; the proposed function remains an interpretation, and the account gives no secure excavation context.

passages.title: Authority, ornaments and historical evidence
passages.text: Within Powhatan’s political world, leadership followed the female line, and chiefs consulted councillors rather than acting entirely alone. Tribute could include food, skins, beads and copper. This regional system helps explain Appamattuck institutions, but an individual town’s decisions and relationships cannot all be reconstructed from a general description.

passages.title: Travel knowledge and encounters
passages.text: Percy’s entry for 8 May 1607 describes armed residents challenging the English landing at Apamatica before accepting signs of peace. His hostile vocabulary belongs to a colonist’s account. Read carefully, the episode also records Indigenous people controlling access to their country and deciding whether visitors could come ashore.

passages.title: Travel knowledge and encounters
passages.text: Bland’s 1651 pamphlet names Pyancha as the Appamattuck guide on a journey made the previous year. He describes Pyancha explaining river branches and neighboring settlements and advising a different return route after receiving a warning through a local relationship. The expedition’s knowledge came through Indigenous expertise and social connections.

passages.title: Travel knowledge and encounters
passages.text: At a path marked by two trees, Bland observed Pyancha clear one side before continuing. Another guide supplied a political story explaining different groups’ use of the route. The passage reveals a landscape carrying remembered relationships and conflict; it also shows the limits of an outsider’s account when Pyancha himself declined to explain.

passages.title: Treaties, petitions and what followed
passages.text: The 1677 treaty’s final memorandum says that Pericuhtah sought to join but was excluded because English officials accused him or his people of killings. The document records an accusation and exclusion, not a demonstrated verdict of guilt. Its own text therefore qualifies modern catalogue headings that simply list Appomattoc among the original signatories.

passages.title: Treaties, petitions and what followed
passages.text: The treaty promised land protection and access to fishing and gathering, while requiring submission to the English Crown and permission for some travel. These terms joined recognition with control. Their wording describes obligations and promises, not proof that colonial settlers respected every protected right after Appamattuck participation in the expanded agreement.

passages.title: Treaties, petitions and what followed
passages.text: A petition dated 24 April 1691 was made by an Appamattuck female ruler for herself and her people to live among English settlers. A later ferry-payment record names Appamattuck travelers to Jamestown. Such documents preserve collective representation and movement after the earlier devastation, even when they tell us little about individual households.

Colonial warfare, land loss and dependent treaty relations transformed Appamattuck political life. Families remained identifiable in Beverley’s 1705 account. These sources do not establish the later fate of every family or a single extinction date. The imported map’s endpoint of 1500 is not a historical ending.

passages.text: The Apsáalooke, often called Crow, are a living Northern Plains people with a homeland in and around present-day Montana. Their history includes seasonal bison hunting, three major bands, extensive family relationships and the preservation of language and community life through profound changes in landholding and government.

passages.title: Food, families and movement
passages.text: Smaller winter villages could come together in the warmer part of the year, when the major bands gathered and hunted. Dried meat, roots and berries helped sustain households in winter. Food preservation mattered alongside the hunt: the ability to store and share provisions supported community life through seasons with very different opportunities.

passages.title: Food, families and movement
passages.text: Matrilineal clans and an extended network of relatives shaped responsibility for children. A mother’s sisters were also mothers, and a father’s brothers were also fathers in the kinship system described by the college. These relationships made care and belonging broader than the small household model familiar to many outsiders.

passages.title: Food, families and movement
passages.text: Horses increased the loads families could move and the distances hunters could cover. Larger tipi loads became practical as transport changed. The approximate early eighteenth-century adoption date describes a transformation in an existing society, not its beginning; horse expertise was developed through learning, use and exchange.

passages.title: Objects as records of knowledge
passages.text: The NMAI’s robe 1/2558 combines bison hide, pigment, trade cloth, beads and porcupine quillwork. Its approximately 1850 date is a museum attribution; acquisition at Fort Benton in 1861 is a separate event. Bringing different materials together required hide preparation, painting and decorative skills, and also reflects access to traded goods.

passages.title: Objects as records of knowledge
passages.text: Apsáalooke historian Patrick J. Hill and Timothy P. McCleary interpret the robe’s six scenes as a public account of martial accomplishments. They explain its pictorial conventions as narrative writing. The object is therefore evidence of a way to communicate remembered deeds, rather than merely an ornamental surface.

passages.title: Objects as records of knowledge
passages.text: Tipi liner 18/9242 preserves cotton canvas, deer hooves, glass beads and porcupine quills, with bead stitching and quill wrapping recorded in its catalogue. The museum bought it from a New York dealer in 1936. Its maker, manufacture date and earlier ownership are not supplied, so that purchase cannot be presented as an excavation or a date of invention.

passages.title: Objects as records of knowledge
passages.text: Liners helped manage drafts, dampness and ventilation inside tipis. During the reservation period, some families carried their use into log houses. Crow house interiors could retain a central stove, an east-facing entrance and decorated wall linings. New construction materials did not automatically erase established ways of organizing domestic space.

passages.title: Land, education and adaptation
passages.text: The 1868 treaty made a reservation the prescribed permanent home while retaining specified hunting rights on unoccupied United States land, subject to conditions in its text. Reading both provisions matters: reservation boundaries did not by themselves describe every place the agreement allowed Crow people to use. These are the treaty’s historical terms.

passages.title: Land, education and adaptation
passages.text: Boarding schools separated children from their families as part of federal assimilation policy. Families established camps near reservation missions, keeping themselves closer to children attending those schools. This response shows parents working within severe constraints to preserve relationships; attendance cannot be read simply as willing abandonment of Crow social life.

passages.title: Land, education and adaptation
passages.text: Plenty Coups’ preserved homestead near Pryor includes a log house, farm and store. Montana’s state park account dates his residence there from 1884 until his death in 1932. The buildings provide concrete evidence of a leader negotiating new economic conditions through farming and commerce, alongside his public responsibilities.

passages.title: Continuing institutions and achievements
passages.text: Crow Fair brings people together in a large gathering that includes a tipi encampment and public cultural activities. In the college’s account it belongs to continuing social life, alongside smaller family and community relationships. A historical card should place such gatherings in the present as well as discuss nineteenth-century objects.

passages.title: Continuing institutions and achievements
passages.text: In March 2016, Apsáalooke researchers at the Smithsonian examined beadwork and horn-reinforced bows, documenting construction for possible recreation and teaching. They treated museum holdings as resources for living knowledge. The project’s proposed digital archive was a goal described at the time, not a product whose completion this account establishes.

passages.title: Continuing institutions and achievements
passages.text: The same visitors viewed a film of the 1908 Crow Fair and listened to later commentary recorded by Dean Bear Claw. Their own explanations added another layer of knowledge. This work connects community interpretation with museum records; collecting an old film alone does not preserve all the meanings that knowledgeable viewers can recognize.

passages.title: Continuing institutions and achievements
passages.text: The tribe’s official website describes executive, legislative and judicial branches under its 2001 Constitution. Tribal government is a continuing institution, with public responsibilities extending beyond cultural representation. Its existence makes it particularly misleading to treat the final year of an imported historical map polygon as the disappearance of a people.

The Apsáalooke continue as a people and a self-governing tribe. Treaties and reservation policies profoundly restricted land and reshaped institutions, but did not end their community. The imported 1492 to 1500 map interval is not their historical lifetime or an extinction date.

sectionTitles: Featherwork and the evidence in collections

passages.text: The Apyãwa, widely known as Tapirapé, are an Indigenous people of the middle Araguaia region of Brazil. Their history connects forest gardens, fishing places and village ceremonies with struggles to recover land. Apyãwa is their own name; Tapirapé remains common in historical writing and museum catalogues.

passages.title: Gardens, villages and sharing food
passages.text: Villages combine access to non-flooding forest suitable for gardens with streams, fishing places and seasonally useful open country. Houses traditionally surround a central takara. Farming, hunting, fishing and collecting require knowledge of different environments, so a village’s livelihood cannot be represented by a single crop or occupation.

passages.title: Gardens, villages and sharing food
passages.text: Koria Valdvane Tapirapé’s research records Imakopy’s account of collective garden work and distribution of the harvest among families. Cassava, beans, squash, yams and maize appear among the crops he discusses. The account connects agricultural work with education and ceremonial responsibilities, rather than treating cultivation as an isolated economic activity.

passages.title: Gardens, villages and sharing food
passages.text: The same researcher describes tataopãwa eating groups through Korako’s explanations. Family affiliations, participation in a shared fish meal and remembered group names connect food with belonging. The study distinguishes groups maintained at the time of research from those recalled in ceremonial knowledge; it does not describe every historical arrangement as unchanged.

passages.title: Gardens, villages and sharing food
passages.text: His 2020 dissertation also examines the increasing place of industrially produced foods. Using field notes, photographs and recordings in Tapi’itãwa, he asks how communities can draw on their territory’s resources while maintaining knowledge and relationships around eating. This is an Apyãwa investigation of contemporary change.

passages.title: Featherwork and the evidence in collections
passages.text: The Met’s mask 2017.100 is dated to 1950 to 1965. Its semicircular wooden structure carries feather mosaics in yellow and green, a central blue-green division and shell details around the face. Combining wood, feathers, shells and bindings required several kinds of material knowledge. The catalogue does not identify the individual artist.

passages.title: Featherwork and the evidence in collections
passages.text: The mask entered the Met as a gift in 2017. That acquisition date is different from the museum’s earlier date for the work itself. Its description makes the construction visible: shaped wooden elements frame the face, while individual feathers radiate above it and decorated fibre pendants hang below.

passages.title: Featherwork and the evidence in collections
passages.text: Madrid’s Museo de América holds another example, 1993/02/007, catalogued as made before 1993. It combines a wooden support, stitched feathers, vegetable fibres and shell. Eyes and mouth are cut through the support. The two collections show related forms with different arrangements; their accession records are not archaeological excavation dates.

passages.title: Featherwork and the evidence in collections
passages.text: Objects can also be chosen to explain history by the people who made and used them. At the NMAI consultation, Apyãwa representatives selected palm baskets, body-painting tools, feather headdresses and masks. The selection linked everyday making and ceremonial life with migrations, land and the struggle to return to it.

passages.title: Featherwork and the evidence in collections
passages.text: The museum’s report names Xywaeri José Pio, Ararawytygi Paulo Tapirapé and Xario Domingos Tapirapé among the participants. Discussion of a flour basket concerned its selection and display, not simply its appearance. Their participation supplied knowledge that a materials list alone could not convey.

passages.title: Teaching, research and new institutions
passages.text: Teacher Nivaldo Korira’i Tapirapé describes a 2014 project in which pupils learned words while studying practical knowledge. Kaxowari’i and his class drew a fish and worked on names for its parts, including fins and gills. The lesson joined literacy with close knowledge of animals familiar to the community.

passages.title: Teaching, research and new institutions
passages.text: Yrywaxã researched a flat canoe with a knowledgeable community member, then worked with children on its construction and use. Other classes studied different arrow types. A gathering brought pupils, parents and grandparents together. These activities made observing, making and speaking parts of the same educational work.

passages.title: Teaching, research and new institutions
passages.text: Gilson Ipaxi’awyga Tapirapé entered UFG’s intercultural education course in 2007 and became a university professor in 2023. The university identifies this as its first Indigenous faculty appointment. His path connects education in the community with teaching in a university, while bringing Apyãwa experience into academic work.

passages.title: Teaching, research and new institutions
passages.text: A 2024 paper coauthored by Koria Valdvane Tapirapé describes plans for a museum in Tapi’itãwa. The design drew on the form of a large-face mask and a feather diadem. The authors also discuss recording songs, managing collections and protecting territory. Their paper documents a collaborative project in progress, not proof that the building had opened.

The Apyãwa continue as communities with their own language, schools, researchers and territorial responsibilities. Severe losses and displacement were followed by recovery and renewed institutions. The map’s 1492 to 1500 coverage does not mark their disappearance, and recognition of Indigenous lands does not mean that every land conflict has ended.

sectionTitles: What objects and archaeological camps reveal
Continuing achievements and care for Country

passages.text: Arabana Country lies around Kati Thanda, also known as Lake Eyre, in northern South Australia. Springs, waterholes and the knowledge needed to care for them connect livelihoods, family histories and cultural responsibilities. Arabana people continue to maintain those relationships through community institutions, teaching and work on Country.

passages.title: Water, food and everyday knowledge
passages.text: The 2015 water report describes creeks and waterholes as places for longer stays, fishing and gathering. The value of a water place includes its history and relationships as well as its immediate supply. Meeting, washing and harvesting connect practical needs with remembered journeys and responsibilities.

passages.title: Water, food and everyday knowledge
passages.text: Soakages can be recognized through soil colour, texture, cracks and vegetation that indicate water below the surface. Elders and parents teach younger people how to recognize and use water places. This is learned knowledge of particular landscapes, not a single technique that can be assumed to work throughout Australia.

passages.title: Water, food and everyday knowledge
passages.text: The research employed Arabana co-researchers and included field visits. Indicators considered plants, animals, soil, use and pressures on water. Community participation shaped what counted as evidence of environmental condition and why a place mattered.

passages.title: Water, food and everyday knowledge
passages.text: The corporation’s Kutha work connects water management with Arabana decision-making. Its project account describes partnerships involving Rangers, Elders, conservation volunteers and environmental researchers. Considering the health of plants and animals alongside water conditions helps turn knowledge of Country into practical monitoring and management priorities.

passages.title: What objects and archaeological camps reveal
passages.text: The Museums Victoria ornament is a netted form made from hand-spun string. Its catalogue tentatively identifies animal fur and human hair among the fibres. The object records skilled work with flexible materials, but the uncertain identification should remain visible: a museum description is not a laboratory confirmation of every component.

passages.title: What objects and archaeological camps reveal
passages.text: The museum associates the ornament with Arabana people near Lake Eyre and records Spencer’s collecting in 1917. It does not name its maker. Collection history therefore gives one point in the object’s journey, while leaving important questions about manufacture, ownership and use unanswered.

passages.title: What objects and archaeological camps reveal
passages.text: At Strangways Springs, archaeologists identified flaked, thick amethyst glass derived from telegraph battery containers in Arabana camps. Reworking these materials shows people selecting and reshaping new supplies for their own uses. The finds document technological choices in a colonial setting, not simply the passive receipt of imported goods.

passages.title: What objects and archaeological camps reveal
passages.text: Camp S355 contained buttons, pipe fragments, cooking vessels and other household goods. Broken shears may have been reused as knives, although the authors present that interpretation cautiously. Such finds help reconstruct activities around work and home; the presence of purchased goods alone cannot establish the abandonment of Arabana identity.

passages.title: What objects and archaeological camps reveal
passages.text: Colonial employment could be paid in food and clothing rather than cash. Ration distribution also gave outsiders power over access to necessities. Archaeological evidence of new goods must be read alongside these unequal working conditions.

passages.title: Families, photographs and language
passages.text: David Moore’s 1959 photograph at Finniss Springs depicts Old Finke Bob and his wife Jessie. The gallery identifies Bob as Southern Arrernte, with an Arabana mother, Kantyara Nhuka. That specific family history matters: a photograph taken on Arabana Country does not make every person in it exclusively Arabana.

passages.title: Families, photographs and language
passages.text: The gallery catalogue connects Finniss Springs with Francis Warren and Laura Paralta, an Arabana woman. It describes the mission’s protection of children from removal and its eventual closure amid drought, water shortages and fire. The photograph survives as a record of people within that wider history; the museum print was made in 2000.

passages.title: Families, photographs and language
passages.text: The 2022 exhibition Arabana Yanhi! Tanganekald Yan! brought together two distinct language communities. For Arabana, Elders’ knowledge and memories were connected with archival spoken and written records. Artwork and word cards supported teaching. The exhibition’s Tanganekald materials belong to their own language history and should not be relabelled as Arabana evidence.

passages.title: Continuing achievements and care for Country
passages.text: Arabana Rangers monitor springs, care for threatened species and address feral animals and weeds. Cultural heritage work and learning from Elders are part of the same program. Training and employment help community members practise this knowledge on Country while developing skills needed for long-term management.

passages.title: Continuing achievements and care for Country
passages.text: The November 2025 burn targeted excessive reed growth around springs associated with the threatened salt pipewort, Eriocaulon carsonii. Arabana Elders and Rangers participated with partners. The project was a trial intended to protect spring habitat; its announcement does not establish that the plant had already recovered or that every spring needs burning.

passages.title: Continuing achievements and care for Country
passages.text: The Arabana Aboriginal Corporation represents community responsibilities for land, water and culture. Its public account links those responsibilities to native title recognition and to continuing family connections. These institutions give contemporary form to relationships whose significance extends beyond the dates displayed by a historical map.

Arabana people and their relationships with Country continue. Colonial stations, mission closure and changes in work altered community life without bringing it to an end. The map’s 1600 to 1815 interval is a coverage range, not a founding date, disappearance or transfer of Arabana identity to another people.

passages.text: The Arabela are an Indigenous people living around the Arabela River in Peru’s Loreto region. Their language belongs to the Zaparoan family. Tapueyocuaca, meaning family or siblings, is another name recorded for the people.

passages.title: Work, homes and materials
passages.text: A minga brings neighbours together for substantial jobs such as clearing a garden or building a house. The ILV account describes collective work followed by food, drink and conversation. Production therefore includes relationships of cooperation as well as the household that requested help.

passages.title: Work, homes and materials
passages.text: The Ministry of Culture describes an earlier pattern of related families sharing a maloca, followed by greater use of separate family houses. This is a history of changing domestic arrangements, not evidence that all households followed one permanent design.

passages.title: Work, homes and materials
passages.text: Historical clothing descriptions record women’s tubular bark garments with painted hexagonal designs and men’s woven ornaments with feather tassels. Cotton and chambira fibres, bark, feathers and beeswax appear in these accounts. They show the selection and combination of forest materials; they do not date the invention of those techniques.

passages.title: Work, homes and materials
passages.text: ILV describes hunting, fishing and collecting alongside cultivation. Its missionary account records customary divisions of work as well as collaboration, rather than demonstrating that all households followed an identical pattern.

passages.title: Coercion, trade and schooling
passages.text: Rubber extraction and patronage subjected Arabela people to exploitation. ILV describes goods advanced against labour and forest products at valuations that kept workers indebted. It connects literacy and arithmetic with households’ ability to track transactions and challenge abuse. Schooling had practical consequences within an unequal trading system.

passages.title: Coercion, trade and schooling
passages.text: The 1999 dictionary’s stated purpose was reciprocal communication: helping Arabela speakers learn Spanish and helping Spanish speakers communicate with them. Its listed contents include Arabela-to-Spanish entries, a Spanish-to-Arabela section, grammatical notes and guidance on the alphabet. The publication documents substantial linguistic work rather than the creation of a previously nonexistent language.

passages.title: Coercion, trade and schooling
passages.text: The 2016 alphabet resolution provides a different kind of evidence: a dated administrative record concerning a standardized way to write Arabela. Official recognition and the earlier dictionary are separate milestones. Neither establishes that language transmission was secure or that every speaker used the same written conventions beforehand.

passages.title: Recorded voices and continuing knowledge
passages.text: Casa de la Literatura credits Alfredo Pacaya Torrejón, Edgar Pastor Rosero and Ester Rosero Vásquez in the 2012 Buena Vista recording, with Vivian Wauters and Alfredo Pacaya as collectors. Naming these participants makes visible the people behind a recording that might otherwise appear only as an anonymous language sample.

passages.title: Recorded voices and continuing knowledge
passages.text: In the published translation’s opening, the narrator frames the account through writing and knowledge from elders, then tells of a child emerging from the earth and being welcomed into a household. This is a particular recorded narrative, not a statement that all Arabela people share one unchanging religious interpretation.

passages.title: Recorded voices and continuing knowledge
passages.text: Berkeley’s 2019 update describes more than 36 hours of Arabela recordings, along with field notes and a lexical database. These preserve different kinds of evidence: spoken examples, research observations and organized vocabulary. The announced deposit documents preservation work; it does not demonstrate that the entire collection was transcribed or that every recording is unrestricted.

passages.title: Recorded voices and continuing knowledge
passages.text: The 2023 classroom resource contains eight illustrated sheets intended for children aged three to five. Its catalogue says the scenes concern community calendars, including activities of other Indigenous peoples and Afro-Peruvian communities. The resource therefore should not be read as eight ethnographic photographs of Arabela life.

passages.title: Recorded voices and continuing knowledge
passages.text: Publishing materials for children is one part of the work of sustaining language and knowledge. A catalogue can establish that a resource was produced and whom it was designed for; it does not by itself establish how widely teachers used it or measure changes in children’s fluency.

Arabela communities continue, despite coercion, displacement and serious pressure on their language. Changes in housing, schooling and multilingual life do not mean the people disappeared. The map’s 1492 to 1500 interval is only imported coverage.

sectionTitles: Objects made for care, work and art
Homes, food and the surrounding land

passages.text: Arapaho history includes distinct northern and southern communities, skilled making, family relationships and a living language. Homes, museum objects and recorded voices help us explore particular lives across generations.

passages.title: Objects made for care, work and art
passages.text: A Northern Arapaho cradleboard in the Smithsonian collections is dated to about 1890. It combines wood, hide, cotton canvas, sinew and porcupine-quill decoration. The catalogue records collection from Elizabeth Sunroad at Wind River in 1924. It preserves skilled sewing and quill work in a baby carrier, but the record does not name its maker or the child it carried.

passages.title: Objects made for care, work and art
passages.text: A hide scraper from Wind River joins an antler body to an iron blade. The museum places it in a group collected from five Northern Arapaho people in 1923. This practical tool combines materials with different origins. Its history of collection does not establish its manufacture date or which of those five people owned this individual scraper.

passages.title: Objects made for care, work and art
passages.text: Donna Shakespeare-Cummings made a doll dated to about 2000 that brings together hide, glass beads, porcupine quills, wood and other materials. Its construction includes sewing, carving, painting and beadwork. A small figure can hold a remarkable amount of skilled work. This museum artwork is evidence of a named Northern Arapaho artist’s practice, not proof that a child used it as a toy.

passages.title: Children, friendship and everyday care
passages.text: Agnes Yellow Plume and Ann Wolf recalled making toy horses from bent willow, with weed tails and little rawhide saddles. Dolls rode them on pretend journeys, sometimes with tiny tipi poles. Their memories, published in 1952, show children turning familiar travel into play. A twig could become transport for an entire imaginary household.

passages.title: Children, friendship and everyday care
passages.text: Ann Wolf remembered a lifelong friendship that began at boarding school. The two women exchanged clothing and other gifts; their husbands became friends too. Agnes Yellow Plume described a group of friends instead of one closest companion. Their accounts show variation within a community, not a rule that everyone must have exactly one best friend.

passages.title: Children, friendship and everyday care
passages.text: Hilger’s interviews also recorded ordinary baby care: some mothers recalled powdered, aged buffalo dung as absorbent cradle filling and sitting toddlers on a can during toilet training. These are historical accounts from particular women, not evidence that the practices were universal, safe or medically effective.

passages.title: Homes, food and the surrounding land
passages.text: In Boulder’s ethnographic report, Arapaho representatives explain why camps could not all remain together: people and horses needed water and food. Smaller family camps and larger gatherings served different purposes. Frank Medicine Water describes journeys between water sources. Planning where to sleep also meant planning where a horse could drink; the travel arrangements included thirsty passengers with four legs.

passages.title: Homes, food and the surrounding land
passages.text: The Arapaho Language Project records food plants including chokecherries, serviceberries, wild onions and biscuitroot. Buffalo mattered greatly, but gathering required knowledge of a varied landscape too. This list identifies documented foods; it does not tell us what every family ate on a particular day.

passages.title: Learning and community life continue
passages.text: In research published in 2023, Northern Arapaho elders explored places and a tipi through virtual reality. A 2019 session showed Nii’eihii Neecee’s view on a large screen so others could follow. Working with the Language and Culture Commission, researchers used these settings to prompt speech and memories. The virtual world supported learning from elders; it did not replace their knowledge.

passages.title: Learning and community life continue
passages.text: The Cheyenne and Arapaho Tribes describe language classes in their communities and online, outreach to Head Start and child-care programmes, and intensive adult learning with experienced speakers. Language work crosses generations: children learn, adults practise and elders contribute knowledge. Sharing a tribal government does not make Cheyenne and Arapaho the same language.

passages.title: Learning and community life continue
passages.text: In its January 2025 description, the Cheyenne and Arapaho Buffalo Program reports quarterly distributions of buffalo meat, recipes and food information to elders and eligible members, including people with diabetes or at risk of it. The programme also supports herd restoration. This describes community food provision, not a claim that one food cures a disease.

passages.title: Records, loss and remembrance
passages.text: In 2000, manuscript copies of letters by Silas Soule and Joseph Cramer were found in Denver. The National Park Service explains that these eyewitness accounts document the Sand Creek Massacre and soldiers who resisted participating. Written evidence helps examine what happened alongside the continuing work of descendant communities to remember the people who were killed.

Arapaho communities continue at Wind River in Wyoming and within the Cheyenne and Arapaho Tribes in Oklahoma. Displacement changed political life without ending the people. Families, institutions and language teaching continue; 1783 is only this map entry’s endpoint.

passages.text: Asante architecture joined construction skill with visual language and religious practice. Surviving shrine buildings near Kumasi preserve parts of a tradition that remained meaningful beyond the period of imperial power.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Builders arranged timber and bamboo structures around courtyards, applying mud plaster to walls and originally roofing them with thatch.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Wall reliefs combine spirals with animal, bird and plant forms. Motifs related to Adinkra convey meanings as well as decorate surfaces.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Shrines are places for consultation with deities before important decisions. Their symbolic features belong to continuing religious practice.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Maintaining earthen buildings requires responding to heavy rain, humidity and damage to organic materials. Architectural survival depends on repeated care.

sectionTitles: Families, food and a portable home
What objects and pictures can tell us

passages.text: Assiniboine history includes family-based communities, far-reaching trade and continuing traditions of skilled making and teaching. Nakoda and Nakota are names people use for themselves; individual communities have their own histories.

passages.title: Families, food and a portable home
passages.text: Assiniboine bands comprised families who camped together, often linked through marriage and other kinship, according to historian David Reed Miller. Membership could change and new bands could form. A camp was also a political community.

passages.title: Families, food and a portable home
passages.text: Buffalo supported more than dinner: meat provided food, while hides supplied clothing and tipi covers. People also used many other food sources; this was not a buffalo-only menu.

passages.title: Families, food and a portable home
passages.text: The National Park Service describes cooking by placing fire-heated stones in water. Heat travelled with the stones into the vessel. In this kitchen, the hot part could arrive inside the pot.

passages.title: Families, food and a portable home
passages.text: Assiniboine traders exchanged meat and pelts with Missouri River villagers, including Mandan and Hidatsa people, for crops such as corn, beans and squash. Dinner could depend on relationships reaching well beyond one camp.

passages.title: What objects and pictures can tell us
passages.text: Excavations at Fort Union recovered a bone comb, fishhook, metal bell, ornaments and gunflints. These finds reveal grooming, fishing, decoration and weapons at a nineteenth-century trading place. They do not identify the Assiniboine person, other visitor or post resident who owned each object.

passages.title: What objects and pictures can tell us
passages.text: George Catlin painted Assiniboin Woman and Child at Fort Union in 1832. His accompanying account described hide clothing decorated with porcupine quills and elk teeth. The painting and description preserve an outsider’s view of particular clothing, not a photograph or a complete account of the sitters’ lives. Their names are not supplied in this museum record.

passages.title: What objects and pictures can tell us
passages.text: Joyce Growing Thunder Fogarty’s Toy Cradleboard, dated 1989, combines beadwork, leather, cloth and painted wood. Its museum label traces the form to Kiowa and Comanche cradles, while identifying her individual style. An Assiniboine-Sioux artist can learn from neighbouring traditions and create something distinctive. This is a documented modern artwork, not an excavated ancient Assiniboine cradle.

passages.title: A family’s art and generosity
passages.text: For the Give Away Horses dress featured in a 2007 Smithsonian account, Joyce Growing Thunder Fogarty sewed blue and white beads onto elk skin. She worked for ten months, often at her kitchen table. Her daughter Juanita made accessories including a belt and sewing-tool case, while granddaughter Jessica made a beaded blanket strip. This was a family collaboration with a formidable number of tiny parts.

passages.title: A family’s art and generosity
passages.text: The dress’s horses recalled Joyce’s grandfather Ben Gray Hawk. She remembered him giving away horses to honour his grandchildren, with the person who caught a released horse keeping it. Her design turned a family memory of generosity into wearable art. The account describes this family’s experience, not a rule followed at every Assiniboine celebration.

passages.title: Learning, museums and living communities
passages.text: Nakóda teachers approached Indiana University’s research institute in December 2017 about new school materials. The collaboration used elders’ recorded stories and Nakóda artists’ illustrations to create early-grade books and an app. A child could hear an elder’s voice while learning with modern technology. The project described its first materials; it did not claim the entire planned school curriculum was finished.

passages.title: Learning, museums and living communities
passages.text: In a 2025 account from Aaniiih Nakoda College, student Kassi Buckles read Fifteen Animals in English and Nakoda to four- and five-year-olds, then introduced counting words. The library’s collection also included work by local writers and translators such as Assiniboine educator Minerva Allen. Story time could bring language learning, animals and numbers into the same room.

passages.title: Learning, museums and living communities
passages.text: Fort Peck’s Cultural Resources Department, established in 1995, looks after a museum and a landscape containing campsites, stone-working sources, rock art and historic buildings. Heritage care includes recording and protecting places, not simply putting attractive objects behind glass. Its public mission connects that work with Dakota and Nakoda culture, history, language and life.

passages.title: Learning, museums and living communities
passages.text: Carry the Kettle’s ancestors joined Treaty 4 at Fort Walsh on September 25, 1877. FHQ Developments’ community history names the chiefs and explains their wish for a reserve in their Cypress Hills homeland. This Canadian history belongs alongside the Montana stories; a present-day border should not make one part of a people’s history disappear.

Assiniboine communities continue in the United States and Canada. Land loss and reservation policies transformed political life without ending the people. Fort Belknap, Fort Peck and Carry the Kettle have distinct histories. The map’s 1500 and 1783 endpoints are not extinction dates.

sectionTitles: Families, food and a portable home
What objects and pictures can tell us

passages.text: Assiniboine history includes family-based communities, far-reaching trade and continuing traditions of skilled making and teaching. Nakoda and Nakota are names people use for themselves; individual communities have their own histories.

passages.title: Families, food and a portable home
passages.text: Assiniboine bands comprised families who camped together, often linked through marriage and other kinship, according to historian David Reed Miller. Membership could change and new bands could form. A camp was also a political community.

passages.title: Families, food and a portable home
passages.text: Buffalo supported more than dinner: meat provided food, while hides supplied clothing and tipi covers. People also used many other food sources; this was not a buffalo-only menu.

passages.title: Families, food and a portable home
passages.text: The National Park Service describes cooking by placing fire-heated stones in water. Heat travelled with the stones into the vessel. In this kitchen, the hot part could arrive inside the pot.

passages.title: Families, food and a portable home
passages.text: Assiniboine traders exchanged meat and pelts with Missouri River villagers, including Mandan and Hidatsa people, for crops such as corn, beans and squash. Dinner could depend on relationships reaching well beyond one camp.

passages.title: What objects and pictures can tell us
passages.text: Excavations at Fort Union recovered a bone comb, fishhook, metal bell, ornaments and gunflints. These finds reveal grooming, fishing, decoration and weapons at a nineteenth-century trading place. They do not identify the Assiniboine person, other visitor or post resident who owned each object.

passages.title: What objects and pictures can tell us
passages.text: George Catlin painted Assiniboin Woman and Child at Fort Union in 1832. His accompanying account described hide clothing decorated with porcupine quills and elk teeth. The painting and description preserve an outsider’s view of particular clothing, not a photograph or a complete account of the sitters’ lives. Their names are not supplied in this museum record.

passages.title: What objects and pictures can tell us
passages.text: Joyce Growing Thunder Fogarty’s Toy Cradleboard, dated 1989, combines beadwork, leather, cloth and painted wood. Its museum label traces the form to Kiowa and Comanche cradles, while identifying her individual style. An Assiniboine-Sioux artist can learn from neighbouring traditions and create something distinctive. This is a documented modern artwork, not an excavated ancient Assiniboine cradle.

passages.title: A family’s art and generosity
passages.text: For the Give Away Horses dress featured in a 2007 Smithsonian account, Joyce Growing Thunder Fogarty sewed blue and white beads onto elk skin. She worked for ten months, often at her kitchen table. Her daughter Juanita made accessories including a belt and sewing-tool case, while granddaughter Jessica made a beaded blanket strip. This was a family collaboration with a formidable number of tiny parts.

passages.title: A family’s art and generosity
passages.text: The dress’s horses recalled Joyce’s grandfather Ben Gray Hawk. She remembered him giving away horses to honour his grandchildren, with the person who caught a released horse keeping it. Her design turned a family memory of generosity into wearable art. The account describes this family’s experience, not a rule followed at every Assiniboine celebration.

passages.title: Learning, museums and living communities
passages.text: Nakóda teachers approached Indiana University’s research institute in December 2017 about new school materials. The collaboration used elders’ recorded stories and Nakóda artists’ illustrations to create early-grade books and an app. A child could hear an elder’s voice while learning with modern technology. The project described its first materials; it did not claim the entire planned school curriculum was finished.

passages.title: Learning, museums and living communities
passages.text: In a 2025 account from Aaniiih Nakoda College, student Kassi Buckles read Fifteen Animals in English and Nakoda to four- and five-year-olds, then introduced counting words. The library’s collection also included work by local writers and translators such as Assiniboine educator Minerva Allen. Story time could bring language learning, animals and numbers into the same room.

passages.title: Learning, museums and living communities
passages.text: Fort Peck’s Cultural Resources Department, established in 1995, looks after a museum and a landscape containing campsites, stone-working sources, rock art and historic buildings. Heritage care includes recording and protecting places, not simply putting attractive objects behind glass. Its public mission connects that work with Dakota and Nakoda culture, history, language and life.

passages.title: Learning, museums and living communities
passages.text: Carry the Kettle’s ancestors joined Treaty 4 at Fort Walsh on September 25, 1877. FHQ Developments’ community history names the chiefs and explains their wish for a reserve in their Cypress Hills homeland. This Canadian history belongs alongside the Montana stories; a present-day border should not make one part of a people’s history disappear.

Assiniboine communities continue in the United States and Canada. Land loss and reservation policies transformed political life without ending the people. Fort Belknap, Fort Peck and Carry the Kettle have distinct histories. The map’s 1500 and 1783 endpoints are not extinction dates.

passages.text: The Atakapa-Ishak are a Gulf Coast Indigenous people associated with southwestern Louisiana and eastern Texas. Their history connects waterways, local communities and related language varieties. Craft objects and named speakers’ records preserve evidence of their knowledge.

passages.title: Life along coast and bayou
passages.text: Fishing, hunting and gathering supplied communities that moved within familiar territories. Historical descriptions identify alligator meat, hides and oil as resources, with oil applied against insects. These uses demonstrate knowledge of an animal’s different properties.

passages.title: Life along coast and bayou
passages.text: Trade connected local bands with neighbors and with French and Spanish visitors. Akokisa and Deadose histories belong within the wider regional picture. Colonial names sometimes covered populations larger than a speaker’s own community, so the regional label should not erase local distinctions.

passages.title: Objects, manufacture and archaeological limits
passages.text: Covered basket 22/8845 in the National Museum of the American Indian is catalogued as Atakapa. It is made from river cane using twill plaiting and double weaving. Edward Leverich bought it from local people near Franklin, Louisiana, between 1882 and 1886; his family later donated it in 1959. Neither date is an excavated manufacture date.

passages.title: Objects, manufacture and archaeological limits
passages.text: This basket’s recorded sale provides evidence of craft entering an outside market, while its woven construction preserves a maker’s technical choices. The catalogue does not name that maker or identify the vessel’s original contents. A useful account can explain material and technique without inventing a biography or assigning a specific household use.

passages.title: Objects, manufacture and archaeological limits
passages.text: Another Smithsonian basket, E360927, shows why museum labels need scrutiny. Its public record calls it Atakapa, but also reports a basket maker’s identification of Mississippi Choctaw style and an older possible Cherokee label. It cannot securely demonstrate a uniquely Atakapa pattern. The disagreement is evidence about collecting and classification, not proof that the peoples were interchangeable.

passages.title: Objects, manufacture and archaeological limits
passages.text: Campbell’s Caplen-site report likewise cautions against a simple ethnic assignment. Old pottery and European beads indicate material from different periods, while collecting and weak stratigraphic control limit interpretation. Geographical location alone cannot establish that every object at an upper Texas coast site belonged to the same historically named community.

passages.title: Language records and lasting achievements
passages.text: Louison Huntington and Delilah Moss supplied much of the language material recorded in 1885. Gatschet used small school notebooks; the published introduction describes black-ink entries subsequently checked and corrected with Moss in red ink. The archive therefore records Indigenous intellectual work and revision, not simply a linguist discovering an otherwise voiceless people.

passages.title: Language records and lasting achievements
passages.text: Kimball’s 2022 reference grammar returns to those notes, analyzes the language’s structure and presents surviving texts in revised transcription and translation. Its public description credits the speakers alongside Gatschet and later contributions collected by Swanton. The achievement is a new analysis of inherited records, not evidence that a new language was created in 2022.

passages.title: Language records and lasting achievements
passages.text: David Kaufman, language researchers and Ishāk community members collaborated on the Living Dictionary. Its searchable vocabulary makes earlier records available for renewal work. The resource does not by itself establish restored everyday fluency or a particular number of speakers.

Epidemics and colonial disruption severely reduced historical communities, but Ishāk people and organized language work continue. Older reports of disappearance should not be read as proof that all descendants vanished. The map’s 1500 and 1783 endpoints are coverage boundaries, not extinction dates.

passages.text: Grand Bayou Indian Village is a living Atakapa-Ishak Chawasha community in coastal Plaquemines Parish, Louisiana. Reached by boat, it connects homes, livelihoods and cultural memory with the surrounding marshes and waterways. Residents work collectively to protect those relationships as land disappears.

passages.title: Waterways, work and community life
passages.text: Boat access shapes everyday connections between households and the wider coast. The community’s own account describes land and water as sources of food, materials, medicine and shelter. Protecting a wetland therefore also protects the practical resources on which a village depends.

passages.title: Waterways, work and community life
passages.text: Commercial fishing was a principal livelihood described in the 2012 community profile. Fishing knowledge connects the work of earning a living with close observation of changing water and marsh conditions. The village’s experience of environmental change comes through people whose daily work depends on those places.

passages.title: Waterways, work and community life
passages.text: The same profile emphasizes mutual aid, self-sufficiency and adaptation. Residents and university partners worked to connect local experience with officials and other communities. Their collaboration supported residents’ ability to shape decisions about their future, including difficult choices about remaining in place or moving.

passages.title: Knowledge, research and discoveries
passages.text: The 2011 coastal study combined historical imagery from 1968 to 2009 with residents’ ecological knowledge and scientific information about marsh conditions. Its maps distinguished areas vulnerable to change from places especially important to sustaining community life. That distinction added local priorities to measurements of physical land loss.

passages.title: Knowledge, research and discoveries
passages.text: Maurice A. Phillips of Grand Bayou appears among the study’s authors alongside university, restoration-agency and NASA researchers. The collaboration is a concrete example of community expertise contributing to research design and interpretation. The public abstract describes the method; it does not establish that every proposed restoration priority was subsequently funded.

passages.title: Knowledge, research and discoveries
passages.text: Rosina Phillipe described visitors arriving from several countries to learn from Grand Bayou. Sharing building, recovery and environmental experience turned the village into a place of exchange as well as a place facing danger. Residents presented themselves as contributors of knowledge, with experience useful beyond their own shoreline.

passages.title: Making protective shorelines
passages.text: Recycled oyster shells move through a deliberate process: restaurants separate them, the shells are taken to a curing site, and volunteers place them in marine-grade mesh bags. Returned to coastal water, they provide surfaces for new oysters and help form a living shoreline. The technique connects food waste, manual construction and habitat restoration.

passages.title: Making protective shorelines
passages.text: At Grand Bayou’s residential area, the 2024 project used bagged shells placed by hand to build a reef along the shore. CRCL records this separately from its earlier mound-site project. These are modern structures made through community partnerships, with the purpose of supporting habitat and reducing erosion around places people continue to use.

passages.title: Making protective shorelines
passages.text: CRCL compares protected and unprotected shorelines and revisits reefs to assess new oyster growth. For its Plaquemines mound-site reef, aerial images before and after Hurricane Ida indicated less damage along protected marsh. That observation supports local monitoring; a result from one reef is not a guarantee that all coastlines will respond identically.

passages.title: Sacred places and collective action
passages.text: Lemon Tree Mound, sacred to the community, was returned by St. Paul’s Episcopal Church on 20 September 2024. The transfer accompanied continuing shoreline protection.

passages.title: Sacred places and collective action
passages.text: Grand Bayou joined other coastal Indigenous communities in the First Peoples Conservation Council. The community describes this alliance as a way to protect waters, land, resources and health for coming generations. The work joins cultural survival with practical conservation.

The Atakapa-Ishak Chawasha community continues while erosion and storms threaten its land and livelihoods. Conservation, research partnerships and the care of sacred places are parts of that ongoing history. The imported 1492 to 1500 map interval is not a founding or extinction date.
