passages.text: Aboriginal peoples of Australia comprise many nations with their own languages, knowledge and relationships to Country. A continent-wide label cannot describe one kingdom or one way of life. The examples here come mainly from the mainland and identify particular places; Torres Strait Islander peoples have distinct histories.

passages.title: Food preparation preserved in stone
passages.text: At Madjedbebe in Mirarr Country, researchers examined grinding stones from deposits spanning the Ice Age and later periods. Wear patterns and chemical residues indicate processing of seeds and other plants. Two stones from the oldest occupation phase, GS39 and GS73, carry evidence interpreted as seed grinding.

passages.title: Food preparation preserved in stone
passages.text: A shaped sandstone whetstone, GS79, occurs in that early phase alongside an axe and flakes removed from ground tools. Together they support the interpretation that people made and maintained sharpened stone edges. Shape alone would be weaker evidence than this combination of objects and wear.

passages.title: Food preparation preserved in stone
passages.text: Red pigments on some stones also indicate grinding, but the researchers rejected many stains as contamination. Surviving pigment does not identify the images once painted, and preservation favours mineral traces over many food residues. An archaeological sample is therefore not a complete picture of daily activity.

passages.title: Engineering a wetland food supply
passages.text: At Budj Bim in south-western Victoria, Gunditjmara builders used volcanic stone to redirect water through channels, dams and weirs. These structures helped trap and hold short-finned eels. Their operation depended on knowledge of water flow and the animals’ seasonal movement.

passages.title: Engineering a wetland food supply
passages.text: Kurtonitj preserves stone house sites, eel traps, channels and trees used for smoking eels. These connected traces show a landscape of food production, processing and settlement. They are specific evidence from Gunditjmara Country, not a template for every Australian environment.

passages.title: Clothing, tools and exchange
passages.text: Wooden boomerangs recovered at Wyrie Swamp in South Australia in 1973 were dated to about 10,000 years ago. They demonstrate ancient woodworking, while their survival cannot establish when the first boomerang was invented. Most Australian boomerangs are not the returning form familiar from popular imagery.

passages.title: Clothing, tools and exchange
passages.text: Boomerangs served as hunting tools, digging implements and percussion instruments, with forms adapted to different tasks. Hooked examples from north-central Australia and heavy carved examples from the Darling and Cooper river systems travelled through exchange networks. Technique and decoration varied among makers and communities.

passages.title: Clothing, tools and exchange
passages.text: People in colder regions made clothing from animal skins. In Noongar language, kangaroo-skin cloaks are called booka. The museum also holds a 2005 reproduction by Lee Darroch and Treahna Hamm of a possum-skin cloak collected at Echuca in 1853, linking practical clothing to cultural renewal.

passages.title: Knowledge and community action
passages.text: Seasonal knowledge guides activities on Country. In recent collaborations, Indigenous knowledge holders and CSIRO have created calendars that communicate local environmental understanding. Ngan’gi, Walmajarri and Kunwinjku projects are distinct examples, not different versions of one national calendar.

passages.title: Knowledge and community action
passages.text: From 1792, Pemulwuy led resistance near the Parramatta, Hawkesbury and Georges rivers. His actions and the punitive colonial response show that occupation was contested. This Sydney-region history should not be assigned automatically to distant communities with different experiences of invasion.

passages.title: Knowledge and community action
passages.text: The 1967 campaign drew on petitions, community organising and alliances. Joe McGinness and Faith Bandler were among its leading organisers. The resulting constitutional change did not first grant voting rights: the federal franchise had already been extended in 1962.

Colonisation brought profound losses of land, lives and self-government, but Aboriginal peoples did not disappear. Communities continue in urban, regional and remote Australia, maintaining and renewing distinct identities. A change or ending in this broad map label records the atlas’s categories, not a single surrender or the end of a people.

passages.text: Ayutthaya, founded on an island in the Chao Phraya in 1351, ruled Siam for four centuries and was one of the great trading cities of Asia. Its kings took the Khmer idea of divine kingship, and its port welcomed Chinese, Japanese, Persian, Dutch, Portuguese and French merchants.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Rice, deer hides, sappanwood and tin left through the royal warehouses; Chinese junks and, from 1511, Portuguese ships came to buy them.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Foreign quarters ringed the city: Japanese, Portuguese, Dutch from 1608, French and Persian; the Greek Constantine Phaulkon rose to chief minister under King Narai.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: King Narai sent an embassy to Louis XIV at Versailles in 1686.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Prang towers in the Khmer manner and the tall chedis of Wat Phra Si Sanphet, with gilded Buddhas.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Court poetry, the Ramakien, the Thai Ramayana, and masked dance drama.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Theravada Buddhism with royal patronage and hundreds of temples in the capital.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Khmer court ritual and the devaraja idea of the king as a god shaped kingship; the law code of 1805 preserves Ayutthaya's laws.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The Historic City of Ayutthaya was listed by UNESCO.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Thai kingship, law and court culture descend from Ayutthaya.
A Burmese army took and burned the city in April 1767. Within the year Taksin had rallied Siam from a new capital at Thonburi.

passages.text: Tenochtitlan brought canals, markets, workshops and ceremonial architecture into a large lake city. This card focuses on the capital's civic and artistic life within the Aztec imperial world.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Canals and raised causeways connected the capital to surrounding lakeshore towns. Canoes carried people and goods through the urban network.

passages.title: Water and daily life
passages.text: Aqueducts supplied fresh water, while neighborhood communities maintained local temples and markets.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Stone carvers used stone and hardwood tools, fiber cords, water and sand to shape even hard materials into detailed sculpture.

passages.title: Architecture
passages.text: The Templo Mayor paired shrines to Tlaloc and Huitzilopochtli. Successive rulers enlarged the complex, sometimes also responding to flooding and unstable ground.

passages.title: Craft and exchange
passages.text: The capital's markets offered food and luxury goods. Its neighborhoods included potters, weavers, sculptors, lapidaries and featherworkers.
Tenochtitlan fell in 1521. Spanish rulers built a new colonial capital over the devastated city.

passages.text: Baekje held the southwest of the Korean peninsula and was the most refined of the Three Kingdoms, trading by sea with China and Japan. Its monks, scholars and craftsmen carried Buddhism, Chinese learning and temple architecture to the Yamato court.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Sea routes linked Baekje to the southern Chinese dynasties and to Japan, and possibly further south.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: King Seong sent a Buddha image, sutras and monks to the Yamato court, the official introduction of Buddhism to Japan; Japanese sources date it to 538 or 552.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: The Baekje smile, the gentle expression of its stone and bronze Buddhas, as on the rock-cut triad at Seosan.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Gilt-bronze Buddhas, reliquaries and roof tiles stamped with lotus designs.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: The Gilt-bronze Incense Burner of Baekje, found at Neungsan-ri in 1993, a mountain of peaks, musicians and animals on a lotus base.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The monk Marananta arrived from Eastern Jin and the court adopted Buddhism, building temples and monastic communities.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Confucian learning and the Chinese classics were taught to the aristocracy; Baekje scholars such as Wang In took the classics to Japan.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The Baekje Historic Areas were listed by UNESCO.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Baekje's transmission of Buddhism, writing and craft shaped early Japanese civilization.
A Silla army and a Tang fleet took the capital Sabi in 660; a restoration movement was crushed at the Baekgang river in 663, and Silla absorbed the land by 676.

Making music, costumes and public memory

passages.text: The Bahamas became independent in 1973 after a much longer history of Lucayan communities, colonial settlement, slavery and struggles for political rights. Pottery, house yards and living craft traditions reveal how people worked, raised families and made things together across the islands.

passages.title: Discoveries: clay, weaving and island food
passages.text: A pottery recipe began with a surprising ingredient: dust blown across the Atlantic from the Sahara. Researchers sampled red deposits on Long Island and experimented with Palmetto Ware, the Lucayan pottery containing burned, crushed conch shell. The shell helped difficult local material hold its shape. Experiments indicate relatively low firing temperatures, showing careful adaptation to the islands’ available resources.

passages.title: Discoveries: clay, weaving and island food
passages.text: At Long Bay on San Salvador, impressions preserved in pottery reveal woven materials that have largely decayed. Hutcheson’s study compares these with other Late Lucayan sites; at Palmetto Grove, impressions even preserve evidence of woven spun thread. Clay kept a record of fibre work. Different patterns suggest variation in craft, but do not automatically identify a specific ethnic group.

passages.title: Discoveries: clay, weaving and island food
passages.text: At Clifton on New Providence, excavators distinguished two Lucayan settlements using radiocarbon dates and objects, rather than assuming all nearby remains belonged to one village. Griddles, hollow vessels, shell beads and tools differed between the sites. Marine remains show the importance of conch and other seafood. The researchers favoured successive settlement over a long-lived pair of simultaneous villages.

passages.title: Household work and family knowledge
passages.text: Laundry left clues at early nineteenth-century Clifton. Buttons, beads and fasteners clustered between houses and outdoor kitchens; the excavators interpreted them as losses during washing and drying. Food remains and cooking tools marked other activity areas. The yards supported sewing, childcare and conversation as well as chores, within the constrained lives of enslaved households.

passages.title: Household work and family knowledge
passages.text: On Cat Island, Iva Thompson passed skills to her family, including Sheena Woodside and Peggy Johnson. The tourism ministry’s family profile describes Woodside plaiting dried palm leaves into bags, baskets and rugs from childhood. Ordinary plants became useful household objects through learned patterns and patient hands. This is one documented family’s story, not a rule for every Bahamian home.

passages.title: Household work and family knowledge
passages.text: The same Cat Island family remembers bush teas made from local plants, including cerasee, breadfruit and guava. Peggy Johnson describes this knowledge as part of an inherited tradition of care. The account tells us what this family practised and valued; it does not demonstrate that a tea cures an illness.

passages.title: Making music, costumes and public memory
passages.text: For Junkanoo, families and groups transform cardboard and crepe paper into towering costumes. Skills pass between generations in preparation spaces called shacks and at home. A child can learn by helping someone who already knows the craft. UNESCO’s 2023 inscription recognizes the shared work and creativity behind the spectacle.

passages.title: Making music, costumes and public memory
passages.text: The street music of Junkanoo includes whistles, cowbells, horns and goatskin drums. A 2022 postal-service account describes months of preparation and costumes whose materials changed over time, from cloth and natural materials to elaborate cardboard constructions. The exact origin remains debated. The parade is the part you see; much of the work happens beforehand.

passages.title: Making music, costumes and public memory
passages.text: At Clifton, Antonius Roberts carved female figures from unwanted casuarina tree trunks, leaving them in place as a memorial. Tyrone Ferguson added metal bells. The work, called Sacred Space, connects art, ancestry and the landscape. These contemporary sculptures commemorate history; they are not excavated Lucayan statues.

passages.title: Work, votes and independence
passages.text: The Burma Road unrest of 1942 grew from workers’ anger over unequal pay at an airfield construction project. Bahamian labourers learned that Americans received more for comparable work. The dispute helped connect workplace demands with the wider struggle over racial inequality and political power.

passages.title: Work, votes and independence
passages.text: Mary Ingraham, Doris Johnson, Eugenia Lockhart and other campaigners pressed for women’s voting rights through organizing and petitions. Women voted in the general election of 26 November 1962. That achievement widened participation before majority rule in 1967.

passages.title: Work, votes and independence
passages.text: After the September 1972 election, the Bahamas legislature requested independence and government and opposition delegates attended a London conference. The resulting settlement fixed 10 July 1973 as independence day. This was a negotiated end to British colonial rule, not a conquest or the disappearance of an island community.
British colonial rule ended with independence in 1973. The Bahamas continues as a country. The map’s separate entries represent coverage of the same islands, not vanished and refounded societies.

passages.text: Balhae was founded in 698 by Dae Joyeong, a former Goguryeo general, in the hills of eastern Manchuria, and grew into a power that Tang writers called the Flourishing State of the East. Its capitals were laid out on the Tang model and its envoys sailed regularly to Japan.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Embassies went to Tang China and, more than thirty times, across the sea to Japan, carrying furs, ginseng and horses.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Balhae sat on the routes between Manchuria, the Korean peninsula, north China and the steppe.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Buddhism was practiced in the capitals, alongside the native beliefs of the Mohe majority.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: A Tang-style government of three chancelleries and six ministries ran a state of many peoples; the capital Sanggyeong copied the grid of Chang'an.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Korea, China and Russia each claim Balhae's story in their national histories.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Excavations of its walled capitals and tombs show a state that mixed Goguryeo, Mohe and Tang traditions.
The Khitan under Yelü Abaoji, founder of what became the Liao dynasty, took the capital Sanggyeong in 926 after a campaign of a few weeks. Refugees from the ruling class moved south into Goryeo.

sectionTitles: Work, homes and the struggle for freedom

passages.text: Barbados’s island history long predates the plantation colony. Archaeology records shell tools, pottery and fishing, while Bridgetown’s buildings reveal the organization of colonial trade and slavery. Independence in 1966 and the republic established in 2021 are distinct political changes within a continuing society.

passages.title: Discoveries and earlier island life
passages.text: At Heywoods, a conch-shell adze from archaeological Context 7 produced a calibrated date range of 2530 to 2200 BCE. The shaped shell is evidence of toolmaking before pottery became common on the island. The dating study also discusses contamination and marine-shell problems, so this evidence does not establish an exact arrival year for the first islanders.

passages.title: Discoveries and earlier island life
passages.text: Excavators at Heywoods washed deposits through fine mesh to recover small fish bones. Elizabeth Wing identified an assemblage dominated by open-water fish, especially flying fish and tuna, alongside fewer reef fish. Shell remains also point to collecting around mangroves and the shore. These finds reveal varied coastal food gathering in the precolonial settlement landscape.

passages.title: Discoveries and earlier island life
passages.text: The later Heywoods settlement produced footed bowls, animal and human pottery ornaments, and a spindle whorl. Shell adzes, beads and cut conch added evidence of manufacture. These finds connect food preparation, ornament and textile-related work; pottery classifications describe material traditions rather than proving a single ethnic identity.

passages.title: Work, homes and the struggle for freedom
passages.text: The 1661 slave code tried to control movement through written passes and ordered overseers to search enslaved people’s houses twice weekly for fugitives. It also specified an annual clothing allowance. These provisions expose intrusion into domestic life and mobility; a written requirement does not demonstrate that clothing was actually supplied or that people complied.

passages.title: Work, homes and the struggle for freedom
passages.text: The rebellion that began on 14 April 1816 was organized across estates. Participants included Bussa, an estate ranger, the carpenter King Wiltshire and Nanny Grigg, a literate domestic worker. Colonial forces defeated the uprising, but its organization shows enslaved people using occupational contacts and knowledge in their struggle for freedom.

passages.title: Work, homes and the struggle for freedom
passages.text: Much surviving documentation of the rebellion comes from officials who suppressed it. The National Archives presents governors’ letters and military reports for critical reading, alongside a sketch of an insurgent flag. These sources preserve evidence of resistance through the language and interests of colonial authorities; their viewpoint requires interpretation.

passages.title: Work, homes and the struggle for freedom
passages.text: For some Barbadian families, moving house meant moving the actual house. Wooden chattel houses stood on blocks and could be taken apart and relocated. Residents might own the building but rent plantation land beneath it, so portability helped preserve their home when a landowner required them to leave. A clever building method answered a very real insecurity.

passages.title: Buildings, representation and creative achievement
passages.text: Bridgetown’s winding streets, warehouses and dock facilities record a port built around commerce. Buildings adapted European forms to tropical conditions, including storage designed against storms and damage to goods. The same harbour infrastructure supported the traffic in enslaved people, so architectural achievement and the coercive economy that sustained it must be considered together.

passages.title: Buildings, representation and creative achievement
passages.text: Samuel Jackman Prescod entered the House of Assembly in 1843, after free men of colour meeting property requirements had gained voting rights. More than a century later, Edna Bourne became the first woman elected to the House in the 1951 adult-suffrage election. These changes broadened institutions whose early membership had been tied to property.

passages.title: Buildings, representation and creative achievement
passages.text: Crop Over developed from end-of-harvest celebrations and was revived as a national festival in 1974. The decorated cart parade recalled plantation transport and drew extensive local participation. Other early events attracted criticism for favouring visitors and wealthier audiences, making the festival’s development a debate about who could take part and whose culture it represented.

passages.title: Buildings, representation and creative achievement
passages.text: Kamau Brathwaite made Barbadian places central to works including Mother Poem, Sun Poem and Barabajan Poems. The editors of Poui describe his attention to beaches, villages, canefields and threatened landscapes, as well as experiments in rhythm and language. His writing gave these environments literary importance while questioning how they were being transformed.

passages.title: Buildings, representation and creative achievement
passages.text: In a 2021 interview, spoken-word artist Adrian Green emphasized differences among the speech of Barbadian parishes and neighbourhoods. His performances use the language he speaks in daily life. Rather than treating the island as having one uniform voice, he describes local variation as a resource for artistic expression and communication.

British colonial rule ended with independence in 1966. Becoming a republic in 2021 changed the head of state of an already independent country. Barbados continues as a nation, and its separate map records represent coverage intervals rather than successive disappearances and refoundings.

sectionTitles: A mountain in history and memory
Homes that are works of art
Music at work, at home and in healing

passages.text: Lesotho’s national story took shape around Moshoeshoe I’s mountain stronghold at Thaba Bosiu. Clay sculptures of parents, children and musicians bring everyday lives into this history alongside rulers and political events.

passages.title: A mountain in history and memory
passages.text: Thaba Bosiu became Moshoeshoe I’s political centre in 1824. Lesotho’s heritage account describes stone walls, gateways and lookout posts strengthening the plateau’s natural defences. It also records an oral tradition that the mountain grew taller at night. That story belongs to how the place was remembered and understood; it is not a measurement of a mountain changing height.

passages.title: Homes that are works of art
passages.text: Writing in 2020, artist ‘Matsooana Sekokotoana explains how Basotho women decorated homes with litema. Designs were worked into damp earth plaster, sometimes with coloured stones making a mosaic. Cow dung helped bind the mud. The wall was a surface for skilled pattern-making as well as shelter. Her account describes a practice that has become less common as building methods change.

passages.title: Homes that are works of art
passages.text: Sekokotoana also describes a ceramic plate she made using two litema designs: boliba, associated with deep water, and lihlaba, with hills or mountains. She arranged them to evoke Lesotho’s landscape. She recalls her father encouraging patience, a lesson she connected with the careful painting. Family advice and the patterns of home found another life on a plate.

passages.title: Getting dressed for the mountains
passages.text: A blanket made around 2012 and held by the British Museum combines black and turquoise with four red vertical stripes. Its feather design belongs to the Victoria England range. The catalogue identifies wool and cotton, and manufacture at Aranda’s mill in Randfontein, South Africa. An object associated with Basotho dress can also reveal production and trade across the border.

passages.title: Getting dressed for the mountains
passages.text: The museum explains that wearing blankets are wrapped around the body and secured at the shoulders, providing warmth in Lesotho’s cold mountain conditions. The familiar stripes usually run vertically when worn. A blanket can be part of getting dressed as well as going to bed. The catalogue describes a living clothing tradition with different designs, rather than one outfit worn by everyone.

passages.title: Little sculptures, everyday people
passages.text: Samuele Makoanyane, who lived from 1909 to 1944, made small clay figures of people around him. Iziko’s collection includes a woman feeding a baby and another rolling a sleeping mat. These are an artist’s representations, not photographs of every household. Their subjects put childcare and ordinary work into a museum collection alongside portraits of kings and warriors.

passages.title: Little sculptures, everyday people
passages.text: In 1935, collector Percival Kirby commissioned Makoanyane to model musicians and their instruments. Seven figures were completed, including a herdboy playing the lesiba and a woman with a drum. The exhibition lets viewers examine these fragile sculptures as digital models. Close attention to the tiny players helps preserve evidence of performance as well as the sculptor’s individual skill.

passages.title: Music at work, at home and in healing
passages.text: A lesiba combines a stick, a stretched string and a quill. Pusetso Nyabela’s 2022 museum report describes players using their breath to make the quill vibrate, rather than simply plucking a tune. Associated with shepherds, the instrument also supplied a familiar sound before Radio Lesotho’s news. Small materials can make a very distinctive voice.

passages.title: Music at work, at home and in healing
passages.text: A revival project in 2007 and 2008 found older women in Leribe who still played the lekope, with instruments hanging on their house walls. The report describes a string stretched along a reed and a player’s mouth shaping the sound. Skills that seemed to be disappearing were still present in particular homes.

passages.title: Music at work, at home and in healing
passages.text: Recordings from the late 1950s and early 1960s documented the lekope in hlophe, a ritual healing dance. Nyabela discusses music, singing, clapping and beliefs about ancestral help. These recordings preserve accounts of healing and performance; they do not test the medical effectiveness of a treatment.

passages.title: Reading, learning and remembering families
passages.text: Morija’s archives preserve Leselinyana, a newspaper first published in 1863, alongside church registers, letters, government reports and Sesotho hymnals. French, Sesotho and English all appear in the collections. Such records let researchers follow reading, music and public debate through time. A newspaper’s small notices can open questions quite different from those answered by a royal portrait.

passages.title: Reading, learning and remembering families
passages.text: The Hub at Morija opened in 2015 as a place for digital creativity. The museum describes internet access and training in photography, film, writing and information technology. It connects a town known for historical collections with new ways of making and sharing stories. Learning about the past can happen in the same community as learning to use a camera or computer.

passages.title: Reading, learning and remembering families
passages.text: David-Frédéric Ellenberger collected oral histories and genealogies from 1866 to 1905. His interview notes, letters and maps survive at Morija, and a British Library project digitised the archive. The notes offer evidence about families and remembered events, but they also reflect what a missionary asked and chose to record. Preserving a source includes understanding the viewpoint through which it was made.

passages.title: Paintings older than the kingdom
passages.text: A 2013 heritage evaluation describes Sehlabathebe’s rock paintings in shelters and overhangs: human figures, animals including eland, and colours from earthy yellow to dark red and white. These works belong to San histories that extend beyond the later story of the Basotho kingdom. Interpreting their spiritual meanings takes research; a painted animal is not automatically a literal record of a hunting trip.

British rule ended on 4 October 1966. Lesotho continues as an independent kingdom, with later changes of government forming part of its history. The map’s Basutoland and Lesotho records do not represent the extinction and replacement of three separate peoples.

sectionTitles: Care, creative tools and political change

passages.text: Belize’s communities share knowledge through food, music and learning. Cassava bread, house-to-house celebrations and teaching in several languages offer glimpses of everyday creativity across its diverse traditions.

passages.title: Discoveries: homes and gathering places
passages.text: At Ta’ab Nuk Na in southern Belize, wooden posts survive beneath a lagoon. A building dated about 650 to 780 CE contained serving bowls, a spindle whorl for spinning fibre and part of a maize-grinding stone. Researchers interpret it as a home beside salt kitchens. Making salt could be household work, with the workshop very close to the front door.

passages.title: Discoveries: homes and gathering places
passages.text: The same site yielded a small ceramic whistle shaped as a woman, with its sound chamber behind the figure. It belongs to the Late Classic phase and resembles examples from Lubaantun, where it may have been made. This object adds music to a place studied for its industry, although we cannot identify its player or its occasions of use.

passages.title: Discoveries: homes and gathering places
passages.text: South of Lamanai’s first Spanish-period church, archaeologists uncovered broad descending terraces edged with stone. The church dates to roughly 1544 to 1550. Elizabeth Graham interprets the terrace space as a courtyard where religious gatherings and teaching could take place. The stones show the layout; descriptions of exactly how people used it remain a reconstruction from comparative evidence.

passages.title: Work, food and family knowledge
passages.text: Colonial timber exports depended on enslaved Africans working in Belize’s forests, first for logwood and later mahogany. NICH’s historians describe dangerous camp conditions as well as resistance. The people doing this work also brought and reshaped languages, traditions and skills. A shipment of timber therefore represents human lives and coerced labour, as well as trees.

passages.title: Work, food and family knowledge
passages.text: Garifuna writer I. Myrtle Palacio describes making ereba, cassava bread, through grating, straining, sifting and baking. Her 2024 publication documents the specialised work behind a familiar food. A root does not simply volunteer to become bread. Tools, practiced hands and knowledge turn it into something to share.

passages.title: Work, food and family knowledge
passages.text: In the same book, Palacio captions a photograph of a child pounding plantain in a hana, a mortar, for hudut. It is a small, specific glimpse of a child taking part in food preparation. The photograph does not tell us the child’s name or daily chores, but it records learning and work happening beyond a classroom.

passages.title: Social life and education
passages.text: At Gales Point Manatee, Krismos Bram takes music from house to house at Christmas and on Boxing Day. Singers, drummers and dancers move through the village, and host families offer homemade cakes and drinks. The songs use call and response and tell of community experiences. Here a celebration has both a rhythm and a route.

passages.title: Social life and education
passages.text: A new building for Gulisi Primary School in Dangriga opened in 2011. Belize’s report to UNESCO describes the National Garifuna Council’s school teaching Garifuna, English and Spanish, alongside music, dance and other cultural knowledge. The example shows a community bringing language preservation into formal education, with children participating in several linguistic worlds.

passages.title: Social life and education
passages.text: The same heritage report describes a programme at Bullet Tree where children learned gardening and plant knowledge from community practitioners. The work connected growing things with local traditions concerning medicinal plants. This is evidence of how knowledge was shared; the report does not establish whether particular remedies worked. A garden could be a place for learning across generations.

passages.title: Care, creative tools and political change
passages.text: The wooden building that now houses the San Ignacio-Santa Elena House of Culture served as a hospital from the 1920s to 2009. NICH describes its later use for exhibitions, workshops, music and community activities. A building once associated with medical care gained another public role. Its changing uses preserve a local history that extends beyond monuments to rulers.

passages.title: Care, creative tools and political change
passages.text: In 2024, NICH staff and visiting Maya university interns used photogrammetry, creating three-dimensional models from photographs, to document cultural objects. These included Garifuna drums and a contemporary Maya ceramic bowl. The project brought technical learning together with living traditions, allowing objects to be studied digitally while their makers’ and communities’ knowledge remained essential to understanding them.

passages.title: Care, creative tools and political change
passages.text: Belize’s steps toward independence happened at different times: internal self-government in 1964, the change of name from British Honduras in 1973, and independence in 1981. Changing a name and changing political status are distinct events. Keeping them separate helps explain why older records use another name for the country.

British colonial rule ended with independence on September 21, 1981. Belize continues as an independent country, and its communities sustain their cultural life. The earlier map interval ending in 1715 does not mark their disappearance.

passages.text: Benin's court commissioned brass sculpture to preserve royal memory and express authority. This Edo kingdom was centered in present-day Nigeria, distinct from the modern country named Benin.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: An incoming oba commissioned a commemorative head honoring his predecessor. These idealized royal images emphasize kingship rather than individual facial likeness.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Brass-casting guild artists produced rectangular plaques for the palace. A surviving example is dated approximately 1540 to 1570.

passages.title: Architecture
passages.text: Palace courtyards and galleries included wooden pillars covered with cast brass plaques.

passages.title: Historical memory
passages.text: Scholars interpret palace plaques as an archive later consulted about court ritual and regalia.

passages.title: Historical evidence
passages.text: British removal of royal works in 1897 disrupted their original contexts. Scholars therefore combine stylistic and material evidence when reconstructing their chronology.

sectionTitles: Homes and food in the archaeological record

passages.text: The Beothuk were an Indigenous people of Newfoundland whose food, travel and settlement connected the island’s coasts with its interior. Archaeologists trace their history through the Little Passage complex and later sites containing European materials. Houses, tools, food remains and Shanawdithit’s drawings preserve evidence of skills and choices that written colonial accounts often overlooked.

passages.title: Homes and food in the archaeological record
passages.text: At Boyd’s Cove, discarded shellfish helped neutralize acidic soil, preserving tiny fish bones that usually disappear at Newfoundland sites. Smelt bones and remains of seals, caribou, birds and other animals reveal a varied diet. This preservation accident matters: what an excavation recovers depends partly on soil conditions, not only on what people once ate.

passages.title: Homes and food in the archaeological record
passages.text: Excavators identified eleven house pits at Boyd’s Cove. Most were roughly round or many-sided, while two were oval. Depressions, bark-covered frameworks and earth around the edges offered substantial shelter. Refuse deposited in abandoned pits records later use of those spaces; it should not all be treated as objects left exactly where residents used them.

passages.title: Homes and food in the archaeological record
passages.text: Seasonal movement allowed people to obtain foods that appeared at different times and places. Coastal marine animals, inland caribou, fish and berries required different knowledge and equipment. A community’s territory therefore included routes and temporary camps as well as larger settlements; one village cannot stand for every household’s annual movements.

passages.title: Homes and food in the archaeological record
passages.text: Drying and sometimes smoking made salmon and other foods keep longer. Accounts also describe cooking in birchbark containers by adding heated stones to water. These methods joined knowledge of heat, materials and storage with the work of feeding a household. The surviving descriptions do not establish that every meal or every community used identical methods.

passages.title: Making tools and interpreting discoveries
passages.text: Little Passage arrowheads and small hide scrapers from Inspector Island show skilled working of chert. At other sites, such stone tools occur below later deposits containing reworked iron. This sequence is one reason archaeologists connect the Little Passage tradition with the historical Beothuk, rather than interpreting European metal as evidence of an entirely new population.

passages.title: Making tools and interpreting discoveries
passages.text: Nails recovered from seasonally abandoned European fishing stations became projectile points and hide-working tools; fishhooks could become awls. Wrought iron could be reshaped without a forge and bent back when damaged. This was selective adaptation of a useful material to local needs, not the invention of iron or simple dependence on finished European products.

passages.title: Making tools and interpreting discoveries
passages.text: An oval house at Boyd’s Cove contained a long central hearth with finely broken, burnt bone. Researchers compare it with Innu feasting practices in which processed caribou bones had nutritional and spiritual importance. The hearth and bone are excavated evidence; the precise ceremony is an interpretation by comparison, not a witnessed Beothuk ritual.

passages.title: Communities, encounters and surviving records
passages.text: Campsites and burials are known from many of Newfoundland’s bays, while house depressions also survive beside the Exploits River and the lake historically called Red Indian Lake. This distribution records occupation across different times. It does not establish that one centralized government controlled the entire island at every date shown on the map.

passages.title: Communities, encounters and surviving records
passages.text: A larger camp could serve as a base while smaller parties used other places for particular resources. Pastore’s reconstruction of Boyd’s Cove contrasts nearby summer foods with harp-seal hunting farther out toward islands and headlands. Such patterns help explain why access to coast and interior both mattered as European settlement increasingly restricted movement.

passages.title: Communities, encounters and surviving records
passages.text: Shanawdithit’s drawings depict tools, foods, dwellings and encounters with settlers. They preserve knowledge offered by a Beothuk observer, alongside archaeological evidence and outside descriptions. Her work was produced under painful conditions after severe losses in her family and community; it is testimony with a particular history, not an anonymous illustration of a timeless culture.

Colonial encroachment, violence, reduced access to food and disease devastated Beothuk communities. Shanawdithit’s death in 1829 is often used to mark their disappearance as a distinct recorded society. Accounts of possible survivors and descendants complicate a claim that every Beothuk person died then. The map’s earlier endpoints are not extinction dates.

passages.text: Botswana’s history includes many communities and languages. Colonial Bechuanaland became an independent republic in 1966. Family teaching, craft businesses, schools and community museums reveal histories that continue beyond changes of government.

passages.title: Family lessons in clay
passages.text: Among the Bakgatla ba Kgafela in Kgatleng, UNESCO’s 2012 account describes women shaping pots by hand. They build from the base toward the rim, smooth the clay with a wooden paddle and fire the finished vessels in a pit kiln. A useful pot begins well before dinner: preparing the earth, shaping it and firing it all take skill.

passages.title: Family lessons in clay
passages.text: The same account describes daughters and granddaughters learning by watching experienced potters and practising. Pots serve several household purposes, including storing water, cooking and fermenting sorghum beer. This is education through repeated, practical work. UNESCO also recorded difficulties passing on the craft as experienced makers became fewer and cheaper mass-produced containers competed with their pots.

passages.title: Baskets, family and conversation
passages.text: Basket maker Thitaku Kushanya recalls starting at home in Etsha 6 when she was five, learning from her mother. She says she sold her first basket at eight for one pula and fifty thebe. This is her own remembered childhood, not a rule about when all children learned. A carefully made basket could be both a family lesson and a first sale.

passages.title: Baskets, family and conversation
passages.text: Research published in 2017 describes women weaving together in courtyards while children played nearby. In interviews, makers explained how sales paid for food, schooling and healthcare. The basket on a shop shelf was therefore connected to conversation, patient work and household budgets. These accounts come from particular communities in Ngamiland, rather than a survey of every family in Botswana.

passages.title: Baskets, family and conversation
passages.text: The study photographs patterns called Ribs of the Giraffe and Flight of the Swallow in baskets from Gumare and Maun. Makers used narrow palm strips, coloured with roots and bark. One photograph shows a needle opening a hole for the next stitch. The animal belongs to the design: no giraffe is required in the sewing kit.

passages.title: Baskets, family and conversation
passages.text: The Kavora women’s basketry collective explains that its name comes from its home ward within the Etsha villages. Putting that name on a basket identifies the people and place behind it. The group connects sharing its craft with its ambition to provide a sustainable livelihood for daughters and granddaughters. A basket can carry a maker’s hopes for the future as well as a pattern.

passages.title: Learning, with a little help from cattle
passages.text: Botswana’s 1976 university appeal invited public support for a larger campus. The university later recorded donations of cattle, money, grain and eggs. Contributions took forms that different households could offer. The campaign is remembered in a statue outside the library. A university can begin with books and building plans, but in this case its fundraising history also includes a herd.

passages.title: Learning, with a little help from cattle
passages.text: At Swaneng Hill near Serowe, Patrick van Rensburg developed an approach linking secondary education with practical skills. An account written in 1999 explains that its associated brigades offered school-leavers work and training in construction trades. Lessons could involve making and building as well as reading. This was a particular educational experiment, not the curriculum of every Botswana school.

passages.title: A new country, and a very big evening
passages.text: For part of the colonial period, the Attorney General’s office serving Bechuanaland was in Mafikeng, across the border in South Africa. Its own institutional history records a move to Gaberones by 1965. Following an office’s address can reveal political change: administrative work was moving into the territory as independence approached. The older spelling Gaberones refers to today’s Gaborone.

passages.title: A new country, and a very big evening
passages.text: A contemporary Kutlwano announcement looked ahead to independence celebrations in September 1966. It promised hilltop bonfires as the new flag replaced the British flag at midnight leading into 30 September. Reading the announcement brings the anticipation into view: the political change was also being planned as a public occasion. It records what organizers intended, rather than proving every planned bonfire took place.

passages.title: Everyday work becomes history
passages.text: A women’s club in the BORAVAST area, active from the late 1960s, brought together activities such as sewing, crochet and baking bread. Research completed in 2024 traces how this work developed into a community museum project, with fundraising and local partnerships. A museum’s story can begin with people making useful things together, rather than with a royal collection.

passages.title: Everyday work becomes history
passages.text: The Tsodilo hills preserve thousands of rock paintings alongside a much longer archaeological record. UNESCO describes traces of human activity across at least 100,000 years, with gaps. That does not make all the paintings 100,000 years old. Their individual dates are often uncertain, and the painted record extends into much more recent centuries. Different kinds of evidence keep different clocks.

passages.title: Everyday work becomes history
passages.text: Tsodilo is also a sacred landscape for Hambukushu and San communities. UNESCO records continuing associations with ancestral spirits, hills and water holes. Archaeologists study physical traces, while communities maintain relationships with the place. These are distinct kinds of knowledge, and a heritage designation does not turn a living sacred place into merely an outdoor picture gallery.

British rule ended with independence on 30 September 1966. Botswana continues as a republic. The older map record’s endpoint in 1938 and the later record’s opening in 1960 are coverage dates, not the disappearance and rebirth of the country’s people.

passages.text: Buganda grew around the Kabaka, chiefs and clans in the Lake Victoria region. Its history can also be read in barkcloth workshops, the wooden architecture of Kasubi and recordings of court musicians. Royal government changed under colonial rule and was later abolished; Baganda cultural life and a restored royal institution continue.

passages.title: Buildings that preserve knowledge
passages.text: Kasubi's palace became a royal burial ground in 1884. The main building, Muzibu Azaala Mpanga, used a circular plan, a domed thatched roof and wooden supports. Monumental architecture here depended on skilled work with plant materials, rather than masonry.

passages.title: Buildings that preserve knowledge
passages.text: The documented interior combined palm-frond structural rings with long poles wrapped in barkcloth. A drum house and gatehouse faced the courtyard. These details connect construction, textile work and ceremonial movement within one royal compound.

passages.title: Buildings that preserve knowledge
passages.text: After the destructive 2010 fire, restoration drew on surviving building knowledge as well as documentation. Kasubi left UNESCO's danger list in 2023. Conservation work announced in 2026 addresses disaster preparation, site management and community participation.

passages.title: Barkcloth and household work
passages.text: Craftspeople harvest the Mutuba tree's inner bark in the wet season and beat it with wooden mallets. Working under an open shed keeps it from drying too quickly. Repeated skilled handling produces a soft sheet from bark, without weaving threads.

passages.title: Barkcloth and household work
passages.text: Barkcloth served as bedding, curtains, storage material and clothing as well as ceremonial dress. Its household uses place the craft within ordinary work and comfort, alongside the royal and funerary settings in which it remains especially visible.

passages.title: Barkcloth and household work
passages.text: UNESCO identifies Ngonge clan craftspeople and a hereditary chief craftsman as custodians of this knowledge. Imported cotton reduced demand during the nineteenth century. Continued ceremonial use and later promotion helped sustain skills through a changing textile economy.

passages.title: Listening to musicians across generations
passages.text: The 2021 album Buganda Royal Music Revival places archival sessions beside recordings made in 2017. Its credits name recordists and dates, allowing listeners to distinguish historical documentation from later performances rather than treating all tracks as one ancient sound.

passages.title: Listening to musicians across generations
passages.text: The collection includes the endongo lyre, the large akadinda xylophone and an entenga ensemble of tuned drums. These are different approaches to melody, resonance and ensemble coordination, not interchangeable examples of drumming.

passages.title: Listening to musicians across generations
passages.text: Performers credited include lyre player Albert Bisaso Ssempeke and royal harpist Temutewo Mukasa. Naming musicians preserves individual artistic work within a court tradition too often described only through kings and ceremonies.

passages.title: Councils and changing authority
passages.text: The Lukiiko developed from advisory councils of chiefs and clan heads. Its organization changed during the nineteenth century and under the 1900 agreement. Its present cultural and consultative role should not be projected unchanged onto earlier royal government.

passages.title: Councils and changing authority
passages.text: Article 118 of Uganda's 1967 constitution explicitly abolished royal offices. For Buganda it made that provision effective from 24 May 1966. This distinction explains why histories mention both years when describing the suppression of the kingdom.

Buganda's royal political institutions were suppressed during the 1966 crisis and the constitutional changes of 1967. Their restoration in 1993 established a cultural role within Uganda. Baganda communities, crafts and music continued across that interruption; the map's final snapshot is not their disappearance.

passages.text: Bunyoro in western Uganda connected royal institutions with farming, exchange and specialist production. At Kibiro, pottery and living salt-working practices reveal a history beyond royal genealogies. British conquest reshaped the kingdom; later abolition and cultural restoration of the monarchy are separate from the continuing lives of Banyoro communities.

passages.title: What Kibiro's archaeology reveals
passages.text: Excavations at Kibiro on Lake Albert uncovered abundant pottery associated with a salt-producing settlement. In his 1991 report, Graham Connah placed the origins of this important economic center early in the second millennium CE. This is evidence about a settlement and livelihood, not a secure founding date for Bunyoro.

passages.title: What Kibiro's archaeology reveals
passages.text: Many Kibiro pots carried patterns impressed with roulettes, including carved rollers. Connah interpreted these as connections toward the upper Nile or regions farther west. Similar decoration supports comparison and contact; it does not by itself identify the makers' language or ethnicity.

passages.title: What Kibiro's archaeology reveals
passages.text: Uganda's heritage submission identifies pottery used in leaching and boiling salt. Broken vessels therefore preserve traces of an industrial process as well as decorative choices. Its broad dates are less precise than a dated excavation context and should be used cautiously.

passages.title: Women's work and salt-making skill
passages.text: At Kibiro, workers spread and recycle earth over salt gardens so saline water rises into it. They collect the salty material, leach it and boil the resulting liquid to crystallize salt. The sequence combines knowledge of soil, water and heat.

passages.title: Women's work and salt-making skill
passages.text: Women carry out the salt work and inherit rights to garden plots through female relationships. These arrangements tie expertise to access to a productive place. Fishing complements salt production in the lakeshore economy.

passages.title: Women's work and salt-making skill
passages.text: Kibiro was proposed on Uganda's World Heritage Tentative List in 2025. That proposal documents a living workplace, not simply an abandoned ruin. Tentative status is distinct from inscription on the World Heritage List.

passages.title: Names, meals and social ties
passages.text: Empaako is an additional name used among Banyoro and neighboring communities. Addressing someone by this name can express affection and respect or ease tension. It identifies a relationship between people rather than merely distinguishing one individual from another.

passages.title: Names, meals and social ties
passages.text: In UNESCO's documented naming ceremony, paternal aunts consider the child's resemblance to relatives and the clan head announces the name. A meal of millet and smoked beef, gifts and a planted tree follow. Household ritual joins kinship with food and obligations of care.

passages.title: Names, meals and social ties
passages.text: The tradition entered UNESCO's Urgent Safeguarding List in 2013 because transmission and use of its associated language were weakening. Recognition concerns support for a living practice; it does not mean that the community or naming tradition had ended.

passages.title: Political change and its consequences
passages.text: The British-Buganda coalition defeated and deported Kabarega in 1899. Colonial incorporation and the transfer of territory changed the scale and authority of Bunyoro. These events concerned a political kingdom whose people and dynasty continued afterward.

passages.title: Political change and its consequences
passages.text: Historian G. N. Uzoigwe interprets Bunyoro's contraction through interacting causes: decisions by rulers, disease affecting people and animals, and violent British conquest. This is a historical argument about a long crisis, not evidence for one battle explaining every loss.

passages.title: Political change and its consequences
passages.text: In the 1964 referendum, voters in Buyaga and Bugangaizi chose a return to Bunyoro after their earlier transfer to Buganda under colonial rule. The vote shows that territorial change also involved local political choices, not only decisions made at royal courts.

Conquest in the late nineteenth century ended Bunyoro's independent political power. Uganda abolished kingship in 1967, and the monarchy returned with cultural functions in 1994. Banyoro communities and practices continued through those changes. Neither the salt village's age nor the map's last snapshot establishes a single lifetime for the kingdom.

passages.text: Caddo peoples built distinct river-valley communities linked by language, kinship and exchange. House traces, a surviving canoe and pottery reveal skilled work alongside farming and ceremonial life. Colonial dispossession forced major movements, but Caddo people continued and today sustain the Caddo Nation and renewed artistic traditions.

passages.title: Homes, hearths and travel
passages.text: At the George C. Davis site in east Texas, excavators found overlapping post patterns left by wooden buildings. Radiocarbon evidence places the main community between the ninth and early fourteenth centuries. Buildings were repeatedly renewed as people lived around ceremonial mounds.

passages.title: Homes, hearths and travel
passages.text: A magnetic survey detected structures invisible on the surface. Excavation in 2003 confirmed one large building with a central hearth and four internal roof supports. The pattern reveals engineering and interior space, although it does not identify every activity or occupant.

passages.title: Homes, hearths and travel
passages.text: A dugout canoe eroding from a Red River bluff in northwestern Louisiana was radiocarbon dated to about 1000 CE. The surviving wooden vessel gives direct evidence of water transport beyond later written descriptions.

passages.title: Food and shared work
passages.text: Late-seventeenth-century accounts describe corn stored in raised granaries, seed kept for planting and dried beans, squash and fruit. Storage helped households bridge seasonal shortages. These accounts mainly concern Hasinai communities and cannot describe every Caddo settlement.

passages.title: Food and shared work
passages.text: Housebuilding, planting and harvest brought people together. Maternal kinship connected households, while chiefs consulted community elders. Such relationships organized practical work as well as public decisions.

passages.title: Pottery as technology and art
passages.text: Caddo potters built vessels by joining coils of prepared clay to a base, then thinning and smoothing the walls. Temper mixed into clay and controlled drying helped a vessel survive manufacture and firing. Cooking pots and decorated bottles required different choices of shape and finish.

passages.title: Pottery as technology and art
passages.text: Engraved designs cut across a vessel's surface, unlike incised lines pressed into damp clay. Researchers and potters debate whether some ancient engraving occurred before or after firing. Modern experiments illuminate the skill without proving one method was universal.

passages.title: Pottery as technology and art
passages.text: Jereldine Redcorn's 1998 bottle Taysha has hollow tripod feet containing clay balls that rattle. Its form joins visual pattern with sound. It is a documented modern artwork drawing on ancestral pottery, not an excavated ancient vessel.

passages.title: Pottery as technology and art
passages.text: Redcorn learned through study, experiment and conversations with archaeologists when there was no local group of elder potters to teach her. Her work shows renewal as active investigation and artistic choice, not simply copying old designs.

passages.title: Dispossession and a continuing Nation
passages.text: The 1835 cession forced Caddo groups from lands in present Louisiana and Arkansas. Families moved toward Texas and, in some cases, Mexico. The agreement did not give them a secure replacement home.

passages.title: Dispossession and a continuing Nation
passages.text: In 1859, renewed pressure forced people from the Brazos reservation to Indian Territory. They left cultivated land and family graves behind. This was a rupture in community life, not the disappearance of Caddo people.

passages.title: Dispossession and a continuing Nation
passages.text: The Caddo Nation's education services include cultural learning and vocational support. These are contemporary institutions serving people with changing needs, alongside the continued importance of language, arts and family histories.

Caddo communities endured repeated dispossession, including the forced move of 1859. The Caddo Nation and Caddo cultural life continue. The end of an imported map interval is not an extinction date, and the many earlier communities should not be treated as a single kingdom with one fall.

passages.text: Cao Wei was the most powerful of the Three Kingdoms, controlling the northern heartland of China. Founded by Cao Cao's son Cao Pi, it inherited the Han administrative system and produced significant literary and military achievements.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Cao Cao and his sons Cao Pi and Cao Zhi wrote some of the finest poetry of the age, the Jian'an style named for the last Han reign period.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Cao Pi's Discourse on Literature, the first systematic essay of Chinese literary criticism, argues that writing outlasts rank and wealth.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Ma Jun builds a south-pointing chariot, a cart whose figure keeps pointing south as it turns, through gearing whose design is reconstructed with differential gears.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: The tuntian system of military-agricultural colonies, begun by Cao Cao in 196 under the last Han emperor, settled soldiers and refugees on frontier land.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Administrative innovations passed to the Jin dynasty, among them the nine-rank system for grading officials, introduced in 220.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The fourteenth-century novel Romance of the Three Kingdoms later romanticized this era.
Sima Yan forced the last Wei emperor to abdicate and founded the Jin dynasty, in the last month of 265 by the Chinese calendar, February 266 by ours.

passages.text: Carolingian rulers made learning, Christian worship and patronage part of imperial government. Their workshops and scholars adapted older traditions into books, buildings and objects that influenced medieval Europe.

passages.title: Writing
passages.text: The drive for accurate, readable texts encouraged Carolingian minuscule, a clear script based on Roman letter forms.

passages.title: Learning
passages.text: Charlemagne gathered scholars including Alcuin, Theodulf and Paul the Lombard. Court patronage supported educational and liturgical reform.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Illuminated books and carved ivory panels combined classical figures with local ornamental traditions. Precious bindings could include gems and pearls.

passages.title: Architecture
passages.text: The palace chapel at Aachen has an octagonal core, an encircling aisle, upper galleries and a dome. Its antique columns were probably brought from Rome and Ravenna.

passages.title: Ideas and institutions
passages.text: Charlemagne received the imperial crown in Rome in 800. The ceremony tied royal authority to a Christian interpretation of Roman imperial tradition.

passages.title: Change and continuity
passages.text: Carolingian art continued after Charlemagne's death and political fragmentation. The end of a unified realm did not end its workshops or manuscript traditions.

passages.text: Carthage grew on the Gulf of Tunis into a major center of Punic civilization and Mediterranean commerce. Its ports connected communities, goods and artistic traditions. This card concerns the Punic city and its power before Roman destruction, rather than the later Roman city built on the same site.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: The surviving Punic harbor remains make maritime infrastructure central to understanding Carthage's commercial power.

passages.title: Arts and beliefs
passages.text: Stelae from the sacred tophet show varied cultural influences. The imagery is evidence of artistic exchange as well as religious practice.

passages.title: Knowledge
passages.text: Magon was remembered as an agronomist and Hannon as a navigator. Agriculture and seafaring both belonged to Carthage's intellectual legacy.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Later Roman buildings at Carthage belong to a refounded city. They should not be attributed automatically to Punic builders.
Rome destroyed Punic Carthage in 146 BCE. A Roman city was later established on the site.

passages.text: Champa was a string of Cham kingdoms along the coast of what is now central Vietnam, first recorded by the Chinese as Lin-yi in 192 CE. Seafarers and traders, the Chams built brick towers to Shiva and fought the Khmer and the Vietnamese for more than a thousand years.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Brick tower temples at My Son, built from the seventh to the thirteenth century, with sandstone carving of a fineness that rivals Angkor.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Sandstone images of Shiva, Vishnu, Ganesha and dancing apsaras in the Cham styles of Tra Kieu and Dong Duong.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Cham ports sold agarwood, ivory, gold and cinnamon to China and the archipelago and sheltered ships waiting for the monsoon.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Cham sailors traded and raided across the South China Sea and up the Mekong; they sacked Angkor in 1177.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Shaivism was the royal cult, with Buddhism strong at Dong Duong in the ninth century; Islam reached the Chams from the fifteenth century.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Sanskrit and Cham inscriptions record kings and gifts to temples; the Dong Yen Chau stone of the fourth century is the oldest text in any Southeast Asian language.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: My Son Sanctuary was listed by UNESCO.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Cham communities in Vietnam and Cambodia keep the language and, in Cambodia, Islam.
The Vietnamese took the capital Vijaya in 1471; the last Cham principality, Panduranga, was absorbed by the Nguyen emperor Minh Mang in 1832.

sectionTitles: A writing system becomes a printed public voice

passages.text: Cherokee history includes distinct southeastern communities and continuing nations in Oklahoma and North Carolina. Writing, newspapers, basketry and food knowledge record achievements made by individuals and families as well as governments. Forced removal devastated communities, but Cherokee people rebuilt institutions and maintained connections to their homelands.

passages.title: A writing system becomes a printed public voice
passages.text: Sequoyah developed a syllabary for writing Cherokee. In 1825 the Nation commissioned English and Cherokee type for a press. Adapting a writing system to movable type connected linguistic invention with practical publishing equipment and organization.

passages.title: A writing system becomes a printed public voice
passages.text: The first Cherokee Phoenix appeared at New Echota on 21 February 1828. Its Cherokee and English columns made the same newspaper accessible across languages. Surviving issues are material evidence of Cherokee authorship and political communication before removal.

passages.title: A writing system becomes a printed public voice
passages.text: Publication continued in a new setting with the Cherokee Advocate, established in Tahlequah in 1844. It printed both languages as the Nation rebuilt schools, homes, businesses and government buildings after removal.

passages.title: Baskets, materials and teaching
passages.text: A rivercane basket from the Qualla Boundary, catalogued as 15/8659, was collected in 1927 or 1928. The museum records its twill-plaited construction but does not name its maker. The collection date should not be mistaken for the year it was woven.

passages.title: Baskets, materials and teaching
passages.text: Lottie Queen Stamper recalled her family making white-oak baskets after work in the fields. Preparing splints required carefully splitting wood into usable strips. Her recollection connects an admired finished object to seasonal farm work and demanding preparation.

passages.title: Baskets, materials and teaching
passages.text: Stamper expanded into rivercane and plant dyes, then recorded patterns in notebooks and on graph paper for students. Teaching changed how designs circulated between families and materials while preserving close attention to technique.

passages.title: Baskets, materials and teaching
passages.text: In 1940, Stamper studied a photograph of an older double-weave basket held in Britain and worked out its pattern. Other Cherokee elders still knew this technique. Her achievement strengthened its teaching; describing her as the sole rediscoverer would erase those weavers.

passages.title: Food, language and family knowledge
passages.text: Eastern Cherokee speaker Tommy Cabe describes gathering sochan greens with relatives in spring and later teaching his own children. His account includes care for the plant and gratitude before picking. It documents one living family tradition in its own voice.

passages.title: Food, language and family knowledge
passages.text: Cherokee Nation offers immersion education in Tahlequah, online teaching and a master-apprentice language program. Different ways of learning connect children and adults with speakers, continuing the language beyond what any historic printed page can preserve.

passages.title: Displacement, government and continuity
passages.text: In May 1838, federal troops and state militias began forcing Cherokee families into detention. People often had little time to collect possessions. Subsequent travel by roads and waterways brought further hardship, illness and death.

passages.title: Displacement, government and continuity
passages.text: The 1839 constitution was part of rebuilding, but it did not immediately resolve conflicts between earlier western migrants, removal supporters and those forced west. A new government should not be mistaken for an uncomplicated recovery from dispossession.

passages.title: Displacement, government and continuity
passages.text: Cherokee Nation and the United Keetoowah Band are based in Oklahoma; the Eastern Band is based in North Carolina. Each has its own government and citizenship system. The broad label Cherokee on this map includes histories that need these distinctions.

United States removal policies caused enormous loss of life, homes and land. They did not end Cherokee peoples or political life. Cherokee Nation, the United Keetoowah Band and the Eastern Band continue as distinct nations; the map's eighteenth-century endpoint describes only its available historical coverage.

passages.text: The Chimu kingdom made Chan Chan a major center on Peru's north coast. Its earthen compounds, craft production and water systems show how a large city organized resources in a dry coastal environment.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Canals and irrigation supported agriculture around Chan Chan. Roads helped connect the kingdom along the northern coast.

passages.title: Architecture
passages.text: Large walled compounds contained open courts, temples, dwellings, storage spaces, reservoirs and funerary platforms.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Earthen walls carried relief decoration with abstract patterns and human or animal subjects.

passages.title: Craft and work
passages.text: Specialized production areas supported weaving, woodworking and metalworking. These activities were part of the city's planned fabric.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Storage and water-management installations supported the city alongside agricultural land beyond its monumental center.

passages.title: Change over time
passages.text: The kingdom reached its height in the fifteenth century before incorporation into the Inca Empire. The source used here does not establish a precise conquest year.

passages.text: The Cholas of the Kaveri delta, restored under Vijayalaya in 848, ruled the Tamil south for four centuries and sent fleets across the Bay of Bengal. Their bronze Natarajas, the great temples of Thanjavur and Gangaikonda Cholapuram and their village assemblies are the high point of Tamil civilization.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Rajaraja I finished the Brihadisvara temple at Thanjavur, its granite tower about 66 meters high.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Bronze images of Shiva Nataraja, cast by the lost-wax method, reached their classic form in the tenth and eleventh centuries.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Rajendra I sent a fleet against Srivijaya in 1025 and sacked its ports along the Strait of Malacca.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Merchant guilds such as the Ayyavole Five Hundred traded across the Indian Ocean, and Chola embassies reached Song China in 1015 and 1077.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Tanks, sluices and the Kaveri's old anicuts irrigated the delta's rice fields.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Ocean-going ships carried armies to Sri Lanka, the Maldives and Sumatra.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Village assemblies chose their committees by lot from eligible landholders, as the Uttaramerur inscriptions of the 920s record.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The Great Living Chola Temples were listed by UNESCO.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Chola bronzes and temple styles were carried to Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia.
The Pandyas of Madurai defeated the Cholas repeatedly from the 1210s and absorbed the last of the kingdom by 1279.

sectionTitles: Titles, records and what remains uncertain

passages.text: Medieval Croatian kingship developed among communities whose lives survive in inscriptions, church buildings, tools and human remains. Royal titles and land grants show relationships between rulers and religious institutions; archaeology adds evidence of riding, food and health. The accession of an Arpad ruler in 1102 changed the dynasty while Croatian kingship and local society continued.

passages.title: Titles, records and what remains uncertain
passages.text: Tomislav's royal title survives through copies of papal letters associated with the Split councils, preserved in a much later compilation. The source tradition matters: a copied title is evidence to assess, not a surviving contemporary coronation record.

passages.title: Titles, records and what remains uncertain
passages.text: The familiar coronation at Duvno in 925 arose from later historical reconstruction. The Croatian Encyclopedia explains why that location claim was rejected and why a precise ceremony cannot be confidently reconstructed from the surviving evidence.

passages.title: Titles, records and what remains uncertain
passages.text: The Baska Tablet is a limestone slab originally belonging to the church screen at St Lucy's near Jurandvor on Krk. Carved around 1100, it placed a written record within a building used by a religious community.

passages.title: Titles, records and what remains uncertain
passages.text: Its text records King Zvonimir's gift of land, witnesses and an abbot's account of church construction. The inscription links property, prayer and patronage; damage and difficult readings prevent every personal name and clause from being treated as certain.

passages.title: Titles, records and what remains uncertain
passages.text: The tablet uses Croatian Church Slavonic and Glagolitic letters between rounded and angular forms. Its later reuse in the church floor damaged the surface. Both its script and its wear are part of the evidence for how the stone was used.

passages.title: Objects and ordinary lives
passages.text: A bronze fitting from the cemetery near St George at Putalj was first catalogued as a Gothic buckle. Petrinec reidentified it as part of an early Carolingian spur set, dating to the late eighth or early ninth century.

passages.title: Objects and ordinary lives
passages.text: The Putalj fitting has parallels in the Solin area and graves at Biskupija. It documents connections in riding equipment before the later royal-title evidence, but one imported style cannot establish every rider's birthplace or a whole community's identity.

passages.title: Objects and ordinary lives
passages.text: Bone-collagen analysis at sites including Glavice-Gluvine and Radasinovci-Vinogradine suggests millet contributed to early medieval diets. This is a chemical inference about food consumed, not a surviving meal or proof that everyone followed the same menu.

passages.title: Objects and ordinary lives
passages.text: The later Sibenik-Sveti Lovre sample differs from the other early medieval groups in that study. Its chemistry suggests a different protein mix, possibly including freshwater fish. The researchers' uncertainty is more informative than a single supposed national diet.

passages.title: Objects and ordinary lives
passages.text: At the ninth- to eleventh-century Konjsko cemetery, researchers recorded dental and skeletal signs of stress and disease. Their comparisons help recover the lives of people absent from royal documents, while the small sample limits conclusions about the wider population.

passages.title: Dynastic change and continuing institutions
passages.text: St Mary's cartulary at Zadar records Coloman's 1102 coronation at Biograd. An inscription at St Mary's also supports Zadar's recognition of his rule in 1105, connecting written accounts with a surviving architectural setting.

passages.title: Dynastic change and continuing institutions
passages.text: Pacta conventa survives as a note appended to a manuscript from the 1380s. Most recent scholarship rejects it as an authentic contemporary treaty. A possible agreement with nobles should be distinguished from accepting this later text as its original record.

In 1102 Coloman became king of Croatia and Dalmatia, bringing Croatian kingship under an Arpad ruler. This marks dynastic change rather than the extinction of Croatian society or the royal title. The terms of any contemporary agreement with nobles cannot simply be read from the much later Pacta conventa.
