sectionTitles: Discoveries: houses, handles and carved seats
Toilets, rubbish and traces of leisure

passages.text: Cuba’s history lives in household objects as well as public events. Wooden tools, discarded dishes, readers at work and music shared between generations reveal different kinds of knowledge. The examples below distinguish particular communities and periods across the island’s changing political history.

passages.title: Discoveries: houses, handles and carved seats
passages.text: At Los Buchillones on Cuba’s north coast, archaeologists recovered palm thatch and wooden parts of collapsed buildings. A 2006 study placed occupation before 1220 CE through 1640 or later. One partly excavated structure appeared to stand on pilings over water. The surviving pieces let researchers investigate how homes were built; the precise arrangement of every building is still a matter of reconstruction.

passages.title: Discoveries: houses, handles and carved seats
passages.text: The Los Buchillones wood collection includes axe handles with holes prepared for stone heads, and two grooved fragments interpreted as knife handles. The grooves could hold stone blades. Woodworking supplied the part that fitted a tool to a human hand. The collection combines excavated finds and earlier collected objects, so individual pieces do not all have equally precise find records.

passages.title: Discoveries: houses, handles and carved seats
passages.text: Carved seats called dujos also survive from Los Buchillones. Some were made from a single piece of wood, with sculpted human or animal features and supporting legs. Researchers classify them as ceremonial seats. Their careful carving shows skilled work, but they should not be treated as a sample of every household’s everyday furniture.

passages.title: Toilets, rubbish and traces of leisure
passages.text: At Habana 958 in Old Havana, a latrine cut into bedrock held pottery, glass, bones and seeds from the late eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. Excavators distinguished waste left during use from later rubble used to fill it. An old toilet can preserve clues to meals and household possessions. Archaeology sometimes finds its best reading material in very unglamorous places.

passages.title: Toilets, rubbish and traces of leisure
passages.text: Excavations in 1999 and 2000 at El Padre, a nineteenth-century coffee plantation near Madruga, recovered two circular pieces cut from discarded crockery. The report interprets them as game counters. Such small objects offer glimpses of activities beyond imposed plantation work. They do not establish which game was played or who used each piece.

passages.title: Learning, medicine and family knowledge
passages.text: In a tradition traced to nineteenth-century Cuba, a lector read aloud to cigar workers as they worked. Reading brought literature and political information into the workshop. Historian Araceli Tinajero studied newspapers and interviewed readers to investigate the practice. It is a little like sharing an audiobook with the whole workplace, except the person doing the reading is actually there.

passages.title: Learning, medicine and family knowledge
passages.text: In 1881, Cuban physician Carlos Finlay proposed that mosquitoes carried yellow fever between people. The Yellow Fever Board led by Walter Reed confirmed mosquito transmission in 1900. Finlay’s insight helped change how people investigated and prevented the disease. The distinction between proposing an explanation and testing it is part of the story of scientific discovery.

passages.title: Learning, medicine and family knowledge
passages.text: A photograph taken by the Kaweiro Group in 2015 shows a mother and daughter joining other Native families in eastern Cuba for a workshop about local medicinal plants. The Smithsonian included it in its 2018 Taíno exhibition announcement. It records knowledge being discussed across generations and challenges the idea that Indigenous people vanished. The photograph does not establish whether a particular remedy works.

passages.title: Learning, medicine and family knowledge
passages.text: Cassava bread connects Cuban households with a wider Caribbean tradition. UNESCO’s 2024 account describes variations in thickness, texture and flavour across Cuba and four other countries, with skills commonly passed on at home and within communities. Learning to make a familiar food can also mean learning from an older relative or neighbour. There is no single recipe that represents every family.

passages.title: Music and neighbourhood surprises
passages.text: Rumba combines singing, movement and percussion, with roots in communities including Havana and Matanzas. Instruments can include household or workplace utensils, and the audience joins the exchange through clapping and response. UNESCO’s 2016 account describes children and adults learning through imitation within families and neighbourhoods. A musical education can begin by watching someone nearby and joining in.

passages.title: Music and neighbourhood surprises
passages.text: Punto brings poetry and melody together. Singers perform ten-line stanzas, sometimes learned in advance and sometimes made up as they sing. UNESCO’s 2017 account describes learning by imitation and workshops in Houses of Culture. Improvising a rhyme while keeping a tune takes practice. It gives thinking on your feet a very musical meaning.

passages.title: Music and neighbourhood surprises
passages.text: For Las Parrandas in central Cuba, competing neighbourhoods spend months preparing floats, costumes, lights and decorations. UNESCO’s 2018 account even mentions people trying to discover the other side’s surprise before the celebration. The preparations combine craft skills with friendly suspense: imagine keeping a spectacular float secret from the neighbours. Participation and practices vary between communities.

Spanish sovereignty ended after the 1898 war, followed by U.S. occupation and the republic in 1902. Batista’s government ended in the 1959 revolution. These political transitions did not end Cuban communities or culture, including Indigenous descendants and traditions shared across generations.

passages.text: At Abomey, the royal palaces combined government, skilled craft production and the storage of royal treasures. Their architecture and imagery expressed Aja-Fon traditions and preserved memories of successive rulers.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Palace builders used earthen walls and traditional materials to organize enclosed compounds around courtyards.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Polychrome reliefs gave palace walls a visual language of royal history and symbolism.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Outer, inner and private courtyards structured access through each palace, making social distinctions part of the built environment.

passages.title: Continuity
passages.text: Royal families continue ceremonies and care for sacred places, including royal tombs and structures associated with a king's spirit.

passages.text: Five dynasties of Turkic and Afghan sultans ruled from Delhi from 1206 to 1526, at their height under the Khaljis and Tughluqs reaching the far south. They brought Persian letters, Islamic architecture and Sufi shrines to northern India, and their India shaped the Mughals.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: The Qutb Minar was begun under Qutb al-Din Aibak and finished by Iltutmish; at 72.5 meters it is the tallest brick minaret in the world.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: The true arch and dome arrived with the sultanate; the Alai Darwaza of 1311 is the first building in India built entirely on those principles.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Amir Khusrau of Delhi wrote Persian verse and is credited with the beginnings of Hindustani music and poetry.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Chishti Sufis such as Nizamuddin Auliya drew Hindus and Muslims alike to their shrines and their music.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Persian was the language of court and chancery, and Indo-Persian history writing began with Minhaj-i Siraj and Barani.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Alauddin Khalji fixed market prices and had the land measured for revenue; paper and the spinning wheel spread through India in these centuries.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Persian wheels lifted water for irrigation.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Indo-Islamic culture and the Persian chancery passed to the Mughals.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The Qutb Minar and its monuments were listed by UNESCO.
Babur's guns and cavalry defeated Sultan Ibrahim Lodi at Panipat in April 1526, and the Mughal Empire began.

passages.text: Twentieth-century Copenhagen became a meeting place for physicists working on quantum theory. This focused chapter follows the institute, discussions and everyday arrangements that helped international collaboration take root.

passages.title: Science
passages.text: Bohr's Institute for Theoretical Physics was dedicated in Copenhagen in March 1921, after fundraising and approval of the project.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: During the 1920s, visiting researchers exchanged ideas in Copenhagen. Discussions could happen in small groups and at dinners with the Bohr family.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: In 1927, Bohr presented complementarity: different experimental arrangements can require different, mutually exclusive descriptions of a quantum phenomenon. The proposal became a focus of debate.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: In the 1930s, a new mathematics institute was built beside the physics institute. Shared classrooms and a canteen were intended to support closer collaboration.

passages.text: This chapter follows sixteenth-century Denmark-Norway through astronomy, printing and royal architecture. Tycho Brahe's observatory shows how scientific work depended on buildings, instruments and supporting crafts.

passages.title: Science
passages.text: Under Danish royal patronage, Tycho Brahe built Uraniborg on Hven between 1576 and 1580. The island is now Swedish but was then Danish.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Uraniborg included a printing office and a water mill for making paper. Publishing and material production supported the observatory's work.

passages.title: Science
passages.text: Tycho established Stjerneborg in 1584. Sheltered instrument spaces reduced exposure to wind and helped stabilize observations.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Frederik II began rebuilding Kronborg as a Renaissance castle in 1574. Its courtyard, carved sandstone and decorated chapel formed a major royal setting.

sectionTitles: Discoveries and the limits of the evidence

passages.text: Dominica’s history includes Indigenous pottery, plantation slavery, resistance and an independent republic established in 1978. Its earlier archaeological sites and continuing craft traditions reveal more than changes of government. Creole music, dance and language research show communities making and teaching knowledge across generations.

passages.title: Discoveries and the limits of the evidence
passages.text: At Woodford Hill, Andre Samuel found two nearly complete Cayo pottery jars in an eroding headland in 2004. A later survey recovered pottery, stone flakes, charcoal, fish bones and shells behind an old warehouse. These finds illuminate manufacture and food use, but older material was mixed with modern glass, metal and ceramics.

passages.title: Discoveries and the limits of the evidence
passages.text: At the Eden River mouth, pottery includes incised and modelled decoration, possible griddle fragments and pieces assigned to different ceramic traditions. The mixed deposit records repeated use of the locality. It cannot be treated as one household assemblage or used to prove that a change in pottery meant one people replaced another.

passages.title: Slavery, resistance and freedom
passages.text: Jacko escaped from enslavement at Castle Comfort Estate and established a refuge in the mountainous interior near Belles, at the place now called Jacko Flats. His community sheltered people escaping coastal plantations. He was killed by colonial Rangers in July 1814 during the suppression of Maroon resistance.

passages.title: Slavery, resistance and freedom
passages.text: Dominica’s emancipation observances remember both legal abolition in 1834 and the end of apprenticeship in 1838. Lectures, exhibitions, drumming and bèlè performances connect public history with artistic practice. Remembering the two dates separately helps explain why the first legal change did not immediately end coerced work.

passages.title: Kalinago work and community
passages.text: Sandra Thomas made a wicker-plaited larouma-fibre basket in Dominica in 2002. The Smithsonian records both the artist and the material; its staff member Susan Secakuku bought the basket directly from Thomas the following year. This is documented contemporary craft, with an identified maker, rather than an anonymous archaeological object.

passages.title: Kalinago work and community
passages.text: Kalinago Barana Aute presents craft, cassava-bread making and canoe-building demonstrations led by community practitioners. Its model cultural village includes a covered communal meeting place. These activities make skills available for teaching and paid cultural work; the buildings are a modern interpretation of heritage, not surviving ancient houses.

passages.title: Kalinago work and community
passages.text: The Kalinago account of their territory describes colonial land sales and dispossession, followed by retreat toward the east coast. Recognition of communal land in 1903 did not begin their history. Even when colonial authorities suspended the chief’s office, community members continued to recognize elders as leaders.

passages.title: Music, dance and language
passages.text: Pearle Christian’s description of traditional instruments explains how a tambou bèlè uses rope and pegs to tension its skin: greater tension raises the pitch. Drum bodies can be made from kegs, metal cans or hollowed trunks. The instrument joins practical knowledge of materials with the demands of dance and collective performance.

passages.title: Music, dance and language
passages.text: The bamboo flute has a blowing hole and six finger holes, allowing the player to change pitch. In jing ping music, the accordion supplies a reed-driven melody. These instruments show different routes to a local sound: shaping plant material into an instrument and adapting an imported instrument to Dominican performance.

passages.title: Music, dance and language
passages.text: Daryl Phillip’s 1994 account describes quadrilles as coordinated sequences for four couples. Musicians must understand the steps and change rhythm to suit them. Sequence names vary with place and language: Woodford Hill uses Kokoy terms alongside the Creole names found elsewhere. The dances preserve local differences within a shared form.

passages.title: Music, dance and language
passages.text: Mabel Cissie Caudeiron composed Creole songs, founded the Kairi Artistic Troupe and researched music, dress and dance. She also helped organize the 1965 National Day celebrations. Her work brought practices associated with ordinary Dominican life onto public stages and into written accounts, years before political independence.

passages.title: Music, dance and language
passages.text: Established in 1981, Kommité pou Etid Kwéyòl organized literacy classes and the first Jounen Kwéyòl celebration that October. Its publications include proverbs, riddles called timtim, and a Kwéyòl-English dictionary. This work treats a spoken community language as a medium for reading, teaching and research.

Colonial association with Britain ended in 1978, when Dominica became an independent republic. Kalinago community life and Creole cultural institutions continue. The end of a map interval is not the end of these communities or of the country.

sectionTitles: Discoveries: baskets, containers and colonial buildings
Community learning and looking after one another
Music at gatherings, knowledge at home

passages.text: Craft, care, learning and music illuminate the Dominican Republic’s everyday history. Archaeological finds and living traditions reveal different communities and periods.

passages.title: Discoveries: baskets, containers and colonial buildings
passages.text: Divers at La Aleta, a flooded cavern in the southeast, recovered a woven basket fragment with a published date range of about 1275 to 1435 CE. It unravelled after recovery. The team left other baskets underwater until suitable conservation could be arranged. Keeping fragile finds intact is part of archaeology.

passages.title: Discoveries: baskets, containers and colonial buildings
passages.text: La Aleta also yielded a carved tree-gourd container, dated in the report to roughly 1020 to 1180 CE. Its cut designs resemble patterns on pottery. It shows how a plant could become both a useful vessel and decorated work. Researchers interpret the cavern finds as possible offerings, so a container found there is not automatically kitchen rubbish.

passages.title: Discoveries: baskets, containers and colonial buildings
passages.text: At La Isabela on the north coast, the remains of a warehouse include traces of its outer walls and inner posts. The 1490s settlement combined substantial buildings with palm-thatched housing. Columbus’s residence used rammed earth and cut limestone. These differences show how a colonial town combined several building techniques. They do not mean all residents had the same space, comfort or authority.

passages.title: Care, homes and family records
passages.text: The ruins of San Nicolás de Bari in Santo Domingo preserve the site of a hospital begun in 1503 and enlarged during the early sixteenth century. A government heritage guide describes rebuilding with earth, stone and brick, and later service as a royal and military hospital. Buildings can document organised care even when they cannot tell us how a particular patient felt or whether a treatment succeeded.

passages.title: Care, homes and family records
passages.text: Casa de Tostado is a sixteenth-century stone house now used to display the furnishings of a wealthy nineteenth-century Dominican family. That is two different historical layers: the age of the building and the period represented by its collection. A handsome museum room can reveal household tastes and resources, but it is not a typical home for every family.

passages.title: Care, homes and family records
passages.text: Birth, marriage and death registers help researchers connect generations of Dominican families. The Library of Congress guide points to digitised records and warns that not everything has been indexed for name searches. Sometimes an original register must be browsed page by page. A family-history search can therefore resemble detective work, with handwriting instead of fingerprints.

passages.title: Community learning and looking after one another
passages.text: English-speaking Caribbean migrants and their descendants built Cocolo communities in the Dominican Republic. Alongside work in the sugar economy, they established churches, schools, benevolent societies and mutual assistance lodges. These institutions supported learning and community ties. Their history shows that migration involves creating places to gather and help one another, as well as moving from one island to another.

passages.title: Community learning and looking after one another
passages.text: Cocolo dance drama brings together African musical and dance traditions with stories from biblical and European literature. UNESCO describes performances including David and Goliath, presented at celebrations such as Christmas and carnival. Music, costumes and acting turn a familiar story into a shared community event. Passing on the performances requires opportunities for younger people to learn.

passages.title: Community learning and looking after one another
passages.text: In Villa Mella, members of the Brotherhood of the Holy Spirit play hand-drums called congos. UNESCO describes music, prayer and dancing at festivals and in ceremonies of mourning. Here music helps people celebrate together and remember those who have died. These are practices of a particular community and brotherhood, rather than funeral customs shared by every Dominican household.

passages.title: Music at gatherings, knowledge at home
passages.text: Merengue is danced in pairs to music that can include accordion, drum and saxophone. UNESCO’s 2016 account describes children learning by observing, joining in and imitating others. Social gatherings can become informal classrooms, with the lesson carried in movement and rhythm. It is one kind of homework for which sitting perfectly still would miss the point.

passages.title: Music at gatherings, knowledge at home
passages.text: Bachata groups combine lead guitars with instruments such as bongos, maracas, a güiro and bass. Songs often explore affection, longing and memories. UNESCO’s 2019 description places this music at celebrations and social gatherings, with learning both informally and in schools. A song can give a roomful of people a shared feeling, even though their own stories are different.

passages.title: Music at gatherings, knowledge at home
passages.text: Cassava bread is a round bread made from the cassava root. UNESCO’s 2024 account links Dominican practice with traditions in four other countries, while emphasising differences in texture and flavour. Skills pass through households and communities. A familiar food can carry family knowledge across generations.

The Dominican Republic emerged from Haitian rule in 1844, underwent Spanish annexation in 1861, and regained independence in 1865. Political institutions have changed while communities continue to create, learn and share traditions. The map’s 1878 starting point is not the country’s founding date.

sectionTitles: Discoveries: a cookhouse and its contents
Food tools with stories to tell
Homes, clothes and travelling by river

passages.text: Suriname’s history includes Indigenous and Maroon communities, colonial settlements and migration across oceans. Cooking tools, carved gifts, writing and family records offer different views of everyday knowledge. The examples identify particular places and communities.

passages.title: Discoveries: a cookhouse and its contents
passages.text: At Jodensavanne, excavations of House de Meza in 2020 to 2022 recovered pottery identified as Indigenous and Maroon alongside colonial objects. Work at a nearby cookhouse in 2023 and 2024 found Indigenous pottery in the same layer as colonial artifacts, plus a stone mortar. These finds support research into shared materials and cooking practices. They do not identify the maker or user of every pot, or prove equal relationships in a society shaped by slavery.

passages.title: Discoveries: a cookhouse and its contents
passages.text: The Jodensavanne Foundation’s 2023 cookhouse record includes a nearly complete porcelain plate, part of a stoneware jug and an incomplete iron cauldron undergoing conservation. Different materials brought different qualities to serving, storing and cooking. Even fragments help reconstruct a working household. A recovered jug does not, by itself, reveal what someone drank from it on a particular day.

passages.title: Food tools with stories to tell
passages.text: A basket sifter from Pikin Saron, a Kalina village, has a square wooden frame and loosely woven palm fibres. The Lam Museum’s 2022 account explains how such sifters remove lumps from cassava flour and make its texture more even. Weaving knowledge becomes useful kitchen equipment. Lumpy flour has met its match, without a plug or a battery in sight.

passages.title: Food tools with stories to tell
passages.text: In 2018, visiting Matawai community members explained a decorated calabash spoon in the Smithsonian’s collection. They described this small spoon as a personal utensil for eating rice, with larger examples used for soup. Its bowl was cut from a hard-shelled gourd and decorated with incised designs. Community knowledge helps a museum understand how an object fits into meals and daily life.

passages.title: Food tools with stories to tell
passages.text: A Ndyuka wooden food stirrer in Milwaukee’s collection carries carved personal messages. The museum describes carved utensils given as expressions of affection, with some stirrers used for cooking and more delicate examples kept for their beauty. A practical object can also hold a relationship’s meaning. The caption does not translate this particular message, so its exact words remain unstated here.

passages.title: Homes, clothes and travelling by river
passages.text: The Surinaams Museum preserves a mahogany four-poster bed made in 1829 by the furniture maker Podekowitz on Paramaribo’s Wagenwegstraat. It belongs to a collection rich in furniture associated with the colonial elite. This was substantial, carefully made furniture, rather than a picture of how everyone slept. A single grand bed cannot represent all the country’s bedrooms.

passages.title: Homes, clothes and travelling by river
passages.text: Needlework samplers in the same museum record how young European women practised embroidery and mending in the late nineteenth century. Surviving stitches make learning visible: someone had to repeat a movement, control the thread and improve. The collection also preserves early-twentieth-century baby clothes. These are particular surviving objects, rather than evidence that every family dressed or taught its children alike.

passages.title: Homes, clothes and travelling by river
passages.text: Gerrit Schouten’s 1817 miniature scene shows a riverboat with six enslaved rowers, a steersman and a covered passenger compartment. The shelter has windows with shutters propped open by sticks. The model records both ingenuity and inequality: passengers could travel out of the sun and rain while others did the rowing. It is an artist’s carefully constructed view, not a photograph of a named journey.

passages.title: Writing, families and learning together
passages.text: In the early twentieth century, Afáka Atumisi developed a writing system for Ndyuka. Its signs represent syllables. A 2012 study explains that the sign for tu, meaning two, uses two strokes, while fo, meaning four, uses four. A little counting can help a reading lesson. The system is a distinctive achievement in making spoken language visible, though some signs can represent more than one sound.

passages.title: Writing, families and learning together
passages.text: Immigration registers for indentured workers arriving from British India between 1873 and 1916 can record parents, siblings and other relatives. Officials later added marriages, children and sometimes grandchildren born in Suriname. These documents help descendants reconnect family stories across oceans. Some registers were lost or badly damaged, and spelling varies, so an unsuccessful name search does not show that a person never existed.

passages.title: Writing, families and learning together
passages.text: In September 2024, nineteen volunteers aged 12 to 70 joined a supervised archaeology project at Jodensavanne. Four young participants came from neighbouring Redi Doti, an Indigenous village. The work included excavation, maintenance and conservation; a caption records young volunteers sifting earth for artifacts. Learning about the past can involve patient observation and teamwork as well as books.

passages.title: Writing, families and learning together
passages.text: Jodensavanne’s heritage is cared for through cooperation with Redi Doti. UNESCO describes the Indigenous village and the Jodensavanne Foundation sharing responsibility for preservation and agreeing together on changes to the management plan. This recognises living communities as participants in caring for history. A historic site is also part of someone’s present-day neighbourhood.

Suriname gained internal autonomy in 1954 and became an independent republic in 1975. These changes ended colonial government, not the histories of its communities. Crafts, languages and family knowledge continue through living people, with traditions changing as they are shared.

passages.text: Eastern Wu controlled the Yangzi delta and southern coast under the Sun family. Its naval power and maritime trade connected China to Southeast Asia, while southern China developed economically and culturally.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Shipbuilding for the Yangzi and the sea: the stern-mounted rudder, attested in Han tomb models, and ships with several masts, described by Wu envoys who sailed to the south.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Maritime trade with Southeast Asia and India; in 226 a merchant from the Roman east named Qin Lun reached the Wu court.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Exotic goods imported from the south: pearls, ivory, rhinoceros horn.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Economic development of the Yangzi delta laid foundations for later southern prosperity.
The Jin dynasty launched a massive invasion with naval forces sailing down the Yangzi, forcing Wu to surrender and reunifying China.

passages.text: The Eastern Zhou saw the Zhou kings reduced to figureheads while rival states competed for power. This political fragmentation paradoxically produced China's greatest intellectual flowering, as philosophers offered competing visions of the good society.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Confucius born in the state of Lu; he teaches ethics, proper conduct and the restoration of Zhou ritual.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Mozi advocates universal love and utilitarian ethics as alternatives to Confucianism.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The Daodejing, attributed to the sage Laozi, is in circulation by about 300 BCE, the date of the earliest copies found in a tomb at Guodian; it founds the Daoist philosophy of naturalness and non-action.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Mencius develops Confucian ideas of innate human goodness and the right to rebel against unjust rulers.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Cast iron production begins, allowing mass production of agricultural tools.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Crossbows with bronze trigger mechanisms appear in warfare.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Iron tools replace stone and bronze in agriculture and crafts.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: The Spring and Autumn Annals compiled in Lu, the first Chinese chronicle history, covering 722 to 481 BCE.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: The Zuozhuan and other commentaries elaborate on historical events with narrative detail.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Lacquerware production reaches new heights of craftsmanship, above all in the southern state of Chu.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Walled cities grow as commercial centers with specialized crafts and markets.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Coinage in bronze spade and knife shapes facilitates trade between states.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Professional bureaucrats and scholars travel between courts seeking employment.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Trade networks connect the Yellow River states with the Yangzi valley and the southern coast.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Salt and iron become major commodities in interstate commerce.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The Hundred Schools of Thought established the major philosophical traditions of East Asia.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Military innovations and statecraft from this period influenced later imperial administration.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The concept of a unified Chinese cultural sphere emerged despite political division.
The Qin state conquered the last Zhou territories in 256 BCE, and the last Zhou king died that year, ending the dynasty.

passages.text: Ancient Egypt brought together royal power, skilled workshops and a durable written culture along the Nile. Its art changed substantially across the Old and Middle Kingdoms. Pyramids, family memorials and ordinary letters reveal different parts of that society; surviving evidence is often weighted toward elite tombs.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: At Saqqara, Djoser's Step Pyramid formed the center of a complex of stone buildings and underground chambers. Later builders developed smooth-sided pyramids.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Papyrus sheets were made by layering strips of the stalk's inner pith and drying them under pressure. Sheets could be joined into writing rolls.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Old Kingdom tomb chapels depicted food offerings and agricultural work. These images were meant to sustain the dead, so they are more than documentary pictures of daily life.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Middle Kingdom jewelers placed tiny inlays on ornaments and sometimes decorated their backs with elaborate chasing, visible principally to their wearers.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Unis had religious spells carved inside his pyramid late in Dynasty 5. Later kings, and eventually queens, also received these Pyramid Texts.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Middle Kingdom memorials increasingly pictured extended families and associates. Such monuments show religious commemoration reaching beyond the ruler alone.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Papyrus carried accounts, letters and legal agreements as well as religious works. Black ink usually supplied the main text; red ink could mark emphasis.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: The same marsh plant also supplied material for baskets, sandals, ropes and small boats. A writing technology belonged to a much wider craft economy.

passages.text: Elam was one of the oldest civilizations, centered on Susa and the highlands of Anshan in southwestern Iran. Its language belongs to no known family; its kings built ziggurats and fought, traded and intermarried with Mesopotamia for more than two thousand years.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: King Untash-Napirisha built the ziggurat of Chogha Zanbil, the best preserved ziggurat anywhere, with baked-brick stairways and glazed tiles.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Irrigation canals from the Karun and Karkheh rivers watered the Khuzestan plain.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Bronze casting on a large scale: the statue of Queen Napir-Asu from Susa weighs 1,750 kilograms.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Proto-Elamite, one of the earliest scripts, was written on clay at Susa around 3100 BCE and is still undeciphered.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Cylinder seals and rock-cut reliefs of kings and processions, as at Kul-e Farah.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: A pantheon headed by Inshushinak, the god of Susa, with the goddess Kiririsha and the highland god Napirisha.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Kingship passed between brothers and nephews, and some scholars read the record as descent through the female line, unusual in the ancient Near East.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Chogha Zanbil was among the first Iranian sites listed by UNESCO.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Elamite was one of the three languages of the Achaemenid royal inscriptions, and Elamite scribes kept the Persepolis archives.
Assyria sacked Susa in 647 BCE. The small Elamite kingdoms that followed passed under the Persians of Anshan, and Cyrus's empire, which took Babylon in 539 BCE, made Susa one of its capitals.

passages.text: The medieval Soninke empire of Ghana prospered through trans-Saharan exchange. Its power rested on commercial connections and political centers such as Kumbi Saleh, rather than a fixed border enclosing one people.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Gold moved north while salt moved south. Taxing imports and exports helped support imperial rule.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Camel caravans made long desert journeys possible; traders connected different ecological regions rather than transporting goods within a single uniform landscape.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Savanna agriculture and livestock breeding supported the societies through which the trade routes passed.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Al-Bakri described gold-adorned court equipment and clothing. Such written testimony records royal display, not the possessions of every household.

passages.title: Political change
passages.text: By the late twelfth century Ghana had lost its dominant position in the western Sudan gold trade as routes shifted. Its decline was a process, not a securely dated disappearance of Soninke society.

passages.text: This chapter looks at scientific institutions in seventeenth-century England within the map's combined England-and-Ireland record. It also marks the later union of England and Scotland, which did not merge Ireland into Great Britain.

passages.title: Science
passages.text: The Royal Society's first meeting followed Christopher Wren's astronomy lecture in London in 1660. Its members gathered observations, performed experiments and discussed results.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Henry Oldenburg began Philosophical Transactions in 1665. The same year, Robert Hooke published the close observations collected in Micrographia.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: The early Royal Society drew members from professional and aristocratic circles and admitted only men. Its meeting rooms represented a restricted part of society.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The English and Scottish Acts of Union created Great Britain on 1 May 1707. The new parliament first met that October.

sectionTitles: A burial and its surviving objects

passages.text: The kingdom of the East Saxons included communities with very different material circumstances. Prittlewell's elaborate burial preserves music, painted wood and international connections; Mucking reveals changing settlements and textile work. Written accounts document royal patronage and religious reversals. Essex later entered West Saxon government, while its inhabitants and local institutions continued.

passages.title: A burial and its surviving objects
passages.text: Excavators at Prittlewell in 2003 found a timber-lined chamber with a copper-alloy bowl still hanging from a wall hook. The arrangement preserves evidence of how mourners furnished a privileged burial, rather than a typical household interior.

passages.title: A burial and its surviving objects
passages.text: Radiocarbon samples from horn and wood gave a range of 575-605; Frankish coins narrowed the burial to about 580-605. That interval spans 597, so it cannot by itself prove burial before Augustine's mission.

passages.title: A burial and its surviving objects
passages.text: Two gold-foil crosses lay near the coffin's head, perhaps originally over the eyes. They support a Christian interpretation of this individual's burial, without establishing that every East Saxon had adopted the same beliefs.

passages.title: A burial and its surviving objects
passages.text: The Prittlewell lyre survived largely as a soil stain with wood fragments and fittings. Laboratory excavation identified a maple body and ash tuning pegs. Reconstructing its shape depended on recording fragile traces in their original positions.

passages.title: A burial and its surviving objects
passages.text: The lyre had been broken and repaired with iron, gilded copper-alloy and silver fittings. Raman analysis identified almandine garnets, probably from India or Sri Lanka. The instrument records both repair work and far-reaching material connections.

passages.title: A burial and its surviving objects
passages.text: Micro-excavation of a soil block exposed painted maple fragments interpreted as a box lid. Yellow borders and red and white designs preserve wood decoration that ordinary excavation might have missed. The proposed fish-scale motif remains an interpretation.

passages.title: Settlements, skilled work and belief
passages.text: At Mucking, postholes and sunken building features form changing groups across a gravel terrace. Researchers describe a settlement that shifted over time. These remains do not establish one permanent town plan or a royal palace.

passages.title: Settlements, skilled work and belief
passages.text: Mucking's building GH84 contained roughly 140 loomweights. Hamerow considers storage on a rack more plausible than several looms operating inside the small building. Textile equipment proves work and provisioning without fixing exactly where every loom stood.

passages.title: Settlements, skilled work and belief
passages.text: In Mucking GH105, about 30 unfired clay loomweights and freshly broken pots rested on the trampled floor. Such contextual detail helps distinguish material associated with a building's use or abandonment from unrelated objects dumped into a later hollow.

passages.title: Settlements, skilled work and belief
passages.text: Bede describes London as a trading centre and says that Aethelberht of Kent supported St Paul's for Mellitus. His account places the East Saxon king Saeberht within a network of Kentish overlordship and Christian patronage.

passages.title: Settlements, skilled work and belief
passages.text: After Saeberht's death, Bede says his sons rejected Mellitus's religious authority and the bishop departed. This was a reversal in royal religious policy, not the disappearance of the East Saxon kingdom.

passages.title: Settlements, skilled work and belief
passages.text: A charter calls Sigeric both a Mercian ruler's follower and an East Saxon king. Ann Williams uses this evidence to complicate a simple, abrupt end to local kingship.

Essex entered West Saxon overlordship around 825 and Wessex in 860. Administration changed while local society continued. Williams treats Sigered's expulsion by Ecgberht as probable, rather than a fully documented event.

passages.text: Ethiopia’s history includes a long-lived empire and later governments, alongside communities with distinct languages, religions and institutions. Abyssinia was a European name used for the empire. Manuscripts, buildings, farming landscapes and living craft traditions reveal histories that cannot be reduced to the careers of emperors.

passages.title: Books as objects of knowledge
passages.text: A Gospel manuscript now at the Metropolitan Museum dates from the late fourteenth or early fifteenth century. Its parchment pages combine Ge’ez text with painted Gospel scenes. The museum identifies two artists, whose shared visual language transformed models connected to the eastern Mediterranean.

passages.title: Books as objects of knowledge
passages.text: The book was made at a northern Ethiopian monastic centre. A possible connection to Dabra Hayg Estifanos is a scholarly attribution, not a recorded excavation find. Notes associate its recipient church with the Archangel Michael, while the paintings were intended for viewing during worship and processions.

passages.title: Books as objects of knowledge
passages.text: The late seventeenth-century Arganonä Maryam prayer book organises prayers using decorated headings for days of the week. Geometric borders help readers navigate the text. Its parchment, pigments, script and binding required several kinds of practical skill as well as religious learning.

passages.title: Books as objects of knowledge
passages.text: Pencil additions, erased and rewritten red text, and smudges reveal the prayer book’s later use. Its colophon names Baselyos, but scholars debate whether the scribe also painted the hornbill image associated with this group of manuscripts. Evidence of authorship is therefore more complex than one modern artist label.

passages.title: Buildings and water management
passages.text: Fasil Ghebbi’s royal compound contains more than castles. Its surviving structures include a library, a chancellery and a banqueting hall, alongside palaces and nearby churches. The ensemble shows how a settled court brought administration, ceremony and skilled construction into a permanent urban centre.

passages.title: Buildings and water management
passages.text: At the Bath of Fasilidas, a canal carried water from the nearby river into a rectangular pool around a pavilion. The building stands on pier arches and was reached by a stone bridge. Water supply and structural engineering were integral to the royal landscape.

passages.title: Farming, households and collective work
passages.text: Konso communities shaped steep land with dry-stone terraces that retain soil, collect rainfall and discharge excess water. Their maintenance depends on organised communal labour. These southern Ethiopian landscapes represent local environmental knowledge rather than a technology that can be credited to the imperial dynasty.

passages.title: Farming, households and collective work
passages.text: Within Konso settlements, communal spaces called moras organise social and ceremonial life. Reservoirs are built and maintained collectively, while generation-marking stones record transfers of responsibility. Farming infrastructure and local institutions belong to the same cultural landscape.

passages.title: Textiles, skill and contemporary livelihoods
passages.text: Designer Hana Getachew describes Habesha dresses made from fine cotton with coloured geometric decoration called tibeb. On a simple two-harness loom, artisans must pick decorative patterns by hand or add embroidery. The cloth’s apparent lightness conceals patient, technically demanding work.

passages.title: Textiles, skill and contemporary livelihoods
passages.text: At the contemporary Sabahar workshop, local women spin cotton by hand, yarn is dyed, and weavers thread the loom before weaving panels. Washing and careful stitching finish the cloth. Getachew’s account links design, distributed labour and changing markets without implying that all Ethiopian households follow this practice.

passages.title: Institutions beyond the palace
passages.text: The Oromo Gada system provides a distinct tradition of community governance. Assemblies and elected leadership address administration, disputes and social responsibilities, while knowledge is passed between generations. It operates at a local level and should not be confused with the institutions of Ethiopia’s imperial or federal governments.

passages.title: Institutions beyond the palace
passages.text: Haile Selassie’s 1931 constitution drew on foreign constitutional models but strengthened imperial authority. Written government rules did not necessarily mean independent parliamentary power. This distinction helps explain why institutional reform and political participation did not always advance together.

passages.title: Expansion, resistance and political change
passages.text: Menelik II’s army defeated the Italian invasion at Adwa in 1896. His reign also brought conquest and annexation in the south. Resistance to European colonial rule and expansion over neighbouring communities were different processes within the same imperial history.

passages.title: Expansion, resistance and political change
passages.text: The constitution adopted in December 1994 speaks in the name of Ethiopia’s nations, nationalities and peoples, emphasising equality and shared political life. Its wording records the new constitutional project; it is not proof that subsequent governments fulfilled every stated aim.

The emperor was removed in September 1974 and the Derg assumed power. That ended imperial government, not Ethiopia or its peoples. The Derg itself fell in 1991, followed by a transitional administration and a federal republic. These regime changes must be distinguished from the country’s continuing history.

passages.text: The Etruscans lived in a network of central Italian city-states. Metalworking, imported luxury materials and distinctive funerary art reveal communities deeply involved in Mediterranean exchange.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Bucchero pottery has a glossy black surface and often uses shapes associated with metal vessels.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Bronze workers made decorated chariots, vessels, mirrors and sculpture. Access to copper and iron supported their craft traditions.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Greek painted pottery was highly valued in Etruria. Trade also brought ivory, amber and other materials used by local artists.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: At Cerveteri, rock-cut tombs reproduce features of houses. Their arrangement into streets and small squares offers clues to settlement planning.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Painted tombs at Tarquinia preserve scenes of living, dying and religious belief. Funerary images provide evidence that short surviving inscriptions often cannot supply.

passages.title: Change and continuity
passages.text: Roman expansion absorbed the Etruscan cities over time. Their culture did not end on the map's current 323 BCE snapshot boundary.

passages.text: Fiji's history includes distinct iTaukei societies, Indo-Fijian communities and other peoples linked by settlement, trade and migration. Barkcloth, port buildings and labor records reveal skilled production and unequal colonial relationships. This card follows the colonial and independent country while identifying older traditions and later diaspora examples explicitly.

passages.title: Barkcloth and technical knowledge
passages.text: A painted masi cloth from the Lau Islands, dated to the late nineteenth or early twentieth century, survives at the Metropolitan Museum of Art. Its stencilled designs provide a specific example of Fijian textile work; the collection record does not identify an excavated findspot.

passages.title: Barkcloth and technical knowledge
passages.text: Barkcloth makers softened strips of inner bark in water and beat them on a wooden anvil. Overlapping and beating the edges fused smaller pieces into larger sheets, turning plant fibers into flexible cloth without a loom.

passages.title: Barkcloth and technical knowledge
passages.text: A 1996 photograph records Mereia Johnston stencilling a border on paper-mulberry cloth in New Zealand. The named maker and workshop context show craft knowledge being practiced in the diaspora, rather than treating masi as only an anonymous museum survival.

passages.title: What the built landscape reveals
passages.text: At Levuka on Ovalau, warehouses and port buildings developed around the indigenous settlements of Totoga and Nasau. The surviving layout shows local communities shaping a colonial trading town, rather than an empty landscape simply filled by newcomers.

passages.title: What the built landscape reveals
passages.text: Beach Street's sea wall, lanes leading inland and traces of transport to the wharf connect buildings with movement of goods. Copra sheds, workers' cottages and the Baba labor settlement extend the story beyond official government buildings.

passages.title: What the built landscape reveals
passages.text: The colonial capital moved from Levuka to Suva in 1882, but commercial activity at Levuka continued. Losing capital status was a change in political function, not the abandonment of the town.

passages.title: Work, migration and daily life
passages.text: Indian indentured laborers first arrived in Fiji on 14 May 1879. Their contracts, remembered as girmit, tied them to harsh plantation labor. Their work and later community building are central to Fiji's history, while the coercion of the system must remain visible.

passages.title: Work, migration and daily life
passages.text: Yaqona, also called kava, is prepared from a plant root. It has ceremonial importance in iTaukei life and is also shared socially across communities. Its continued use overseas connects everyday gathering with relationships to Fiji.

passages.title: Work, migration and daily life
passages.text: Migration changed the circulation of food and household goods. Te Ara describes Indo-Fijian businesses in New Zealand helping make island and Indian ingredients, clothing and utensils more accessible to Fijian communities.

passages.title: Language, belief and community
passages.text: Fijian, Fiji Hindi and English connect different communities. Family use, contact with Fiji and language teaching help sustain them overseas, although language fluency and choices vary across generations.

passages.title: Language, belief and community
passages.text: Christian, Hindu and Muslim networks support worship, festivals and community relationships among migrants. These distinct institutions reveal the plurality of Fijian experience; no single religious practice represents the entire country.

passages.title: Independence and continuing history
passages.text: Fiji became independent on 10 October 1970. The independence ceremony transferred political authority from colonial rule; it did not mark the beginning of the islands' peoples, craft traditions or community histories.

British colonial rule ended with Fiji's independence in 1970. Fiji continues as a country whose communities maintain different histories, languages and traditions, including overseas. The colonial endpoint must not be turned into a claim that Fijian society ended.

passages.text: Seventeenth-century French projects joined engineering, landscape design and royal display. This chapter pairs a working waterway with Versailles to show different purposes of large-scale construction.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: The Canal du Midi project used locks, aqueducts, bridges, spillways and tunnels to make an inland water route. UNESCO dates the wider historic works to 1667 through 1694.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: The canal's water-supply system drew on the Montagne Noire. The Saint-Ferreol dam was a major engineering component.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: After 1661, Louis XIV enlarged Versailles through work directed first by Le Vau and later by Jules Hardouin-Mansart. Its architecture developed across successive campaigns.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Andre Le Notre organized Versailles' gardens with long axes, planted beds, hedges, water and fountains. The landscape formed part of the royal residence's design.

passages.text: Frankish communities expressed wealth and identity through dress and skilled metalwork. The map's Frankish Kingdom record covers only part of a longer history and should not imply that Frankish culture began in 600.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Women wore belted tunics with a wrap or cloak. Pendants hung from belts, and jewelry included earrings, necklaces and hairpins.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Small paired brooches were common in earlier centuries; large single disk brooches became fashionable in the 600s.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: A mid-seventh-century disk brooch combines gold with garnet, colored glass and mother-of-pearl. Small fastening objects could display elaborate material contrasts.

passages.title: Change and continuity
passages.text: Charlemagne became king of the Franks in 768 and emperor in 800. Imperial culture grew from earlier Frankish traditions of patronage and fine metalwork.

sectionTitles: Discoveries: pots, fields and traces of food
Skilled work and care at Loyola

passages.text: French Guiana’s history comes into view through ancient fields, cooking equipment, family records and living traditions of craft and celebration.

passages.title: Discoveries: pots, fields and traces of food
passages.text: At Chemin Saint-Louis on the lower Maroni, archaeologists found pottery vessels fitted inside one another in a pit. The site included occupation around 50 to 220 CE. Some pottery carried a red coating and geometric incisions. Its unfamiliar forms raised questions about local development and outside influence; a striking pot alone does not settle where its maker came from.

passages.title: Discoveries: pots, fields and traces of food
passages.text: At K-VIII near Kourou, ancient farmers built raised plots and long ridges in a seasonally flooded landscape. Their arrangement varied with the ground: researchers interpret some ridges as helping drainage and others as retaining water. Farming involved shaping the land as well as planting seeds. These fields belong to a wider late precolonial landscape, with dates varying by site.

passages.title: Discoveries: pots, fields and traces of food
passages.text: Tiny plant traces help reconstruct food history. Researchers identified maize remains in raised-field soils, squash at Piliwa, and maize and manioc starch on griddle fragments from Sable Blanc. The last traces connect particular cooking surfaces with crops. A fragment too small to hold your lunch can still preserve clues about someone else’s.

passages.title: Skilled work and care at Loyola
passages.text: At Loyola in Rémire-Montjoly, Jesuits operated a plantation from 1668 to 1764 using enslaved labour. Excavation of its forge yielded hoes, hooks, hinges and locks. Unfinished hoe blades show stages in shaping an agricultural tool. These finds reveal skilled work, although they cannot identify which individual made or used each object.

passages.title: Skilled work and care at Loyola
passages.text: Excavation beside Loyola’s kitchen recovered thousands of pottery fragments. A masonry cooking structure called a potager and a bread oven also survived. Here, potager means a place for heating cooking pots, rather than a vegetable garden. These remains reveal a particular plantation kitchen, not the meals or equipment available to everyone who lived and worked there.

passages.title: Skilled work and care at Loyola
passages.text: Loyola’s hospital stood against its kitchen. Archaeologist Nathalie Cazelles suggests that the arrangement may reflect a belief that warmth hastened recovery. The building layout is evidence; that explanation is an interpretation. Neither proves that the treatment worked, nor that enslaved patients experienced the institution as benevolent.

passages.title: Family records, homes and learning
passages.text: Registers made for newly freed people in 1848 to 1853 preserve names, ages, occupations and places. The Manioc research project makes these details searchable and connects the work with questions about individuals and families. Official paperwork can help recover a person’s story, while remaining a partial account written within the institutions of its time.

passages.title: Family records, homes and learning
passages.text: At Boniville and Loka, Aluku heritage houses include timber walls, steep gabled roofs and often a carved front gable called a koppo. The preservation project links buildings with family and community history. It also brings apprentices together with local experts and carpenters. Saving a house can mean passing on the knowledge needed to make its next repair.

passages.title: Family records, homes and learning
passages.text: At Antecume Pata, the Yépé association’s workshops have taught basketry, weaving and pottery since 2015. The park reports that around thirty children participated in 2017, with Wayana and Apalaï craftspeople guiding their work. Young adults also learned to make objects for sale. Learning here involves watching skilled hands, practising and gradually making something of your own.

passages.title: Science and celebrations
passages.text: On April 9, 1968, a Véronique sounding rocket became the first rocket launched from the Guiana Space Centre. The flight tested the new launch site’s operating systems and recovery at sea of its radio-equipped payload. Space work began with practical trials on the ground and in the atmosphere, before the centre’s satellite-launching era.

passages.title: Science and celebrations
passages.text: The 2017 carnival inventory describes Touloulou costumes that conceal identity with dresses, masks, head coverings and gloves. Some participants even change their usual perfume. Women in these disguises invite partners to dance at the bal paré-masqué. Recognizing a friend can require more detective work than simply spotting their favourite shoes.

passages.title: Science and celebrations
passages.text: Carnival also has a social life around the table. The 2017 inventory describes sharing filled galettes des Rois with family, colleagues, schoolmates and associations during the season. A small token is hidden in the pastry, and finding it helps decide who provides refreshments next time. That slice of cake may come with a future hosting assignment.

The 1946 departmental law changed French Guiana’s administrative status; combined territorial institutions followed in 2016 within France. These changes did not end its communities. Craft teaching, family memory and celebrations continue to connect generations.

passages.text: Funan, known from the reports of Chinese envoys in the third century, was the first of Southeast Asia's Indian-influenced states, in the Mekong delta. Its port at Oc Eo linked the trade of Rome, India and China.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Oc Eo's canals and warehouses handled goods between the Gulf of Thailand and the Mekong; coins of Antoninus Pius and Marcus Aurelius were found there.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Indian beads and seals, Chinese bronze mirrors and local tin amulets came out of the excavations of the 1940s.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Sanskrit inscriptions and images of Vishnu and Shiva show Indian religion at court, with Buddhism beside it.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The Chinese envoys Kang Tai and Zhu Ying, who visited about 245, described walled towns, taxes paid in gold and a written script.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: A network of canals, one of them nearly 90 kilometers long, drained and linked the delta towns.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Funan set the pattern of the Indianized kingdom that Chenla, the Chams and the Khmer followed.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Oc Eo is among the earliest excavated urban sites in mainland Southeast Asia.
In the sixth century the inland Khmer state the Chinese called Chenla absorbed Funan; by about 550 its kings ruled the delta.

passages.text: The Funj Sultanate ruled from Sennar in present-day Sudan. Local centres within its sphere kept distinct institutions. Excavated households at Old Dongola reveal everyday work in a northern community.

passages.title: Homes, neighbours and meals
passages.text: In sixteenth- and seventeenth-century Old Dongola, some dwellings shared a courtyard. One excavated compound grouped four homes around the same open space. Builders used sun-dried bricks or frameworks of twigs covered with mud. Shared access helps archaeologists study relationships between neighbours, although it cannot establish exactly how every household was related.

passages.title: Homes, neighbours and meals
passages.text: Dongola’s courtyards contained grinding stones, hearths and storage vessels. Plant samples included sorghum and wheat. Together, these finds place food preparation in the open spaces around homes. Grinding grain was part of making a meal, not just a task represented in a royal account. The evidence does not supply a complete menu or identify every cook.

passages.title: A pantry preserved
passages.text: A deposit in room U50 at Old Dongola contained storage pots standing on woven mats, with some covered by basketry lids or reused bowls. The deposit dates to roughly the late sixteenth or early seventeenth century. These objects preserve a practical system for storing things, including an economical second job for an old bowl.

passages.title: A pantry preserved
passages.text: One rectangular basket in that deposit held a small pot with a basketry cover, a wooden key, a grinding stone and two spindle whorls. These finds bring household equipment into view together. The key survived; what it opened is less certain. Objects found together do not necessarily all belong to one task.

passages.title: Learning and local government
passages.text: The traveller Evliya Çelebi reported six schools at Dongola in 1672/1673. A modern archaeological study compares that written account with a survey that could not clearly identify the reported religious buildings. The account is evidence for educational activity, but its numbers are not a verified count of excavated classrooms or of children attending lessons.

passages.title: Learning and local government
passages.text: An Arabic order from Old Dongola, studied in 2026, instructs a man named Khidr to arrange exchanges involving goods interpreted as textiles and a ewe with her young. It names King Qashqash and his scribe Hamad. The document, dated broadly to the sixteenth or seventeenth century, shows government handling material transactions. Some commodity names remain difficult to read.

passages.title: Learning and local government
passages.text: The royal order uses both sides of an irregular piece of paper. The reverse adds further instructions, probably concerning cotton cloth or headwear. Scholars distinguish the readable names and commands from damaged or ambiguous words. A small piece of paperwork can reveal people who are scarcely visible in grand political histories, without settling every detail of their lives.

passages.title: Clothes, colour and changing habits
passages.text: Chemical analysis of seventeen wool, cotton and silk samples from seventeenth- and eighteenth-century Dongola identified dyes from plants and animals. The researchers distinguished fabrics they considered local from imported textiles. Small scraps can therefore reveal choices about colour and connections beyond the city, even when the original garment has disappeared.

passages.title: Clothes, colour and changing habits
passages.text: The same study identified kermes and lac colourants, made from insects, alongside plant dyes. One crimson knitted wool fragment was interpreted as part of a fez. Getting dressed could involve surprisingly varied raw materials. The possible hat identification remains an interpretation of a fragment, not a complete surviving wardrobe.

passages.title: Clothes, colour and changing habits
passages.text: Seeds identified as tobacco were recovered at Old Dongola and dated approximately to 1664 to 1760. Their presence supports research into local cultivation and changing habits. The study treats the exact timing and route of tobacco’s arrival as uncertain. This is evidence of a historical practice, rather than proof that every household grew or used the plant.

passages.title: Crafts and discoveries today
passages.text: A 2025 study of excavated pottery at Sennar and Al Khandaq found differences in production. Handmade forms with relatively simple decoration were prominent at Sennar, while the Al Khandaq material included wheel-made wares and more varied surface treatments. Comparing the two places shows local choices continuing within a connected region; one technique does not rank an entire community’s skill.

passages.title: Crafts and discoveries today
passages.text: In a 2026 account of the Dongola research, the University of Warsaw describes local residents as partners who exchange knowledge with archaeologists. Residents still use a name meaning the King’s House for a building studied by the team. Such remembered names can guide questions about a place, while excavated documents provide a different kind of evidence.

Turco-Egyptian forces conquered the Funj Sultanate in 1821 after prolonged internal struggles. Its independent government ended, while communities and their local histories continued. The map’s separate endpoints in 1530 and 1815 do not mark two destructions of the sultanate.

passages.text: In late-sixteenth- and early-seventeenth-century Genoa, mercantile wealth reshaped streets, houses and hospitality. The Rolli palaces reveal how private residences served the republic's public business.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: In the late sixteenth and early seventeenth centuries, Genoa developed the Strade Nuove as a coordinated district of streets and aristocratic palaces above the older city.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: The palaces adapted to steep and confined sites with open staircases, courtyards and garden-facing loggias. Frescoes and stucco decorated their interiors.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: The Senate established the Rolli list of private palaces used to lodge distinguished official visitors. Hosting state guests became an obligation attached to selected elite homes.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The Rolli system sorted residences into categories corresponding to different ranks of guest. Hospitality made social hierarchy part of the organization of official visits.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Architectural treatises spread knowledge of Genoa's new streets and palaces beyond the city in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries.

passages.text: British rule joined the coastal Gold Coast colony and several differently administered territories under a changing constitutional framework. The history of the communities living there is much broader than colonial government. Farmers, fishers, potters, traders, teachers and writers shaped the society that became independent Ghana.

passages.title: Buildings and archaeological discoveries
passages.text: Coastal forts such as Ussher and James in Accra and Christiansborg in Osu predate the formal British colony. Their courtyards, bastions, storerooms and accommodation reveal how commercial and military functions were combined within enclosed compounds. Their architecture records repeated occupation and adaptation by different European powers.

passages.title: Buildings and archaeological discoveries
passages.text: The forts served trade in gold and later the Atlantic traffic in enslaved Africans. Their survival is evidence of those coercive systems and the international networks surrounding them. They are not simply monuments to construction skill or neutral symbols of overseas exchange.

passages.title: Buildings and archaeological discoveries
passages.text: At Christiansborg, archaeologists working with descendant communities found house foundations, local and imported ceramics, beads and smoking pipes. Three stones with charcoal suggested a cooking area, but that identification is interpretive. These discoveries bring nearby households into a history often told only through the castle.

passages.title: Buildings and archaeological discoveries
passages.text: Pottery studied from the 2016 Christiansborg garden excavations includes soot-marked vessels consistent with cooking. Stepped rims may have supported lids. The report had not yet obtained chronometric dates, so its broad post-seventeenth-century context does not justify assigning each sherd to a particular colonial year.

passages.title: Buildings and archaeological discoveries
passages.text: Incised bowls known as weika are compared with vessels used to grind condiments, while other forms served food or carried liquids. These functional comparisons help reconstruct household work, but vessel shapes could have overlapping uses. A surviving fragment does not identify the exact meal once prepared in it.

passages.title: Buildings and archaeological discoveries
passages.text: Regional pottery traditions include hand coiling, apprenticeship and open firing. Engmann uses those traditions as comparisons, not direct observation of the excavated pots’ manufacture. Clay suitable for pottery is scarce at Osu, and the origins of most recovered vessels remain uncertain.

passages.title: Fishing, innovation and coastal livelihoods
passages.text: Fishing supported an extensive division of labour. Men generally worked at sea, while women processed catches and organised trade into inland markets. Women also advocated more productive nets. Decisions about equipment therefore affected fishers, processors and traders differently, rather than benefiting a single undifferentiated community.

passages.title: Fishing, innovation and coastal livelihoods
passages.text: African entrepreneurs developed and adapted large ali drift nets and yevudor beach seines. Accounts disagree over their first introduction. From 1898 to 1923, disputes concerned juvenile fish, declining catches, prices and the larger rewards claimed by equipment owners. More productive technology also raised questions about conservation and access to earnings.

passages.title: Cocoa farming and scientific work
passages.text: Tetteh Quarshie, a blacksmith from Osu, returned from Fernando Po with cocoa in 1879 and cultivated it at Akwapim Mampong. Farmers obtained pods from his farm and spread cultivation. Earlier Dutch and missionary introductions mean that his contribution is better understood as successful propagation than the first arrival of cocoa.

passages.title: Cocoa farming and scientific work
passages.text: From 1886, the Aburi Botanical Garden also supplied cocoa planting material. Expansion depended on farmers establishing and tending trees as well as these distribution networks. The crop’s spread was a process of agricultural adoption involving many cultivators, not the work of one planter alone.

passages.title: Cocoa farming and scientific work
passages.text: The Central Cocoa Research Station opened at Akim Tafo in 1938 to investigate pests and diseases affecting farms. Its successor, the West African Cocoa Research Institute, expanded the programme in 1944 to include soils and cultivation practices. Scientific investigation developed around practical problems in a major agricultural livelihood.

passages.title: Education, print and political change
passages.text: Achimota opened in 1927 and developed school, teacher-training and higher-education branches. Its curriculum brought science and vocational work together with art, music and African dance. The institution provides a concrete example of education combining technical preparation and cultural expression, without implying that such opportunities were available to every child.

passages.title: Education, print and political change
passages.text: The University of Ghana preserves a catalogue record for Gold Coast Leader issues from April to July 1907, published at Cape Coast. Its description identifies local and international political and social reporting. This archival record documents a local newspaper culture; it does not establish the views of every resident.

passages.title: Education, print and political change
passages.text: The Ghana Independence Act ended British governmental responsibility for the new country from 6 March 1957. It also restricted future British legislation for Ghana to measures requested and consented to by Ghana. The legal change concerned sovereignty, not the disappearance of the communities previously governed as colonial subjects.

The colonial constitutional order gave way to independent Ghana on 6 March 1957. The Gold Coast name and British responsibility ended; the population, settlements and working traditions continued into a new political history. The map’s earlier record endpoints are coverage boundaries, not separate dates of national independence.

passages.text: Goguryeo was the largest and most martial of Korea's Three Kingdoms, holding the north of the peninsula and much of Manchuria from its mountain fortresses. Its painted tombs are the fullest picture of life in early Korea, and its art reached Japan through Baekje and its own monks.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Tomb murals show hunts, processions, wrestlers, dancers, the sun crow and the moon toad, and the four directional animals, painted with a sense of movement.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Gilt-bronze crown ornaments, earrings and belt fittings show skilled metalwork.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Buddhist sculpture and temple building grew after the religion arrived in 372; the gilt-bronze Buddha of 539 from Yeonga is the oldest dated Korean Buddhist image.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Mountain fortresses of fitted stone, built to the ridgelines, guarded the valleys and river crossings.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Iron lamellar armor for horse and rider equipped heavy cavalry, as the tomb paintings show.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The monk Sundo arrived from Former Qin with images and sutras, and the court adopted Buddhism; a Confucian academy, the Taehak, was founded the same year.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Native shamanic and ancestral rites continued alongside Buddhism and Confucian learning.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The Complex of Koguryo Tombs in North Korea and the capitals and tombs of the kingdom in China were both listed by UNESCO.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The name Korea comes from Goryeo, the tenth-century dynasty that took its name from Goguryeo.

After decades of war with Silla and Tang China, Goguryeo fell when Pyongyang was taken in 668. Tang set up a protectorate over the north; Silla held the peninsula south of the Taedong river and pushed the Tang armies out by 676.

passages.text: The Göktürk Khaganate was the first empire to bear the name Türk. Founded by Bumin in 552, it stretched from Manchuria to the Black Sea, split into eastern and western halves in 583, submitted to Tang in 630 and 657, and rose again as the Second Khaganate in 682. Its stone inscriptions are the oldest Turkic writing.

passages.title: Inventions
passages.text: The stelae of Kül Tegin (732) and Bilge Qaghan (735) in the Orkhon valley carry the oldest long texts in the Old Turkic script, the first Turkic writing.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Tengri, the sky, gave the khagan his mandate; shamans and the sacred Ötüken forest stood at the center of belief.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Taspar Qaghan patronized Buddhism and had sutras translated into Turkic, though Tengri worship remained the rule.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: The khaganate held the Silk Road from China to Persia, with Sogdian merchants as its traders and scribes.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: The Sogdian Maniakh, an envoy of the khagan, reached Constantinople to open a silk route around Sasanian Persia.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The name Türk first appears in history with this empire.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The Orkhon inscriptions remain the chief source for early Turkic language and history.
An alliance of Uyghur, Basmyl and Karluk tribes overthrew the khaganate; the Uyghur Khaganate rose in its place in 744.
