passages.text: Kanem, east of Lake Chad, was the earlier heartland of Sayfawa power. Its beginnings remain uncertain; excavated settlements illuminate elite buildings and working materials.

passages.title: Building and working materials
passages.text: At Tié Kalaté S2, discarded bricks lie in a depression where clay was extracted and fired. Nearby residences stood on dunes.

passages.title: Building and working materials
passages.text: Tié’s substantial enclosure is a candidate for Njimi, the royal capital. The identification remains argued rather than confirmed by a naming inscription.

passages.title: Building and working materials
passages.text: A study of excavated iron nails distinguishes four main forms used in twelfth- to fourteenth-century Kanem. These ordinary fasteners preserve metalworking choices that monumental buildings alone cannot show. Their precise use must be established from archaeological context.

passages.title: Adornment and long-distance exchange
passages.text: At Tié, glass dominates the recovered beads, alongside smaller numbers made from ostrich eggshell, metal and stone. Bone pendants and cowries also served as ornaments. This assemblage describes personal adornment at the excavated site, not everyone’s dress.

passages.title: Adornment and long-distance exchange
passages.text: Many glass beads are tiny cylinders or rounded forms. Makers cut drawn glass and often reheated it to soften sharp edges. Red-brown and yellow shades were common in the recovered collection.

passages.title: Adornment and long-distance exchange
passages.text: Chemical analysis links a few beads with the glass industry around Ile-Ife in present-day Nigeria. Much of the remaining glass has affinities farther east. The results support African exchange connections, while the exact routes and intermediaries remain uncertain.

passages.title: Writing, travel and unequal exchange
passages.text: The Arabic Diwan preserves a royal succession record. Historians compare its chronology with other texts and archaeological dates.

passages.title: Writing, travel and unequal exchange
passages.text: Saharan exchange included enslaved people, horses and cloth. The court’s connections rested partly on coercion as well as commerce.

passages.title: Writing, travel and unequal exchange
passages.text: Cairo was an important meeting point for pilgrims from Kanem and later Borno travelling toward Mecca. Dewière’s study treats pilgrimage as religious practice that also carried people, goods and ideas between African regions.
In the late fourteenth century, the Sayfawa court left Kanem for Borno under pressure from Bulala rivals. Kanem continued under other rulers while the dynasty rebuilt its power west of the lake.

passages.text: Borno developed west of Lake Chad as a centre of Sayfawa government and scholarship. Its history includes scholarly communities, farming settlements and changing dynasties, as well as royal capitals.

passages.title: Farming, fishing and exchange
passages.text: At Garumele, a settlement associated with Borno’s history, excavators found abundant fish remains together with sheep, goat and cattle bones. Oral traditions connect it with royalty, but its precise occupation dates and capital status remain debated.

passages.title: Farming, fishing and exchange
passages.text: The range and quantity of fish at Garumele suggest specialist fishing. Researchers propose that some fish arrived already processed, while herders supplied livestock. These are interpretations of bone distributions, not proof of a known market organisation or preservation recipe.

passages.title: Farming, fishing and exchange
passages.text: Nineteenth-century Borno depended on agriculture. Many people combined farming with seasonal crafts or trade. Kyari Mohammed stresses the importance of regional commerce alongside Saharan routes, challenging a picture of an economy sustained only by distant caravans.

passages.title: Learning and manuscript arts
passages.text: Some scholarly villages combined study with farming and enjoyed royal exemptions. Students advanced from Quran memorisation to Arabic grammar, Old Kanembu translation and interpretation. Education rested on organised communities as well as individual teachers.

passages.title: Learning and manuscript arts
passages.text: The Konduga Quran survives as loose leaves kept in a leather folder and satchel. Italian watermarks identify imported paper. Different hands added Arabic commentary and Old Kanembu glosses around the main text, preserving several readers’ work.

passages.title: Learning and manuscript arts
passages.text: A later copy of the Konduga manuscript’s final page preserved its annotations as well as its Quranic text. The copy used a different page layout. This unusual duplication protected a record of teaching, not only the main scriptural passage.

passages.title: Learning and manuscript arts
passages.text: Owners patched the Konduga Quran with paper strips and stitches after moisture damaged its lower margins. Repeated repairs show care across generations. A surviving manuscript can record maintenance and reuse alongside the original scribe’s achievement.

passages.title: Learning and manuscript arts
passages.text: Extensive written annotations became less common during nineteenth-century upheaval, but handwritten Qurans and oral translation continued. Bondarev proposes links with political and educational changes; he does not establish one decree that ended the practice.

passages.title: Power and its human costs
passages.text: Rabih’s administration demanded produce and other revenues through local authorities under military supervision. Mohammed’s research describes confiscation and punishment as tools of rule. These burdens make the occupation a history of households and livelihoods as well as battles.

Rabih conquered Borno in 1893. French forces and African allies defeated him in 1900; colonial partition followed. Royal institutions and regional communities continued under altered authority, while the independent state’s political order ended through successive conquests rather than a single timeless “fall.”

passages.text: Early medieval Kent joined royal households, farming communities, monasteries and overseas connections. Excavations at Lyminge preserve traces of feasting, games, textile work and changing diets; surviving manuscripts transmit Kentish laws. Royal independence ended through changing overlordship and West Saxon incorporation, while Canterbury's religious and educational institutions continued.

passages.title: Written law and religious learning
passages.text: Queen Bertha worshipped at St Martin's before Augustine's arrival in 597. Aethelberht welcomed the mission and gave it land outside Canterbury. Conversion therefore developed through existing relationships, royal decisions and new institutions.

passages.title: Written law and religious learning
passages.text: The abbey probably founded in 598 combined churches and a cemetery with gardens, orchards and vineyards. Its school drew monks from far away, connecting learning with the practical support of a resident community.

passages.title: Written law and religious learning
passages.text: Textus Roffensis preserves early Kentish laws in a manuscript compiled in the early 1120s. Its survival makes older legal writing accessible, but the date of this copy must be distinguished from the seventh-century rules it transmits.

passages.title: Written law and religious learning
passages.text: Aethelberht's law code sets compensation for injuries and property offences, with distinctions among rulers, clergy, free people and enslaved people. It reveals ranked legal categories; it does not prove that every prescribed payment was enforced.

passages.title: Food, textiles and entertainment
passages.text: At Lyminge, a gaming piece was made from a hollow bone cylinder with turned end caps and a bronze rivet. Found in a royal hall setting, it gives tangible evidence of skilled manufacture and play, though the game's exact rules remain unknown.

passages.title: Food, textiles and entertainment
passages.text: Broken luxury drinking glass and animal bones accompanied Lyminge's late-sixth- and seventh-century royal complex. Together with the halls and gaming piece, these finds support an interpretation of gatherings organised around feasting and display.

passages.title: Food, textiles and entertainment
passages.text: Lyminge's eighth- and ninth-century deposits contain more large marine fish bones, including cod and whiting, than its earlier occupation. The study identifies increasing consumption while warning that recovery methods and different deposits affect comparisons.

passages.title: Food, textiles and entertainment
passages.text: Sheep became more prominent in later Lyminge animal remains, while pigs declined. Loomweights, bone needles, pin-beaters and spindle whorls also occur. The researchers suggest increased wool production, but reserve judgment pending fuller analysis of the flocks.

passages.title: Food, textiles and entertainment
passages.text: A 741 grant records a fishery on the River Lympne for Lyminge. Written landholding evidence helps explain how an inland religious community could obtain coastal foods; fish bones alone cannot establish a particular fasting rule.

passages.title: Survival and institutional change
passages.text: After a raid in 804, Lyminge's community received refuge in Canterbury. Coins, building activity and dated butchered bones show subsequent occupation at Lyminge, challenging the assumption that one recorded attack immediately destroyed the monastery.

passages.title: Survival and institutional change
passages.text: By the late ninth century the Lyminge monastery appears to have been abandoned. Sustained military pressure is the researcher's likely explanation. Tenth-century settlement returned under Canterbury's archbishops, showing that the place's history outlasted that institution.

passages.title: Survival and institutional change
passages.text: At Canterbury, tenth-century monastic reform organised prayer, reading and manual work. In 978 the abbey's dedication was extended to include Augustine. This later institutional history should not be mistaken for continued Kentish royal independence.

Kent entered a subordinate West Saxon kingdom around 825; separate kingship ended in 860. Communities and religious institutions continued, as Canterbury's later reforms and Lyminge's renewed settlement demonstrate.

passages.text: Kerma was the capital of a Nubian kingdom on the Nile in present-day Sudan. Its prosperity rested on herding, cultivation and exchange between African interiors and Egypt. This page follows the kingdom, its earlier background and what archaeology reveals about its people.

passages.title: What excavations reveal
passages.text: Excavators mapped houses with courtyards containing kitchens and grain silos. These remains show how households organized cooking and storage around shared outdoor space.

passages.title: What excavations reveal
passages.text: Temple workshops and storerooms clustered around the Western Deffufa. A palace contained a large circular building interpreted as a royal audience hall, revealing distinct religious and political spaces.

passages.title: What excavations reveal
passages.text: At Middle Kerma grave 253, researchers recorded 4,899 cattle skulls. They interpret the association between large tombs and numerous skulls as a display of the deceased person's wealth and power.

passages.title: What excavations reveal
passages.text: Some cattle horns had been deliberately reshaped; cut marks and altered growth preserve evidence of the practice. Researchers suggest specially valued animals were distinguished this way, while warning against copying modern herders' beliefs directly onto ancient Kerma.

passages.title: Arts and technology
passages.text: Kerma potters shaped exceptionally thin cups by hand, then polished their red surfaces. Controlled firing produced black rims and interiors, evidence of skilled handling of both clay and the firing atmosphere.

passages.title: Arts and technology
passages.text: A tulip-shaped beaker in Manchester Museum was excavated at Kerma in 1913. Its smooth, shining finish was made by burnishing the clay before firing; the form was achieved without a potter's wheel.

passages.title: Arts and technology
passages.text: Cattle also appeared in small figurines found in the city and in paintings in a funerary chapel. Their presence in art as well as graves suggests a significance extending beyond food and exchange.

passages.title: Daily life and food
passages.text: Animal bones from the capital show that domestic livestock supplied most of the meat evidence. Cattle, sheep and goats dominated; the researchers observed a later increase in sheep and goats relative to cattle.

passages.title: Daily life and food
passages.text: Fine beakers existed alongside heavier storage jars, sometimes stamped around the rim. Stone implements remained in use beside metal technology, preserving evidence of practical choices in everyday tools.

passages.title: Burial, belief and social rank
passages.text: Graves preserve wooden beds, personal ornaments, sandals and containers for oils or ointments. Larger, richer tombs show growing inequality; some also contained accompanying people interpreted as victims of funerary killing.

passages.title: Trade and cultural connections
passages.text: A Kerma-style beaker now at the Metropolitan Museum was excavated at Abydos in Egypt. Such finds demonstrate connections across the Nile Valley, but the museum cautions that pottery alone cannot establish whether the people buried with it were Nubian traders.

passages.title: What continued after conquest
passages.text: Survey finds include Egyptian pottery together with Nubian pottery. Stuart Tyson Smith interprets the settlement pattern as evidence that some local elites retained cultural and political latitude under Egyptian rule; conquest did not erase Nubian society.

passages.title: What remains uncertain
passages.text: The relationship between the earlier Pre-Kerma settlement and the royal city is not fully demonstrated. Excavated buildings and objects reveal much, but their locations do not establish precise kingdom borders.

Egyptian New Kingdom campaigns ended Kerma's independence. The excavation mission places the capital's destruction around 1450 BCE, after a longer conquest associated with Thutmose I and Thutmose III; this is an approximate endpoint, not a known single day of collapse.

passages.text: The Hawaiian Kingdom joined islands with much older political and cultural traditions. Its people developed newspapers, constitutional institutions and international connections while maintaining knowledge of land, water and the arts. This card follows the monarchy from Kamehameha I's consolidation in 1795 to its overthrow in 1893; unification of the principal islands was completed in 1810.

passages.title: Food and environmental engineering
passages.text: At Heeia, parallel basalt walls packed mainly with coral slowed the movement of water. Sluice gates controlled freshwater and seawater flows, maintaining brackish conditions in which algae could feed herbivorous fish. This engineering tradition long predates the unified kingdom.

passages.title: Food and environmental engineering
passages.text: Fishponds helped maintain a food supply when rough seas interrupted ocean fishing. Heeia remained part of the kingdom's lived landscape: Abner Paki received much of the surrounding land during the Mahele of 1848.

passages.title: Discoveries in surviving newspapers
passages.text: Ka Lama Hawaii began publication at Lahainaluna Seminary on Maui in 1834. Surviving issues preserve Hawaiian-language writing from the kingdom itself, giving readers access to contemporary voices alongside later histories.

passages.title: Discoveries in surviving newspapers
passages.text: A letter from Hanalei printed in Ka Hae Hawaii on 14 January 1857 set out Hawaiian month names and day counts. Its author, J. W. Q. Kaia, worried that younger readers no longer knew them. The museum cautions that month names varied between islands.

passages.title: Discoveries in surviving newspapers
passages.text: A surviving Ka Nupepa Kuokoa issue displays the Hawaiian flag in color on 1 January 1862. The original held at Hamilton Library is evidence of printing and national expression that can be lost in poor reproductions; conservation and digitization make such details easier to study.

passages.title: Work, government and public life
passages.text: The Kuhina Nui shared governing authority with the monarch, including land distribution, treaties and justice. Women of high chiefly rank held the office first. Calling it simply a prime ministership understates the authority of these early co-regents.

passages.title: Work, government and public life
passages.text: The constitution of 1840 provided for a council of nobles and a representative body chosen by the people. Early legislative rules developed over time; a written constitution did not immediately create equal political power for everyone.

passages.title: Work, government and public life
passages.text: Lahaina linked local households with visiting whaling ships, trade and, later, sugar plantations. From the 1850s Chinese immigrants worked under plantation contracts, and some settled on Maui after those contracts ended. The kingdom's economic history includes these workers as well as its rulers.

passages.title: Arts, education and the royal court
passages.text: Completed in 1882, Iolani Palace combined a royal home with rooms for official receptions and visiting dignitaries. Hula performances and grand balls formed part of its public and ceremonial life.

passages.title: Arts, education and the royal court
passages.text: Liliuokalani composed Aloha Oe in 1878, before becoming queen. Her work as a composer forms part of a larger musical legacy remembered alongside her political life.

passages.title: Arts, education and the royal court
passages.text: In 1886 Liliuokalani founded an educational society to support schooling for Hawaiian girls with limited means. Her public work connected royal patronage with access to education beyond the court.

passages.title: Arts, education and the royal court
passages.text: The Highways Act of 1892 protected public trails and rights of access. Its continuing importance to Hawaiian trail preservation shows how a kingdom-era law can shape the landscape after a change of government.

passages.title: After the overthrow
passages.text: A royalist attempt to restore Liliuokalani in 1895 failed. She was tried in the palace throne room and confined in an upstairs room, turning the royal residence into a place of imprisonment.

passages.title: After the overthrow
passages.text: Hawaiians organized petitions against annexation in 1897, and Liliuokalani continued to protest. These records preserve organized political opposition after the monarchy had been overthrown.

passages.title: After the overthrow
passages.text: Congress passed its annexation resolution on 7 July 1898. This later US action must be distinguished from the overthrow of the monarchy in 1893.

On 17 January 1893, the Committee of Safety overthrew Liliuokalani with support from the US minister and US Marines, establishing a Provisional Government. A republic followed in 1894. The removal of the monarchy did not end Hawaiian people, culture or opposition to annexation.

passages.text: The Kuba kingdom brought together several principalities in Central Africa. Royal and aristocratic patronage encouraged inventive textiles, carved vessels and images through which rank and historical memory became visible.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Kuba makers wove raffia palm fibers into cloth. Women joined, dyed and embellished panels with embroidery and applique.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Cutting embroidered raffia threads created a dense pile surface. Some panels were displayed as prestige objects and used as currency rather than worn.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Multiple cloth panels formed wrappers whose gathered edges moved with the wearer. Dress combined bodily movement with elaborate surface design.

passages.title: Historical memory
passages.text: Ndop sculptures memorialized rulers through idealized seated figures and identifying symbols. A strategy board identifies Shyaam aMbul aNgoong.

passages.title: Knowledge
passages.text: Kuba chronologies preserve references to a solar eclipse and Halley's comet, giving historians points for comparison with independently dated celestial events.

passages.text: Gunaikurnai people maintain Country, kinship and cultural knowledge across Gippsland. Stoneworking traces at the Knob and exceptionally preserved wood at Cloggs Cave connect material evidence with knowledge held by communities. Their history includes colonial displacement, the survival of family connections and continuing care for land and waters.

passages.title: People, names and Country
passages.text: Gunaikurnai brings together the recorded names Gunnai and Kurnai in a form agreed by the community. Different spellings in older records often reflect how outsiders transcribed speech; they should not automatically be treated as different peoples.

passages.title: People, names and Country
passages.text: The Gunaikurnai Land and Waters Aboriginal Corporation recognizes five major clans across Gippsland. Clan connections place responsibilities in particular landscapes, while families share wider relationships. A single outline on a map cannot capture all those connections.

passages.title: Material evidence and discovery
passages.text: At the Knob on Brayakaulung Country, deep grooves in sandstone beneath the bluff record repeated sharpening of stone axe heads. Stone scatters, camps and scarred trees also survive, making this a landscape of skilled work as well as a gathering place.

passages.title: Material evidence and discovery
passages.text: Research published in 2024 described small fireplaces at Cloggs Cave near Buchan containing trimmed Casuarina sticks and fatty residues. Dating places these features about 11,000 to 12,000 years ago. The preserved wood provides unusually direct evidence of how people prepared and used plant materials.

passages.title: Material evidence and discovery
passages.text: Working with Gunaikurnai Elders, the Cloggs Cave researchers compared those finds with nineteenth-century descriptions of ritual specialists using treated sticks. They interpret a long transmission of ritual knowledge. The excavated objects and residues are observations; the connection across millennia is the study's argued interpretation.

passages.title: Food, travel and shared work
passages.text: Dooyeedang, the Avon River, linked high country with the Gippsland Lakes. Gunaikurnai accounts describe travel along it and foods including eels and fish. Moving through this river landscape connected meals and material resources with visits, exchange and relationships.

passages.title: Food, travel and shared work
passages.text: The Knob hosted meetings where clans feasted, exchanged goods, shared news and held ceremonies. Such gatherings joined practical provisioning with social and cultural obligations; the place mattered for much more than a single activity.

passages.title: Food, travel and shared work
passages.text: Cultural fire is guided by knowledge of the season, the place and the purpose of a burn. Gunaikurnai accounts connect fire with land health, ceremony and communication. Renewing this practice draws on Elders' knowledge rather than treating every fire as an identical operation.

passages.title: Displacement, recognition and learning
passages.text: During the mission era, people continued to meet at the Knob, sometimes secretly, to maintain family ties despite enforced separation. In 2010 the same place hosted the native title determination ceremony, linking legal recognition with a much older community history.

passages.title: Displacement, recognition and learning
passages.text: Established in 2007, GLaWAC provides a community institution for representing Gunaikurnai people and caring for Country. Its public cultural protocols recognize that knowledge belongs to people and families and that perspectives within the community can differ.

passages.title: Displacement, recognition and learning
passages.text: The Cultural Hub at Forestec supports community programs and cultural learning. Stories and songlines connect knowledge with ancestors and places; teaching involves relationships and responsibilities as well as information that can be written down.

Gunaikurnai communities continue. Colonial displacement and mission control disrupted families and access to Country, but neither ended the people or their knowledge. Native title recognition, cultural learning and care for Country are later chapters of that continuing history.

passages.text: Kush was an African kingdom of the Middle Nile whose centers included Napata and Meroe. Its rulers and craftspeople developed distinctive monuments while exchanging ideas with neighboring societies. The royal city, religious settlements and industrial remains show a civilization extending well beyond its famous pyramids.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Iron-working remains and ceramic production areas at Meroe document skilled manufacture. They establish local production, not a claim that Kush invented iron smelting.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Reservoirs helped support settlements away from the Nile. Their remains are evidence for both engineering and the environmental conditions in which people lived.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Steep-sided pyramids, decorated funerary chapels and painted burial chambers gave Kushite royal commemoration a distinctive appearance.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Architecture at Meroe, Naqa and Musawwarat combined Kushite forms with elements associated with Egypt, Greece and Rome.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Gebel Barkal was a sacred landscape. Temples at its foot connected royal authority with the worship of Amun.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The Meroitic political order ended in late antiquity, but burial traditions continued afterward. A kingdom's disappearance should not be read as the disappearance of its people.

passages.text: The Kushans, a Yuezhi clan from Bactria, built an empire from the Oxus to the Ganges in the first three centuries CE. They struck gold coins, stood at the crossing of the Silk Road, and under Kanishka became the great patrons of Buddhism and the art of Gandhara.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Gandharan sculptors, drawing on Greek and Roman models, made some of the first images of the Buddha in human form, at the same time as the workshops of Mathura.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Stupas and monasteries rose at Taxila, Peshawar and Hadda; Chinese pilgrims reported Kanishka's stupa at Peshawar as the tallest building they had seen.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: The empire held the passes between the Silk Road, the Indus ports and the Ganges plain, and traded with Rome by sea and with Han China by land.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Gold coins on the Roman weight standard, showing Greek, Iranian, Indian and Buddhist gods, circulated from Central Asia to the Ganges.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Kanishka's reign, beginning about 127 CE, is remembered in Buddhist tradition for a council in Kashmir that fixed the canon of the Sarvastivada school.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Zoroastrian, Greek, Hindu and Buddhist deities all appear on Kushan coins, and Bactrian, written in Greek letters, was the language of the state.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Gandharan Buddhist art traveled along the Silk Road to Central Asia and China.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Kushan patronage helped carry Buddhism to Central Asia and on to China.
The Sasanians took Bactria and the west in the third century and set up Kushano-Sasanian governors; the last Kushan kings ruled in the Punjab in the shadow of the Guptas until about 375.

passages.text: Later Liang was the first of the Five Dynasties that ruled northern China between the Tang and Song. Founded by Zhu Wen, a former rebel who deposed the last Tang emperor, it controlled only part of northern China and faced constant military threats.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Kaifeng developed as the capital, though smaller and less cosmopolitan than Tang Chang'an.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The Five Dynasties period saw the rise of military strongmen who dominated politics.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Printing technology continued to develop during this unstable period.
Li Cunxu of Later Tang conquered Later Liang and captured its capital Kaifeng in 923.

sectionTitles: A mountain in history and memory
Homes that are works of art
Music at work, at home and in healing

passages.text: Lesotho’s national story took shape around Moshoeshoe I’s mountain stronghold at Thaba Bosiu. Clay sculptures of parents, children and musicians bring everyday lives into this history alongside rulers and political events.

passages.title: A mountain in history and memory
passages.text: Thaba Bosiu became Moshoeshoe I’s political centre in 1824. Lesotho’s heritage account describes stone walls, gateways and lookout posts strengthening the plateau’s natural defences. It also records an oral tradition that the mountain grew taller at night. That story belongs to how the place was remembered and understood; it is not a measurement of a mountain changing height.

passages.title: Homes that are works of art
passages.text: Writing in 2020, artist ‘Matsooana Sekokotoana explains how Basotho women decorated homes with litema. Designs were worked into damp earth plaster, sometimes with coloured stones making a mosaic. Cow dung helped bind the mud. The wall was a surface for skilled pattern-making as well as shelter. Her account describes a practice that has become less common as building methods change.

passages.title: Homes that are works of art
passages.text: Sekokotoana also describes a ceramic plate she made using two litema designs: boliba, associated with deep water, and lihlaba, with hills or mountains. She arranged them to evoke Lesotho’s landscape. She recalls her father encouraging patience, a lesson she connected with the careful painting. Family advice and the patterns of home found another life on a plate.

passages.title: Getting dressed for the mountains
passages.text: A blanket made around 2012 and held by the British Museum combines black and turquoise with four red vertical stripes. Its feather design belongs to the Victoria England range. The catalogue identifies wool and cotton, and manufacture at Aranda’s mill in Randfontein, South Africa. An object associated with Basotho dress can also reveal production and trade across the border.

passages.title: Getting dressed for the mountains
passages.text: The museum explains that wearing blankets are wrapped around the body and secured at the shoulders, providing warmth in Lesotho’s cold mountain conditions. The familiar stripes usually run vertically when worn. A blanket can be part of getting dressed as well as going to bed. The catalogue describes a living clothing tradition with different designs, rather than one outfit worn by everyone.

passages.title: Little sculptures, everyday people
passages.text: Samuele Makoanyane, who lived from 1909 to 1944, made small clay figures of people around him. Iziko’s collection includes a woman feeding a baby and another rolling a sleeping mat. These are an artist’s representations, not photographs of every household. Their subjects put childcare and ordinary work into a museum collection alongside portraits of kings and warriors.

passages.title: Little sculptures, everyday people
passages.text: In 1935, collector Percival Kirby commissioned Makoanyane to model musicians and their instruments. Seven figures were completed, including a herdboy playing the lesiba and a woman with a drum. The exhibition lets viewers examine these fragile sculptures as digital models. Close attention to the tiny players helps preserve evidence of performance as well as the sculptor’s individual skill.

passages.title: Music at work, at home and in healing
passages.text: A lesiba combines a stick, a stretched string and a quill. Pusetso Nyabela’s 2022 museum report describes players using their breath to make the quill vibrate, rather than simply plucking a tune. Associated with shepherds, the instrument also supplied a familiar sound before Radio Lesotho’s news. Small materials can make a very distinctive voice.

passages.title: Music at work, at home and in healing
passages.text: A revival project in 2007 and 2008 found older women in Leribe who still played the lekope, with instruments hanging on their house walls. The report describes a string stretched along a reed and a player’s mouth shaping the sound. Skills that seemed to be disappearing were still present in particular homes.

passages.title: Music at work, at home and in healing
passages.text: Recordings from the late 1950s and early 1960s documented the lekope in hlophe, a ritual healing dance. Nyabela discusses music, singing, clapping and beliefs about ancestral help. These recordings preserve accounts of healing and performance; they do not test the medical effectiveness of a treatment.

passages.title: Reading, learning and remembering families
passages.text: Morija’s archives preserve Leselinyana, a newspaper first published in 1863, alongside church registers, letters, government reports and Sesotho hymnals. French, Sesotho and English all appear in the collections. Such records let researchers follow reading, music and public debate through time. A newspaper’s small notices can open questions quite different from those answered by a royal portrait.

passages.title: Reading, learning and remembering families
passages.text: The Hub at Morija opened in 2015 as a place for digital creativity. The museum describes internet access and training in photography, film, writing and information technology. It connects a town known for historical collections with new ways of making and sharing stories. Learning about the past can happen in the same community as learning to use a camera or computer.

passages.title: Reading, learning and remembering families
passages.text: David-Frédéric Ellenberger collected oral histories and genealogies from 1866 to 1905. His interview notes, letters and maps survive at Morija, and a British Library project digitised the archive. The notes offer evidence about families and remembered events, but they also reflect what a missionary asked and chose to record. Preserving a source includes understanding the viewpoint through which it was made.

passages.title: Paintings older than the kingdom
passages.text: A 2013 heritage evaluation describes Sehlabathebe’s rock paintings in shelters and overhangs: human figures, animals including eland, and colours from earthy yellow to dark red and white. These works belong to San histories that extend beyond the later story of the Basotho kingdom. Interpreting their spiritual meanings takes research; a painted animal is not automatically a literal record of a hunting trip.

British rule ended on 4 October 1966. Lesotho continues as an independent kingdom, with later changes of government forming part of its history. The map’s Basutoland and Lesotho records do not represent the extinction and replacement of three separate peoples.

sectionTitles: A mountain in history and memory
Homes that are works of art
Music at work, at home and in healing

passages.text: Lesotho’s national story took shape around Moshoeshoe I’s mountain stronghold at Thaba Bosiu. Clay sculptures of parents, children and musicians bring everyday lives into this history alongside rulers and political events.

passages.title: A mountain in history and memory
passages.text: Thaba Bosiu became Moshoeshoe I’s political centre in 1824. Lesotho’s heritage account describes stone walls, gateways and lookout posts strengthening the plateau’s natural defences. It also records an oral tradition that the mountain grew taller at night. That story belongs to how the place was remembered and understood; it is not a measurement of a mountain changing height.

passages.title: Homes that are works of art
passages.text: Writing in 2020, artist ‘Matsooana Sekokotoana explains how Basotho women decorated homes with litema. Designs were worked into damp earth plaster, sometimes with coloured stones making a mosaic. Cow dung helped bind the mud. The wall was a surface for skilled pattern-making as well as shelter. Her account describes a practice that has become less common as building methods change.

passages.title: Homes that are works of art
passages.text: Sekokotoana also describes a ceramic plate she made using two litema designs: boliba, associated with deep water, and lihlaba, with hills or mountains. She arranged them to evoke Lesotho’s landscape. She recalls her father encouraging patience, a lesson she connected with the careful painting. Family advice and the patterns of home found another life on a plate.

passages.title: Getting dressed for the mountains
passages.text: A blanket made around 2012 and held by the British Museum combines black and turquoise with four red vertical stripes. Its feather design belongs to the Victoria England range. The catalogue identifies wool and cotton, and manufacture at Aranda’s mill in Randfontein, South Africa. An object associated with Basotho dress can also reveal production and trade across the border.

passages.title: Getting dressed for the mountains
passages.text: The museum explains that wearing blankets are wrapped around the body and secured at the shoulders, providing warmth in Lesotho’s cold mountain conditions. The familiar stripes usually run vertically when worn. A blanket can be part of getting dressed as well as going to bed. The catalogue describes a living clothing tradition with different designs, rather than one outfit worn by everyone.

passages.title: Little sculptures, everyday people
passages.text: Samuele Makoanyane, who lived from 1909 to 1944, made small clay figures of people around him. Iziko’s collection includes a woman feeding a baby and another rolling a sleeping mat. These are an artist’s representations, not photographs of every household. Their subjects put childcare and ordinary work into a museum collection alongside portraits of kings and warriors.

passages.title: Little sculptures, everyday people
passages.text: In 1935, collector Percival Kirby commissioned Makoanyane to model musicians and their instruments. Seven figures were completed, including a herdboy playing the lesiba and a woman with a drum. The exhibition lets viewers examine these fragile sculptures as digital models. Close attention to the tiny players helps preserve evidence of performance as well as the sculptor’s individual skill.

passages.title: Music at work, at home and in healing
passages.text: A lesiba combines a stick, a stretched string and a quill. Pusetso Nyabela’s 2022 museum report describes players using their breath to make the quill vibrate, rather than simply plucking a tune. Associated with shepherds, the instrument also supplied a familiar sound before Radio Lesotho’s news. Small materials can make a very distinctive voice.

passages.title: Music at work, at home and in healing
passages.text: A revival project in 2007 and 2008 found older women in Leribe who still played the lekope, with instruments hanging on their house walls. The report describes a string stretched along a reed and a player’s mouth shaping the sound. Skills that seemed to be disappearing were still present in particular homes.

passages.title: Music at work, at home and in healing
passages.text: Recordings from the late 1950s and early 1960s documented the lekope in hlophe, a ritual healing dance. Nyabela discusses music, singing, clapping and beliefs about ancestral help. These recordings preserve accounts of healing and performance; they do not test the medical effectiveness of a treatment.

passages.title: Reading, learning and remembering families
passages.text: Morija’s archives preserve Leselinyana, a newspaper first published in 1863, alongside church registers, letters, government reports and Sesotho hymnals. French, Sesotho and English all appear in the collections. Such records let researchers follow reading, music and public debate through time. A newspaper’s small notices can open questions quite different from those answered by a royal portrait.

passages.title: Reading, learning and remembering families
passages.text: The Hub at Morija opened in 2015 as a place for digital creativity. The museum describes internet access and training in photography, film, writing and information technology. It connects a town known for historical collections with new ways of making and sharing stories. Learning about the past can happen in the same community as learning to use a camera or computer.

passages.title: Reading, learning and remembering families
passages.text: David-Frédéric Ellenberger collected oral histories and genealogies from 1866 to 1905. His interview notes, letters and maps survive at Morija, and a British Library project digitised the archive. The notes offer evidence about families and remembered events, but they also reflect what a missionary asked and chose to record. Preserving a source includes understanding the viewpoint through which it was made.

passages.text: The Liu Song was the first of the Southern Dynasties, ruling from Jiankang. Despite political instability, this period saw significant cultural and intellectual achievements in the south.

passages.title: Science
passages.text: Zu Chongzhi proposes the Daming calendar, the first in China to allow for the precession of the equinoxes.

passages.title: Science
passages.text: Zu Chongzhi (429 to 500) bounds pi between 3.1415926 and 3.1415927, a precision not bettered anywhere for about nine centuries.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: The poet Xie Lingyun (385 to 433) develops landscape poetry as a major genre.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Southern culture developed distinctive characteristics that influenced later periods.
The last Liu Song emperor was deposed by Xiao Daocheng, who founded the Southern Qi dynasty.

passages.text: Luba political life joined sacred kingship with council authority. Artworks could carry political knowledge, embody ancestral relationships, or serve highly practical purposes within elite daily life.

passages.title: Knowledge and memory
passages.text: Lukasa boards use carved forms or attached beads and shells to organize histories, genealogies and significant places. Their interpretation depends on trained specialists.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The mbudye association includes women and men who interpret political principles and can restrain or reinforce chiefly authority.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Female figures on royal seats, staffs and other court objects relate to ancestral kings and the sacred character of rule.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Carved headrests protected elaborate hairstyles while their owners slept. A nineteenth-century example repeats the hairstyle in the sculpture itself.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: A headrest can create a strong sculptural composition with slender limbs and open spaces while still supporting the sleeper's head.

passages.text: Lunda rulers adapted aspects of Luba kingship while maintaining their own political independence. Trade routes and relationships with neighboring courts supported the movement of materials, artistic forms and political ideas.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: By 1650, Mwaant Yaav Naweej had connected his capital with Atlantic trade. This commerce included enslaved people as well as forest products.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Lunda outposts participated in copper exchange, while settlements near Lake Mweru linked the interior with eastern commercial routes.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Rulers commissioned artists from client peoples, including Chokwe carvers, to make prestigious court objects.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Accounts of Chibinda Ilunga describe a founding culture hero. They are traditions of legitimacy, not a dated eyewitness biography.

passages.title: Music and memory
passages.text: In related Chokwe court art, a chief holds a lamellophone associated with historical recitation and praise. The object shows how music and political knowledge could meet.

passages.text: Majapahit, founded in eastern Java in 1293, was the last great Hindu-Buddhist kingdom of the archipelago. Under Hayam Wuruk and his minister Gajah Mada it claimed overlordship from Sumatra to the Moluccas and set the pattern that Indonesia's founders looked back to.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: The Nagarakretagama, a poem by Mpu Prapanca finished in 1365, describes the court, the royal progress and the lands that sent tribute.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Red brick temples and gateways at Trowulan, and terracotta figures and piggy banks from the capital.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Wayang shadow plays and gamelan are named in Majapahit texts and carved on its reliefs.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Javanese rice bought the cloves, nutmeg and mace of the Moluccas, which Majapahit ships carried west.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Chinese cash coins were the currency; missions went to the Ming court, and Chinese and Muslim traders lived in the ports.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Shiva and the Buddha were worshipped together; the court poem Sutasoma's line Bhinneka Tunggal Ika, unity in diversity, is Indonesia's motto.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The realm was a mandala of vassals around a divine king, held by ritual and tribute more than by garrisons.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Indonesia's founders invoked Majapahit's reach when they drew the nation's borders.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Its Hindu-Javanese culture lives on in Bali, where nobles and priests moved as Islam spread in Java.
The kingdom shrank after Hayam Wuruk's death in 1389 and a civil war; the Muslim sultanate of Demak took the last Majapahit capital around 1527.

sectionTitles: Learning, writing and keeping track of things
Buildings that changed purpose, and discoveries today

passages.text: Makkura is the map’s name for Makuria. Its capital, Dongola, grew around a fortified centre beside the Nile. Houses, churches and workshops reveal a city of builders and makers as well as rulers.

passages.title: At home, including the bathroom
passages.text: House A at Old Dongola had a bathroom with heated water and painted walls, plus a toilet upstairs. These excavated features show that some residents devoted considerable effort to comfort and sanitation. An upstairs toilet belongs in the history of medieval engineering too. This particular house does not tell us that every family enjoyed the same facilities.

passages.title: At home, including the bathroom
passages.text: A study of four Dongola house compounds, spanning the fourteenth to seventeenth centuries, examined chemical traces in floors. Comparisons with reference samples helped locate activities, especially food preparation, where few visible objects remained. A swept floor can still hold clues. The researchers found that similar-looking homes could be used in different ways as residents’ needs changed.

passages.title: At home, including the bathroom
passages.text: From the fourteenth century onward, many Dongola dwellings grouped small residential buildings around a shared courtyard. Rooms included benches and storage spaces for vessels and equipment. Archaeologists examine how shared and separate working areas shaped household relationships. A floor plan can suggest how people met and worked together, but it cannot establish every resident’s family tree.

passages.title: Learning, writing and keeping track of things
passages.text: A rubbish deposit beside Dongola’s monastery church contained pottery fragments used for writing exercises. Examples include a Coptic alphabet and archangels’ names written in an unpractised hand. Other pieces carry Greek grammar exercises. Broken pottery could serve as a writing surface. These finds show learning, although they do not reveal every pupil’s age or how many children attended lessons.

passages.title: Learning, writing and keeping track of things
passages.text: A monastery room yielded two groups of dishes bearing the names of religious leaders Lazaros and Stephanos. Each group included roughly ten pots. Writing could identify belongings as well as record prayers. These names connect ordinary tableware with particular people, though the finds do not prove whether each leader ate alone or shared meals with others.

passages.title: Learning, writing and keeping track of things
passages.text: Some Dongola inscriptions switch between Greek and Old Nubian. Other texts present psalms in both languages, sometimes alternating the language from verse to verse. This makes multilingual religious life visible on the walls. The texts preserve written choices, but they do not tell us that every resident spoke both languages fluently.

passages.title: Families, land and neighbours
passages.text: A land-sale document from Qasr Ibrim names a woman, Kapopi, selling property inherited from her mother to Neuesi, an official’s daughter, and Anenikoli. A 2019 reanalysis dates it to November 1, 1191, while noting an older discussion using 1190. This northern Nubian record preserves a woman acting in a property transaction, without proving that every woman had identical rights or wealth.

passages.title: Families, land and neighbours
passages.text: Old Nubian land sales often described a plot by naming neighbouring owners and the land upstream and downstream along the Nile. The 2019 study argues that descriptions normally proceed from south to north. Finding your field depended on relationships between people and places: the neighbours were part of the address. Some readings and exact locations remain uncertain.

passages.title: Small objects and skilled making
passages.text: A pot beneath the pavement of the church on Kom D at Dongola contained a necklace of about one hundred beads. Materials included coloured glass, faience, shell, bone and stone. Researchers interpreted it as a seventh-century foundation deposit. The necklace shows materials brought together in an unusual setting; its placement does not tell us who previously wore it, or whether anyone did.

passages.title: Small objects and skilled making
passages.text: Dongola ornaments included marine shells altered for suspension. Some cowrie shells had their upper surfaces removed or pierced; larger cone shells had their tips cut off. One pierced shell still had a leather thong. These objects connect inland adornment with marine materials and skilled preparation, while the route taken by each shell remains unknown.

passages.title: Buildings that changed purpose, and discoveries today
passages.text: Dongola’s Mosque Building preserves an Arabic foundation inscription dated 1317. Architectural study shows the earlier monumental hall being adapted for worship, including a prayer niche and new plaster over painted walls. Its earlier role as a royal audience hall is an interpretation of its plan and decoration. One building’s conversion did not mean that every resident changed religion that year.

passages.title: Buildings that changed purpose, and discoveries today
passages.text: In a discovery announced in 2023, archaeologists investigating a later house found an opening into a small painted chamber below its floor. One scene shows a Nubian ruler with Christ and Archangel Michael. Preliminary reading of a difficult inscription mentions a King David and protection for a city. The identification and historical occasion were still being investigated: a dramatic painting is not a photograph of a known event.

Makuria fragmented during the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries. The court left Dongola in the 1360s, but the city continued under a smaller kingdom and later within the Funj sphere. Changes of government and religion unfolded over time. The map’s 1492 endpoint does not establish a single conquest or the disappearance of Nubian communities.

passages.text: Malacca, founded about 1400 by Parameswara, a prince from Palembang, became within a century the greatest port of Asia, where the monsoons met. Its sultans made Islam and Malay the faith and language of the archipelago's trade.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Ships from China, Gujarat, Bengal, Arabia, Java and the Spice Islands met at Malacca to exchange cloth, spices, tin, gold and porcelain.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Tomé Pires, writing just after the conquest, counted 84 languages spoken in the city and wrote that whoever was lord of Malacca had his hand on the throat of Venice.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Zheng He's fleets called at Malacca from 1405, and the sultanate sent missions to the Ming court.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The ruler adopted Islam around 1414, taking the name Iskandar Shah; Malacca became a center from which Islam spread to Java and the islands.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The Undang-Undang Melaka, the laws of Malacca, and the Malay Annals were written in Malay in the Arabic script.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Malay spread as the lingua franca of maritime Southeast Asia and became Malaysian and Indonesian.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Malacca's laws and court customs set the model for the Malay sultanates.
Afonso de Albuquerque took the city in August 1511 after a month's fighting; the sultan fled and his heirs founded Johor.

passages.text: Mali connected West African gold-producing regions with a wider commercial and intellectual world. Mansa Musa became internationally famous through his pilgrimage, while architecture and oral performance preserved different forms of cultural memory.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Gold and salt served long-distance commerce; cowrie shells also entered local exchange during the fourteenth century.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Mansa Musa passed through Cairo during his pilgrimage in 1324 to 1325. His distribution of gold made a strong impression on contemporaries.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Timbuktu's Djingareyber Mosque traces its initial construction to Musa's return from pilgrimage. Later rebuilding means the surviving fabric represents multiple periods.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Mande jeliw transmit historical epics through skilled performance. Musical accompaniment helps structure and pace narratives.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Mosque architecture and scholarship connected Timbuktu to Islamic networks while local building practices remained central.

sectionTitles: Crafts that carry names and meanings

passages.text: The Mamluk sultanate centred on Cairo and governed Egypt and much of Syria. Rulers drawn from military households supported institutions and specialised crafts. Surviving buildings and objects illuminate urban services, skilled labour, trade and the public display of authority.

passages.title: Institutions and exchange
passages.text: Military recruits entered the ruling system through enslavement, education and training, followed by manumission and service. Advancement was not solely hereditary. This path to elite office depended on coercive recruitment and should not be confused with freedom from social hierarchy.

passages.title: Institutions and exchange
passages.text: Trade in silks and spices helped finance patronage. Textiles and carpets also circulated internationally. Skilled production connected merchants and workshops with wealthy buyers well beyond the sultanate.

passages.title: Water, teaching and care
passages.text: Qalawun’s complex on Cairo’s al-Mu’izz Street joined a school, mosque, tomb and hospital. The arrangement brought teaching and care into an architectural foundation that also preserved the ruler’s memory. The building’s functions were broader than royal burial alone.

passages.title: Water, teaching and care
passages.text: Shaykhu’s sabil, established in 1354, supplied water to passers-by. Its rock-cut rooms have openings to cisterns below, and jars were used in distribution. The surviving structure shows how storage and service worked together in a city street.

passages.title: Water, teaching and care
passages.text: Qayitbay’s fifteenth-century complex combined a madrasa, a public water facility and a kuttab for Qur’anic teaching to poor Muslims. A courtyard and surrounding halls organised the school. Education, water supply and commemoration shared one foundation.

passages.title: Water, teaching and care
passages.text: Wooden furnishings at Qayitbay’s madrasa include a pulpit and a Qur’an reciter’s chair inlaid with ivory. Their construction demonstrates skilled joinery and ornament in objects used for teaching and worship, alongside the stonework of the building.

passages.title: Crafts that carry names and meanings
passages.text: A glass lamp made for Amir Qawsun around 1329 to 1335 combines a blown body and applied foot with enamel and gilding. Its inscription identifies the patron. The museum regards a mosque or tomb-hospice as its probable destination, rather than a proven findspot.

passages.title: Crafts that carry names and meanings
passages.text: A fourteenth-century tray stand bears a cup emblem and an inscription naming Husain, son of Qawsun. Brass was worked and inlaid with contrasting metals. Stands of this kind held trays of fruit and other food, connecting elite dining with symbols of court office.

passages.title: Crafts that carry names and meanings
passages.text: The Five Medallion Carpet, dated around 1500, uses wool for its foundation threads and knotted surface. Repeated geometric forms organise the long design. Its attribution to Egypt, probably Cairo, remains an attribution, not a documented excavation location.

passages.title: Crafts that carry names and meanings
passages.text: A fifteenth-century engraved brass box names Muhammad al-Hamawi, the timekeeper at Damascus’s Umayyad Mosque. His office supervised prayer times and announcements concerning Ramadan. The box probably held food; it documents a specialist’s role without itself being a timekeeping instrument.

Ottoman conquest ended the Egyptian sultanate in 1517. Tuman Bey was captured and executed in Cairo after resisting the invasion. Mamluk elites retained influence under Ottoman rule, so the loss of the sultanate did not immediately eliminate its military households or social power.

sectionTitles: What the Wairau Bar settlement preserves
Growing food in a cooler environment

passages.text: East Polynesian voyagers established communities in Aotearoa around the thirteenth-century transition to the fourteenth. This early-period card follows settlement, food production and watercraft through named archaeological sites. Māori histories encompass distinct communities and traditions; this map label does not identify a single kingdom.

passages.title: What the Wairau Bar settlement preserves
passages.text: At Wairau Bar, unfinished adzes and stone-working waste record the shaping of argillite brought from the Nelson and D’Urville Island region. The concentration suggests organised production, potentially supplying other communities, rather than only occasional tool repair.

passages.title: What the Wairau Bar settlement preserves
passages.text: Wairau Bar fishing equipment adapts Polynesian designs to local materials, including moa bone and stone where tropical pearl shell was unavailable. Middens also contain fish, shellfish, birds, dogs and marine mammals. Early livelihoods drew on several resources.

passages.title: What the Wairau Bar settlement preserves
passages.text: Isotope analysis distinguishes childhood environments recorded in tooth enamel from later diets recorded in bone. Wairau Bar ancestors show differences in food and likely mobility; those signals do not identify a precise birthplace for every person or a uniform diet for the settlement.

passages.title: What the Wairau Bar settlement preserves
passages.text: Ornaments and equipment accompanied some Wairau Bar burials, including drilled moa eggs, worked teeth and adzes. These objects document distinctive treatment of the dead. They cannot, by themselves, establish a complete hierarchy of occupations or rank among the living.

passages.title: Growing food in a cooler environment
passages.text: At Triangle Flat in Golden Bay/Mohua, planting pits dated to 1290 to 1385 contained microscopic starch interpreted as kūmara-like, alongside evidence attributed to taro and yam. The finding places horticultural experimentation within the early settlement period.

passages.title: Growing food in a cooler environment
passages.text: Triangle Flat lies within the customary jurisdiction of Manawhenua ki Mohua. Its garden evidence challenges the assumption that early southern settlers relied almost entirely on hunting and gathering after abandoning tropical crops. That conclusion concerns this investigated landscape, not every settlement.

passages.title: The Anaweka canoe
passages.text: A surviving canoe hull from Anaweka on the South Island’s northwest coast was shaped from native mataī wood. Internal ribs and a longitudinal stringer were carved into the hull, while lashing holes joined components. These features reveal construction knowledge beyond simply hollowing a log.

passages.title: The Anaweka canoe
passages.text: Additional holes beside damaged lashings show repairs to the Anaweka hull. Caulking helps date its final use to approximately 1400; older wood dates do not establish when the canoe was built. Researchers reconstruct the wider vessel from a surviving component.

passages.title: The Anaweka canoe
passages.text: A turtle carved in relief on the Anaweka hull resembles motifs in other Polynesian traditions. The researchers interpret it as evidence of cultural connections. It does not establish a uniquely identifiable departure island or the biography of the people aboard.

passages.title: Communities across generations
passages.text: Local groups maintained their own authority and relationships through genealogy, mana and tapu. Exchange carried valued materials such as pounamu, obsidian and harakeke among communities. Shared practices coexisted with regional histories and changing social ties.

The map’s 1530 endpoint is a change in coverage, not the disappearance of Māori. Colonial confiscations later dispossessed many communities, while iwi, hapū and whānau continued. The kōhanga reo movement, beginning in 1982, is one example of community-led language transmission across generations.

sectionTitles: Fishing and the meaning of clothing
Carving, memory and a documented removal

passages.text: Māori communities maintained distinct iwi and hapū histories through trade, technological change and colonisation. This card follows named examples of food production, fishing, carving and language education. The imported interval ending in 1914 does not mark an end to Māori society.

passages.title: Food and childhood at Tamahere
passages.text: A study of seven ancestors from Tamahere site S14/487, dated about 1700 to 1780, found diets predominantly based on plants. Archaeological context supports cultivated root crops as important foods. Isotopes do not identify each meal, and this small sample cannot describe all Māori diets.

passages.title: Food and childhood at Tamahere
passages.text: The teeth of two children in the Tamahere study preserve a changing dietary signal consistent with weaning onto plant foods within their first two to three years. This is a finding about those children, not a universal rule for childhood across iwi.

passages.title: Fishing and the meaning of clothing
passages.text: Te Papa’s pā kahawai lure OL000106/10, dated broadly to 1750 to 1850, combines a shaped and polished pāua-shell shank with a shell barb and tightly bound muka fibre. Fine notches decorate the shell. It preserves several stages of skilled manufacture in one small fishing implement.

passages.title: Fishing and the meaning of clothing
passages.text: Kākahu provided warmth and protection, while particular cloaks also expressed status and relationships. Their continued use as esteemed gifts and at funerals connects material workmanship with honour, care and ancestral memory. Everyday use and ceremonial importance should not be treated as interchangeable.

passages.title: Carving, memory and a documented removal
passages.text: In the early 1840s, carvers led by Raharuhi Rukupo created Te Hau ki Tūranga at Orakaiapu pā, Manutuke. The whare whakairo belongs to Ngāti Kaipōhō of Rongowhakaata. Its carved ancestors and memorial purpose joined artistic work to hapū history and relationships.

passages.title: Carving, memory and a documented removal
passages.text: In 1867 Crown troops dismantled Te Hau ki Tūranga and removed it despite objections. Rukupo recorded that he had refused requests to give it up. This documented removal is part of the building’s history alongside its artistry.

passages.title: Carving, memory and a documented removal
passages.text: The Rongowhakaata settlement deed signed in 2011 acknowledges the wrongful taking of Te Hau ki Tūranga and records the Crown’s apology. The account recognises the harm caused by separating the taonga from its community.

passages.title: Authority, land and continuing knowledge
passages.text: The Treaty signed in 1840 survives in texts with different meanings. The Māori text speaks of kāwanatanga in Article 1 and guarantees tino rangatiratanga over lands, villages and taonga in Article 2; the English text uses sovereignty. Treating these as identical obscures the historical disagreement.

passages.title: Authority, land and continuing knowledge
passages.text: The New Zealand Settlements Act of 1863 enabled land confiscation from communities labelled rebellious. Confiscation also took land from Māori who had remained neutral or supported the government. The effects differed by region, with severe losses in Waikato and Taranaki.

passages.title: Authority, land and continuing knowledge
passages.text: For many iwi, Matariki connects seasonal knowledge with remembrance and sharing the harvest. Communities observe it in different ways and at different times. Its significance joins practical attention to the year with relationships among the living and the dead.

passages.title: Authority, land and continuing knowledge
passages.text: Pukeatua kōhanga reo opened in Wainuiomata in April 1982. The movement places children in Māori-language immersion environments and gives whānau responsibility for running centres. Education here includes language, relationships and cultural knowledge transmitted through daily life.

Māori have no cultural fall date. Colonial war and confiscation transformed landholding and political authority, while communities persisted. Te Tiriti remains central to the history of their relationship with the Crown. Kōhanga reo exemplifies continuing whānau-led work to pass language and knowledge to future generations.

sectionTitles: Ōtuataua: a worked and inhabited landscape
Gardening and the work of clothing

passages.text: This record follows Māori communities in the sixteenth and early seventeenth centuries. Gardens, crafts and ancestral taonga reveal knowledge rooted in particular places. Iwi and hapū had distinct histories and authority, not a single state.

passages.title: Ōtuataua: a worked and inhabited landscape
passages.text: Ōtuataua Stonefields at Ihumātao preserve rows, heaps and mounds associated with cultivation on volcanic ground. The specialised system may have developed by the fifteenth or sixteenth century. Adding sand and gravel and arranging stone helped growers manage soil and growing conditions.

passages.title: Ōtuataua: a worked and inhabited landscape
passages.text: Shell middens at Ōtuataua, including deposits dated to the sixteenth or seventeenth century, show that coastal foods accompanied gardening. Habitation areas and storage features place food production within a lived landscape rather than an isolated agricultural installation.

passages.title: Ōtuataua: a worked and inhabited landscape
passages.text: Today’s stonefields contain features from different periods. Māori gardens, house sites, cooking shelters and terraces share the landscape with nineteenth-century European drystone walls. A visible wall is therefore not automatically evidence of a pre-contact Māori garden boundary.

passages.title: Gardening and the work of clothing
passages.text: In the middle Waikato Basin, modified soils and borrow pits record intensive horticulture from the sixteenth century. Gardeners moved gravel into cultivation areas. Storage pits and planting features add evidence of sustained labour in managing root crops.

passages.title: Gardening and the work of clothing
passages.text: Whatu forms cloth by twining horizontal threads around vertical ones with the fingers. Muka fibre extracted from harakeke supplied material for cloaks. Raranga uses plaiting, commonly for mats and baskets. These related crafts solve different structural problems.

passages.title: Gardening and the work of clothing
passages.text: Rain capes combine a worked foundation with overlapping plant strips that shed water. Scraped sections allowed the strips to be attached as the garment grew. The construction joined knowledge of fibre preparation, fastening and weather protection; no exact invention date is established here.

passages.title: Knowledge, ancestry and the seasons
passages.text: Te Papa presents weaving’s whakapapa through Hine-te-iwaiwa, guardian of weaving, childbirth and lunar cycles. In this tradition, women transmit the skills and knowledge. Craft is understood through relationships among people, ancestors and the natural world as well as through technique.

passages.title: Knowledge, ancestry and the seasons
passages.text: Uenuku, an ancestral carving held at Te Awamutu Museum, represents an atua of Tainui. Tainui tradition associates the spirit of Uenuku with the voyaging waka. The museum gives a broad traditional dating range; this card does not convert it into a precise manufacture year.

passages.title: Knowledge, ancestry and the seasons
passages.text: For many iwi, Matariki’s return to the winter dawn sky marks a new year. Remembrance, harvest thanksgiving and sharing food connect observation of the heavens with community life. Timing and observance vary among iwi; there was no single uniform national calendar.

Māori communities continue beyond this map interval. Ōtuataua retains local ancestral connections. Later colonial confiscation caused dispossession, while iwi and hapū persisted. Kōhanga reo supports continuing cultural transmission.

passages.text: The Maratha state founded by Shivaji in the Western Ghats broke Mughal power in the eighteenth century and, as a confederacy of chiefs under the Peshwa at Pune, ruled or taxed most of India by the 1750s. Its horsemen, hill forts and revenue administration made it the last great Indian power before the British.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Light cavalry that lived off the country and struck and withdrew defeated slower Mughal armies.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Shivaji's chain of hill forts, Raigad, Pratapgad and Sinhagad among them, controlled the passes of the Western Ghats.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: A navy under Kanhoji Angre held the Konkan coast against the Portuguese, the Siddis and the East India Company.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Shivaji was crowned Chhatrapati at Raigad in a Vedic ceremony asserting independent Hindu kingship.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The Ashtapradhan, a council of eight ministers, ran war, revenue, foreign affairs and religion.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Marathi, with Sanskrit terms replacing Persian ones in Shivaji's chancery, became the language of state.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Revenue came as chauth and sardeshmukhi, a quarter and a tenth of the yield, collected directly from the land.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The Maratha wars drained the Mughals; after the defeat at Panipat in 1761 the confederacy recovered and held Delhi's emperor as a client.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Marathi identity and the memory of Shivaji remain central in Maharashtra.
The East India Company beat the confederacy in three wars; the Peshwa surrendered in 1818 after the Third Anglo-Maratha War and his lands were annexed.

sectionTitles: Discoveries beneath the shore and town

passages.text: Martinique’s history spans a plantation colony and a continuing Caribbean society within France. Writers and musicians developed distinctive cultural forms. Its separate map intervals do not represent an unchanged government.

passages.title: Discoveries beneath the shore and town
passages.text: At Anse Trabaud in Sainte-Anne, excavators recovered wood, seeds and probable calabash fragments from deeply buried coastal deposits. These fragile materials add evidence that ordinary pottery assemblages cannot supply. The report describes exceptionally good preservation, while treating several botanical identifications as preliminary.

passages.title: Discoveries beneath the shore and town
passages.text: Manchineel stones in one sediment sample suggest a coastal environment where the poisonous tree grew. They are not evidence that people ate its fruit. Together with the sequence of sand and organic deposits, plant remains help reconstruct the changing surroundings in which the village’s inhabitants lived.

passages.title: Discoveries beneath the shore and town
passages.text: Saint-Pierre’s port area preserved stacks of imported porcelain and earthenware sealed by the 1902 disaster. Researchers identified heat-marked impressions of straw used as packing. Plates that had been stored for sale therefore reveal both overseas supply and the practical work of transporting fragile goods.

passages.title: Discoveries beneath the shore and town
passages.text: The same ceramics research distinguishes imported tableware from locally made water vessels and industrial pottery. Sugar moulds, molasses pots and roof tiles served different tasks from cups and plates. Marks and clay types help investigate workshops, although several proposed manufacturing places remain tentative.

passages.title: Work, records and freedom
passages.text: Plantation slavery survived the changes of imperial control around 1800. When France recovered Martinique in 1802, the incoming administration maintained an existing system of coercion. The island’s chronology therefore differs from that of colonies where the 1794 abolition had actually taken effect.

passages.title: Work, records and freedom
passages.text: The events of May 1848 involved enslaved workers at Le Prêcheur, Morne-Rouge and Saint-Pierre. Their mobilization and the ensuing violence forced an early local proclamation of abolition. The distinction between the uprising on 22 May and the decree on 23 May makes the participants’ agency visible.

passages.title: Work, records and freedom
passages.text: Freedom left difficult questions about land and work unresolved. Compensation was eventually arranged for those claiming losses from emancipation, while formerly enslaved people received none. Abolition ended legal enslavement but did not itself create equal access to property.

passages.title: Work, records and freedom
passages.text: Copies of parish and civil registers were collected to safeguard legal rights and administration. These records let researchers follow particular households through births, marriages and deaths.

passages.title: Writing, music and public knowledge
passages.text: Tropiques began in 1941 through collaboration among teachers and writers including Aimé and Suzanne Césaire and René Ménil. Its essays and poetry treated Caribbean experience as a subject of intellectual creation. Literary scholar Olga Hel-Bongo explains how apparently cultural subjects could carry criticism of colonial authority.

passages.title: Writing, music and public knowledge
passages.text: Suzanne Césaire helped bring manuscripts to the censorship authorities. The journal’s contributors used indirection as well as open argument; censorship interrupted publication in 1943. Their achievement involved editing, securing print and reaching readers under pressure, alongside the writing itself.

passages.title: Writing, music and public knowledge
passages.text: The community association AM4 describes the tibwa as two dry hardwood sticks that maintain a repeating rhythm, struck against a drum’s rear or sometimes bamboo. The bèlè drum uses a wooden barrel body and an animal-skin head; the player sits astride it and works with hands and heel.

passages.title: Writing, music and public knowledge
passages.text: Singing moves between a lead voice and a responding chorus. Instrument combinations vary by region and kind of music, so one ensemble cannot represent every Martinican practice. The tradition depends on shared timing, remembered verses and skilled interaction as much as on the construction of instruments.

passages.title: Writing, music and public knowledge
passages.text: In 1946, Césaire presented a parliamentary report supporting departmental status. The record of his interventions also includes food supply, protections for agricultural workers and bringing unused land into cultivation. These questions connect constitutional change with the daily concerns of households and labourers.

passages.title: Writing, music and public knowledge
passages.text: The 1902 catastrophe gave the Pelean eruptive type its name and helped scientists understand violent volcanic processes. The forests and volcanoes of northern Martinique entered UNESCO’s World Heritage List in 2023 for their geological and ecological importance. Recognition preserves both scientific evidence and places inseparable from local memory.
Colonial administration gave way to departmental status in 1946. Territorial institutions changed again in 2015, within France. Martinican society continues across these changes.
