passages.text: The Parthian Empire, ruled by the Arsacid dynasty from 247 BCE to 224 CE, held Iran and Mesopotamia between Rome and the steppe for nearly five centuries. Its armored lancers and horse archers, its great noble houses and its grip on the Silk Road made it Rome's only equal in the East.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: The Parthian shot: horse archers turned in the saddle to shoot behind them at full gallop.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: At Carrhae in 53 BCE, horse archers and cataphracts, riders and horses in scale armor, destroyed a Roman army under Crassus.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: The empire sat astride the Silk Road; Chinese silk reached Rome through Parthian middlemen who kept the two ends apart.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Envoys from Han China reached the Parthian court in the 110s BCE, and in 97 CE the Han envoy Gan Ying got as far as the Persian Gulf.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Zoroastrian, Greek, Babylonian and Jewish communities kept their own cults, and the kings styled themselves friends of the Greeks on their coins.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The Arsacids claimed descent from the Achaemenid king Artaxerxes II.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The Sasanians inherited Parthian cavalry, provinces and great noble houses.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Parthian, a Middle Iranian language written in its own script, was still used in the Sasanian royal inscriptions.
Ardashir I of Persis defeated and killed the last Arsacid king, Artabanus IV, at Hormozdgan in 224 and founded the Sasanian dynasty.

passages.text: Pictish communities and kingdoms occupied parts of early medieval Scotland. Their history survives in carved stones, workshops, food remains and outside accounts. The evidence reveals connected regional societies, not a single unchanged state. Political authority and language changed as Alba emerged, without a securely established single date when all Picts disappeared.

passages.title: Peoples, places and evidence
passages.text: Written references to Picts begin in the late third century. This first surviving name is not a secure founding date for a people or kingdom.

passages.title: Peoples, places and evidence
passages.text: Fortriu, a powerful kingdom by the seventh century, is now located around the Moray Firth. Its full extent and relationship with smaller regions remain debated.

passages.title: Peoples, places and evidence
passages.text: Rhynie's fifth- and sixth-century settlement had successive ditches and a larger timber palisade. The Craw Stane stood near an entrance. These excavated relationships connect symbol stones with an inhabited, repeatedly remodelled place.

passages.title: Making, exchange and ordinary work
passages.text: An iron axe-shaped pin from Rhynie resembles the axe on the Rhynie Man stone. Clay moulds for comparable pins establish local manufacture, linking a carved image to the work of metalworkers.

passages.title: Making, exchange and ordinary work
passages.text: Rhynie's ditch deposits contained imported amphora fragments, continental glass, crucibles and metalworking tools. The vessels demonstrate exchange connections, while production debris shows that the settlement also made valuable objects.

passages.title: Making, exchange and ordinary work
passages.text: Around 700, Portmahomack's workers carved stone, worked metal and glass, and processed hides interpreted as parchment production. Combined with its burial pattern and infrastructure, this supports identification as a monastery.

passages.title: Making, exchange and ordinary work
passages.text: Cattle bones dominate Portmahomack's animal remains. The researchers connect cattle with food, possible dairying and hides for parchment. Supporting a religious community required husbandry and skilled processing as well as prayer.

passages.title: Making, exchange and ordinary work
passages.text: After the monastic phase, a Portmahomack workshop became a kiln barn with an upper floor and flue. Its alteration, together with grain remains, makes a change in everyday work visible in the buildings.

passages.title: Making, exchange and ordinary work
passages.text: Charred barley and evidence for oats and wheat at Lairg document cultivation from about 450 onward. Such environmental traces reveal food production even where early medieval houses are difficult to identify.

passages.title: Images, learning and change
passages.text: The Hilton of Cadboll cross-slab, erected around 800, places a woman prominently in a hunting scene. The original was later cut and reused as a grave marker; the stone at the site today is a replica.

passages.title: Images, learning and change
passages.text: Bede reports that King Naiton asked Ceolfrid for guidance on Easter and builders for a stone church. His account shows royal interest in religious calculation and imported expertise, although it presents these exchanges through Bede's Christian viewpoint.

passages.title: Images, learning and change
passages.text: Burning and broken sculpture mark Portmahomack's destruction around 800. A Viking raid is a proposed explanation, not an identified attacker. Workers subsequently cleared debris and resumed metal and glass production.

Pictish power centres shifted during the later ninth century, and Alba extended uneven authority into the Highlands in the tenth. This was a prolonged political and cultural transformation. The evidence does not support one conquest date or the disappearance of an entire population.

sectionTitles: Learning, patronage and the wider state

passages.text: Medieval Poland developed from Piast centres into a kingdom with towns, religious communities, mining enterprises and a university. Its political geography changed through fragmentation and renewed royal authority. Bridges, excavated buildings, municipal layouts and written records offer different views of everyday work and learning. The union with Lithuania in 1569 transformed the state while the Polish Crown continued within the Commonwealth.

passages.title: Discovering the early centres
passages.text: Remains of two tenth-century wooden bridges lie in Lake Lednica beside the island stronghold. They connected its palace and chapel complex with routes towards Poznan and Gniezno. The timbers document organised construction and access across water, beyond the history of individual rulers.

passages.title: Discovering the early centres
passages.text: Excavators uncovered two depressions in the Lednica chapel in 1988 and 1989. The museum interprets them as baptismal basins. They support discussion of early Christian practice, but identifying them with Mieszko's own baptism remains an interpretation rather than a witnessed event.

passages.title: Discovering the early centres
passages.text: At Giecz, foundations of an unfinished palace and chapel belong to the late tenth century; a stone stronghold church dates to the early eleventh. Unfinished work is evidence too: a surviving plan does not mean the planned building was completed or used.

passages.title: Urban communities and salt workers
passages.text: Krakow's charter of 1257 helped shape a merchants' town whose market, streets and public buildings remain legible. Wawel formed a distinct royal and episcopal centre. The city's accumulated buildings reflect repeated construction, not a single medieval building campaign.

passages.title: Urban communities and salt workers
passages.text: Kazimierz, chartered in 1335, began as a separate town beside Krakow. Catholic and Jewish communities shaped its later streets, religious buildings and customs. Its medieval origin should not be used to assign every surviving synagogue or house to the founding year.

passages.title: Urban communities and salt workers
passages.text: Wieliczka produced salt from brine before deep mining expanded in the thirteenth century. An exploratory shaft found in the Saltworks Castle courtyard preserves evidence of that transition. The casing shown to visitors has been reconstructed, so the presentation includes both remains and modern interpretation.

passages.title: Urban communities and salt workers
passages.text: By the late thirteenth century, the Cracow Saltworks joined mines and salt-processing facilities at Wieliczka and Bochnia. Administration and sales connected underground labour to royal income and distant markets. The enterprise needed coordination above ground as well as extraction below it.

passages.title: Urban communities and salt workers
passages.text: The mines preserve galleries, tools and spaces later adapted for chapels or storage. UNESCO cautions that much surviving technical evidence is from the eighteenth century onward. Medieval methods are partly known from documents and reconstructions; the whole visitor route is not a medieval workplace.

passages.title: Learning, patronage and the wider state
passages.text: Casimir III founded the University of Krakow in 1364. Teaching faltered after his death, and a renewed charter followed in 1400 through the patronage of Jadwiga and Wladyslaw Jagiello. Institutional continuity required renewed resources and organisation rather than one founding act alone.

passages.title: Learning, patronage and the wider state
passages.text: Endowed university chairs supported subjects including astronomy, mathematics, grammar and rhetoric. The Corpus Academicum project identifies patrons such as Jan Stobner and Katarzyna Mezykowa. Teaching depended on people financing particular posts, not only on royal sponsorship.

passages.title: Learning, patronage and the wider state
passages.text: Fifteenth-century Krakow attracted scholars in law and mathematical astronomy. Nicolaus Copernicus began his studies there in 1491. His attendance belongs to the history of this teaching community; it should not imply that all his later astronomical work was completed at the university.

passages.title: Learning, patronage and the wider state
passages.text: The 1569 Act of the Union of Lublin records a new constitutional relationship between the Kingdom of Poland and the Grand Duchy of Lithuania. A surviving legal act makes the transition more specific than describing Poland as simply falling to a neighbouring country.

The Union of Lublin joined the Polish Crown and the Grand Duchy of Lithuania in the Commonwealth in 1569. Polish institutions and communities continued within that arrangement. The imported map interval ending in 1400 is neither the kingdom's extinction nor the date of this constitutional transformation.

passages.text: This chapter follows Renaissance planning and learning in Poland-Lithuania. Zamosc offers a local view of how architectural ideas, commerce and education could meet in one deliberately planned town.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The Union of Lublin joined the Polish Crown and Grand Duchy of Lithuania in the Commonwealth under one monarch in 1569.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: In the late sixteenth century, Bernardo Morando designed Zamosc using Italian Renaissance ideas of an ideal city, adapted to Central European architectural traditions.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Zamosc was conceived as a trading centre on a route connecting western and northern Europe with the Black Sea. Arcaded merchants' houses enclosed its main market square.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Founder Jan Zamoyski established the Zamosc Academy. The planned town combined education with residential, commercial and civic functions.

passages.text: This chapter follows Portuguese architecture and learning from the sixteenth to eighteenth centuries, through Lisbon's Belem complex and Coimbra's colleges, laboratories and printing facilities.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: In sixteenth-century Belem, the Hieronymites monastery combined richly carved Manueline decoration with spaces for worship, meals, study and communal life.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: The Belem tower incorporated ribbed cupolas inspired by Islamic architecture. Its design records artistic exchange across cultural boundaries.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Coimbra University has occupied the Royal Palace of Alcacova since 1537 and expanded through a network of colleges.

passages.title: Science
passages.text: In the eighteenth century, Coimbra added chemistry and other laboratories, a botanical garden and a university press. These facilities linked teaching, experimentation and the circulation of books.

passages.text: This chapter follows the designed landscapes and museum ambitions associated with Prussia in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. It focuses on architects, craftspeople and the institutions that organized their work.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Frederick II commissioned Sanssouci between 1745 and 1747. The palace later hosted the French writer Voltaire.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: In the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, Potsdam's parks combined architecture with landscape gardening. Builders, painters, sculptors and gardeners contributed to the ensemble.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: During the nineteenth century, Peter Joseph Lenne planned changes to the Havel landscape around Potsdam. Designed parkland linked water, buildings and views.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The Museum Island project in Berlin began in the nineteenth century. It treated museum architecture and the display of art and archaeology as a connected public undertaking.

passages.text: The Ptolemies governed Egypt from Alexandria as Macedonian monarchs and Egyptian pharaohs. Their kingdom brought Greek-speaking rulers into a society with enduring Egyptian languages, temples and crafts. Surviving decrees and estate papers reveal both royal institutions and everyday work.

passages.title: Discoveries and what they reveal
passages.text: The Rosetta Stone preserves a priestly decree honoring Ptolemy V in 196 BCE. Soldiers found it reused in a fort at el-Rashid in 1799, so its discovery location is not the original setting of the decree.

passages.title: Discoveries and what they reveal
passages.text: Hieroglyphic Egyptian, Demotic Egyptian and Greek versions address different readers of the same royal decree. This is evidence of multilingual administration and priestly authority, not three different spoken languages.

passages.title: Discoveries and what they reveal
passages.text: Villagers digging for fertilizer uncovered the Zenon archive near ancient Philadelphia in 1914 to 1915. The documents illuminate a third-century BCE estate, but their exact original findspot was not recorded.

passages.title: Daily life and agricultural work
passages.text: A lease copied in a lawsuit prepared by Zenon required tenants to grow wheat and barley and deliver grain rent at Philadelphia. Clauses about seed advances and outstanding debts reveal how agricultural work depended on both produce and credit.

passages.title: Daily life and agricultural work
passages.text: The same document allowed recovery from debtors, their guarantors and their property. Read beside its crop instructions, it shows the unequal bargaining power behind estate production, rather than an idyllic picture of farming.

passages.title: Daily life and agricultural work
passages.text: A papyrus dated 7 May 254 BCE records a stolen donkey. This small dispute survives because estate papers were kept, giving a glimpse of transport animals and ordinary losses outside royal histories.

passages.title: Science and learning
passages.text: Eratosthenes worked at the Alexandrian library in the third century BCE. He compared summer-solstice shadows at Syene and Alexandria with an estimated distance between them to calculate Earth's circumference.

passages.title: Science and learning
passages.text: His original measurement treatise is lost; the method survives in later authors. Uncertainty about the length of the stadium makes a single modern claim for his percentage accuracy misleading.

passages.title: Science and learning
passages.text: The sieve associated with Eratosthenes identifies prime numbers by removing multiples. It is a concrete example of mathematical reasoning connected with Alexandria's scholarly world.

passages.title: Arts and religious life
passages.text: Temple workshops made faience vessels and colorful glass inlays. Egyptian and Greek forms coexisted, and royal portraits could combine Greek hair with Egyptian poses.

passages.title: Arts and religious life
passages.text: Egyptian temples remained centers of scholarship and worship, supported by rulers who also promoted their own royal cults.

passages.title: Trade and correspondence
passages.text: Zenon's files include letters about shipments of wheat and wine as well as official and personal business. Their survival connects agricultural production with transport and administration, rather than treating trade as an abstract royal achievement.
Roman takeover in 30 BCE ended the dynasty after Cleopatra VII's defeat. Egyptian religious and artistic traditions continued beyond the change of rulers.

passages.text: Pueblo societies comprise distinct communities and histories. Chaco Canyon and Mesa Verde preserve ancestral building and farming landscapes; Taos Pueblo is a living community with its own traditions and government.

passages.title: Architecture
passages.text: At Chaco, builders planned multistory Great Houses whose construction could span generations. Their masonry and shared layouts mark a regional architectural tradition.

passages.title: Science and landscape
passages.text: Many Chaco structures were oriented toward solar, lunar or cardinal directions. Their placement linked buildings to a meaningful surrounding landscape.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Mesa Verde preserves farming terraces, check dams, reservoirs and ditches as well as houses. These remains document the engineering of everyday subsistence.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Roads connected Chaco Great Houses across the region. Some major buildings may have hosted periodic ceremonies and exchange rather than dense permanent populations.

passages.title: Living architecture
passages.text: At Taos, families maintain adobe homes by renewing earthen plaster. Taos describes that work as an ongoing connection between ancestors and the present.

passages.title: Continuity
passages.text: Changes in ancestral settlements did not end Pueblo life. Mesa Verde remains a living connection to present-day Pueblo peoples, and Taos continues as a sovereign community.

sectionTitles: Discoveries: spaces for gathering and living

passages.text: Puerto Rico’s history includes knowledge passed through hands, families and neighbourhoods. Hammock makers work plant fibres, coffee farmers teach younger growers, and dancers exchange ideas with drummers. These living practices belong to an island shaped by Indigenous, African and European histories and a wider Puerto Rican diaspora.

passages.title: Discoveries: spaces for gathering and living
passages.text: At Caguana in Utuado, a ceremonial centre dating broadly to 1200 to 1500 CE, excavators uncovered rows of limestone slabs around a levelled plaza. Some bore carved faces. Builders cut into the hillside to create the flat gathering space. The remains show organised construction and a setting for communal ceremonies, although every activity cannot be reconstructed from the stones alone.

passages.title: Discoveries: spaces for gathering and living
passages.text: Between two of Caguana’s courts, excavators recorded postholes outlining a circular wooden building, along with two hearths, decorated pottery and a carved stone cemí, a spiritual object. A piece of Spanish glazed pottery appeared with Taíno objects in an undisturbed context. This association suggests activity into the contact period, rather than a perfectly clean break between two worlds.

passages.title: Homes, water and learning
passages.text: Smithsonian researchers documented an elderly Puerto Rican woman making hammocks with fibres from the maguey plant. Textile specialist Soraya Serra Collazo helped the team find this living craft tradition. Turning a tough plant into a place to rest takes considerable skill. A good nap can begin with somebody else’s hard work.

passages.title: Homes, water and learning
passages.text: The builders of Castillo San Cristóbal designed the fort to collect rain. Five cisterns beneath its plaza stored water for use inside. Those underground reservoirs were part of the engineering that made the eighteenth-century fortress workable. Beneath the impressive courtyard lay a practical answer to a very ordinary problem: everyone gets thirsty.

passages.title: Homes, water and learning
passages.text: A January 1942 photograph by Jack Delano shows children outside a wooden building in Aibonito. Above the doorway, the sign reads “Comedor Escolar,” meaning school dining room. Open shutters and a corrugated roof are visible. School history includes places to eat as well as classrooms, although this photograph does not tell us what lunch tasted like.

passages.title: Health, food and practical knowledge
passages.text: In the early twentieth century, Bailey Ashford and Pedro Gutiérrez worked on Puerto Rico’s hookworm problem. Their programme combined investigation and treatment with teaching about infection and improving waste disposal to reduce contact with contaminated soil. The historical account shows that caring for health extended beyond a doctor’s consulting room into public facilities and everyday surroundings.

passages.title: Health, food and practical knowledge
passages.text: In a 2022 interview, filmmaker Russell Oliver described learning about farming at Hacienda Masini in the mountains of Yauco. He met older coffee farmers who wanted to pass their knowledge to the next generation. His team’s documentation project grew from those relationships. Behind a cup of coffee are people learning about plants, land and the work of growing a crop.

passages.title: Music, family and social life
passages.text: In bomba, the lead drummer responds to a dancer’s movements, turning gestures into rhythms. Your feet can give the drummer homework. Singing often uses call and response, while barrel-shaped drums, a maraca and wooden sticks contribute different sounds. The tradition developed among African-descended communities in Puerto Rico and continues through performances and workshops on the island and in its diaspora.

passages.title: Music, family and social life
passages.text: Margarita “Tata” Cepeda’s bomba dress entered the story told by the Smithsonian’s Latino museum in its 2023 exhibition rotation. The museum connects the garment to the Cepeda family’s work performing and teaching bomba and plena. Clothing can preserve a history of movement and family learning, as well as fabric and colour.

passages.title: Freedom, government and living heritage
passages.text: Puerto Rico’s March 22, 1873 abolition law declared an end to slavery, yet required freed people to enter labour contracts lasting at least three years. Former enslavers received compensation, while full political rights for the freed people were delayed. The law’s clauses show why a legal declaration of freedom did not immediately remove every coercive restriction on daily life.

passages.title: Freedom, government and living heritage
passages.text: Voters approved a Puerto Rican constitution in 1952, followed by congressional approval. It organised the island’s internal government, including elected leaders and courts. Constitutional self-government and independent national sovereignty are different things: Puerto Rico continued within the United States territorial system.

passages.title: Freedom, government and living heritage
passages.text: Caguana is also a place of living spiritual meaning. In a 2007 account, Taíno advocates described their campaign for ceremonial access and a voice in caring for the site, including a 2005 protest. Their perspective reminds us that an archaeological park can be someone’s sacred place. Present-day communities have their own knowledge, responsibilities and views about its future.

Spanish rule ended in 1898, followed by United States administration and later commonwealth government. Puerto Rico remains a U.S. territory. Its communities and Indigenous heritage continue through changing institutions and cultural practices.

passages.text: Qin began as a frontier state of the Zhou in the Wei River valley in 770 BCE and grew, by reform and conquest, into the power that unified China in 221 BCE. The empire created a centralized bureaucratic state that replaced feudal fragmentation. Though the dynasty lasted only fifteen years, its institutional innovations became the foundation of all subsequent Chinese empires.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Shang Yang's reforms in the state of Qin reward farming and soldiering, punish by fixed law and break the power of the old nobility, the Legalist programme the empire would follow.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Legalism becomes state orthodoxy, emphasizing strict laws, harsh punishments and absolute state power.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Books of rival philosophies are ordered burned, and by tradition scholars are executed the next year.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The First Emperor seeks immortality through alchemy and travels to sacred mountains.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Standardization of weights, measures, axle widths and written script across the empire.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Construction of the Great Wall begins, connecting earlier defensive walls along the northern frontier.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: The Terracotta Army, some 8,000 life-size soldiers, is completed to guard the First Emperor's tomb; work had begun on his accession in 246 BCE.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Bronze mirrors, crossbow mechanisms and standardized coinage show unified artistic standards.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: The small seal script standardized for official use, later replaced by clerical script.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: The empire divided into thirty-six commanderies governed by appointed officials rather than hereditary lords.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Corvée labor conscripted for massive public works: roads, the Lingqu canal linking the Yangzi and Pearl river systems, and the Epang palace.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Harsh legal code applied uniformly across the empire.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Standardized bronze coins in round shape with square hole become the empire's currency.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Imperial highways facilitate military movement and commercial exchange.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The name China probably derives from Qin, by way of Sanskrit and Persian.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Centralized bureaucratic administration replaced feudalism in all subsequent dynasties.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Standardized writing enabled cultural unity across linguistic diversity.
After the First Emperor's death, popular rebellions and civil war led to the dynasty's collapse in 206 BCE; Liu Bang, the victor of the wars that followed, founded the Han.

passages.text: For four centuries one government ruled every shore of the Mediterranean, from the Atlantic to the Euphrates and from Hadrian's Wall to the first cataract of the Nile. Rome invented little that was wholly new and perfected almost everything it borrowed: Greek architecture became concrete vaults, Etruscan drains became aqueducts, and a city-state's customs became a body of law that most of Europe still lives under. Its language, Latin, is the parent of Spanish, Portuguese, French, Italian and Romanian.

passages.title: Inventions and building
passages.text: Roman concrete, opus caementicium, mixed with volcanic ash so that it set even under water. The harbour moles built with it at Caesarea and Portus still stand.

passages.title: Inventions and building
passages.text: Vitruvius completes De architectura, ten books on building, water, machines and city planning that guided Renaissance architects fifteen centuries later.

passages.title: Inventions and building
passages.text: The Colosseum opens: about 50,000 seats, a retractable awning, and eighty entrances so the whole crowd could leave in minutes.

passages.title: Inventions and building
passages.text: The Pantheon's concrete dome, 43.3 meters across, is completed under Hadrian. It is still the largest unreinforced concrete dome in the world.

passages.title: Science
passages.text: Pliny the Elder publishes the Natural History, thirty-seven books that try to gather everything then known about the natural world.

passages.title: Science
passages.text: Ptolemy, working in Alexandria, writes the Almagest, the geocentric model of the heavens that stood for 1,400 years, and a Geography that placed the known world on a grid of coordinates.

passages.title: Science
passages.text: Galen arrives in Rome. His dissections of animals describe the nerves, the heart and the pulse, and his anatomy is taught in Europe until the sixteenth century.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Aqueducts: eleven serve the city of Rome by 226 CE, feeding public fountains, baths and a sewer system, the Cloaca Maxima, that still drains the Forum.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Roads: about 80,000 km of paved highway across the empire by the second century, cambered for drainage, with milestones and way stations a day's ride apart.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: The codex, pages bound at the spine, begins to replace the scroll; by the fourth century it is the normal form of the book.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: The mills at Barbegal near Arles: sixteen water wheels in two descending rows, grinding grain for a whole town.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Virgil dies leaving the Aeneid unfinished. Augustus orders it published against the poet's wishes, and it becomes Rome's national epic.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Ovid completes the Metamorphoses, the retelling of Greek and Roman myth that fed European painting and poetry for two thousand years.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Trajan's Column: a 30-meter spiral of carved relief telling the story of the Dacian wars in 155 scenes.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Portrait sculpture that shows the sitter warts and all, mosaic floors from Britain to Syria, and the wall paintings of Pompeii, sealed by Vesuvius in 79 CE.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Roman law: the praetors' edicts and the jurists' commentaries, later gathered under Justinian, are the root of the civil law systems of continental Europe and Latin America.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Seneca, Stoic philosopher and tutor to Nero, is ordered to kill himself, leaving the Letters to Lucilius. Stoicism was the working philosophy of the Roman elite.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Constantine's Edict of Milan grants freedom of worship. Christianity, persecuted a decade earlier, becomes the religion of the emperors.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The Edict of Thessalonica makes Nicene Christianity the state religion.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Public baths in every town, with hot and cold rooms, exercise yards and libraries. Entry cost a quadrans, the smallest coin.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: A market the size of the Mediterranean: Spanish olive oil, Egyptian grain, Gaulish wine and Indian pepper moved in amphorae. Monte Testaccio in Rome is a hill made of an estimated 53 million broken oil jars.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Insulae, apartment blocks of five or more storeys, housed most of Rome's roughly one million people, the largest city in the world until the nineteenth century.

On the death of Theodosius I in 395 the empire was divided between his sons Arcadius and Honorius and never reunited. The Western half fell in 476; the Eastern half, which we call Byzantine, lasted until 1453.

passages.text: The Safavids, who took Tabriz in 1501, made Twelver Shia Islam the religion of Iran and gave the country the shape and identity it has kept since. Shah Abbas I's Isfahan, the carpets, the painted manuscripts and the long wars with the Ottomans mark their two centuries.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Shah Abbas I made Isfahan his capital and laid out the Naqsh-e Jahan square with the Shah Mosque, the Sheikh Lotfollah mosque and the Ali Qapu palace.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: The Ardabil carpet of 1539 to 1540 and the court workshops set the standard for Persian carpets, which reached European palaces by the thousands.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Reza Abbasi and the Isfahan painters, and the Shahnameh made for Shah Tahmasp with its 258 miniatures.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Ismail I proclaimed Twelver Shia Islam the state religion at Tabriz and brought Shia scholars from Lebanon and Iraq to teach it.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: A clerical hierarchy, the shrines of Mashhad and Qom and the mourning rites of Muharram took root.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Armenian Christians, Jews and Zoroastrians lived as protected communities, with periods of pressure.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Shah Abbas moved Armenian merchants from Julfa to New Julfa in Isfahan; their network carried Iranian silk to Venice, Amsterdam and India.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Isfahan grew into one of the largest cities of the seventeenth century, with its bazaar, bridges and gardens.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Twelver Shia Islam remains Iran's state religion.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Naqsh-e Jahan square was listed by UNESCO.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Carpets and miniature painting remain the arts Iran is known for.
Afghan rebels took Isfahan in 1722 after a siege. Nader, an Afshar Turkmen general, drove them out, ruled through puppet Safavid shahs, and took the crown himself as Nader Shah in 1736.

passages.text: Saint Kitts and Nevis became an independent federation in 1983. Its history also lives in household objects, classroom craftwork and Christmas street theatre.

passages.title: Archaeology: ornaments, supper and toilets
passages.text: At Coconut Walk on Nevis, the 1998 excavations recovered a polished shell pendant shaped like a tooth, with a tiny suspension hole drilled from both sides. Most pottery in the assemblage was assigned broadly to about 500 or 600 to 1500 CE. The finds reveal skilled work before European colonization.

passages.title: Archaeology: ornaments, supper and toilets
passages.text: At colonial Jamestown, excavators found handmade cooking jars with soot, a handled cooking bowl and a coalpot or brazier. These Afro-Caribbean vessels show food preparation alongside imported European pottery. The clay was thought local, but the report explicitly left that identification awaiting scientific examination.

passages.title: Archaeology: ornaments, supper and toilets
passages.text: Toilets leave history behind, too. Jamestown deposits dated around 1850 to 1880 included decorated chamber pots and washing basins. These are tangible evidence of household hygiene; the pots alone cannot tell us exactly where each family kept them or how waste was disposed of.

passages.title: Building, homes and work
passages.text: Brimstone Hill’s impressive walls depended on the skill and forced labour of enslaved Africans. Builders used locally quarried basalt blocks around a rubble core, with limestone around openings and corners. Construction developed from 1690 over the following century. Britain’s military abandoned the fortress in 1853; that was the end of its garrison role, not the end of island society.

passages.title: Building, homes and work
passages.text: After apprenticeship ended in 1838, plantation workers still faced a difficult bargain: employment could be tied to a home and a plot for growing food on estate land. Losing a job could mean eviction. Some workers moved into Basseterre, where overcrowding and inadequate sanitation became major concerns. Work, family housing and public health were closely connected.

passages.title: Building, homes and work
passages.text: The St. Kitts sugar factory stopped operating on 23 July 2005. This closed a major chapter of plantation-linked industrial work, rather than ending the country’s history. The date is a useful reminder that an economic institution can disappear while the communities shaped by it continue.

passages.title: Learning, nursing and community life
passages.text: Ismay Burt began as a pupil teacher and later trained in Antigua. After receiving a craft-training grant in 1946, she shared skills with teachers at Warner Park: hats, bags, fans and baskets made from screw pine. Learning could turn leaves into useful objects and an income. Her home also became a meeting place for people entering teaching.

passages.title: Learning, nursing and community life
passages.text: May Stevens became matron of Cunningham Hospital in 1949, the first person born in the St. Kitts-Nevis-Anguilla presidency to hold that post. Student nurses also worked as staff, making regular training difficult. Stevens supported further study, including evening English and mathematics classes in 1960. Better healthcare involved teaching and organization as well as treatment.

passages.title: Learning, nursing and community life
passages.text: Burt’s teaching extended into neighbourhood celebrations. She trained the Newtown Junior Choir, organized a Christmas programme and helped provide gifts for less privileged children. After retiring, she continued craft teaching and hosted a Golden Age Club. One person’s biography shows how school, music and care across generations could overlap.

passages.title: Street theatre and living traditions
passages.text: Christmas Sports are street performances, so the name does not mean a football tournament. Masquerade dancers wear ribbons, mirrors and bells, accompanied by bamboo fife and drums. Moko Jumbie performers dance on stilts above the crowd. The National Archives describes changing costumes and participation, reminding us that living traditions keep adapting.

passages.title: Street theatre and living traditions
passages.text: The Mummies are actors, rather than wrapped archaeological remains. Their name comes from mummers, and the play brings together figures such as saints, a captain and a doctor in staged confrontations. Fife and drum accompany the troupe. The National Archives notes that their costumes changed to resemble those of the masquerade.

passages.title: Street theatre and living traditions
passages.text: Kindergartens and primary schools helped pass on masquerade dance, especially around Christmas. Groups also performed at private parties and tourism events beyond the holiday. A cultural-department registration programme began in 1995. Preservation here includes children learning steps and performers earning fees, alongside the older street celebrations.

British sovereignty ended with independence in 1983. The federation joined St. Kitts and Nevis, while Anguilla followed a separate political path. Nevis received its own island administration under the new constitution. Communities, crafts and performance traditions continued through these institutional changes; the imported map’s 2020 endpoint is not a date when the country ceased to exist.

sectionTitles: Work, slavery and the struggle for freedom

passages.text: Saint Lucia’s island history reaches far beyond the independent state established in 1979. Archaeological sites preserve evidence of earlier craft and coastal life. French and British colonization brought plantation slavery, while struggles over freedom and self-government changed political institutions. Kwéyòl celebrations, scholarship and literature are continuing parts of this history.

passages.title: Discoveries and earlier island life
passages.text: At Morne Lezard, a 2002 survey recovered small chert flakes, blade tools and hammerstones in test pits above the Balenbouche River. These remains, alongside previously collected ground-stone axes, identify an area of stoneworking. Their concentration helps researchers study where tools were made, without identifying the makers from pottery labels alone.

passages.title: Discoveries and earlier island life
passages.text: At Saltibus Point, the team excavated shell tools, griddle fragments and bones of turtles and fish. A fragment of a spindle whorl and a shaped shell inlay added evidence of craft. The refuse deposit brings food preparation and manufacture into view together; some shell fragments initially described as scoops may instead be natural breakage.

passages.title: Work, slavery and the struggle for freedom
passages.text: A government order of 1832 regulated the time enslaved plantation workers could spend cultivating allotted food plots. During the first twelve weeks of the harvest season it allowed every second Monday, followed by every Monday for the remaining forty weeks. The schedule expressly accommodated planters’ needs, exposing how control of working time reached into household subsistence.

passages.title: Work, slavery and the struggle for freedom
passages.text: The same order set Monday as market day. It treated workers who received statutory food rations differently from those cultivating allotted plots, and named particular holidays. These are rules prescribed by colonial authorities, not proof that every estate obeyed them or that enslaved people accepted the arrangements.

passages.title: Work, slavery and the struggle for freedom
passages.text: The people whom colonial accounts called brigands included Africans who had left plantations and lived in forests. In 1796, formerly enslaved defenders fought alongside French revolutionary forces against a British invasion that threatened renewed enslavement. Their struggle concerned personal freedom as well as imperial control; it was not yet the independence of the modern state.

passages.title: Knowledge, writing and public memory
passages.text: Arthur Lewis, born in Castries, won a scholarship to Britain in 1932 and studied at the London School of Economics. His later university career included Manchester and Princeton. In 1979 he shared the economics prize for research into development, bringing questions about poorer countries into the centre of economic analysis.

passages.title: Knowledge, writing and public memory
passages.text: Lewis examined economies where a large agricultural workforce coexisted with expanding capitalist industry. He also studied the terms on which countries exporting tropical products traded with industrial economies. These models asked how growth and its benefits were distributed across sectors and countries; they were analytical contributions, not a single technology invented on Saint Lucia.

passages.title: Knowledge, writing and public memory
passages.text: Derek Walcott described an English-language education at Saint Mary’s College within a world shaped by French Creole, African rhythms and Catholic practice. His mother was a teacher and encouraged his writing. In his account, literary work grew through family, teachers, theatre and the multilingual life around him.

passages.title: Knowledge, writing and public memory
passages.text: Discussing Omeros, Walcott said he wanted to celebrate the island and people he knew. He resisted describing the poem as a simple rewriting of the Odyssey: classical references mattered, but Caribbean lives had their own meanings. His 1992 literature prize recognized a career rooted in this creative engagement with history and place.

passages.title: Knowledge, writing and public memory
passages.text: Researcher Winston Phulgence interviewed people involved in the Freedom Monument project. Debate over Ricky George’s design included whether a seated man conveyed resistance and why women’s participation was absent. The resulting discussion shows how public monuments select and interpret the past, rather than simply reproducing it.

passages.title: Community organization and living traditions
passages.text: La Rose and La Marguerite are flower societies whose preparations extend far beyond their August and October feast days. Groups organize singing and dancing gatherings in owned or rented halls, raising funds through refreshments and games. The chantwèl, or lead singer, sustains the performance and the gathering’s energy.

passages.title: Community organization and living traditions
passages.text: The societies maintain repertoires that include quadrilles, lancers and other dances. More spontaneous gatherings and the formal feast have different expectations. The Folk Research Centre does not claim a precise origin date for the festivals; their continuing importance rests on collective organization, musical skill and participation.

passages.title: Community organization and living traditions
passages.text: Jounen Kwéyòl brings language, food, dress, traditional practices and technology into public celebration. Host communities and activities across the country contribute to a month of cultural events around October’s international Creole observance. This work makes local knowledge something to teach and use, as well as something to remember.

passages.title: Community organization and living traditions
passages.text: The 1978 constitutional order records the Saint Lucian House of Assembly’s request for the independence arrangements. Its commencement date was 22 February 1979. Reading the document distinguishes the legal end of association with Britain from earlier steps toward internal self-government.

British rule ended with independence in 1979. Saint Lucia continues as a nation, with living cultural institutions and traditions. The map’s separate Saint Lucia records are intervals of geographic coverage, not repeated endings of its people or society.

sectionTitles: Discoveries, buildings and a surviving object
Land, forced migration and continuing communities

passages.text: Saint Vincent and the Grenadines became independent in 1979. This geographic history includes the earlier Kalinago and Garifuna presence, colonial rule and struggles over land and labour. Indigenous village remains, farming practices and community knowledge reveal lives beyond changes of government.

passages.title: Discoveries, buildings and a surviving object
passages.text: At Argyle, archaeologists recovered the plans of eleven houses. Two larger elongated structures were interpreted as men’s houses through comparison with Raymond Breton’s historical descriptions. The excavated outlines provide evidence of building arrangements; their proposed social functions depend on interpretation as well as the physical remains.

passages.title: Discoveries, buildings and a surviving object
passages.text: The village also yielded pottery, beads, axe heads and European wares. Ceramic connections extend toward South America and the Greater Antilles. Reconstruction involved local experts and Kalinago and Garifuna participants in choices about wood, binding and roofing, bringing archaeological evidence into discussion with living building knowledge.

passages.title: Discoveries, buildings and a surviving object
passages.text: A carved coconut-shell ladle in the West India Committee collection bears Chatoyer’s name and the date 1773 on a silver rim. Its exact provenance is unknown, and its handle may be a later addition. Association with a diplomatic gift is plausible, not proven by the inscription alone.

passages.title: Land, forced migration and continuing communities
passages.text: The 1763 treaty speaks in the language of possession by crowns. Saint Vincent’s Indigenous inhabitants were not parties to that agreement. The treaty therefore documents an imperial claim, while later negotiations and wars show that control on the ground remained contested.

passages.title: Land, forced migration and continuing communities
passages.text: The Garifuna Heritage Foundation connects the forced exile of 1797 with communities in Honduras, Belize, Guatemala and Nicaragua. Its account also stresses enduring ties with people on Saint Vincent. Deportation was a catastrophic loss of homeland and autonomy, followed by cultural survival across new places.

passages.title: Land, forced migration and continuing communities
passages.text: UNESCO’s recognition concerns Garifuna language, dance and music in Central America. Oral narratives, songs and participatory performances transmit knowledge associated with cassava cultivation, fishing and canoe building. Their 2008 inscription followed a 2001 proclamation; neither date marks the beginning of the culture.

passages.title: Farming, household work and craft
passages.text: Research on women estate workers links their withdrawal from plantation labour after apprenticeship to abusive working conditions. Growing and selling provision crops offered an alternative. This helps explain emancipation through choices about work and household survival, alongside the legal dates that changed labourers’ status.

passages.title: Farming, household work and craft
passages.text: Arrowroot cultivation and starch processing have supported families in northern and northeastern Saint Vincent, particularly Indigenous communities. A 2019 design brief describes the crop’s dense roots and leafy cover as useful on loose volcanic soils, while noting that unusually heavy rain could still erode fields. Agricultural knowledge here involves both production and care for sloping land.

passages.title: Farming, household work and craft
passages.text: The same brief describes an existing factory where grinding had to pause while starch settled under gravity. Its proposed replacement aimed to connect processing more effectively with pulverizing and packing. The document reveals how growers’ livelihoods depended on factory maintenance and processing capacity; the proposal alone does not prove the new plant was operating.

passages.title: Farming, household work and craft
passages.text: Craftworkers use bamboo, banana fibre, palm leaves and grasses for baskets, mats, hats and other objects. Wood carving, clothing, steel pans and goatskin drums also appear among documented local industries. These practices combine knowledge of materials with the needs of households, performers and markets.

passages.title: Scientific work and public participation
passages.text: During the 2020 to 2021 eruption, the UWI Seismic Research Centre, Montserrat Volcano Observatory and local monitoring staff combined earthquake records, gas measurements, cameras and ground movement data. Expanding the instrument network made changes in activity easier to observe. Scientists interpreted several kinds of evidence together rather than relying on a single warning signal.

passages.title: Scientific work and public participation
passages.text: On 8 April 2021, increased activity prompted a red alert and evacuation before explosions began the next day. The researchers emphasize preparedness, communication and uncertainty in forecasting. The achievement was a coordinated response involving scientists, authorities and residents, with decisions made before the eventual course of the eruption was known.

passages.title: Scientific work and public participation
passages.text: After the eruption, northern residents used photography and community walks to document changes in their surroundings. Participants also helped identify locations for rain gauges and monitored rainfall with scientific support. Their photographs were exhibited in Kingstown and Sandy Bay in 2022, making local experience part of the record of recovery.

passages.title: Scientific work and public participation
passages.text: Adult suffrage and self-government developed through several institutional changes. The 1951 voting reform was followed by ministers in 1956 and associated statehood in 1969. These dates distinguish broader political participation from full independence, which required another constitutional settlement.

Colonial rule ended with independence in 1979, and Saint Vincent and the Grenadines continues as a nation. The earlier defeat and deportation of Garifuna communities did not end their culture or ties with the island. Separate map intervals do not represent repeated national extinctions.

passages.text: The Samanids, a Persian dynasty ruling from Bukhara from 819 to 999, presided over the revival of Persian as a written language after two centuries of Arabic. Their court fed the poets and scholars of the Islamic Golden Age in Central Asia.

passages.title: Science
passages.text: Avicenna was born near Bukhara; his Canon of Medicine remained a standard medical text in Europe and the Islamic world into the seventeenth century.

passages.title: Science
passages.text: Al-Biruni was born in Khwarazm and began his work in astronomy and mathematics as the Samanid age ended.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Rudaki, called the father of Persian poetry, wrote at the court of Nasr II.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Ferdowsi began the Shahnameh, the Persian epic, under Samanid rule; he finished it in 1010.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Bowls and plates from Nishapur and Samarkand carry black Kufic proverbs on white slip.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Persian became a language of court and literature beside Arabic; the vizier Bal'ami's Persian version of Tabari's history was made for the amir.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The dynasty was Sunni and patronized Hanafi scholars, and Bukhara became a center of Islamic learning.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Bukhara and Samarkand were the Silk Road's markets between China and the Islamic west.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Samanid silver dirhams were carried north along the Volga in such numbers that hoards of them turn up across Russia and Scandinavia.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The Persian literary revival shaped the Ghaznavid, Seljuk and later courts.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The mausoleum of the Samanids in Bukhara, a cube of patterned brick, is among the oldest surviving Islamic monuments in Central Asia.
The Karakhanids took Bukhara in 999 while the Ghaznavids, once Samanid slave-governors, took Khurasan south of the Oxus.

passages.text: The Sámi are an Indigenous people whose homeland, Sápmi, crosses northern Norway, Sweden, Finland and Russia’s Kola Peninsula. They speak several related languages and have pursued varied livelihoods, including fishing, hunting, handicrafts and reindeer husbandry. No single occupation or modern national border defines the whole people.

passages.title: Food, movement and household knowledge
passages.text: Fishing in seas, lakes and rivers supported many Sámi communities, while organized hunting required knowledge of animal routes and behavior. Surviving pit systems record collective work in hunting landscapes. Reindeer herding became highly visible, but treating every Sámi family as a herd-owning household obscures this wider economic history.

passages.title: Food, movement and household knowledge
passages.text: A seasonal herding camp needed pasture, fresh water, fuel, building materials and suitable dry ground. Cold springs or ground suitable for storage helped keep milk. Choosing a location therefore involved practical knowledge of several resources at once, rather than simply following animals without a planned pattern of return.

passages.title: Food, movement and household knowledge
passages.text: Reindeer milking was labor-intensive and could involve the whole family. Herders moved among different milking grounds during summer; mountain routes also used snow patches where animals found relief from insects and heat. These are descriptions of particular herding systems, not evidence that the same schedule applied to coastal fishers or every Sámi region.

passages.title: Food, movement and household knowledge
passages.text: Sámi languages are related but distinct. In Finland, Northern Sámi, Inari Sámi and Skolt Sámi each have their own communities and histories. Language is part of work and the transmission of skills, as well as schooling and literature. Calling all of these languages a single uniform tongue would hide that diversity.

passages.title: Craft, buildings and historical evidence
passages.text: Duodji joins making, use and cultural knowledge. Materials include birch bark, roots, hide, sinew and reindeer antler. Portable containers, knives and clothing were shaped for particular tasks and for movement where required. Craftsmanship also continues as art and a livelihood; a museum object is one moment in an evolving practice.

passages.title: Craft, buildings and historical evidence
passages.text: The náhppi, a vessel for milking reindeer, illustrates how a household object’s form addressed a practical problem: limiting spillage. Containers could be carved from birch burls or root growths. Such work required understanding the material as well as the task. This is a documented object type, not a claim about an excavated specimen’s date.

passages.title: Craft, buildings and historical evidence
passages.text: Tirro Farm at Siida represents nineteenth-century Sámi life in permanent houses. Its place among movable tents, shelters and storage buildings makes an important distinction visible: Sámi architecture included several forms, suited to different livelihoods. The museum setting is a curated presentation, rather than an untouched nineteenth-century village.

passages.title: Craft, buildings and historical evidence
passages.text: Siida also preserves Mirhamintupa, a courthouse moved from the Inari-Kittilä border. Names and inscriptions left by people awaiting sentences survive on its walls. The building offers a different kind of evidence from hunting tools: a physical trace of encounters with judicial authority, preserved in a structure relocated for interpretation.

passages.title: Craft, buildings and historical evidence
passages.text: Medieval sagas and chronicles describe Sámi people through their authors’ interests. Ottarr’s account, for example, connects northern resources with tribute. Such texts can reveal trade and relations of power, but they should not be read as a complete census, a neutral ethnography or proof that every named northern group was identical.

passages.title: Restrictions, organizing and continuing institutions
passages.text: Border closures divided grazing systems that had crossed what became national frontiers. Some herders moved from Kautokeino to Karesuando after 1852 and continued using Finnish winter pasture as Swedish subjects, until the later closure blocked that route too. State lines changed practical access to land without making Sámi relationships stop at those lines.

passages.title: Restrictions, organizing and continuing institutions
passages.text: The Swedish school system distinguished children by their families’ livelihoods and offered mobile herders’ children inferior conditions. Sámi delegates challenged both the physical accommodation and the limited educational expectations in 1918. Their demands show parents and organizers seeking the knowledge children needed for a changing society, while resisting policies imposed upon them.

passages.title: Restrictions, organizing and continuing institutions
passages.text: Elsa Laula Renberg helped bring together the cross-border Sámi congress held in Trondheim on 6 February 1917. Organizing across state boundaries became an enduring part of Sámi public life. The event is commemorated by Sámi National Day, linking contemporary civic expression with an earlier achievement in collective representation.

passages.title: Restrictions, organizing and continuing institutions
passages.text: Finland’s Sámi Parliament works on language, culture and Indigenous status, while the Skolt Sámi also have a separate decision-making body. Norway and Sweden have their own Sámi parliaments. These institutions should be understood in their particular settings; they are not a single sovereign state governing all of Sápmi.

The Sámi continue as a people across several states, maintaining languages, livelihoods, cultural institutions and political representation. Borders and state policies restricted land use and shaped community life, but there was no single event in which a unified Sámi kingdom fell. The imported map intervals describe coverage, not the people’s lifetime.

passages.text: Samoa has a long history of Pacific voyaging, skilled craft and family-based social institutions. This card follows the western islands through colonial government and independence, with clearly identified earlier background. Samoan people and culture also extend to American Samoa and overseas communities; the modern state is not the whole Samoan world.

passages.title: Discoveries and the deeper past
passages.text: Pottery fragments recovered during construction of the Mulifanua ferry berth on Upolu in 1973 included the tooth-stamped decoration associated with Lapita. Their context links the islands to a much older Pacific settlement history, long before the modern state.

passages.title: Discoveries and the deeper past
passages.text: A 2001 radiocarbon study placed occupation of the Mulifanua site around 930 to 800 BCE. These are calibrated estimates for a particular archaeological site, not an exact founding date for Samoa or a date assigned from a later genealogy.

passages.title: Craft knowledge and achievement
passages.text: A Samoan tattooing implement in Te Papa combines a bone comb, turtle-shell plate and wooden handle. A mallet drives the toothed edge, while combs of different widths make broad areas or fine lines. The object makes the precision of the tattooist's craft visible.

passages.title: Craft knowledge and achievement
passages.text: Ie Samoa fine mats are woven from narrow pandanus strips and finished with feathers and fringe. Preparing and weaving such fine material takes sustained skill and labor; the mats are valued for workmanship and the histories they acquire through exchange.

passages.title: Craft knowledge and achievement
passages.text: Fine mats circulate at weddings, funerals and other gatherings, reaffirming relationships between families. Village committees and master weavers teach the practice, making production a form of shared knowledge as well as individual artistry.

passages.title: Daily life and social obligations
passages.text: The aiga, or extended family, connects daily life with service, respect and reciprocal care. Family members exchange food, money and practical support, including across national borders. These obligations are lived and debated differently by different generations.

passages.title: Daily life and social obligations
passages.text: Matai titles, genealogies, language and ceremonial responsibilities are parts of fa'asamoa. Together they organize belonging and public relationships; the term does not describe an identical way of life for every Samoan household.

passages.title: Daily life and social obligations
passages.text: Christian teaching introduced by John Williams in 1830 became part of a changing religious landscape. Samoan forms of church life developed in close relationship with fa'asamoa, rather than simply replacing every earlier social institution.

passages.title: Colonial rule and political agency
passages.text: The arrival of the influenza-infected Talune in 1918 led to a devastating epidemic under New Zealand administration. The disaster affected families and food production, making colonial governance part of everyday experience as well as constitutional history.

passages.title: Colonial rule and political agency
passages.text: The Mau pursued self-government through organized, nonviolent resistance. In December 1929, colonial police killed peaceful demonstrators, including Tupua Tamasese Lealofi III. The movement's history records Samoan political action, not merely a transfer between foreign rulers.

passages.title: Colonial rule and political agency
passages.text: In 1936 New Zealand recognized the Mau as a legitimate political organization and repealed the Samoan Offenders Ordinance. Independence still required a longer struggle and arrived on 1 January 1962.

passages.title: Language and continuity
passages.text: Samoan language nests and school programs in New Zealand connect language learning with shared leadership and cultural knowledge. These institutions show how communities maintain and reshape connections to Samoa across generations of migration.

Colonial administration of Western Samoa ended with independence on 1 January 1962. Samoan communities, chiefly institutions and cultural practices continue in the independent state, American Samoa and the diaspora. A last map observation is not the end of the people or their history.

passages.text: The Great Seljuk Empire, founded when Tughril took Nishapur in 1037, brought Oghuz Turkic rule to Iran, Iraq and Anatolia under a Persian administration. Its sultans protected the Abbasid caliphs, built madrasas and mosques, and opened Anatolia to the Turks.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: The vizier Nizam al-Mulk and his rival Taj al-Mulk added the two great brick domes to the Friday Mosque of Isfahan in 1086 and 1088.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Persian poetry, calligraphy and lustre ceramics flourished under Seljuk patronage; Omar Khayyam wrote the quatrains later gathered as the Rubaiyat.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Nizam al-Mulk founded the Nizamiyya of Baghdad, first of a network of madrasas teaching Shafi'i law and theology.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Alp Arslan's victory over the Byzantines at Manzikert opened Anatolia to Turkic settlement.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Nizam al-Mulk's Book of Government set out the Persian art of kingship for the sultans.

passages.title: Science
passages.text: The Jalali calendar, computed by Omar Khayyam and colleagues for Malik Shah, fixed the year to the spring equinox with an error of about one day in 3,770 years, less than the Gregorian calendar's.

passages.title: Science
passages.text: Khayyam's treatise on algebra classified cubic equations and solved them with conic sections.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The Turkic settlement of Anatolia that followed Manzikert led to the Sultanate of Rum and, in time, the Ottomans.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The madrasa became the standard school of Sunni learning.

After Malik Shah's death in 1092 the empire split among his heirs and their atabegs. The last sultan of Iraq, Tughril III, was killed in 1194 by the Khwarazmshah Tekish, who took Iran; the Seljuks of Rum in Anatolia lasted until 1308.

passages.text: Seminole history in Florida grew from several southeastern Indigenous communities, migration and resistance to colonial expansion. It includes related but distinct peoples and governments. This account follows that wider history and the modern Seminole Tribe of Florida, with separate sections about its reservation communities.

passages.title: Homes, food and making a living
passages.text: A chickee’s cypress-log frame and palmetto thatch offered shelter that could be assembled with locally available materials. The Tribe’s account connects its widespread use with movement under military pressure. Building skills continue in commercial work, using newer equipment alongside knowledge of timber and thatching.

passages.title: Homes, food and making a living
passages.text: Corn-based sofk and a pot kept warm at the hearth formed part of household food routines. The Tribe’s food account also emphasizes change: contemporary families buy ordinary groceries and prepare traditional dishes on special occasions. A historical food practice should not be treated as every family’s unchanging daily menu.

passages.title: Homes, food and making a living
passages.text: Early twentieth-century camps traded hides, feathers, fruit and nuts for equipment and goods such as sewing machines and kettles. Everglades drainage and declining markets changed those livelihoods. Agricultural labor, cattle work and tourism became increasingly important ways to earn money.

passages.title: Homes, food and making a living
passages.text: Black Seminole communities included people who had escaped enslavement and established towns in Florida. They maintained alliances with Indigenous Seminoles and fought alongside them. Removal to Indian Territory exposed Black Seminoles to kidnapping and renewed enslavement, showing that a shared military struggle did not remove the distinct dangers they faced.

passages.title: Clothing as invention and historical evidence
passages.text: Hand-sewn appliqué and machine-made patchwork are different techniques. Earlier clothing used traded cotton and applied decoration; sewing machines reached Seminole camps in the late nineteenth century. Around 1920, women developed colored geometric bands sewn into garments, turning an adopted machine into a means of distinctive artistic invention.

passages.title: Clothing as invention and historical evidence
passages.text: Surviving garments, photographs and paintings allow historians to compare changing skirts, capes, shirts and jackets. Patchwork also became a source of income in tourist markets and a skill transmitted within families. Its modern development does not make it less meaningful as Seminole cultural expression.

passages.title: Clothing as invention and historical evidence
passages.text: Tribal archaeologists survey areas before development, record finds and map sites so important places can be protected. Their work combines field investigation with stewardship of the cultural landscape. An object’s presence on a modern reservation, by itself, does not establish that its maker used a modern tribal name.

passages.title: Big Cypress: agriculture and a building’s many lives
passages.text: Big Cypress citrus development began with studies of agricultural suitability and soil. Clearing for a new grove started in 1987, and the first trees were planted in 1989. The project initially emphasized local employment; low industry returns later shifted attention toward efficient production. Economic development required changing plans as conditions changed.

passages.title: Big Cypress: agriculture and a building’s many lives
passages.text: The building reopened as To-Pee-Kee-Ke Yak-Ne in 2019 had been built by the Bureau of Indian Affairs in the 1950s. Elders recalled Council meetings, children’s activities, Head Start and shelter during Hurricane Donna. Its successive uses preserve a history of government, education, recreation and emergency refuge in one place.

passages.title: Big Cypress: agriculture and a building’s many lives
passages.text: The renewed center included exhibits about reservations and cattle raising, together with the museum’s oral-history office. People could share memories where community life already happened. The building is therefore both historical evidence and an active place for creating an archive in the community’s own voices.

passages.title: Brighton: cattle, schooling and recorded everyday life
passages.text: The Red Barn, built in 1941 by the CCC Indian Division, supported Brighton’s developing cattle industry. At its 2013 celebration, elder Stanlo Johns recalled difficulties keeping and treating cattle before adequate fences and facilities. His account gives the building a practical context in animal care and difficult daily labor.

passages.title: Brighton: cattle, schooling and recorded everyday life
passages.text: William D. Boehmer’s 1938 photographs preserve activities at a Field Day celebrating a new school building. Museum photograph 2009.34.142 identifies men preparing barbecue; 2009.34.145 records a pie-eating contest. Together they document food preparation, recreation and a community gathering around education, rather than only formal portraits of leaders.

passages.title: Hollywood: government and new enterprises
passages.text: Hollywood, earlier called Dania, became one of the Tribe’s principal reservation centers. Its institutions include the tribal headquarters. The gaming operation opened in December 1979 and the Hollywood Hard Rock hotel and casino in May 2004 represent different stages of the Tribe’s commercial development.

passages.title: Hollywood: government and new enterprises
passages.text: Organizing in the 1950s responded to the federal threat to terminate tribal relations. The corporate charter created a structure intended to build economic independence, with tribal members sharing ownership. The Board and Council have linked but distinct responsibilities, connecting business decisions with collective government.

passages.title: Hollywood: government and new enterprises
passages.text: A community’s economic history is broader than its most visible casino. The Tribe’s account of its corporate enterprises also includes cattle, citrus, arts and crafts, retailing and finance. These activities show several paths through which land, skills and institutions support livelihoods.

passages.title: Immokalee: work, homes and women’s organizing
passages.text: Residents interviewed in 2015 recalled agricultural work and chickee camps at Immokalee during the mid-twentieth century. Some families came from other Seminole communities for seasonal employment. Nancy Motlow remembered a shared water pump and mosquito nets; these details reveal household conditions behind the later reservation’s formal history.

passages.title: Immokalee: work, homes and women’s organizing
passages.text: Nancy Motlow, Louise Motlow and other women pressed for land, housing and services. A clinic reduced the need to travel elsewhere for care. Land assembled through successive purchases entered trust in a ceremony on 26 October 1989, while residents continued debating how improved housing affected shared daily life.

passages.title: Tampa: family, archives and the costs of growth
passages.text: Tampa’s reservation was established in 1980. An Ah-Tah-Thi-Ki archival aerial photograph, GRP1306.1, shows its early complex with the star-shaped Coo Taun-Cho Bee Museum. Such records recover places subsequently transformed by hotel and casino development and show that the original complex included cultural interpretation as well as gaming.

passages.title: Tampa: family, archives and the costs of growth
passages.text: Ruby Tiger Osceola and her extended family helped form the Tampa community. Later casino expansion displaced residents, creating a long search for new homes together. The Tribe bought Lakeland land in 2006, and a 2019 groundbreaking marked a step toward rebuilding that community. Commercial success carried personal and social costs.

passages.title: Related peoples and distinct governments
passages.text: The Seminole Tribe of Florida and Seminole Nation of Oklahoma are separate governments shaped by the history of removal. The Miccosukee Tribe also asserts its own identity: sustained organizing and diplomacy led to its federal recognition in 1962. Shared history does not make these institutions interchangeable.

Seminole people continue in Florida and Oklahoma. U.S. removal campaigns caused profound losses and displacement, while communities remaining in Florida maintained their lives and later built new institutions. The modern reservations described here did not exist in the imported 1492 map interval, which must not be read as their founding date.
