sectionTitles: Discoveries: tools and a kitchen under the sea
Learning by doing, and political change

passages.text: Trinidad and Tobago have distinct island histories, brought together in one country. Their everyday creativity includes stone tools, skilfully tuned steel, cooking traditions and community teaching. Each example below identifies its place and period.

passages.title: Discoveries: tools and a kitchen under the sea
passages.text: At Banwari Trace in southern Trinidad, a settlement dating to around 5000 BCE, archaeologists found stone pestles, grinders, an axe and cutting flakes. Layers of discarded shells also survive. The tools and refuse reveal practical work and food gathering. A midden, archaeologists’ name for accumulated rubbish, can preserve an excellent record of everyday life, though it is nobody’s idea of a tidy kitchen.

passages.title: Discoveries: tools and a kitchen under the sea
passages.text: At wreck site TRB-5 in Tobago’s Rockley Bay, a 2014 excavation recovered bricks still joined with mortar, copper sheet and wood fragments. Researchers interpreted these as possible remains of a ship’s galley, or kitchen. The finds date broadly to the seventeenth century; association with the 1677 battle is supported, but the vessel’s exact identity remained uncertain in the report.

passages.title: Discoveries: tools and a kitchen under the sea
passages.text: The same test trench yielded four forks and five spoons. These small objects bring eating aboard ship into view alongside the cannon. They show that studying a wreck can recover traces of meals as well as battles. The report does not identify the diners, their food on a particular day, or whether everyone aboard had similar utensils.

passages.title: Food, households and family records
passages.text: NALIS’s account of Indian heritage in Trinidad names a belna, a rolling pin; a chauki, a board for working dough; and a sil and lorha, stones used for grinding. Such equipment accompanied cooking knowledge reshaped in Caribbean homes. Familiar foods involve practiced movements and specialised tools. The kitchen has its own vocabulary, and learning a word can also mean learning a skill.

passages.title: Food, households and family records
passages.text: Chinese shopkeepers became part of village life in Trinidad. NALIS describes a credit arrangement called trusting: customers could take groceries and pay later, while the shopkeeper recorded purchases and repayments in a copy book. A small notebook connected household needs with a local business. This is a documented practice, rather than a claim that every shop offered identical terms.

passages.title: Food, households and family records
passages.text: Trinidad’s immigration registers can record a person’s village in India, relatives, ship and assigned estate. These documents help descendants piece together family histories across oceans. Archivist Helena Leonce also describes missing records and arrivals through other Caribbean colonies. A gap in one register is a research problem, not evidence that a family has no history.

passages.title: Food, households and family records
passages.text: At Christmas, parang musicians visit homes with instruments such as the cuatro, guitar and maracas, while hosts offer food and drink. NALIS recalls nighttime visits that sometimes woke relatives and friends. It gives the idea of an alarm clock a much more musical interpretation. The account describes a particular festive tradition, not a rule followed by every household.

passages.title: Making music and sharing traditions
passages.text: Steelpan developed through experimentation in Trinidad during the 1930s and 1940s. Makers shaped metal containers and tuned parts of the playing surface to different pitches. Earlier tamboo-bamboo groups made percussion music with cut bamboo tubes. The new instrument grew through many people’s work; accounts disagree about assigning its invention to a single person.

passages.title: Making music and sharing traditions
passages.text: A steelband’s engine room is its percussion section, which helps keep the music moving together. NALIS lists bottle and spoon, maracas and assorted iron among its instruments. Here the engine runs on rhythm. The phrase is a useful reminder that a musical ensemble depends on timing and coordination as well as the performers carrying the tune.

passages.title: Making music and sharing traditions
passages.text: In January 2023, Trinidad’s Santa Rosa First Peoples Community helped present the Caribbean Ties exhibition. Community members added baskets, hammocks, ceremonial clothing, photographs and foods including cassava. An ajoupa, a tapia hut, housed the exhibition. People shared their own knowledge and heritage in a community setting, showing that Indigenous history includes living voices as well as excavated objects.

passages.title: Making music and sharing traditions
passages.text: Tobago’s Moriah Ole Time Wedding, documented in July 2017, recreated an older wedding celebration at the village’s Moravian church. A procession then carried the celebration through Moriah with participants and onlookers. It was a heritage performance, using humour and participation to share memories of social life. The staged ceremony should not be mistaken for a record of one historical couple’s marriage.

passages.title: Learning by doing, and political change
passages.text: In a 2015 project concluding at Speyside Secondary School in Tobago, students built solar ovens from boxes, reflective material, insulation and clear plastic wrap. They tested the ovens with bread dough. The winning design baked its loaf all the way through. The exercise turned energy science into something visible and practical, with a result rather easier to inspect than an invisible sunbeam.

passages.title: Learning by doing, and political change
passages.text: Independence and becoming a republic happened in different years. In 1962, Trinidad and Tobago became independent while retaining the monarch as head of state. In 1976, a president replaced that role. The distinction helps explain how a country can govern itself while still sharing a monarch with other countries.

British colonial rule ended at independence in 1962; republican status followed in 1976. Trinidad and Tobago continues as a country. Its communities keep creating and sharing traditions, including First Peoples’ knowledge, music and food.

sectionTitles: Monuments and the evidence for power
Changing institutions and a living legacy

passages.text: The Tu'i Tonga chiefly line was associated with monumental centers on Tongatapu and far-reaching Pacific relationships. Excavated stone tools, royal tombs and collected household objects reveal different aspects of this history. Sacred chiefly rank, practical government and overseas exchange changed over time; they should not be compressed into a single unchanging empire.

passages.title: Monuments and the evidence for power
passages.text: At Heketa in eastern Tongatapu, fieldwork recorded house and seat platforms, a tiered tomb and the Ha'amonga trilithon. Their arrangement joined domestic, ceremonial and chiefly spaces. Clark and Reepmeyer interpret this complex as part of a new political order taking shape in the fourteenth century.

passages.title: Monuments and the evidence for power
passages.text: Ha'amonga is built from two upright coral-limestone slabs supporting a third slab across the top. Tonga's heritage submission links it to Tu'itatui through oral tradition. The monument demonstrates large-stone construction; a proposed astronomical purpose is less securely established.

passages.title: Monuments and the evidence for power
passages.text: The langi at Lapaha are raised burial platforms faced with carefully fitted stone. Moving, shaping and placing those blocks required coordinated labor. The structures preserve evidence of chiefly funerary practice, while continued care connects them with living communities.

passages.title: Voyaging, tools and exchange
passages.text: A 2014 study compared the chemistry of stone tools from Tongan chiefly centers with Pacific stone sources. Many pieces came from Samoa or Fiji, and one adze was traced to the Society Islands. The findings show material moving over long sea routes.

passages.title: Voyaging, tools and exchange
passages.text: In that study, 29 of 44 analyzed adzes and flakes from the state-period sample were nonlocal. The authors interpret the concentration of imports at chiefly centers as evidence of intensified exchange and political connections. Imported stone alone does not establish conquest of its source island.

passages.title: Households and skilled work
passages.text: A wooden kali in the Cook-Forster collection has a narrow head support carried on curved legs. Eighteenth-century observers described Tongans using these objects while sleeping. This household object shows careful woodworking directed toward an ordinary bodily need.

passages.title: Households and skilled work
passages.text: A food hook in the Pitt Rivers Museum retains an original wooden disk painted with bird figures. The hook attached to it is a later replacement. Reading that repair history matters: the whole object on display cannot be treated as untouched evidence from the collecting voyage.

passages.title: Households and skilled work
passages.text: Te Papa's account of eighteenth-century Tonga describes ngatu barkcloth used for bedding and clothing as well as other everyday purposes. Making useful cloth from inner bark connected plant cultivation, beating, joining and decoration with household life.

passages.title: Households and skilled work
passages.text: Clark and Reepmeyer connect Heketa's ceremonial spaces with kava drinking and presentation of first fruits to chiefs. In their interpretation, cultivated food and formal gatherings helped express the sacred standing of the Tu'i Tonga.

passages.title: Changing institutions and a living legacy
passages.text: The Tu'i Ha'atakalaua and Tu'i Kanokupolu lines exercised governing authority as the Tu'i Tonga retained sacred rank. Their relationships developed through succession, marriage and conflict. A list of Tu'i Tonga titleholders is therefore not a complete list of rulers exercising the same powers.

passages.title: Changing institutions and a living legacy
passages.text: Laufilitonga, the last Tu'i Tonga titleholder, died in 1865. George Tupou I's constitutional government followed in 1875, but the earlier transfer of power was a process rather than a single foreign conquest.

passages.title: Changing institutions and a living legacy
passages.text: At Lapaha, community leaders and researchers have worked together to repair stone structures and train residents in conservation. The tombs remain places of cultural responsibility, with archaeological research contributing to their protection.

The Tu'i Tonga title ended with Laufilitonga's death in 1865, after governing power had already shifted among chiefly lines. Tonga developed a constitutional monarchy under George Tupou I in 1875. Tongan communities and their heritage continued; neither date marks their disappearance.

sectionTitles: Discoveries: paddles, fish and practical knowledge

passages.text: In Turks and Caicos, a canoe paddle, fish bones and family homes reveal ingenuity beyond the islands’ beaches. Salt-making connected island workers to distant kitchens and fisheries. Today’s British territory has a long history of Indigenous settlement, slavery, migration and changing political institutions.

passages.title: Discoveries: paddles, fish and practical knowledge
passages.text: A wooden canoe paddle found at North Creek on Grand Turk in 1996 survived in wet peat. Radiocarbon analysis placed its wood around 995 to 1235 CE at the reported 95% confidence range. Conservators treated it with a concentrated sugar solution, then dried it very slowly while checking for distortion. An unusually sweet rescue for a very old paddle. Its pointed blade and T-shaped handle preserve evidence of skilled boat travel.

passages.title: Discoveries: paddles, fish and practical knowledge
passages.text: Fish bones are evidence of dinner. By comparing excavated bones with known species, researchers identified bonefish as the most common food fish at one precolonial Middle Caicos site. Its position beside shallow seagrass flats helps explain the catch. The result describes that site’s food supply, not a single menu shared by every island or every century.

passages.title: Discoveries: paddles, fish and practical knowledge
passages.text: Craftspeople in Conch Bar, Bambarra and Lorimers on Middle Caicos have taught young people basket weaving, palm-leaf plaiting and net making. Hats, containers and working equipment take shape as children learn from experienced neighbours. Practical knowledge passes between generations through making things.

passages.title: Homes, kitchens and water
passages.text: When the museum researched traditional Caicos houses, islanders Berthalee Belle and her mother Olive helped guide architect Jeff Lee to surviving examples. Common features included thick masonry walls, raised wooden floors and a loft for storage or sleeping. Houses differed, so researchers compared several buildings before designing the museum’s reconstruction.

passages.title: Homes, kitchens and water
passages.text: In the traditional homes described by that research, cooking took place over charcoal in a detached or partly detached kitchen called a fire hut. Shuttered openings provided ventilation, and the home included its surrounding working yard. The museum’s Heritage House is a reconstruction informed by buildings and residents’ memories, rather than an untouched nineteenth-century house.

passages.title: Homes, kitchens and water
passages.text: Water conservation connects museum history with daily needs. In a report published in 2014, museum director Patricia Saxton explained that the Grand Turk museum, garden and science building relied on collected rainwater and air-conditioning runoff. A new Providenciales project planned guttering and a cistern to water a demonstration garden. Catching a shower could mean saving water for plants.

passages.title: Salt, labour and family bonds
passages.text: Salt workers guided seawater through evaporation ponds until crystals formed, then raked, shovelled and carried the salt. Small boats ferried it to ships anchored offshore. The product preserved meat and fish far away, but island workers performed exhausting labour to make it. Limited pond space and costly loading helped undermine the industry as larger producers expanded.

passages.title: Salt, labour and family bonds
passages.text: Mary Prince’s 1831 life story gives salt work a human voice. She recalled standing in brine for long hours, hurried meals of corn and soup, painful sores and punishment while enslaved on Turk’s Island. Her testimony challenges any picture of salt-making as a picturesque seaside occupation. This account comes from someone compelled to do the work.

passages.title: Salt, labour and family bonds
passages.text: Prince also remembered an unexpected family reunion when a vessel brought her mother and a little sister she had never met. She took the child, Rebecca, ashore and kept her with her for a week. The episode shows affection and care persisting despite forced separation; it does not make the conditions of enslavement less severe.

passages.title: Music, inventions and public life
passages.text: Ripsaw music puts an ordinary carpenter’s handsaw in the band. Scraping and bending it produces a distinctive sound, accompanied by instruments such as drum, accordion, maracas and guitar. The tool has a musical second job.

passages.title: Music, inventions and public life
passages.text: Grand Turk’s lighthouse arrived as pieces made in England and was assembled on the island in 1852. It helped ships navigate dangerous waters. The museum later saved a rotating Fresnel lens and its clockwork; in 2014 it recreated the mechanism using gravity to drive the movement. A lighthouse could depend on careful mechanics as well as a bright lamp.

passages.title: Music, inventions and public life
passages.text: After orbiting Earth in February 1962, John Glenn came to Grand Turk for medical checks and debriefing. Recovery ships brought him back from the Atlantic before his transfer to the island. The local tracking base connected these small islands to the space programme. Returning from orbit still involved examinations and questions about how the trip had gone.

passages.title: Music, inventions and public life
passages.text: Political participation changed over time. In 1962 voters used secret ballots in an election based on universal adult suffrage. The September 1976 election was contested along party lines and brought the People’s Democratic Movement to government. These were changes in representation within a British territory, rather than dates of national independence.

Turks and Caicos continues as a British territory. Administrative changes and interruptions of elected government changed institutions; its communities continue. The map entries represent the same islands at different times.

sectionTitles: Food, families and going to school

passages.text: Carved shell, handmade pottery, school records and music illuminate daily life in the Virgin Islands. These traces reveal skill and creativity under very different conditions. The islands now called the U.S. Virgin Islands passed from Danish to United States rule in 1917.

passages.title: Discoveries and skilled hands
passages.text: Excavations at Cinnamon Bay on St. John recovered carved shell, stone beads and a small gold-and-copper pendant from layers probably dating to about 1100 to 1200 CE. Kenneth Wild interprets the objects and their placement as evidence of ceremonial offerings. Similar designs elsewhere in the Caribbean suggest connections between communities; matching decoration alone does not prove that one island ruled another.

passages.title: Discoveries and skilled hands
passages.text: At the Danish West India and Guinea Company Warehouse in Christiansted, the Slave Wrecks Project uncovered traces of homes occupied by enslaved people during the 1700s and early 1800s. Finds included locally made pottery known as Afro-Crucian ware. These objects preserve the work of enslaved African craftspeople alongside the imposing buildings of the trading company.

passages.title: Discoveries and skilled hands
passages.text: Christiansted’s historic buildings combined yellow Danish bricks, local stone and coral blocks. The bricks crossed the Atlantic as ships’ ballast, heavy material that helped balance a vessel. Once unloaded, they became building supplies. A brick could have a sea voyage before settling into a wall.

passages.title: Food, families and going to school
passages.text: On St. John, enslavers expected enslaved people to grow their own food on poor plots called provisioning grounds. Cultivation and exchange helped people develop skills and social networks despite coercion. After emancipation in 1848, islanders drew on those connections in activities such as charcoal and bay-rum-oil production. This account concerns St. John, where conditions differed from other islands.

passages.title: Food, families and going to school
passages.text: St. John’s 1849 school rules put children aged five to nine in class from eight to eleven on weekdays. Older children, aged nine to twelve, attended Sunday school. Parents or employers could be fined for preventing attendance. Estate labour shaped these arrangements: a place in school did not mean a childhood free of work.

passages.title: Food, families and going to school
passages.text: Annaberg’s school building was completed in 1847, but a finished classroom did not guarantee money to run it. A mission report dated August 12, 1856 recorded seventy-five children attending the previously unused building. The records reveal the gap between building a school and staffing it. Knight’s article gives differing opening dates, so the dated report is the firmer reference here.

passages.title: Water, toilets and care
passages.text: The Steeple Building in Christiansted became a military hospital under U.S. naval administration. Renovations between 1917 and 1925 added a cistern and toilets. A cistern stores water, a practical concern on islands facing dry seasons. Historic architecture includes the plumbing: a handsome building still needs somewhere for water to go.

passages.title: Water, toilets and care
passages.text: A 1919 naval report described expanded preventive care, maternity services, infant welfare and training for local nurses. Access was unequal. Sick members of the Black Virgin Islands Navy Band were sent to the municipal hospital in Frederiksted, rather than the military ward in Christiansted. New services and racial discrimination existed at the same time.

passages.title: Music and social life
passages.text: Growing up on St. Croix, Stanley Jacobs and his brothers made banjos from sardine cans because their family could not afford instruments. A sardine can could have a second career in music. Jacobs later became a leading player of quelbe, a Virgin Islands tradition whose songs can combine humour with sharp observations about local life.

passages.title: Music and social life
passages.text: Jacobs also worked in elder care, organising social gatherings around music familiar to the residents. A coworker, Stanford Simmonds, taught him melodies and how to make flutes from metal tubing and bamboo. Familiar tunes brought residents together, while practical skills passed from one musician to another.

passages.title: Rights, resistance and political change
passages.text: After emancipation, an 1849 labour law fixed wages and allowed estate workers to change employers only once a year. On October 1, 1878, unrest in Frederiksted developed into the Fireburn uprising. Women remembered as Queen Mary, Queen Agnes and Queen Mathilda were among its leaders. Their titles honour labour resistance, not hereditary monarchies. Freedom from slavery had not brought fair working conditions.

passages.title: Rights, resistance and political change
passages.text: Denmark transferred the islands to the United States in 1917, but citizenship was a separate change: U.S. citizenship was granted in 1927. A change of flag and a change in citizenship were different milestones, a decade apart.

Danish rule ended with the 1917 transfer to the United States. The islands continue as a U.S. territory, with living communities and traditions. The map’s 1878 starting point is a snapshot boundary, not the beginning of U.S. rule.

passages.text: Vanuatu brings together island communities with distinct languages, histories and customary institutions. Lapita pottery, food remains, chiefly places and sand drawings reveal settlement, skilled work and ways of remembering. The republic became independent in 1980; the peoples and cultural practices of its islands have much longer histories.

passages.title: Discoveries at Teouma
passages.text: Quarrying at Teouma on Efate exposed a Lapita site in 2003. Archaeologists recovered decorated pottery and a cemetery, bringing evidence of skilled ceramic production together with burial practices. These finds concern early settlement of the islands, long before the modern state.

passages.title: Discoveries at Teouma
passages.text: A 2014 study analyzed stable isotopes in bone collagen from Teouma and compared them with animal and plant samples. The results point to dietary protein from reef and other marine foods, wild land animals and domestic animals. This evidence does not describe every ingredient of a meal.

passages.title: Discoveries at Teouma
passages.text: The researchers interpreted pig and chicken isotope values as consistent with animals feeding freely around the settlement. They also identified possible differences in access to protein. These are hypotheses about husbandry and food distribution, not direct observations of a household's daily routine.

passages.title: Chiefly places and remembered history
passages.text: Chief Roi Mata's Domain connects a residence on Efate, a place of death on Lelepa and a burial site on Artok. UNESCO dates the associated final chief to the early seventeenth century. Archaeology and oral traditions inform the interpretation of these connected places.

passages.title: Chiefly places and remembered history
passages.text: Customary tabu restrictions around Roi Mata's residence and burial place have shaped land use for centuries. Their continued observance makes the landscape part of living authority and memory, rather than only a collection of abandoned remains.

passages.title: Sand drawing, learning and communication
passages.text: In central and northern Vanuatu, a drawer can trace a continuous line across an imagined grid in sand, ash or clay. The resulting design can carry a story, message or body of knowledge. Mastery involves both controlling the line and explaining its significance.

passages.title: Sand drawing, learning and communication
passages.text: Sand drawings help people remember histories, kinship, songs, farming techniques and craft designs. A pattern can have several meanings in different settings. Presenting it merely as decoration leaves out the relationships between the drawing, its performer and its listeners.

passages.title: Food and shared work
passages.text: Laplap combines grated root crops with coconut cream, wrapped in leaves and cooked with heated stones. Contemporary versions use ingredients such as taro, yam or cassava. The preparation brings gardening, grating, wrapping and control of heat into a meal shared at gatherings or sold in markets.

passages.title: Food and shared work
passages.text: Simboro wraps grated plant foods in leaves and cooks them in coconut cream. The dish shows how leaves serve as cooking material as well as food. Recipes and ingredients vary, so a present-day description should not be projected unchanged into the Lapita period.

passages.title: Independence and cultural research
passages.text: The joint British and French colonial system ended when Vanuatu gained independence on 30 July 1980. Political independence concerned the authority of the state; it did not create the island communities or the customary relationships that had sustained them.

passages.title: Independence and cultural research
passages.text: The Vanuatu Cultural Centre's fieldworker network brings community researchers into documentation and teaching. Its 2018 film used interviews and archival material to explain how men and women record knowledge and support cultural renewal in their own communities.

Colonial joint administration ended in 1980, and Vanuatu continues as an independent republic. Island communities maintain and adapt languages, chiefly relationships, food practices and art. The passing of an individual chief or a colonial regime is distinct from the continuation of the people.

passages.text: Venice joined lagoon engineering to a far-reaching artistic culture. This chapter follows the city and its painters during the Renaissance; it does not yet cover the republic's entire history.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: During the republic, canals connected settlements consolidated from lagoon islands. Hydraulic and architectural work continually reshaped the relationship between the city and its surrounding water.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: In sixteenth-century Venice, Titian, Veronese and Tintoretto developed influential approaches to painting. Their work later shaped artists including Rubens and Velazquez.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: After moving from Verona in the 1550s, Veronese found both civic and church commissions in Venice. Artistic employment crossed religious and governmental settings.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: The lagoon included fishing settlements and artisan communities such as Murano. Venice's palaces were part of a larger landscape of work and settlement.

passages.text: Vijayanagara, founded on the Tungabhadra in 1336, ruled the south of India for three centuries and made its capital, today's Hampi, one of the largest cities in the world. It kept the temple culture of the Tamil and Kannada country alive and traded horses and spices with the Portuguese, the Arabs and China.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Gopurams, towered gateways, and pillared halls carried Dravidian temple building to its most elaborate.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Under Krishnadevaraya (1509 to 1529) the Krishna temple was built at Hampi and the Vittala temple gained its stone chariot and musical pillars.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Krishnadevaraya kept eight Telugu poets at court and wrote the Amuktamalyada himself; Kannada, Tamil and Sanskrit letters flourished too.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Arab and Portuguese traders sold the warhorses the empire needed; Hampi's markets sold diamonds, spices and cloth.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: The Portuguese Domingo Paes, who saw the city about 1520, called it as large as Rome and the best provided city in the world.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Estimates of the capital's people run to several hundred thousand, among the largest cities of the sixteenth century.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Canals from the Tungabhadra and large tanks watered the fields around the city.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The Group of Monuments at Hampi was listed by UNESCO; more than 1,600 remains survive.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The empire's temple styles and its Nayaka successors kept Hindu kingship alive in the south.

The Deccan sultanates crushed the imperial army at Talikota in 1565 and sacked the capital. The Aravidu kings ruled a shrinking realm from Penukonda, Chandragiri and Vellore until Bijapur and Golconda took the last of it in 1646.

sectionTitles: Discoveries: spaces for gathering and living

passages.text: Puerto Rico’s history includes knowledge passed through hands, families and neighbourhoods. Hammock makers work plant fibres, coffee farmers teach younger growers, and dancers exchange ideas with drummers. These living practices belong to an island shaped by Indigenous, African and European histories and a wider Puerto Rican diaspora.

passages.title: Discoveries: spaces for gathering and living
passages.text: At Caguana in Utuado, a ceremonial centre dating broadly to 1200 to 1500 CE, excavators uncovered rows of limestone slabs around a levelled plaza. Some bore carved faces. Builders cut into the hillside to create the flat gathering space. The remains show organised construction and a setting for communal ceremonies, although every activity cannot be reconstructed from the stones alone.

passages.title: Discoveries: spaces for gathering and living
passages.text: Between two of Caguana’s courts, excavators recorded postholes outlining a circular wooden building, along with two hearths, decorated pottery and a carved stone cemí, a spiritual object. A piece of Spanish glazed pottery appeared with Taíno objects in an undisturbed context. This association suggests activity into the contact period, rather than a perfectly clean break between two worlds.

passages.title: Homes, water and learning
passages.text: Smithsonian researchers documented an elderly Puerto Rican woman making hammocks with fibres from the maguey plant. Textile specialist Soraya Serra Collazo helped the team find this living craft tradition. Turning a tough plant into a place to rest takes considerable skill. A good nap can begin with somebody else’s hard work.

passages.title: Homes, water and learning
passages.text: The builders of Castillo San Cristóbal designed the fort to collect rain. Five cisterns beneath its plaza stored water for use inside. Those underground reservoirs were part of the engineering that made the eighteenth-century fortress workable. Beneath the impressive courtyard lay a practical answer to a very ordinary problem: everyone gets thirsty.

passages.title: Homes, water and learning
passages.text: A January 1942 photograph by Jack Delano shows children outside a wooden building in Aibonito. Above the doorway, the sign reads “Comedor Escolar,” meaning school dining room. Open shutters and a corrugated roof are visible. School history includes places to eat as well as classrooms, although this photograph does not tell us what lunch tasted like.

passages.title: Health, food and practical knowledge
passages.text: In the early twentieth century, Bailey Ashford and Pedro Gutiérrez worked on Puerto Rico’s hookworm problem. Their programme combined investigation and treatment with teaching about infection and improving waste disposal to reduce contact with contaminated soil. The historical account shows that caring for health extended beyond a doctor’s consulting room into public facilities and everyday surroundings.

passages.title: Health, food and practical knowledge
passages.text: In a 2022 interview, filmmaker Russell Oliver described learning about farming at Hacienda Masini in the mountains of Yauco. He met older coffee farmers who wanted to pass their knowledge to the next generation. His team’s documentation project grew from those relationships. Behind a cup of coffee are people learning about plants, land and the work of growing a crop.

passages.title: Music, family and social life
passages.text: In bomba, the lead drummer responds to a dancer’s movements, turning gestures into rhythms. Your feet can give the drummer homework. Singing often uses call and response, while barrel-shaped drums, a maraca and wooden sticks contribute different sounds. The tradition developed among African-descended communities in Puerto Rico and continues through performances and workshops on the island and in its diaspora.

passages.title: Music, family and social life
passages.text: Margarita “Tata” Cepeda’s bomba dress entered the story told by the Smithsonian’s Latino museum in its 2023 exhibition rotation. The museum connects the garment to the Cepeda family’s work performing and teaching bomba and plena. Clothing can preserve a history of movement and family learning, as well as fabric and colour.

passages.title: Freedom, government and living heritage
passages.text: Puerto Rico’s March 22, 1873 abolition law declared an end to slavery, yet required freed people to enter labour contracts lasting at least three years. Former enslavers received compensation, while full political rights for the freed people were delayed. The law’s clauses show why a legal declaration of freedom did not immediately remove every coercive restriction on daily life.

passages.title: Freedom, government and living heritage
passages.text: Voters approved a Puerto Rican constitution in 1952, followed by congressional approval. It organised the island’s internal government, including elected leaders and courts. Constitutional self-government and independent national sovereignty are different things: Puerto Rico continued within the United States territorial system.

passages.title: Freedom, government and living heritage
passages.text: Caguana is also a place of living spiritual meaning. In a 2007 account, Taíno advocates described their campaign for ceremonial access and a voice in caring for the site, including a 2005 protest. Their perspective reminds us that an archaeological park can be someone’s sacred place. Present-day communities have their own knowledge, responsibilities and views about its future.

Spanish rule ended in 1898, followed by United States administration and later commonwealth government. Puerto Rico remains a U.S. territory. Its communities and Indigenous heritage continue through changing institutions and cultural practices.

sectionTitles: Homes and skilled work at Reccopolis

passages.text: Visigothic royal power had an earlier centre at Toulouse and a later Iberian kingdom associated with Toledo. This card concentrates on the later kingdom, where excavated workshops and houses complement royal gifts, law and Latin scholarship. These different records show inventive adaptation of inherited traditions, but also inequalities and coercion within society.

passages.title: Homes and skilled work at Reccopolis
passages.text: Large houses in the early Visigothic city had circulation spaces leading to rooms, cooking areas and stables. Some were divided and enclosed during the seventh century. Changing walls and multiplying kitchens reveal households adapting existing buildings, rather than a town frozen in its founding plan.

passages.title: Homes and skilled work at Reccopolis
passages.text: Beside Reccopolis's main street, shops opened toward customers while workshops, stores and living spaces extended behind them. A circular glass furnace and associated processing structures survive. These remains place skilled production inside the town, close to both commercial activity and the palace approach.

passages.title: Homes and skilled work at Reccopolis
passages.text: The eastern craft building contained moulds for earrings and rings, balance pans and metalworking waste. Together these objects identify making and weighing, not merely possession of finished jewellery. They show the tools and discarded material behind the ornaments that survive in museum collections.

passages.title: Water engineering and its limits
passages.text: Reccopolis received water through a masonry aqueduct with a channel lined in waterproof mortar containing crushed ceramic. Surveyed remains preserve Roman construction principles in a late sixth-century project. Parts of its route remain missing and are reconstructed through terrain analysis rather than direct excavation.

passages.title: Water engineering and its limits
passages.text: Researchers argue that the aqueduct supplied more than the royal complex, proposing public distribution within the town. The volume of water and the hilltop setting support this interpretation. A complete network of household pipes and public fountains has not been excavated.

passages.title: Water engineering and its limits
passages.text: A tiled drain carried water from the courtyard of house 16000 toward the street. Other small drains and concave street surfaces suggest open channels for rain and overflow. This evidence should not be enlarged into a claim that the city possessed a complete underground sewer network.

passages.title: Goldwork, gifts and survival
passages.text: The Guarrazar treasure includes gold crowns and crosses decorated with stones, pearls and cut crystal. Letters hanging from Recceswinth's crown identify its royal donor. These were offerings for religious settings; the suspended crown should not be imagined as the king's everyday headwear.

passages.title: Goldwork, gifts and survival
passages.text: Guarrazar goldsmiths combined pierced or embossed sheets with settings and chains; some smaller crowns used open latticework. The treasure was concealed and later dispersed after its nineteenth-century discovery. Concealment shows an effort to protect valuable objects, but does not by itself establish one precise historical emergency.

passages.title: Organising and preserving knowledge
passages.text: Isidore of Seville's Etymologies organised subjects from grammar and mathematics to farming, textiles and household equipment through explanations of words. This was a work of compilation and interpretation. Its account of a craft does not establish that Isidore invented it or personally observed every process.

passages.title: Organising and preserving knowledge
passages.text: A manuscript of the Etymologies held by the Real Academia Espanola dates to the twelfth century, centuries after Isidore wrote. Such copies demonstrate the work's continuing transmission. The age of a surviving manuscript must be kept separate from the age of the text it carries.

passages.title: Law and unequal religious life
passages.text: A declaration addressed to Recceswinth in 654 required Jewish converts at Toledo to renounce Sabbath observance, religious festivals and dietary distinctions. Its coercive setting matters: the document records demands on a community, not free evidence that its members welcomed those demands.

passages.title: Law and unequal religious life
passages.text: Erwig's law of 681 threatened Jews who delayed baptism for themselves, their families or enslaved people with physical punishment, exile and confiscation. Royal religious uniformity came at others' expense. A prescribed penalty shows what authorities demanded, not proof that enforcement was identical everywhere.

The Umayyad conquest began in 711 and displaced Visigothic royal government over several years. It did not remove the peninsula's whole population or immediately empty its towns. Reccopolis continued into the Islamic period before declining much later, and Isidore's work continued to be copied. The map endpoint of 800 is not the kingdom's fall date.

passages.text: Mapuche histories encompass autonomous communities, exchange and creative work across southern South America. Relations with neighbours changed over centuries. Colonial resistance and later dispossession belong to this history alongside farming, family knowledge and living artistic traditions.

passages.title: Families, land and local authority
passages.text: The lof organised related families. In the historical model described by the National Library, a longko led a local group with limited authority. Wider alliances could form during war without creating a ruler with permanent jurisdiction over every community.

passages.title: Families, land and local authority
passages.text: The same account describes local leaders allocating fields to families and reassigning plots while depleted ground recovered. Reserve land provided another resource. Access depended on social relationships as well as cultivation, and arrangements changed under later restrictions.

passages.title: Weaving knowledge into daily life
passages.text: Textile specialists Matilde Painemil and Cristina Manquepi contributed family histories and practical knowledge to the museum’s collection study. Their expertise connected the handling of old cloth with forms and meanings still understood by makers.

passages.title: Weaving knowledge into daily life
passages.text: The textiles discussed include makuñ mantles, headbands and chañuntuku, thick woven saddle coverings. These are distinct objects for dress and other uses, rather than interchangeable examples of a single decorative pattern.

passages.title: Weaving knowledge into daily life
passages.text: Painemil describes design as mental and creative work, sometimes connected with dreams. She also teaches classes and makes commissioned textiles. Her account presents weaving as a skilled livelihood and an ongoing artistic practice, not merely repetition of inherited designs.

passages.title: Silver, clay and sound
passages.text: Mapuche silverwork includes the linked breast ornament trapelakucha, earrings called chaway and fastening pins such as tüpu. Specialists Antonio Chihuaicura and Marco Pailamilla examined such pieces with the museum, bringing makers’ knowledge to the interpretation of their construction and use.

passages.title: Silver, clay and sound
passages.text: Following nineteenth-century dispossession, families sometimes exchanged silver objects for food. The museum links these losses to the formation of public and private collections. An ornament’s museum history can therefore record hardship as well as artistic skill.

passages.title: Silver, clay and sound
passages.text: The same account describes craft knowledge surviving within families and being renewed through workshops, new pieces and replicas. Studying an old silver ornament and making a new one can both contribute to this continuing practice.

passages.title: Silver, clay and sound
passages.text: Potter Celinda Huaiquil explains links between water, women’s knowledge and ceramic vessels. Duck-shaped ketru metawe can pour liquids, including muday in ceremonies. Her interpretation joins close observation of living creatures with the practical work of shaping clay.

passages.title: Silver, clay and sound
passages.text: José Cayuqueo makes ritual drums using laurel wood and goatskin. He and Hernán Marinao also describe wooden pifüllka instruments accompanying the drum and supporting a machi’s ceremony. These are named makers’ accounts of living musical practice.

passages.title: People tell their own histories
passages.text: Manuel Manquilef’s writing and Pascual Coña’s orally narrated life preserve Mapuche perspectives on historical change. Coña’s account was recorded by a missionary, so the circumstances of recording matter alongside the narrator’s knowledge.

Chilean and Argentine expansion dispossessed communities and restricted land and movement. Later migration brought many Mapuche people to cities. These transformations did not end Mapuche life: makers, teachers, families and organisations continue to sustain and reshape their cultures.

passages.text: Wadawurrung Country includes landscapes around Geelong, Ballarat and the surrounding coast and plains. Stone arrangements, fishing places, plant knowledge and living art illuminate a history much older than colonial settlement. Wadawurrung people continue to care for Country and sustain cultural life after dispossession and environmental disruption.

passages.title: Stone arrangements and careful interpretation
passages.text: Wurdi Youang is an egg-shaped arrangement of basalt stones near Little River. A published survey describes an east-west axis and prominent stones at the western end. Its construction date is unknown, so the surviving arrangement cannot support a precise founding date or an age-based world record.

passages.title: Stone arrangements and careful interpretation
passages.text: The 2012 study identified two sets of alignments toward solstice and equinox sunsets and tested whether they might arise by chance. The authors interpret deliberate astronomical orientation. That finding does not establish every purpose of the place or recover all the knowledge associated with it.

passages.title: Stone arrangements and careful interpretation
passages.text: A public cultural assessment records stone fish traps at Point Lillias in Corio Bay. Basalt lines in the tidal zone and oral history support their interpretation. One site also has later oyster-industry remains, so the report distinguishes Indigenous use from subsequent modification.

passages.title: Food, materials and everyday knowledge
passages.text: Murnong, or yam daisy, supplied edible tubers on the plains. Accounts assembled in the cultural assessment describe digging sticks used to harvest them, with tubers eaten raw or roasted. Grazing animals introduced during colonization damaged this food landscape.

passages.title: Food, materials and everyday knowledge
passages.text: River red gum bark furnished material for bowls and shields. Golden wattle gum served as food and an adhesive for making implements. The same landscape could supply meals, containers and the means to repair or join tools.

passages.title: Food, materials and everyday knowledge
passages.text: The Wadawurrung Country Plan identifies reeds and grasses as resources for flour, weaving and string, alongside tubers, lilies, ochre and wood. Its priorities connect the health of plants with the continuation of practical and cultural knowledge.

passages.title: Food, materials and everyday knowledge
passages.text: Waterways, wetlands and Sea Country form connected responsibilities in the plan. Fish, eels, birds, camping places and cultural sites matter together, rather than being separated into food resources on one side and culture on the other.

passages.title: Creative practice and continuing authority
passages.text: The community's artists directory includes Tammy Gilson's weaving and Jenna Oldaker's painting, digital art and cultural education. These named practices show people carrying knowledge through both established materials and newer media.

passages.title: Creative practice and continuing authority
passages.text: The corporation was founded on 12 October 1998. Its initial appointment as a Registered Aboriginal Party came on 21 May 2009, with further Country included in 2013. These dates document recognition of an organization's role, not the creation of Wadawurrung identity.

passages.title: Creative practice and continuing authority
passages.text: The Country Plan links language, stories, ceremony and family participation with the protection of places and species. Development, extraction and environmental change therefore affect both ecosystems and the settings where cultural knowledge is practiced.

Wadawurrung people continue. Colonization brought dispossession and major changes to food landscapes, including damage from introduced grazing animals. Community institutions, artists and Country planning sustain cultural responsibilities; the final year shown for a map snapshot is not an extinction date.

passages.text: Wessex was a kingdom in southern England. Under Alfred, royal support for reading and translation linked learned texts with the skilled production of books and precious objects.

passages.title: Learning
passages.text: Alfred commissioned translations of religious works from Latin into Old English. Copies circulated within his kingdom.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Some books were accompanied by reading pointers called aestels. The Alfred Jewel may have formed the head of one, but its function remains an interpretation.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: The jewel combines gold, colored cloisonne enamel and rock crystal. A figure appears beneath the crystal, and an animal-like head forms the base.

passages.title: Writing
passages.text: An inscription names Alfred as the person who ordered the object made. The museum dates it to his reign, 871 to 899.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The figure beneath the crystal may personify sight, fitting a possible reading aid. The museum presents this identification as uncertain.

passages.title: Ideas and institutions
passages.text: Alfred's law code drew on earlier West Saxon, Mercian and Kentish rules. His government also supported fortified market settlements, connecting defense with economic activity.

passages.title: Change and continuity
passages.text: Wessex became the base from which Alfred's successors expanded royal power across England. This was a process of political consolidation, not the disappearance of West Saxon people.

passages.text: The Western Zhou established the political and philosophical foundations of Chinese civilization. Through a system of enfeoffment and the concept of the Mandate of Heaven, they created a model of legitimate rulership that endured for three millennia.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The Mandate of Heaven concept emerges, stating that Heaven grants the right to rule to the virtuous and withdraws it from tyrants.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The Duke of Zhou articulates the theory of dynastic succession and the ruler's moral responsibility.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Ancestor worship becomes formalized in ritual bronze vessels and temple ceremonies.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: The first smelted iron in China, blades set in bronze handles, appears at the very end of the period; iron remained rare beside bronze.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Improved bronze casting techniques for ritual vessels, bells and weapons; the yongzhong bell, hung at an angle and struck at two points, takes its form.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: The songs of the Classic of Poetry (Shijing), court hymns and folk songs, date from this period; the anthology was assembled later.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: The core of the Book of Changes (Yijing), the hexagram and line statements, takes shape as a divination manual; the philosophical commentaries came centuries later.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Bronze inscriptions become longer and more literary, recording royal deeds and land grants; the Mao Gong ding carries about 500 characters.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Regional lords governed territories from walled cities, owing military service and tribute to the Zhou king.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: The well-field system supposedly divided agricultural land into nine plots, with the center plot worked for the lord.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Confucius later idealized the Western Zhou as a golden age of virtue and proper ritual.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The Mandate of Heaven justified political change throughout Chinese history until the empire ended in 1912.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Zhou ritual codes influenced East Asian court ceremonies for centuries.
Quanrong nomads allied with disaffected lords sacked the capital Haojing and killed King You, forcing the court to flee east.

passages.text: Wurundjeri people connect Birrarung and surrounding Country through language, family, leadership and skilled work. Greenstone quarrying, William Barak's drawings and community canoe building reveal different ways of making and sharing knowledge. Colonial dispossession changed access to land, but Wurundjeri identity and cultural responsibilities continue.

passages.title: Greenstone tools and exchange
passages.text: At Wil-im-ee Moor-ring, Mount William, quarry pits, waste stone and working areas preserve the remains of greenstone tool production. Makers shaped rough hatchet heads at the quarry; recipients could then grind and finish them for their own needs.

passages.title: Greenstone tools and exchange
passages.text: Hatchets supported canoe building, food gathering and the manufacture of wooden implements. Mount William greenstone travelled through exchange: visitors brought goods including possum-skin cloaks and spears. The quarry therefore connects household work with relationships between communities.

passages.title: Greenstone tools and exchange
passages.text: In the 1880s, William Barak described quarry access to Alfred Howitt. His account identifies Billibellary as a custodian approached through messengers. It adds evidence of authority and negotiated access to the physical traces of stoneworking.

passages.title: Art as a cultural record
passages.text: Barak's Untitled drawing of 1899, now in the National Gallery of Victoria, uses pencil and watercolor to show a ceremonial gathering. An inscription on its calico wrapping dates the gift to Annie Danks to January 1899, giving the work a documented personal history.

passages.title: Art as a cultural record
passages.text: The drawing includes possum-skin cloaks, feather headdresses, boomerangs used as clapsticks, fires and animals. These details communicate clothing, movement and performance through an artist's composition; the image is a cultural account, not a complete inventory of every Wurundjeri ceremony.

passages.title: Leadership and everyday community life
passages.text: Simon Wonga and William Barak helped establish Coranderrk in 1863 for Wurundjeri and other displaced Kulin people. They sought space for a community amid colonial dispossession. The station provided a place to live, but its administration constrained people's control over their land.

passages.title: Leadership and everyday community life
passages.text: Barak became Ngurungaeta after Wonga's death in 1874. His petitions to retain Coranderrk show leadership exercised through negotiation and written advocacy, alongside the cultural knowledge communicated in his pictures.

passages.title: Leadership and everyday community life
passages.text: In the 2012 Kooroong project, community members worked greenstone into axes and used them to remove bark from a river red gum at Plenty Gorge for a canoe. The project brought stoneworking, tree knowledge and boat construction together in a living practice.

passages.title: Leadership and everyday community life
passages.text: Wurundjeri accounts treat landforms and habitats as integral parts of cultural heritage. Care for Country includes relationships and continuing practices, as well as protecting individual sites or objects.

passages.title: Returns and continuing institutions
passages.text: Descendants established the Wurundjeri corporation in 1985. The return of part of Coranderrk, including its cemetery, in March 1998 restored a connection to a place with deep family significance, without undoing every earlier loss.

passages.title: Returns and continuing institutions
passages.text: Land titles for Wil-im-ee Moor-ring and the Sunbury Rings returned in 2012. In 2017, Elders addressed Victoria's Parliament as part of advocacy for Birrarung. These events show cultural authority expressed through landholding and public decision-making.

Wurundjeri people continue despite dispossession and reserve controls. Coranderrk belongs to that history, but does not define its beginning or end. Descendants sustain leadership, artistic knowledge and responsibilities to Birrarung and Country through family life and community institutions.

passages.text: The Xia is the first dynasty in Chinese tradition, associated by most Chinese scholars with the Erlitou archaeological culture of the middle Yellow River valley. Whether it was a historical state or a later political myth remains debated outside China, but the material culture of the period shows the first large-scale bronze production and palace architecture in the region.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Erlitou casts the earliest Chinese bronze ritual vessels, small jue wine cups, in sectioned clay moulds, the piece-mould method the Shang would carry to its height.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Flood control and irrigation works are attributed by tradition to the founder Yu the Great; the story is legend, but the Yellow River floodplain was being farmed and managed in this period.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Plain bronze jue and jade blades, sceptres and cong tubes from Erlitou set the forms that later dynasties elaborated and decorated.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Turquoise-inlaid bronze plaques with animal designs, and a dragon of some two thousand turquoise pieces laid on a body in an Erlitou tomb.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Ancestor offerings and divination with burnt animal bones appear in the archaeological record, anticipating Shang and Zhou religion.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The legend of Yu controlling the floods established the model of the virtuous ruler who brings order from chaos.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Millet farming and pig husbandry supported growing populations in the Yellow River valley.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Rammed-earth foundations and walls enclosed the palace compound at Erlitou, a walled precinct of about eleven hectares.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: In the traditional histories the cycle of dynasties begins with the Xia: Tang of Shang overthrows its last king, and the Zhou later name the pattern the Mandate of Heaven.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The name Xia later became synonymous with Chinese civilization itself, in the word Huaxia.
According to tradition, the tyrant Jie was defeated by Tang of Shang at the Battle of Mingtiao.

passages.text: The Xin dynasty was a brief interregnum when Wang Mang attempted radical reforms inspired by ancient Zhou ideals. His policies failed to address real economic problems and natural disasters, above all the Yellow River's change of course, and ended in widespread rebellion.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Wang Mang claims the Mandate of Heaven has transferred to him based on omens and classical precedents.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Reforms modeled on the ancient Zhou well-field system and ritual codes.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Private land ownership abolished; all land declared the king's fields, to be redistributed in equal shares. The order was withdrawn within three years.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: The trade in slaves banned, though the ban was widely ignored.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: State monopolies on salt, iron, coinage and liquor, and a bureau to lend to farmers and steady prices.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Wang Mang's failure discredited radical reform and strengthened conservative Confucianism.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: His reign became a cautionary tale about ignoring economic realities for ideological purity.
Rebel armies captured Chang'an in 23 CE and killed Wang Mang; a Han prince, Liu Xiu, restored the dynasty in 25 as Emperor Guangwu.

passages.text: The Xiongnu were the first great steppe empire, united by Modu Chanyu in 209 BCE and ruling Mongolia and the lands to its west for three centuries. Their mounted archers, tribute treaties with Han China and left-and-right administration set the pattern for the Turkic and Mongol empires that followed.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Composite bows of horn and sinew, shot from the saddle, made every herdsman a warrior.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Bronze and iron for weapons and harness; gold plaques of animals in combat for the elite.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The chanyu ruled under Heaven, Tengri, with shamans and seasonal gatherings to sacrifice to ancestors, heaven and earth.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Elite tombs at Noin-Ula held Chinese silks, lacquer and Bactrian textiles beside the dead.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: The heqin treaties from 198 BCE brought Han princesses, silk, grain and wine to the chanyu as the price of peace.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: The Xiongnu taxed the oasis towns of the Tarim Basin and traded horses and furs to China.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The Xiongnu model of steppe empire was followed by the Turkic khaganates and the Mongols.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Their name may lie behind the Huns of European sources, though the link is unproven.

The confederation split into southern and northern halves in 54 BCE. Han armies broke the Northern Xiongnu at Ikh Bayan in 89 CE, and by 93 the Xianbei had taken over the steppe; the Southern Xiongnu lived on as Han clients inside the Great Wall.

passages.text: The Yamato period covers the rise of a single Japanese state from the chiefdoms of the Kofun age. Great keyhole-shaped tombs mark the power of the early rulers; in the sixth and seventh centuries the court took Buddhism, writing and Chinese-style government from Korea and China.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Keyhole-shaped kofun mounds for rulers; the largest, the Daisen Kofun near Osaka, is 486 meters long.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Haniwa clay figures of warriors, horses, houses and dancers stood on the mounds.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Bronze mirrors, iron swords and gilt-bronze horse trappings came from Korea and China and were buried with the chiefs.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Buddhism arrived from Baekje, and the Soga and Mononobe clans fought over whether to accept it.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Prince Shotoku's Seventeen-Article Constitution set out Buddhist and Confucian principles for officials.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Native kami worship, later called Shinto, continued alongside Buddhism and Confucian learning.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Iron tools and weapons improved through smiths and ore from the Korean kingdoms.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Chinese writing was adopted for court records; the inscribed sword from Inariyama, dated to 471, is among the earliest texts written in Japan.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: The Taika Reform began to remodel the court and its land system on Tang lines.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The imperial line that emerged in this period continues to the present.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The Mozu-Furuichi Kofun Group was listed by UNESCO.
The court moved to a permanent capital at Heijo-kyo in 710, the start of the Nara period.

passages.text: Yolngu peoples maintain distinct clan identities in Arnhem Land. Country, law, food, ceremony and art remain connected, while institutions at Yirrkala carry knowledge through contemporary media.

passages.title: Worldview and institutions
passages.text: Dhuwa and Yirritja are complementary moieties connecting people, places and other living beings. In Miwatj, art and ceremony express relationships to fresh and saltwater Country.

passages.title: Food and seasons
passages.text: Seasonal food gathering draws on both land and sea, including yams, fruit, fish and shellfish. Traditional owners connect these practices with law and ceremony.

passages.title: Art and diplomacy
passages.text: Artists framed the Yirrkala petitions with clan designs in ochre, charcoal and pipeclay. These designs expressed relationships to land alongside text in English and Yolngu Matha.

passages.title: Political history
passages.text: Yolngu presented bark petitions to the Australian Parliament in 1963 in response to mining plans made without adequate consultation. They understood the documents as a diplomatic offering between equal powers.

passages.title: Digital knowledge
passages.text: The Mulka Project combines a recording studio, production house, learning centre and cultural archive under Yolngu law and elder leadership. It trains community members and returns audiovisual records to communities.

passages.title: Continuity
passages.text: A bark petition formerly held privately was formally returned to Yolngu at Yirrkala in 2023. Its return forms part of continuing cultural custody.

passages.text: Monte Alban was an important Zapotec capital in the Oaxaca Valley. Its history of urban planning, water management and carved inscriptions is one part of the much wider history of Zapotec societies.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Builders reshaped hillsides with terraces, dams and conduits. Water management and the creation of level spaces were integrated into urban development.

passages.title: Architecture
passages.text: Temples and platforms framed a long ceremonial esplanade. Open spaces were as important to the layout as the buildings themselves.

passages.title: Writing and arts
passages.text: Carved reliefs with hieroglyphic inscriptions survive alongside tombs and temples, giving evidence of visual art and record making.

passages.title: Public life
passages.text: The ceremonial center included a ball court. Its built spaces supported activities beyond the palaces and burial places of elites.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Monte Alban maintained relations with Teotihuacan. Those contacts connect Oaxaca's history to other contemporary Mesoamerican centers.

passages.title: Change over time
passages.text: UNESCO dates Monte Alban's long florescence from about 500 BCE to 850 CE, followed by decline. This is the trajectory of a city, not an extinction date for Zapotec peoples.

sectionTitles: Markets and the people who made cloth

passages.text: The Abdelwadids, also called Zayyanids, made Tlemcen the capital of a kingdom in the central Maghreb. Emerging from Zenata leadership as Almohad power weakened, they supported a city connected to trans-Saharan and Mediterranean trade.

passages.title: Markets and the people who made cloth
passages.text: A marble tablet from Tlemcen’s bazaar carries an inscription dating it to 1328 and identifying it as a cubit measure. Its ruled line is divided into four parts. The object made a common unit of length physically available in a place of commerce.

passages.title: Markets and the people who made cloth
passages.text: The catalogue reports that this tablet was found set into the bazaar wall. It is evidence for a local measurement standard, not proof that the ruler invented the cubit or that every sale followed the rule without dispute.

passages.title: Markets and the people who made cloth
passages.text: Textile production employed both men and women in Zayyanid Tlemcen. A study of the industry links its growth to available raw materials, trading connections and expertise arriving from al-Andalus. Making cloth connected household livelihoods with the city’s wider economy.

passages.title: Markets and the people who made cloth
passages.text: The same study describes demand from different social groups, including elite customers seeking refined fabrics. Quality and finish mattered to makers as well as access to materials. The surviving record does not justify treating every textile worker as prosperous.

passages.title: Architecture and learning
passages.text: An inscription dates the Sidi Bel-Hasan mosque to 1296. Onyx columns support horseshoe arches dividing the prayer hall into three aisles, while cedar roof structures carried tile coverings. A relatively small building brought together stoneworking, carpentry and brick construction.

passages.title: Architecture and learning
passages.text: Traces of coloured paint survive on the mosque’s plaster decoration. Its prayer niche combines inscriptions and floral ornament with a muqarnas dome, formed from small projecting cells. Later alterations mean that the building’s present appearance is not wholly medieval.

passages.title: Architecture and learning
passages.text: At the royal Mechouar, Abu Hammu Musa I completed a mosque in 1317 to 1318. The square minaret preserves panels of small columns and arches against tiled mosaics. Its decoration records skilled work within the court’s architectural setting.

passages.title: Architecture and learning
passages.text: Tlemcen’s teaching took place in mosques and madrasas, with study of Islamic law, Qur’anic interpretation, hadith and Sufism. Rulers’ support helped attract teachers and students from other regions, connecting the city with a wider scholarly world.

passages.title: Architecture and learning
passages.text: The Mechouar began as Yaghmurasan’s royal seat in the thirteenth century and was enlarged by successors. Modern conservation has also shaped it: a project sheet records major work on tile and plaster decoration between 2008 and 2012. Present surfaces need to be read alongside that restoration history.

passages.title: Coins and contested sovereignty
passages.text: Two gold dinars in the Bibliothèque nationale de France, catalogued as Lavoix 986 and 987, name Tlemcen and two rulers. Mohamed Elhadri argues that they belong to sixteenth-century Zayyanids acknowledging the Ottoman sultan Süleyman, rather than an earlier Marinid and Nasrid alliance.

passages.title: Coins and contested sovereignty
passages.text: Elhadri tests that attribution against the names, titles and mint formulas on the coins and the chronology of political alliances. The case shows why a familiar royal name alone may misdate an object, especially when local monetary forms survive changes of overlord.

passages.title: Coins and contested sovereignty
passages.text: In 1517, one Tlemcen faction invited Aruj from Algiers while another backed the Zayyanid ruler with Spanish help. Aruj was killed after fleeing in 1518. Local choices and rivalries were central to this struggle, alongside the ambitions of larger powers.

Ottoman expansion ended Zayyanid rule around the middle of the sixteenth century. Sources date the final transition differently; approximately 1554 is a conventional endpoint. The royal citadel passed into Ottoman use, while Tlemcen and its inhabitants continued beyond the dynasty.
